This working group will integrate (i) ribosome profiling datasets across tissues, development, and stress (GEO), (ii) proteomics quantifying ribosomal protein paralogs and associated factors (PRIDE, CPTAC), (iii) rRNA modification and ribosome biogenesis datasets (public epitranscriptomic studies), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq atlases for tissue context (Tabula Sapiens, HCA), and (v) perturbation datasets targeting ribosomal proteins, snoRNPs, and biogenesis factors (CRISPR screens, DepMap). We will curate metadata on growth conditions, stressors, and cell types, and standardize processing of ribosome profiling to comparable translation efficiency metrics.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity (protein composition, modification patterns, associated factors) across contexts. (2) Test whether specific heterogeneity signatures correlate with selective translation of mRNA subsets (e.g., IRES-containing, uORF-rich, mitochondrial-targeted). (3) Determine whether specialized translation is conserved across species and how it relates to stress adaptation and disease.

Analytical approach: We will build joint models linking ribosome composition proxies (from proteomics and expression of ribosomal paralogs/biogenesis factors) to translation efficiency changes inferred from ribosome profiling. We will use multivariate association methods with careful confounder control (growth rate, global translation shifts) and causal inference leveraging perturbation datasets. We will also develop motif-based and structure-aware predictors of mRNAs sensitive to ribosome state.

NCEMS support is essential because integrating ribosome profiling with proteomics and modification data requires specialized expertise and substantial curation; no single lab typically spans these domains. The working group will coordinate standards for reporting ribosome profiling processing and for mapping ribosomal protein isoforms across datasets.

Deliverables will include a Ribosome Heterogeneity Synthesis Resource with harmonized datasets, inferred heterogeneity axes, and candidate specialized translation programs; reproducible pipelines for ribosome profiling processing; and open benchmarks for detecting specialized translation. Training will be provided through workshops on ribosome profiling analysis, proteomics integration, and open science practices, with trainees leading curation of tissue- and stress-specific modules. The synthesis will clarify whether and how ribosome diversity yields emergent translational control.
original.background_and_significance:
Translation is a central determinant of cellular state, coupling gene expression programs to proteome composition, growth, and adaptation. The ribosome is traditionally modeled as a uniform molecular machine with fixed stoichiometry and function. However, multiple lines of evidence now indicate that ribosomes can vary in composition (e.g., tissue- or lineage-biased usage of ribosomal protein paralogs, differential incorporation of accessory factors, and variable occupancy of ribosome-associated proteins), in rRNA chemical modifications (e.g., 2′-O-methylation and pseudouridylation), and in biogenesis pathways that shape ribosome quality and specialization. These sources of ribosome heterogeneity occur at the mesoscale—between individual biomolecules and organelles—where ensembles of ribosomes collectively influence higher-order outcomes such as stress resistance, differentiation trajectories, and disease phenotypes.

A key unresolved question is whether ribosome heterogeneity is merely correlated with cellular context (a byproduct of transcriptional differences, growth rate, or biogenesis capacity) or whether it constitutes an emergent regulatory layer that causally reshapes which mRNAs are translated. “Specialized translation” hypotheses propose that certain ribosome states preferentially translate mRNA subsets with distinct 5′ leaders (e.g., IRES-like elements), upstream open reading frames (uORFs), codon usage biases, RNA structure features, or subcellular targeting signals (e.g., mitochondrial or ER-targeted transcripts). If true, ribosome heterogeneity would represent a generalizable mechanism for selectively implementing proteome programs without changing mRNA abundance, providing a powerful explanation for context-specific proteome remodeling during stress, development, and disease.

Public data relevant to this problem have grown dramatically: ribosome profiling provides codon-resolved footprints and translation efficiency estimates across hundreds of perturbations and tissues; quantitative proteomics measures ribosomal protein abundances and paralog usage; epitranscriptomic studies map rRNA modifications and snoRNA-guided modification machinery; single-cell atlases provide cell-type context and enable deconvolution of bulk measurements; and CRISPR screens and dependency maps offer perturbation-based constraints on ribosome components and biogenesis factors. Yet these resources remain siloed, processed with inconsistent pipelines, and described with incomplete metadata, preventing robust cross-study inference. Consequently, the field lacks a community-scale synthesis that can quantify reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity and test, with statistical rigor, whether those axes predict selective translation programs across contexts.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze this synthesis because (i) the question centers on emergence at the mesoscale, (ii) resolving it requires integration of heterogeneous molecular datasets and advanced AI/data-science methods, and (iii) the scale of curation, harmonization, and multi-modal modeling exceeds what a single laboratory can sustain. By assembling a multidisciplinary working group spanning ribosome biology, proteomics, epitranscriptomics, statistical genetics, causal inference, and machine learning, we will create a unified, reusable resource and analytical framework. This effort will address a long-standing puzzle—whether ribosome diversity systematically encodes selective translation—and will establish reproducible standards for future synthesis research in translational control.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address whether ribosome heterogeneity constitutes a reproducible, predictive, and partially causal layer of translational regulation across tissues and stress conditions. We will focus on three overarching research questions, each with testable hypotheses that can be evaluated using only publicly available datasets.

Research Question 1: What are the dominant, reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity across biological contexts?
Hypothesis 1A (structured heterogeneity): Across tissues, developmental stages, and stressors, ribosome heterogeneity is not random noise but organizes into a small number of recurrent axes reflecting (i) differential abundance of ribosomal protein paralogs and select core proteins, (ii) variation in ribosome-associated factors (initiation/elongation modulators, quality control factors), and (iii) coordinated patterns of rRNA modification and biogenesis factor activity.
Hypothesis 1B (context specificity with conservation): While the magnitude of heterogeneity varies by context (e.g., proliferative vs. quiescent tissues; acute vs. chronic stress), the underlying axes are partially conserved across species (e.g., yeast, mouse, human) and across dataset modalities.

Research Question 2: Do specific ribosome heterogeneity signatures predict selective translation of defined mRNA subsets beyond global translational shifts?
Hypothesis 2A (selectivity beyond scaling): After controlling for confounders (growth rate proxies, total ribosome occupancy, global initiation/elongation changes, batch effects), certain ribosome states are associated with differential translation efficiency of mRNA subsets defined by mechanistic features: uORF-rich leaders, structured 5′ UTRs, IRES-like elements, specific codon usage patterns, signal peptide/mitochondrial targeting sequences, or stress-response regulons.
Hypothesis 2B (feature-mediated sensitivity): Translation sensitivity to ribosome state is mediated by interpretable mRNA sequence/structure features that can be learned by motif-based and structure-aware models and that generalize across datasets.

Research Question 3: Is there evidence consistent with causality between ribosome components/biogenesis pathways and specialized translation programs, and how does this relate to stress adaptation and disease?
Hypothesis 3A (perturbation consistency): Genetic perturbations of ribosomal proteins, paralogs, snoRNP components, and biogenesis factors produce translation changes that align with the inferred heterogeneity axes, supporting a causal relationship rather than mere correlation.
Hypothesis 3B (fitness and disease relevance): Ribosome states associated with selective translation correspond to differential fitness dependencies in DepMap/CRISPR screens and align with disease-relevant contexts (e.g., cancer lineages, ribosomopathies, neurodegeneration) where translation reprogramming is implicated.

Across all questions, we will explicitly test robustness to alternative processing pipelines and model specifications. We will treat “specialized translation” as an operational, falsifiable claim: a ribosome heterogeneity signature must predict mRNA-specific translation changes with reproducible effect sizes across independent datasets and must remain after accounting for global translation and transcriptional composition. These hypotheses directly target emergent mesoscale behavior—how ensembles of heterogeneous ribosomes yield system-level selectivity in protein synthesis.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis organized around shared curation standards, harmonized processing pipelines, and multi-modal modeling. The team will be divided into cross-cutting task forces: (T1) ribosome profiling harmonization, (T2) proteomics and ribosomal protein isoform/paralog mapping, (T3) rRNA modification/biogenesis integration, (T4) single-cell context and deconvolution, and (T5) modeling/causal inference and benchmarking. All analyses will use existing public data only.

Data acquisition and inclusion criteria. We will compile ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) and matched RNA-seq from GEO/SRA and curated repositories, emphasizing datasets with clear metadata (tissue/cell type, stressor, time, species, replicate structure). Proteomics will be drawn from PRIDE and CPTAC with ribosomal protein quantification or whole-proteome coverage enabling extraction of ribosome-related features. rRNA modification datasets will include published maps of 2′-O-methylation and pseudouridylation, along with snoRNA/biogenesis factor perturbation studies where available. Single-cell atlases (Tabula Sapiens, Human Cell Atlas, mouse atlases) will provide cell-type composition references. Perturbation constraints will come from CRISPR screens and DepMap gene effect matrices.

Harmonized processing.
1) Ribo-seq: Standardized adapter trimming, rRNA/tRNA depletion filtering, alignment, P-site assignment, and footprint periodicity QC. Translation efficiency (TE) will be estimated with generalized linear models that incorporate RNA-seq abundance and library size, producing comparable TE effect sizes across studies. We will compute additional features: initiation vs. elongation proxies, ribosome occupancy along ORFs, and uORF translation where detectable.
2) Proteomics: We will build a ribosomal protein/paralog mapping table resolving gene symbols, isoforms, and shared peptides. Abundances will be normalized within study and transformed into composition signatures (e.g., relative paralog ratios; ribosome-associated factor modules).
3) rRNA modifications/biogenesis: We will represent modification landscapes as site-level or region-level scores and, when direct maps are absent, infer modification/biogenesis activity from expression of snoRNAs and modifying enzymes, with uncertainty estimates.
4) Cell-type context: For bulk tissues, we will deconvolve cell-type proportions using reference atlases and include composition covariates to reduce confounding.

Multi-modal integration and inference.
A) Axis discovery: We will learn latent “ribosome state” axes using multi-view factor models (e.g., MOFA-like frameworks) and regularized matrix factorization that jointly incorporate proteomics, modification proxies, and biogenesis factor expression. Stability will be assessed by bootstrap and replication across independent cohorts.
B) Association with selective translation: For each dataset, we will model gene-level TE changes as a function of ribosome state axes, controlling for stress class, growth proxies, batch, and global translation shifts. Meta-analysis will combine effects across studies with random-effects models.
C) Mechanism-aware mRNA sensitivity models: We will test enrichment of predicted sensitive mRNAs for 5′ UTR motifs, uORFs, RNA structure metrics, codon usage, and subcellular targeting. We will train interpretable predictors (motif/feature-based) and, where feasible, structure-aware sequence models with careful cross-study validation.
D) Causal triangulation: We will use perturbation datasets to test whether manipulating axis-loading genes (ribosomal proteins, snoRNPs, biogenesis factors) shifts TE in the predicted direction. Where matched perturbation Ribo-seq exists, we will apply difference-in-differences designs; otherwise we will triangulate using consistency across TE signatures, expression responses, and fitness dependencies.

Benchmarking and sensitivity analyses. We will run alternative TE estimation methods, evaluate confounder sets, and quantify reproducibility across pipelines. Negative controls (randomized axis assignments; housekeeping mRNAs) will be used to estimate false discovery rates and guard against overinterpretation.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary outcomes will be (1) a harmonized, multi-modal synthesis dataset spanning Ribo-seq, proteomics, rRNA modification/biogenesis proxies, single-cell context, and perturbation constraints; (2) a set of reproducible ribosome heterogeneity axes (“ribosome states”) with quantified uncertainty, cross-context prevalence, and cross-species conservation; and (3) rigorously validated associations between ribosome states and selective translation programs, including interpretable mRNA features that predict sensitivity.

We anticipate three classes of scientific conclusions. First, we will determine whether ribosome heterogeneity collapses into a small number of conserved axes or is largely context-idiosyncratic. Second, we will test whether any axis predicts mRNA-specific translation changes beyond global translation scaling, thereby providing strong evidence for or against specialized translation as a general phenomenon. Third, we will connect ribosome states to stress adaptation and disease relevance by integrating perturbation data and dependency maps, identifying candidate ribosome components or modification pathways that modulate translation programs linked to proliferation, mitochondrial function, proteostasis, or immune signaling.

The broader impact is a community-scale, NCEMS-aligned synthesis that advances understanding of emergent mesoscale regulation: how ensemble-level variation in a core molecular machine yields system-level selectivity. Methodologically, the project will establish best practices for cross-study Ribo-seq normalization, ribosomal protein paralog quantification from proteomics, and integration of modification maps with translation outputs. Practically, the Ribosome Heterogeneity Synthesis Resource will enable researchers to rapidly test new hypotheses, benchmark new algorithms for detecting specialized translation, and prioritize targets for future experimental validation (outside the scope of this synthesis award). Finally, the working group’s training activities will produce a cohort of trainees skilled in reproducible multi-omics synthesis, strengthening the future data-savvy workforce in molecular and cellular biosciences.
original.budget_and_resources:
This proposal is designed as a community-scale synthesis working group that requires NCEMS coordination, convening, and computational support beyond a single laboratory’s capacity. The budget will be structured to maximize collaborative integration, trainee participation, and open deliverables while using only publicly available data.

NCEMS resources requested.
1) Working group convenings: Support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venues) plus regular virtual meetings. Funds cover travel, lodging, and per diem for geographically distributed participants, with priority support for trainees and researchers from under-resourced institutions.
2) Personnel support: Partial support for a project manager/data curator to maintain metadata standards, coordinate cross-team integration, manage releases, and ensure compliance with open-science policies. Trainee support (graduate students/postdocs) will be requested for curation sprints, pipeline development, and tutorial creation.
3) Computational infrastructure: NCEMS-supported compute and storage for large-scale reprocessing of Ribo-seq and proteomics-derived matrices, container registry hosting, and continuous integration. Where cloud/HPC costs are needed, we will use cost-tracked, reproducible environments.

Anticipated cost categories (not generating new data).
- Travel and convening: participant travel, lodging, meeting space, and accessibility services.
- Personnel: project coordination; trainee stipends/salary support for defined synthesis tasks.
- Computing: storage for intermediate files; compute for standardized alignment/QC, TE estimation, and multi-view modeling; long-term hosting of released artifacts.
- Dissemination and training: workshop materials, documentation, and webinar hosting; support for open-access publication fees if allowable.

Feasibility and leveraging existing investments. The project leverages extensive public repositories (GEO/SRA, PRIDE, CPTAC, Tabula Sapiens/HCA, DepMap) and existing open-source tools, reducing costs while increasing impact. NCEMS support is essential to (i) convene domain experts who do not typically collaborate, (ii) maintain a shared, high-quality curation and processing backbone, and (iii) deliver a durable, open resource that the community can extend after the award period.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Molecular biology investigates translational regulation and ribosome biology to address whether ribosome heterogeneity functions as a systematic regulatory mechanism. Current knowledge recognizes ribosome variations in composition and modification but lacks integrated analysis of these siloed public data sources. This project determines if reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity predict selective mRNA translation to explain context specific proteome remodeling.

The study performs a community scale synthesis of public datasets using standardized pipelines and multi view factor modeling. Methods include ribosome profiling harmonization and proteomics based paralog mapping alongside single cell deconvolution and predictive modeling. Results are validated through cross study replication and bootstrap stability analysis and perturbation consistency checks and negative controls.

The project utilizes datasets from GEO and SRA and PRIDE and CPTAC and Tabula Sapiens and DepMap. Datasets are integrated through standardized metadata curation and unified processing pipelines for translation efficiency and joint modeling. Inconsistent metadata and batch effects are mitigated through standardized re processing and deconvolution and statistical models controlling confounders.

The proposal does not address the specific milestones or the overall timeline for the completion of this project. The scope requires cross disciplinary expertise in ribosome biology and proteomics and statistical genetics and machine learning.

The project produces a public Ribosome Heterogeneity Synthesis Resource and reproducible processing pipelines and open benchmarks for translation. The team includes experts in ribosome biology and proteomics and statistical genetics and machine learning with trainees involved.
rephrased.main_idea: This research investigates whether ribosome heterogeneity functions as a systematic regulatory mechanism for selective translation or remains a cellular byproduct. The study employs multi-view factor modeling to integrate siloed proteomics and ribosome profiling data into a unified analytical framework. This project establishes a comprehensive resource that defines the functional relationship between ribosomal composition and context specific protein synthesis.

title: Emergent Properties of Membrane Microdomains: Integrating Lipidomics, Proteomics, and Super-Resolution Imaging of Raft-Like Assemblies

original.abstract:
Membrane microdomains (often described as lipid rafts) are proposed mesoscale assemblies that organize signaling and trafficking, yet their existence and functional roles remain debated due to methodological variability. Public lipidomics, proteomics, and imaging datasets provide an opportunity for a rigorous synthesis to identify when microdomains emerge, what compositions they exhibit, and how they influence cellular outcomes.

This working group will integrate (i) lipidomics datasets across cell types and perturbations (Metabolomics Workbench), (ii) membrane fractionation and detergent-resistant membrane proteomics (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution and single-particle tracking imaging datasets that quantify nanoscale clustering (IDR), (iv) protein palmitoylation and other lipidation resources (SwissPalm, curated PTM databases), (v) perturbation datasets affecting cholesterol/sphingolipid metabolism and signaling (GEO, LINCS), and (vi) interaction networks for membrane proteins (BioGRID). We will curate experimental conditions to distinguish biochemical artifacts from consistent signals.

Scientific questions: (1) Are there reproducible compositional signatures of raft-like assemblies across methods, or are observed domains primarily assay-dependent? (2) Which lipid and protein features predict propensity to form mesoscale clusters (lipidation, transmembrane domain properties, oligomerization)? (3) How do microdomain states modulate emergent signaling behaviors such as ultrasensitivity and receptor crosstalk?

Methodologically, we will develop a cross-assay harmonization framework that models each experimental modality’s biases and extracts latent microdomain states. For imaging, we will standardize clustering metrics (Ripley’s K, pair correlation, cluster lifetime) and implement reproducible pipelines. For lipidomics/proteomics, we will map species and proteins to common ontologies and quantify co-enrichment patterns. Integrative models will connect inferred microdomain states to signaling outputs measured in phospho datasets or transcriptional responses.

NCEMS support is essential to convene lipid biochemists, membrane biophysicists, imaging experts, and data scientists to define standards and evaluate claims with transparent, reproducible analyses. The synthesis requires community-scale effort to curate heterogeneous datasets and build robust meta-analytic models.

Deliverables will include an open Membrane Microdomain Evidence Map with modality-specific and integrated confidence scores; standardized analysis workflows for super-resolution clustering and lipidomics integration; and predictive models linking composition to signaling phenotypes. Training will include modules on lipidomics normalization, spatial statistics for imaging, and open, reproducible meta-analysis. This project will resolve long-standing debates by grounding microdomain concepts in integrated, quantitative synthesis.
original.background_and_significance:
Cell membranes are not uniform fluids; they host heterogeneous, dynamic organization across scales. A central, long-standing hypothesis is that “lipid rafts” or raft-like microdomains—cholesterol- and sphingolipid-enriched assemblies—create mesoscale platforms that concentrate receptors, adaptors, and enzymes to regulate signaling, trafficking, and pathogen entry. Despite decades of research, whether raft-like assemblies constitute reproducible biological states or are largely artifacts of specific assays remains unresolved. This controversy persists because evidence has been fragmented across modalities that probe different physical and biochemical aspects of membranes. Detergent-resistant membrane (DRM) fractionation can enrich cholesterol/sphingolipid components but is sensitive to detergent choice, temperature, and extraction kinetics. Super-resolution imaging and single-particle tracking (SPT) can detect nanoscale clustering and confinement but vary in labeling strategies, localization precision, and analysis methods. Lipidomics and proteomics quantify composition, but cross-study comparability is hampered by differing extraction protocols, ionization biases, protein inference pipelines, and incomplete metadata.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a synthesis that treats raft-like assemblies as an emergent mesoscale phenomenon: patterns of composition and spatial organization that arise from many molecular interactions yet influence higher-level cellular behaviors. The mesoscale focus aligns with NCEMS’ vision to understand how unexpected properties appear between biomolecules and organelles. Raft-like phenomena are an archetypal mesoscale problem: individual lipid–lipid and lipid–protein interactions are weak and transient, but collectively they may generate persistent organizational states that modulate signaling dynamics (e.g., ultrasensitivity, bistability, receptor cross-talk) and trafficking outcomes.

A community-scale synthesis is now feasible because of the growth of publicly available datasets spanning composition, post-translational lipidation, spatial organization, and downstream responses. Metabolomics Workbench contains lipidomics across cell types and perturbations, including cholesterol manipulation and sphingolipid pathway interventions. PRIDE hosts membrane fractionation and DRM proteomics studies with rich protein-level readouts. The Image Data Resource (IDR) aggregates super-resolution and tracking datasets, enabling reanalysis with standardized spatial statistics. SwissPalm and curated PTM resources provide orthogonal evidence for palmitoylation and other lipidation that can drive membrane partitioning. GEO and LINCS provide perturbational transcriptomic signatures of membrane composition changes and signaling pathway activation. BioGRID offers interaction networks that can capture oligomerization and complex assembly, potentially stabilizing microdomains.

However, extracting credible biological conclusions from these resources requires harmonization across assays, explicit modeling of modality-specific biases, and integration into a unified evidence framework. Individual laboratories rarely have the breadth of expertise to curate lipid species nomenclature, proteomics quantification, imaging spatial statistics, and causal inference from perturbation signatures simultaneously. Moreover, the field lacks shared standards for reporting and analyzing clustering metrics and for connecting composition to function in a statistically principled way.

This NCEMS working group will address this gap by synthesizing heterogeneous public datasets to determine when raft-like microdomains emerge, what reproducible compositional and organizational signatures they exhibit, and how these states relate to signaling outcomes. By explicitly separating assay artifacts from consistent cross-modality signals, the project will resolve long-standing puzzles about membrane microdomains and provide reusable, open workflows that elevate rigor and reproducibility across the community.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will test whether raft-like microdomains are best understood as reproducible, latent mesoscale “microdomain states” that can be inferred from multiple orthogonal assays, and whether these states have predictable consequences for emergent signaling behaviors. We focus on three integrated research questions, each with falsifiable hypotheses and measurable predictions.

RQ1: Are there reproducible compositional and organizational signatures of raft-like assemblies across methods, or are observed domains primarily assay-dependent?

H1.1 (Cross-modality reproducibility): After accounting for known biases (e.g., detergent extraction conditions, labeling density, localization precision), independent modalities will converge on a small set of latent microdomain states characterized by consistent co-enrichment patterns (cholesterol/sphingolipid classes; saturated vs unsaturated lipids; specific protein families).

Predictions: (i) DRM proteomics enrichment scores will correlate with imaging-derived clustering/confinement metrics for overlapping proteins in matched or comparable cell contexts; (ii) lipidomics signatures (e.g., sphingomyelin/ceramide ratios, cholesterol proxies, saturation indices) will predict the prevalence of inferred microdomain states across perturbations.

H1.2 (Assay-dependence boundary conditions): Some reported “raft” signatures will be explainable by modality-specific artifacts and will not replicate across orthogonal datasets.

Predictions: (i) studies with harsh detergents/low temperatures will show inflated enrichment of certain proteins without corresponding imaging clustering; (ii) imaging datasets with high labeling density or inadequate drift correction will show spurious clustering that fails to align with compositional evidence.

RQ2: Which lipid and protein features predict propensity to form mesoscale clusters?

H2.1 (Feature-based propensity): Protein palmitoylation, specific transmembrane domain (TMD) properties (length, hydrophobic mismatch, helix-helix motifs), and oligomerization/network connectivity predict microdomain association beyond expression level.

Predictions: (i) palmitoylated proteins (SwissPalm evidence) will have higher inferred microdomain membership probabilities; (ii) proteins with longer TMDs and higher predicted raft affinity will show stronger clustering and DRM enrichment; (iii) BioGRID-derived oligomerization/complex membership will be associated with increased cluster lifetime in SPT.

H2.2 (Compositional coupling): Lipid features—cholesterol availability, sphingolipid abundance, and lipid saturation—modulate microdomain propensity in a context-dependent manner.

Predictions: perturbations that reduce cholesterol biosynthesis or increase membrane unsaturation will shift samples toward low-microdomain states and reduce clustering metrics, while sphingolipid accumulation (e.g., ceramide elevation) will produce distinct microdomain states with different protein recruitment.

RQ3: How do microdomain states modulate emergent signaling behaviors such as ultrasensitivity and receptor crosstalk?

H3.1 (State-dependent signaling gain): High-microdomain states increase signaling gain and apparent ultrasensitivity by co-localizing receptors with kinases/adaptors and excluding phosphatases.

Predictions: across perturbation datasets (GEO/LINCS), inferred high-microdomain states will associate with stronger pathway activation signatures (e.g., MAPK, PI3K/AKT), steeper dose–response proxies, and increased co-activation of receptor programs.

H3.2 (Rewiring/crosstalk): Distinct microdomain states differentially bias receptor crosstalk, producing predictable co-variation patterns among signaling outputs.

Predictions: microdomain states enriched for specific scaffolds (e.g., tetraspanins, flotillins, caveolins where present) will align with distinct transcriptional modules and phospho-signature patterns, indicating state-specific signaling wiring.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will run a community-scale synthesis pipeline with three integrated cores: (A) Data curation and harmonization, (B) Cross-modality latent-state modeling, and (C) Functional linkage to signaling outcomes. The working group will include lipidomics experts, membrane biophysicists, proteomics analysts, imaging/spatial statisticians, and ML/data-integration specialists. No new experimental data will be generated.

A. Data discovery, inclusion criteria, and metadata harmonization.

Data sources: Metabolomics Workbench (lipidomics), PRIDE (DRM/fractionation proteomics), IDR (super-resolution, SPT), SwissPalm and curated PTM databases (palmitoylation/lipidation), GEO and LINCS (perturbational transcriptomics; where available phospho-proteomics links), BioGRID (interaction networks).

Inclusion criteria: (i) public raw or minimally processed data with sufficient metadata (cell type, perturbation, temperature, detergent, labeling strategy, imaging modality), (ii) replicates or clear experimental structure, (iii) identifiable membrane-related readouts. We will create a controlled vocabulary for perturbations (cholesterol depletion, synthesis inhibition, sphingolipid perturbation, cytoskeletal disruption) and map cell types to Cell Ontology.

Harmonization: Lipids will be mapped to LIPID MAPS identifiers; proteins to UniProt/Ensembl; PTMs to PSI-MOD; imaging metadata to OME standards where possible. We will implement normalization strategies per modality (e.g., lipidomics internal standard-aware scaling where available; proteomics batch correction and protein inference harmonization; imaging localization uncertainty propagation).

B. Modality-specific reanalysis with standardized metrics.

Imaging: Reprocess IDR datasets when raw localizations/trajectories are available. Compute standardized clustering/confinement metrics: Ripley’s K/L, pair correlation g(r), DBSCAN/HDBSCAN cluster size distributions, cluster lifetime from SPT, and confinement indices. Implement negative controls via label randomization and spatial bootstrapping; quantify sensitivity to localization precision, drift, and labeling density.

Proteomics: For DRM/fractionation studies, compute enrichment scores relative to total membrane or input fractions; propagate peptide-level uncertainty; annotate extraction conditions to model artifact risk. Quantify co-enrichment modules using robust correlation (biweight midcorrelation) and sparse factor models.

Lipidomics: Standardize lipid class summaries (cholesterol proxies when direct cholesterol absent, sphingomyelin/ceramide, gangliosides, saturation index, acyl chain length distributions). Use compositional data analysis (CLR transforms) to mitigate closure effects.

C. Cross-assay harmonization and latent microdomain state inference.

We will develop a hierarchical Bayesian latent-variable model that treats each assay as a noisy observation of underlying microdomain states. The model will include modality-specific bias terms (e.g., detergent harshness, imaging labeling artifacts) and will output: (i) sample-level microdomain state probabilities, (ii) protein- and lipid-level association weights, and (iii) uncertainty intervals. Where sample matching is imperfect across datasets, we will use semi-supervised alignment via shared covariates (cell type, perturbation class) and domain adaptation methods.

D. Feature-based prediction of microdomain propensity.

We will assemble protein features: palmitoylation evidence strength, other lipidation, TMD length/hydrophobicity, predicted disorder, oligomerization/network centrality (BioGRID), and expression proxies. Use regularized models (elastic net, gradient-boosted trees) with nested cross-validation to predict microdomain membership, emphasizing interpretability and generalization across cell contexts.

E. Linking microdomain states to signaling outcomes.

Using GEO/LINCS perturbation signatures, we will estimate pathway activation scores (e.g., PROGENy, DoRothEA) and transcriptional modules, and relate these to inferred microdomain states via causal-leaning analyses (difference-in-differences across perturbation classes; mediation-style models where composition → microdomain state → signaling signature). We will predefine contrasts around cholesterol/sphingolipid perturbations to reduce researcher degrees of freedom.

Milestones: (1) Evidence Map v1 with curated datasets and QC; (2) standardized imaging/proteomics/lipidomics pipelines; (3) latent-state model and benchmarks; (4) composition/feature predictors; (5) signaling linkage analyses and final integrated synthesis.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative resolution of the raft/microdomain debate framed in terms of reproducible latent microdomain states, including identification of conditions where evidence converges across modalities versus conditions dominated by assay artifacts. This will transform the discourse from binary “rafts exist/do not exist” to testable statements about state prevalence, composition, and uncertainty.

(2) A cross-modality compositional signature atlas: lipid class patterns and protein modules consistently associated with inferred microdomain states, with confidence estimates and explicit dependence on experimental context (cell type, perturbation, extraction/imaging conditions). This will provide the community with a principled reference for what “raft-like” means in data.

(3) Predictive determinants of microdomain propensity: an interpretable model linking protein lipidation (e.g., palmitoylation), TMD biophysics, and interaction-network features to microdomain association and clustering behavior. These results will generate mechanistic hypotheses that can be tested by the broader community (outside this project) and guide annotation of membrane proteins.

(4) Functional integration: evidence for how microdomain states modulate emergent signaling properties, including quantitative associations with pathway activation strength, inferred ultrasensitivity proxies, and receptor crosstalk patterns across perturbation datasets. Even when causal claims are limited by observational synthesis, we will provide robust, uncertainty-aware relationships and boundary conditions.

Community and methodological impact. (5) Standardized, reusable pipelines for super-resolution clustering analysis and for integrating lipidomics/proteomics with compositional and batch-aware statistics. By reducing methodological variability, these workflows will increase reproducibility and comparability across future studies.

(6) The Membrane Microdomain Evidence Map: an openly accessible, continuously extensible resource that scores evidence by modality and in aggregate, enabling researchers to query proteins, lipids, perturbations, and cell contexts.

Training impact. (7) Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary, data-synthesis skills (spatial statistics, omics normalization, Bayesian integration, open science practices), directly advancing NCEMS’ goal of training a data-savvy workforce.

Long-term impact. The project will establish a gold-standard synthesis framework for mesoscale emergence problems where heterogeneous assays provide partial, biased views—generalizable to condensates, cytoskeletal mesoscale organization, and organelle contact sites.
original.budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. The project requires intensive, in-person and hybrid collaboration among experts spanning lipidomics, proteomics, super-resolution imaging analysis, membrane biophysics, and statistical/ML integration. NCEMS resources are essential to convene and coordinate a working group large enough to curate heterogeneous public datasets, build consensus standards, and implement robust, shared pipelines—beyond the capacity of a single lab or bilateral collaboration.

Budget categories (requested through NCEMS working-group mechanisms; exact totals per NCEMS limits).

1) Working group meetings and collaboration (largest direct cost category). Support for 2–3 multi-day synthesis meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue), plus interim virtual workshops. Costs include participant travel, lodging, meeting space, and accessibility services to ensure broad participation across geography and institution types.

2) Personnel support for synthesis labor. Partial support (salary/fringe or stipends, per NCEMS rules) for: (i) a project coordinator/data curator to manage dataset intake, metadata harmonization, and Evidence Map releases; (ii) a research software engineer to productionize workflows, containers, CI, and web-facing resource components; (iii) trainee support (graduate students/postdocs) to lead modality pipelines and cross-validation benchmarks under mentorship.

3) Computing and data infrastructure. Cloud credits or shared compute allocations for large-scale reanalysis (especially imaging reprocessing and Bayesian model fitting), storage for intermediate artifacts, and automated builds/tests. We will prioritize cost-efficient approaches (spot instances, caching, tiered storage) and ensure all compute steps are reproducible locally where feasible.

4) Dissemination and training. Funds for open training materials (recording/captioning), documentation sprints, and maintenance of the Evidence Map (static hosting plus modest backend if needed). Publication costs for open-access dissemination where appropriate.

In-kind and leveraged resources. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing analysis scripts to be standardized, and institutional compute where available. NCEMS will provide convening power, project management scaffolding, and synthesis-center best practices in team science, open science policy, and reproducible analytics.

Deliverable-tied allocation. Spending will be milestone-driven: curation/QC (Evidence Map v1), standardized pipelines, latent-state integration model, functional linkage analyses, and final public releases with training modules.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Cell biology investigates membrane microdomains to understand how these structures organize cellular signaling and trafficking within the plasma membrane. Current knowledge confirms heterogeneous membrane organization but lacks consensus on whether these assemblies represent biological structures or experimental artifacts. This project identifies reproducible microdomain signatures to establish a quantitative framework for understanding mesoscale membrane organization and signaling outcomes.

The study employs a meta analytic synthesis using a hierarchical Bayesian latent variable model to integrate disparate research datasets. Key methods include cross assay harmonization and spatial statistics alongside compositional data analysis and regularized machine learning models. Results are validated by comparing independent modalities for convergence and implementing cross validation benchmarks for all predictive models.

The study utilizes datasets from Metabolomics Workbench and PRIDE and IDR and SwissPalm and GEO and LINCS and BioGRID. These datasets are integrated by mapping species to common ontologies and normalizing across modalities using shared experimental covariates. Known limitations regarding modality specific biases are mitigated by explicit bias modeling and standardized reanalysis of raw data.

The project timeline includes five milestones ranging from evidence map creation to the final analysis of signaling linkage patterns. Multi lab collaboration is required to combine expertise in lipid biochemistry and membrane biophysics and data science for consensus.

The project produces an open Membrane Microdomain Evidence Map and standardized analysis workflows and open access training modules. The team includes lipidomics experts and membrane biophysicists and data scientists who provide mentorship to graduate students and postdocs.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the persistent uncertainty regarding whether membrane microdomains represent genuine biological structures or merely artifacts of specific experimental methods. The study employs a hierarchical Bayesian latent variable model to integrate heterogeneous public datasets while explicitly accounting for modality specific biases. This project establishes a quantitative evidence map that defines the compositional signatures and functional roles of membrane organization across diverse conditions.

title: A Multi-Scale Synthesis of Endocytic Trafficking Emergence: From Coat Assembly to Organelle Identity

original.abstract:
Endocytic trafficking is an emergent system in which local coat assembly and cargo selection generate mesoscale organelles (early/late endosomes) with distinct identities and dynamic maturation. Public datasets include time-resolved imaging, proteomics of endosomal fractions, interaction networks, and perturbation screens, but they have not been unified to understand how organelle identity emerges from molecular interactions.

This working group will integrate (i) imaging datasets tracking endocytic markers and cargo trafficking (IDR, Cell Image Library), (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of endosomal compartments and coat proteins (PRIDE), (iii) interaction networks for adaptors, Rab GTPases, and ESCRT machinery (BioGRID, SIGNOR), (iv) genome-wide perturbation screens affecting trafficking and receptor recycling (CRISPR screens, RNAi datasets), and (v) transcriptomic responses to trafficking perturbations (GEO). We will curate time-course information and experimental contexts (ligand stimulation, inhibitors) to enable dynamic inference.

Scientific aims: (1) Define conserved modules that specify endosomal identity and quantify how these modules assemble and transition over time. (2) Identify emergent checkpoints and bifurcation points that determine cargo fate (recycling vs degradation). (3) Determine how perturbations rewire trafficking networks to produce disease-relevant phenotypes (e.g., altered receptor signaling, lysosomal storage signatures).

Analytical approach: We will develop dynamic network models combining time-lapse imaging-derived trajectories (marker intensity and co-localization over time) with proteomic composition changes. Hidden Markov models and state-space approaches will infer discrete trafficking states and transition probabilities. Perturbation data will be used to assign causal roles to regulators. A methodological deliverable will be a standardized set of trafficking state features and open tools for extracting them from imaging.

NCEMS support is required to coordinate experts in membrane trafficking, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, and to host collaborative curation and benchmarking efforts. The scope—integrating many datasets across modalities and building dynamic inference tools—exceeds individual lab capacity.

Deliverables will include an open Endocytic Emergence Atlas describing trafficking states, modules, and transition maps; reproducible workflows for imaging trajectory extraction and proteomics integration; and a catalog of predicted regulators controlling cargo fate decisions. Training will include hands-on workshops on image-based time-series analysis, network modeling, and open science. This synthesis will reveal how mesoscale organelle identities and trafficking behaviors emerge from molecular-scale interactions.
original.background_and_significance:
Endocytic trafficking is a core cellular process that couples membrane remodeling, cargo selection, signaling, and organelle biogenesis. It is also a paradigmatic example of emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences: local molecular interactions among coat proteins, adaptors, lipids, Rab GTPases, and tethering/ESCRT machineries give rise to mesoscale structures—endocytic pits, vesicles, early endosomes, recycling endosomes, multivesicular bodies, and late endosomes/lysosomes—with distinct identities, lifetimes, and functions. These identities are not encoded by any single molecule; rather, they arise from combinatorial composition, spatial organization, and dynamic transitions across time. Understanding how endosomal identity emerges is central to explaining how cells route receptors and nutrients, terminate or sustain signaling, maintain membrane homeostasis, and adapt to perturbations.

Despite decades of mechanistic work, long-standing puzzles remain. First, endosomal identity is often described using discrete marker proteins (e.g., EEA1, Rab5, Rab7, Rab11), yet imaging reveals heterogeneous and overlapping marker distributions and variable maturation trajectories. Second, cargo fate decisions (recycling versus degradation) appear to occur at specific “checkpoints” along the endocytic route, but the molecular determinants and timing of these bifurcations are incompletely defined and may differ across cell types and stimuli. Third, perturbations to trafficking regulators produce pleiotropic phenotypes that span receptor signaling, metabolism, and neurodegeneration, but causal paths from molecular perturbation to emergent organelle-level dysfunction are difficult to trace.

A major barrier is fragmentation of evidence across modalities. Public repositories now contain extensive time-resolved imaging of endocytic markers and cargo trafficking, quantitative proteomics/phosphoproteomics of endosomal fractions and coat complexes, curated interaction and signaling networks, genome-scale CRISPR/RNAi screens for trafficking phenotypes, and transcriptomic responses to trafficking perturbations. Each modality captures a partial projection of the system: imaging yields trajectories and spatial co-localization; proteomics yields composition and post-translational regulation; interaction databases provide mechanistic priors; perturbation screens provide causal leverage; and transcriptomics provides downstream state readouts. Yet these datasets are rarely integrated into a unified, dynamic model of endocytic emergence.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that is beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. The project requires expertise in membrane trafficking biology, quantitative microscopy, proteomics/omics integration, dynamical systems modeling, and causal inference, as well as coordinated curation of experimental context (cell type, ligand stimulation, inhibitors, temperature, imaging modality, fractionation protocol). The Center’s emphasis on mesoscale emergence aligns directly with the endosomal system, where mesoscale compartments are formed and remodeled by molecular-scale interactions.

By synthesizing publicly available datasets into a coherent framework, this working group will deliver both new biological insight and broadly reusable methodology. Biologically, it will clarify conserved modules that define endosomal identity, quantify maturation and branching trajectories, and map how perturbations rewire routes to generate disease-relevant phenotypes. Methodologically, it will establish standardized “trafficking state” features and open tools for extracting them from imaging and linking them to proteomic composition and regulatory networks. The resulting Endocytic Emergence Atlas will provide a reference for the field, enabling hypothesis generation, benchmarking, and cross-study comparability, while training a new cadre of data-savvy scientists in reproducible synthesis research.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address how mesoscale endosomal identities and cargo fate decisions emerge from molecular interactions and how these emergent behaviors change under perturbation. We focus on questions that require synthesis across imaging, proteomics, interaction networks, and functional genomics, and that can be answered using only publicly available data.

Research Question 1: What are the conserved molecular modules that specify endosomal identity, and how do they assemble and transition over time?
Hypothesis 1A: Endosomal identity is best described by a small number of conserved, partially overlapping “modules” (e.g., Rab5/PI3P/EEA1; Rab7/HOPS; Rab11/recycling adaptors; ESCRT/MVB) whose co-occurrence patterns define mesoscale states more robustly than single markers.
Hypothesis 1B: Transitions between identity states follow constrained trajectories with characteristic ordering (e.g., Rab5→Rab7 conversion) but exhibit quantifiable heterogeneity driven by stimulus context and cell type.
Hypothesis 1C: Proteomic and phosphoproteomic changes provide orthogonal evidence for these modules and reveal regulatory phosphorylation events that precede or accompany state transitions.

Research Question 2: Where and when do cargo fate decisions bifurcate, and what emergent checkpoints govern recycling versus degradation?
Hypothesis 2A: Cargo fate bifurcations correspond to discrete transition points in inferred trafficking state space, detectable as changes in transition probabilities in time-resolved imaging trajectories and as shifts in compartment composition.
Hypothesis 2B: A limited set of regulators (e.g., specific adaptors, sorting nexins, retromer components, ESCRT factors, Rab effectors) act as “gatekeepers” whose perturbation disproportionately alters branching ratios between recycling and degradative routes.
Hypothesis 2C: Cargo class (e.g., GPCRs, RTKs, nutrient transporters) maps onto distinct route preferences that can be predicted from module engagement and checkpoint timing.

Research Question 3: How do perturbations rewire trafficking networks to produce disease-relevant phenotypes and signaling outcomes?
Hypothesis 3A: Perturbations cluster into a small number of “rewiring modes” that correspond to predictable changes in state transition topology (e.g., slowed maturation, increased recycling, impaired MVB formation).
Hypothesis 3B: Disease-associated signatures (e.g., lysosomal storage-like transcriptional programs, sustained receptor signaling) can be explained by specific rewiring modes and their downstream impact on cargo residence times and compartment identity.
Hypothesis 3C: Integrating genetic screens with interaction priors will improve causal attribution, enabling identification of upstream regulators that shift emergent dynamics rather than merely changing steady-state marker abundance.

Research Question 4 (methodological): Can we define a standardized, interoperable representation of “trafficking states” that enables cross-study synthesis and model comparison?
Hypothesis 4A: A consensus feature set—combining imaging-derived trajectories (intensity, co-localization, motion, lifetime), proteomic composition vectors, and network-context embeddings—will yield reproducible state definitions across datasets.
Hypothesis 4B: Models trained on heterogeneous public datasets can generalize to new datasets (held-out studies) when experimental context is explicitly encoded and harmonized.

Collectively, these questions test a unifying premise: endocytic organelle identity and cargo fate are emergent properties of modular molecular assemblies and their regulated transitions, and these properties can be quantitatively inferred by integrating public multi-omic and imaging data into dynamic, causal models.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. We will conduct a community-scale synthesis using only publicly available data, organized around coordinated curation, harmonization, modeling, and validation-by-cross-dataset replication. The working group will include experts in (i) membrane trafficking biology, (ii) quantitative imaging and computer vision, (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics, (iv) network biology and causal inference, and (v) dynamical systems/statistical modeling. NCEMS support is essential for convening repeated working sessions, maintaining shared computational infrastructure, and coordinating open-science curation and benchmarking.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. Imaging: Image Data Resource (IDR) and Cell Image Library time-lapse datasets with endocytic markers (Rab5/7/11, EEA1, LAMP1, clathrin/AP2) and/or cargo (transferrin, LDL, EGFR, GPCRs), with sufficient temporal resolution to track puncta/compartments. Proteomics: PRIDE datasets profiling endosomal fractions, coat complexes, ESCRT assemblies, and phosphoproteomics under stimulation or inhibitor conditions. Interaction priors: BioGRID and SIGNOR for physical and signed regulatory interactions among adaptors, Rabs, kinases/phosphatases, ESCRT, retromer, tethers. Perturbations: genome-wide or focused CRISPR/RNAi screens reporting trafficking phenotypes (receptor recycling, endosome morphology, lysosomal function). Transcriptomics: GEO perturbation-response datasets for trafficking genes or pharmacologic modulation.

Curation and harmonization. We will build a metadata schema capturing cell type, perturbation, ligand, imaging modality, temporal sampling, segmentation/tracking method, fractionation protocol, and quantitative readouts. Controlled vocabularies (e.g., Gene Ontology terms, Cellosaurus cell lines) will standardize labels. Time will be normalized to experimental reference points (e.g., ligand addition) and mapped to common windows when possible. Batch effects will be addressed via hierarchical models and study-level covariates rather than aggressive normalization that erases biology.

Feature extraction and state representation. Imaging: we will implement reproducible pipelines (Napari/CellProfiler/DeepCell options) to segment and track endocytic puncta/compartments, extracting trajectories of intensity, co-localization, size, motion, fusion/fission events, and cargo residence time. Proteomics: we will compute compartment composition vectors and phosphosite activity proxies, with uncertainty estimates from peptide-level evidence. Network context: we will generate embeddings of proteins based on interaction topology and signed regulation.

Dynamic inference and integration. We will infer discrete trafficking states and transitions using hidden Markov models and state-space models, with emissions defined by imaging features and (when available) proteomic composition. For datasets lacking paired modalities, we will use multi-view learning to align state spaces across studies. Transition probabilities will be modeled as functions of context (cell type, stimulus) and perturbations. To identify checkpoints and bifurcations, we will detect branching in inferred transition graphs and quantify how perturbations shift branching ratios.

Causal attribution from perturbation data. Screen hits will be mapped onto the interaction network to prioritize regulators upstream of altered transitions. We will use causal discovery/regularized regression approaches (e.g., do-calculus-inspired scoring, invariant risk minimization across contexts) to distinguish direct regulators of state transitions from downstream effects. Transcriptomic signatures will be linked to inferred rewiring modes using gene set enrichment and latent factor models.

Benchmarking and robustness. We will pre-register evaluation metrics: held-out study prediction of state assignments, replication of module composition across datasets, and stability of checkpoint detection under resampling. All models will report uncertainty; conclusions will require consistency across at least two independent datasets or modalities when possible.

Deliverable tooling. We will release an open “Trafficking State Toolkit” for feature extraction, state inference, and atlas visualization, and produce the Endocytic Emergence Atlas integrating states, modules, transitions, and perturbation effects.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) Endocytic Emergence Atlas: a public, queryable resource describing inferred trafficking states, their molecular modules, and transition graphs across contexts (cell types, stimuli, perturbations). The atlas will include (i) state definitions with feature distributions, (ii) module membership and supporting evidence from proteomics and interaction priors, and (iii) transition probabilities and branching structure with uncertainty. (2) Checkpoint and bifurcation map: a ranked set of emergent decision points where cargo fate diverges, including context dependence and predicted gatekeeper regulators. (3) Rewiring modes under perturbation: a taxonomy of how genetic and pharmacologic perturbations reshape trafficking dynamics, linked to downstream transcriptional programs and disease-relevant phenotypes.

Methodological products. (4) Standardized trafficking state feature set: a community-vetted representation that enables cross-study comparison of endocytic dynamics beyond single-marker labels. (5) Open Trafficking State Toolkit: reproducible pipelines for imaging trajectory extraction, multimodal alignment, dynamic modeling, and visualization, designed to run on public datasets and to be extensible to new studies.

Impact on emergence science. The project will provide a concrete, multi-scale example of how mesoscale organelle identity emerges from molecular-scale interactions and regulation. By explicitly modeling state transitions and branching, it will shift the field from static compartment labels to quantitative, dynamical descriptions of organelle identity. The integration of causal perturbation evidence will connect emergent organelle behaviors to specific regulatory levers.

Broader impacts. The atlas and tools will accelerate hypothesis generation for trafficking, signaling, neurodegeneration, infection, and lysosomal storage disorders by identifying regulators that alter cargo residence time and compartment maturation. The working group will also establish best practices for integrating imaging time series with proteomics and functional genomics—approaches applicable to other mesoscale emergent systems (e.g., stress granules, centrosomes, phase-separated condensates). Finally, the project will train graduate students and postdocs in open, reproducible synthesis science and AI-enabled data integration, directly aligning with NCEMS goals of workforce development and community-scale collaboration.
original.budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (NCEMS working group support). The project’s scope requires coordinated multi-institution collaboration, intensive curation, shared compute, and in-person/virtual synthesis meetings—capabilities that exceed a single lab. We request support in six categories aligned with typical NCEMS working group mechanisms.

1) Meetings and collaboration (travel, lodging, venue, hybrid support). Funds will support 3–4 multi-day working meetings over 18–24 months plus interim virtual sprints. Hybrid meeting infrastructure (AV, facilitation) is needed to include geographically distributed participants and to reduce barriers for trainees and under-resourced institutions.

2) Personnel support (trainees and research staff time). We will support partial effort for (i) a data curator/engineer to maintain metadata, accessions, and provenance; (ii) a research software engineer to package pipelines, containers, and CI; and (iii) trainee stipends/travel to enable graduate students and postdocs to participate meaningfully and lead subprojects (feature extraction, benchmarking, atlas visualization).

3) Computational resources. While much analysis can run on institutional clusters, NCEMS-provided cloud/HPC credits are requested for reproducible re-execution of pipelines on large imaging datasets, model training, and public-facing atlas builds. Storage is required for derived features, intermediate artifacts, and cached public downloads (within repository terms).

4) Data management and dissemination. Costs include DOI deposition (e.g., Zenodo communities), web hosting for the atlas front-end, and accessibility services for training materials (captioning/transcripts).

5) External expertise and facilitation. Modest funds will support short-term consultation (e.g., OME imaging standards, proteomics standards, causal inference methods) and professional facilitation to keep multidisciplinary integration on track.

6) NCEMS-added value and center resources. We will leverage NCEMS convening power, open-science policy guidance, and connections to AI/data-science expertise. NCEMS coordination is essential for recruitment of diverse participants (career stage, institution type), conflict-of-interest management, and ensuring deliverables meet community-scale synthesis standards.

Resource plan and timeline. Year 1 focuses on dataset inventory, metadata harmonization, baseline pipelines, and initial state models. Year 2 focuses on multimodal integration, checkpoint/rewiring analyses, atlas release, and training workshops. All spending directly enables synthesis of existing public data; no funds are requested for generating new experimental data.

rephrased.standardized_text:
The research domain of endocytic trafficking examines how molecular interactions generate organelle identities and determine cargo fate decisions. Current knowledge identifies marker proteins and checkpoints but lacks understanding of maturation trajectories and causal links to organelle dysfunction. This project models how molecular perturbations rewire trafficking networks to provide a quantitative framework for linking regulators to phenotypes.

The study design employs a community scale synthesis of public data through coordinated curation and dynamic network modeling. Methods include hidden Markov models and multi view learning alongside causal discovery algorithms for standardized feature extraction pipelines. Results are validated through held out study prediction and replication of module composition across independent data sources.

The project utilizes datasets from the IDR and Cell Image Library and PRIDE and BioGRID and SIGNOR and GEO. These distinct datasets are integrated by building a unified metadata schema and using multi view learning to align state spaces. Data limitations regarding batch effects are mitigated through hierarchical models and study level covariates rather than aggressive normalization.

The project timeline spans twenty four months with initial phases focused on data harmonization and final phases on atlas release. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the project demands expertise in membrane biology and quantitative imaging and dynamical modeling.

The project releases an Endocytic Emergence Atlas and reproducible workflows and open source toolkits for public data analysis. The interdisciplinary team includes experts in membrane trafficking and network biology with specific provisions for training graduate students and postdocs.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses how molecular interactions generate dynamic endosomal identities and cargo routing decisions by resolving current fragmentation across disparate datasets. The study employs multi-view learning and state space modeling to integrate diverse imaging and proteomic data into a unified analytical framework. This project establishes a quantitative atlas that links molecular regulators to organelle maturation trajectories and provides a predictive model for trafficking.

title: Emergent Control of Cell Cycle Transitions: Integrating Single-Cell Time Series, Proteomics, and Perturbation Screens

original.abstract:
Cell cycle progression is governed by an emergent regulatory system where cyclin-CDK networks, checkpoints, and proteolysis create robust, irreversible transitions. Despite extensive study, open questions remain about how variability arises, how transitions differ across cell types, and which network features ensure irreversibility. Public single-cell time series, proteomics, and perturbation datasets provide an opportunity for a synthesis-driven advance.

This working group will integrate (i) single-cell RNA-seq datasets with cell cycle phase annotations across tissues and conditions (HCA, Tabula Sapiens, GEO), (ii) live-cell imaging time series of cell cycle reporters (IDR), (iii) quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics across cell cycle stages (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iv) ubiquitin-proteasome pathway datasets and degron perturbation time courses (GEO), and (v) CRISPR screens for cell cycle regulators (DepMap, published screens). We will harmonize phase labels using standardized markers and latent phase inference methods.

Scientific questions: (1) Which molecular features (phosphorylation waves, proteolysis timing, feedback loops) best explain emergent irreversibility of transitions (G1/S, G2/M)? (2) How do different cell types tune the same core network to yield distinct cycle lengths and checkpoint sensitivities? (3) Can we predict conditions that push the system toward critical slowing down or catastrophic arrest?

Analytical plan: We will construct integrated dynamical models combining single-cell trajectories (pseudotime/real time) with proteomic and phosphoproteomic dynamics. We will compare mechanistic models (bistable switches, coupled oscillators) using Bayesian model selection informed by multi-omic constraints. Perturbation screen results will provide causal anchors to identify key control nodes and to validate predicted sensitivities.

NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis requires coordinated expertise across cell cycle biology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical systems modeling, as well as substantial infrastructure for harmonizing large datasets. The working group will establish community standards for cell cycle metadata and for integrating time-resolved omics.

Deliverables will include an open Cell Cycle Emergence Resource with harmonized datasets, inferred dynamic parameters, and comparative models across cell types; reproducible pipelines for phase inference and time alignment; and a catalog of predicted regulators governing variability and irreversibility. Training will include workshops on dynamical modeling, single-cell trajectory analysis, and reproducible workflows, with trainees leading dataset curation and benchmark construction. The synthesis will deepen understanding of how robust cell cycle control emerges from molecular interactions.
original.background_and_significance:
Irreversible transitions are a defining feature of the eukaryotic cell cycle. Cells do not merely “pass through” G1/S and G2/M; they commit to DNA replication and mitosis through regulatory architectures that convert graded molecular inputs into switch-like outcomes. This commitment emerges from network interactions among cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), checkpoint pathways, transcriptional programs, and targeted proteolysis. Classic work established that positive feedback, multisite phosphorylation, and ubiquitin-mediated degradation can generate bistability and hysteresis, explaining how a cell can enforce directionality even as individual molecular interactions are reversible. Yet, despite decades of mechanistic studies, key puzzles remain about emergence in real cells and across biological contexts.

First, cell-to-cell variability is ubiquitous. Even in clonal populations, cycle length, checkpoint stringency, and the timing of commitment can vary widely. Some variability reflects extrinsic factors (nutrients, growth signals, stress), but a substantial component is intrinsic, arising from stochastic gene expression, protein turnover, and fluctuating signaling states. A central unresolved question is which molecular features best predict whether variability remains “safe” (buffered by feedback) or becomes destabilizing (leading to arrest, replication stress, or catastrophic mitotic failure). Understanding how robustness emerges from noisy components is a core mesoscale problem: the relevant control variables are not single molecules but coordinated waves of phosphorylation, proteolysis, and transcription that propagate through protein complexes, subcellular compartments, and checkpoints.

Second, cell cycle control is context-dependent. Different cell types and tissues can use the same conserved core (Cyclins, CDKs, APC/C, SCF, p53, RB/E2F) yet display distinct cycle lengths, distinct sensitivity to DNA damage, and distinct coupling between growth and division. Proliferating immune cells, epithelial progenitors, and cancer cell lines can all traverse the same nominal phases while relying on different regulatory “knobs”: alternative cyclin usage, rewired checkpoint thresholds, or altered proteasome capacity. The field lacks a synthesis-level understanding of which parameters are tuned across contexts and which are constrained, and how such tuning preserves irreversibility.

Third, emergent transitions can fail. Many therapies (e.g., CDK4/6 inhibitors, antimitotics) and stresses (DNA damage, replication stress, proteotoxic stress) push the system toward slowing, arrest, or aberrant cycling. Theoretical work predicts early-warning signals near critical transitions (e.g., critical slowing down, increased variance and autocorrelation), but these ideas have rarely been tested systematically with rich, time-resolved molecular data.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to address these gaps through community-scale synthesis. Massive public datasets now exist: single-cell RNA-seq atlases with cell cycle annotations; live-cell imaging of fluorescent reporters capturing real-time trajectories; proteomics and phosphoproteomics across synchronized stages; ubiquitin-proteasome perturbation time courses; and genome-scale CRISPR screens identifying regulators and context-specific dependencies. No single laboratory can harmonize these heterogeneous data types, align them in time, and evaluate competing dynamical models across many cell types. A working group that integrates molecular and cellular datasets with dynamical systems theory will reveal general principles of emergent irreversibility, quantify how tuning occurs across contexts, and establish reusable standards and pipelines that enable future synthesis in mesoscale cell biology.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will pursue three tightly linked research questions about emergent control of cell cycle transitions, focusing on G1/S and G2/M as canonical irreversible commitments.

RQ1: What molecular features best explain emergent irreversibility at G1/S and G2/M across contexts?
Hypothesis 1A: Irreversibility is most strongly predicted by the temporal ordering and steepness of phosphorylation “waves” coupled to proteolysis of key inhibitors, rather than by transcript-level changes alone. Specifically, coordinated multisite phosphorylation of RB/E2F and APC/C substrates, combined with timed degradation of CKIs and mitotic exit regulators, generates hysteresis detectable as direction-dependent molecular trajectories.
Hypothesis 1B: The minimal effective architecture differs between transitions: G1/S irreversibility depends more on transcriptional positive feedback (E2F network) plus CDK2 activation, whereas G2/M depends more on post-translational feedback (CDK1–Wee1/Cdc25 loops) and APC/C switching. Thus, multi-omic constraints will favor distinct mechanistic model classes for each transition.

RQ2: How do different cell types tune the same core network to yield distinct cycle lengths and checkpoint sensitivities?
Hypothesis 2A: Cross-cell-type differences in cycle length can be explained by a small set of tunable parameters—effective cyclin synthesis rates, phosphatase/kinase balance, and proteasome/APC/C capacity—while the topology of the core feedback loops remains conserved.
Hypothesis 2B: Checkpoint sensitivity (e.g., p53-mediated arrest propensity, DNA damage delay magnitude) emerges from how checkpoint signaling is coupled into the core switch. We predict that cell types differ primarily in coupling strength (gain) and basal stress levels, leading to predictable shifts in commitment thresholds and dwell times near transition boundaries.

RQ3: Can we predict conditions that push the system toward critical slowing down or catastrophic arrest, and identify early-warning signatures?
Hypothesis 3A: Approaching arrest states (senescence-like G1 arrest, prolonged G2, mitotic catastrophe) is preceded by quantifiable early-warning indicators in time-resolved trajectories: increased autocorrelation in reporter dynamics, increased variance in inferred phase velocity, and flattening of the potential landscape around the transition.
Hypothesis 3B: Perturbations that impair proteolysis (APC/C, SCF, proteasome) or phosphoregulation (Wee1/Cdc25 axis) disproportionately increase critical slowing down because they directly weaken the feedback that enforces directionality. Therefore, integrating degron/proteasome perturbation time courses with CRISPR dependency profiles will identify a conserved set of “irreversibility enforcers” whose disruption produces predictable dynamical signatures.

Across all questions, we will test an overarching synthesis hypothesis: emergent cell cycle control is best described as a low-dimensional dynamical system embedded in high-dimensional molecular space. Multi-omic measurements provide complementary projections of this system (RNA abundance, protein abundance, phosphorylation state, degradation timing, and phenotypic timing), and reconciling these projections will reveal conserved dynamical motifs and context-specific parameter regimes. This framework yields falsifiable predictions: (i) which mechanistic model class best fits each transition, (ii) which parameters shift across cell types, and (iii) which perturbations move cells toward criticality and arrest.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. We will form a transdisciplinary team spanning cell cycle biology, single-cell genomics, quantitative imaging, proteomics/phosphoproteomics, ubiquitin biology, and dynamical systems/AI. The project will use only publicly available datasets and will produce reusable harmonized resources and benchmarked modeling pipelines.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. (1) scRNA-seq atlases with broad tissue/cell-type coverage and sufficient cycling cells (HCA, Tabula Sapiens, GEO studies), including datasets with experimental perturbations where available. (2) Live-cell imaging time series of cell cycle reporters (e.g., FUCCI, CDK activity sensors) from the Image Data Resource and linked publications, requiring single-cell tracks and metadata. (3) Quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics across cell cycle stages (CPTAC, PRIDE), prioritizing synchronized or fractionated studies with clear stage labels and replicate structure. (4) Ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and degron-based perturbation time courses (GEO/ArrayExpress, proteomics repositories), requiring time points spanning transitions. (5) CRISPR screens for regulators and dependencies (DepMap, published focused screens), including fitness and cell cycle–specific readouts when available.

Harmonization and phase alignment. We will standardize metadata (cell type ontology, perturbations, synchronization method, reporter type, batch variables) and create a “cell cycle phase label” schema with confidence scores. For scRNA-seq, we will harmonize phase assignments using a consensus of marker-based scoring, latent cyclic manifold inference, and RNA velocity-informed directionality where available. For imaging, we will map reporter signals to a common phase coordinate and extract transition times and phase velocities.
