For proteomics/phosphoproteomics, we will align stage-labeled samples onto the same phase coordinate using shared marker proteins/phosphosites (e.g., Cyclin B1, phospho-H3) and optimal transport/time-warping methods.

Integrated dynamical modeling. We will build multi-view dynamical models that connect: (i) latent phase coordinate and velocity, (ii) key molecular modules (CDK activity proxies, APC/C activity proxies, checkpoint signaling proxies), and (iii) observed omic features. Two complementary model families will be compared:
1) Mechanistic coarse-grained ODE/SDE models capturing bistable switches and coupled oscillators (e.g., CDK–Wee1/Cdc25, RB/E2F, APC/C). Parameters will be fit with Bayesian inference using multi-omic constraints (protein/phosphosite dynamics, reporter trajectories) and priors informed by literature.
2) Data-driven state-space and neural ODE models that learn low-dimensional dynamics from time series (imaging) and pseudotime-ordered scRNA-seq, with interpretability layers linking latent dimensions to molecular modules.
Model comparison and selection will use Bayesian model evidence, posterior predictive checks, and out-of-sample validation across datasets and cell types.

Causal anchoring with perturbation screens. CRISPR dependencies and targeted perturbation time courses will be used to (i) constrain network structure (which nodes matter in which contexts), (ii) test predicted control points (sensitivity of transition timing to node perturbation), and (iii) identify context-specific parameter shifts. We will integrate screen results via hierarchical models that map gene perturbations onto changes in latent dynamical parameters (e.g., effective degradation rates, feedback gains).

Early-warning and criticality analysis. Using real-time imaging trajectories and inferred phase velocities from scRNA-seq, we will quantify early-warning indicators (variance, autocorrelation, return rates) near transition boundaries and under perturbations. We will link these indicators to mechanistic parameters (feedback strength, degradation capacity) to predict which perturbations induce slowing versus irreversible arrest.

Feasibility and milestones. Year-1 milestones: curated dataset registry, metadata schema, baseline phase harmonization pipeline, and initial cross-modal alignment on 2–3 benchmark cell types. Year-2 milestones: model comparison for G1/S and G2/M, cross-cell-type parameter maps, and early-warning signature catalog. Continuous integration and code review will ensure robustness and reproducibility.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, cross-context explanation of irreversibility at G1/S and G2/M, identifying which combinations of phosphorylation dynamics, proteolysis timing, and feedback strengths are necessary and sufficient to reproduce observed commitment behavior. This will directly address a long-standing puzzle: how robust directionality emerges from noisy molecular components. (2) A principled map of how cell types tune conserved cell cycle circuitry. By estimating a small set of interpretable dynamical parameters across tissues and cell lines, we will distinguish conserved “hard constraints” from flexible “tunable knobs” that alter cycle length and checkpoint sensitivity. (3) Predictive signatures of proximity to arrest and critical slowing down. We will deliver a validated set of early-warning indicators and perturbation classes that reliably shift the system toward slowing, arrest, or catastrophic failure.

Community-scale resources. We will produce an open Cell Cycle Emergence Resource (CCER): harmonized scRNA-seq phase labels with confidence scores, aligned proteome/phosphoproteome trajectories, curated imaging-derived transition statistics, and integrated perturbation/screen annotations. CCER will include benchmark tasks (phase inference, transition-time prediction, model selection) and reference implementations.

Methodological impact. The project will provide generalizable pipelines for cross-modal time alignment (real time and pseudotime), multi-view dynamical modeling, and causal anchoring with screens—methods broadly applicable to other emergent mesoscale phenomena (stress responses, differentiation switches, organelle biogenesis).

Broader impacts and training. By centering trainees in data curation, benchmarking, and reproducible modeling, the working group will train a cohort of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists. The outputs will accelerate hypothesis generation for experimentalists and inform therapeutic strategies targeting cell cycle vulnerabilities by clarifying which control nodes enforce irreversibility and which produce fragile dynamics when perturbed. The synthesis will also reduce duplication of effort across the community by establishing shared metadata standards and validated analysis workflows.
original.budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. The proposed synthesis exceeds the capacity of a single lab because it requires (i) coordinated curation and harmonization across multiple data modalities and repositories, (ii) substantial compute for repeated model fitting and benchmarking, and (iii) structured, in-person collaboration to converge on shared standards and interoperable pipelines. NCEMS resources (meeting support, coordination, cyberinfrastructure guidance, and community-building) are essential to achieve community-scale integration rather than a one-off analysis.

Budget categories (illustrative, aligned to working group needs). 1) Working group meetings and collaboration: support for 2–3 multi-day meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venues) plus virtual sprints, including travel and lodging for geographically distributed participants, with priority for trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions. 2) Personnel support: partial support for a project coordinator/data steward to manage dataset registry, metadata schema, and release cycles; and limited trainee support (graduate/postdoc) for curation, benchmarking, and tutorial development consistent with NCEMS mechanisms. 3) Computing and storage: cloud/HPC credits for large-scale reprocessing (e.g., scRNA-seq reannotation, imaging feature extraction, Bayesian inference), storage for intermediate harmonized artifacts, and backup/archival costs. 4) Training and outreach: workshop logistics, captioning/recording, and development of open educational materials.

Resource plan and roles. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise and in-kind effort: (i) cell cycle biology and checkpoint interpretation, (ii) imaging analysis and time-series feature extraction, (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics processing and site-level mapping, (iv) ubiquitin/proteolysis biology, (v) dynamical systems and Bayesian inference, and (vi) AI/representation learning for multi-view dynamics. Trainees will lead curated dataset “packs” and benchmark tasks under mentorship.

Timeline and deliverable-linked spending. Year 1 spending emphasizes coordination, curation, and initial pipeline development; Year 2 emphasizes compute-intensive modeling, benchmarking, and dissemination/training. All expenditures will be tied to concrete releases of the Cell Cycle Emergence Resource, reproducible workflows, and training outputs. This budget structure ensures feasibility, accountability, and maximal community benefit while adhering to the requirement to use only existing publicly available data.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Cell cycle biology investigates the regulatory mechanisms governing G1/S and G2/M transitions to address gaps in transition robustness. Core regulatory networks are well characterized but the mechanisms underlying cell to cell variability and catastrophic arrest remain incomplete. This project identifies molecular features enforcing transition irreversibility to reveal general principles of biological robustness and therapeutic vulnerabilities.

The study uses integrated dynamical modeling and Bayesian model selection to compare mechanistic and data driven models across cells. Key methods include single cell trajectory analysis and latent phase inference alongside neural ODEs and early warning indicator analysis. Results are validated through posterior predictive checks and out of sample validation alongside CRISPR perturbation screens as causal anchors.

The project utilizes datasets from HCA and Tabula Sapiens and GEO and Image Data Resource and CPTAC and DepMap. Datasets are harmonized using standardized metadata schemas and consensus phase labeling and time warping to map onto coordinates. Heterogeneity in data types is addressed through standardized metadata and confidence scoring and robust cross modal alignment pipelines.

Year one focuses on dataset curation and metadata standardization while year two focuses on model comparison and resource dissemination. Multi lab expertise is required to harmonize diverse data modalities and to integrate domain specific knowledge with dynamical systems.

The project produces an open Cell Cycle Emergence Resource containing harmonized datasets and reproducible analysis pipelines and regulator catalogs. The transdisciplinary team includes experts in biology and imaging and proteomics and dynamical systems with trainees leading benchmarking tasks.
rephrased.main_idea: This research investigates how robust and irreversible cell cycle transitions emerge from noisy molecular components to address current gaps in understanding. The study employs multi-view dynamical modeling and Bayesian inference to integrate heterogeneous datasets into a unified framework for analyzing transition dynamics. This project establishes a comprehensive resource that identifies novel regulatory principles and therapeutic vulnerabilities governing the stability of cell cycle progression.

title: A Synthesis of Nuclear Body Emergence: Integrating Proteomics, RNA Localization, and Imaging of Speckles, Nucleoli, and PML Bodies

original.abstract:
Nuclear bodies (nucleoli, speckles, PML bodies, Cajal bodies) are mesoscale assemblies with emergent behaviors such as selective sequestration, reaction acceleration, and dynamic remodeling. While many components are known, we lack a unified synthesis linking composition, RNA content, and physical properties to nuclear functions across cell types and stresses.

This working group will integrate (i) proximity labeling and fractionation proteomics of nuclear bodies (PRIDE), (ii) RNA localization and interactome datasets (ENCODE eCLIP, RNA interactome capture studies), (iii) imaging datasets with nuclear body markers across tissues and perturbations (Human Protein Atlas, IDR), (iv) transcriptomic responses to stresses that remodel nuclear bodies (GEO), and (v) sequence/structure features of nuclear body proteins (disorder, low complexity, RNA-binding domains; AlphaFold and annotations). We will curate nuclear body types, experimental assays, and perturbation contexts.

Scientific questions: (1) What compositional “core” is conserved for each nuclear body type, and what peripheral components are condition-specific? (2) How do RNA species contribute to assembly and emergent function—are there common RNA features that promote nuclear body localization? (3) Can we relate nuclear body remodeling to changes in splicing, ribosome biogenesis, DNA repair, or antiviral responses?

Analytical approach: We will build a nuclear body knowledge graph combining protein–protein and protein–RNA interactions with imaging-derived co-localization and abundance features. Community detection will identify modules and condition-specific recruitment. We will develop predictive models for nuclear body targeting from sequence features and interaction context, and link remodeling signatures to functional outputs using transcriptomic and splicing analyses.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans proteomics, RNA biology, imaging, and computational graph modeling, and demands coordinated curation across many studies. The working group will establish shared ontologies and data standards for nuclear body annotation.

Deliverables will include an open Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas with curated components, RNA associations, and remodeling signatures; reproducible workflows for integrating proteomics, eCLIP, and imaging; and benchmarks for predicting nuclear body localization. Training will include trainee-led curation sprints, tutorials on interaction network integration, and reproducible splicing analysis pipelines. The synthesis will reveal general principles by which mesoscale nuclear assemblies emerge and regulate genome function.
original.background_and_significance:
Nuclear bodies are mesoscale, membrane-less assemblies that concentrate specific proteins and RNAs into dynamic microenvironments. Prominent examples include nucleoli (ribosome biogenesis), nuclear speckles (splicing factor organization and RNA processing), promyelocytic leukemia (PML) bodies (DNA damage response, antiviral defense, SUMO-dependent regulation), and Cajal bodies (snRNP and telomerase RNP biogenesis). These structures exhibit emergent behaviors: selective sequestration and release, catalytic acceleration through local concentration, buffering of molecular noise, and rapid remodeling in response to stress, differentiation, and infection. Despite extensive molecular characterization, the field lacks an integrative, cross-assay synthesis that connects (i) composition, (ii) RNA content and RNA-binding interactions, (iii) spatial organization and abundance across cell types, and (iv) functional outputs at the transcriptome level.

A major barrier is that evidence is fragmented across modalities. Proteomic studies (e.g., proximity labeling, fractionation, immunoprecipitation) provide lists of candidate components but differ in bait selection, labeling radius, and background controls, complicating cross-study comparisons. RNA localization and protein–RNA interaction maps (e.g., ENCODE eCLIP; RNA interactome capture) reveal RNA-binding proteins and their targets, yet are rarely integrated with nuclear body residency. Imaging resources (Human Protein Atlas immunofluorescence; Image Data Resource datasets) capture localization patterns and co-localization with markers, but these are typically analyzed qualitatively, with limited harmonized metadata across tissues and perturbations. Finally, transcriptomic datasets documenting stress responses (GEO bulk RNA-seq; public splicing datasets) often measure downstream consequences without a mechanistic bridge to nuclear body remodeling.

NCEMS’s focus on emergence at the mesoscale makes nuclear bodies an ideal target: they represent canonical mesoscale condensates where macromolecular interactions give rise to collective properties not predictable from individual molecules. The availability of vast public datasets across proteomics, imaging, RNA binding, and transcriptomics creates a timely opportunity for synthesis research that can reveal general principles of assembly and function. However, such synthesis is beyond the scope of single laboratories because it requires coordinated curation across many studies, harmonization of ontologies and metadata, and integration of heterogeneous data types into unified analytical frameworks.

This working group addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do nuclear bodies form with distinct compositions and functions, yet share common physical principles such as multivalency, intrinsic disorder, and RNA-mediated interactions? By building an integrated Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas and a knowledge graph that links components, RNAs, spatial phenotypes, and functional readouts, we will enable hypothesis generation and testing at community scale. The proposal aligns with NCEMS priorities by leveraging only publicly available data, developing innovative integrative methods (knowledge graphs, module discovery, predictive targeting models), assembling a multidisciplinary team spanning proteomics, RNA biology, imaging analysis, and network/AI modeling, and training data-savvy trainees through open, reproducible workflows. The resulting synthesis will provide a durable community resource and a conceptual framework for emergent nuclear organization across conditions, cell types, and stresses.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will pursue three tightly linked scientific questions aimed at explaining how mesoscale nuclear bodies emerge from molecular interactions and how their remodeling produces cellular-level outcomes. Across questions, we will explicitly separate “core” components (robust across assays and contexts) from “peripheral” components (context- and perturbation-dependent), and we will quantify uncertainty due to assay-specific biases.

Question 1: What compositional cores define each nuclear body type, and how does peripheral recruitment vary across cell types and perturbations?
Hypothesis 1A (core–periphery principle): Each nuclear body has a conserved core module detectable across orthogonal proteomic assays and imaging co-localization, enriched for multivalent interaction features (intrinsic disorder, low-complexity regions, SUMO/SIM motifs for PML bodies, RNA-binding domains for speckles/Cajal bodies).
Hypothesis 1B (contextual recruitment): Peripheral components are recruited in a condition-specific manner and cluster into functional submodules (e.g., DNA repair proteins to PML bodies under genotoxic stress; antiviral factors under interferon stimulation; ribosome biogenesis factors to nucleoli under growth signaling).
Predictions: Cross-study meta-analysis will yield high-confidence cores with stable membership; peripheral modules will correlate with perturbation classes and with marker intensity/number changes in imaging.

Question 2: How do RNA species contribute to nuclear body assembly and emergent function, and are there shared RNA features that promote localization?
Hypothesis 2A (RNA scaffolding/targeting rules): Nuclear body–associated RNAs share sequence/structure features that promote residency, such as repetitive elements, specific k-mer enrichments, higher propensity for secondary structure, longer length, and binding by sets of core RNA-binding proteins.
Hypothesis 2B (RNP grammar): Distinct nuclear bodies correspond to distinct “RNP grammars,” i.e., characteristic combinations of RNA motifs and protein domain architectures (RRMs, KH domains, RGG boxes) that jointly predict localization.
Predictions: Integrating eCLIP targets with proteomic cores will identify RNA classes enriched for binding by core proteins; machine-learning models using RNA features and interaction context will predict nuclear body association better than expression alone.

Question 3: Can nuclear body remodeling be quantitatively linked to downstream functional outputs such as splicing changes, ribosome biogenesis, DNA repair programs, and antiviral responses?
Hypothesis 3A (remodeling-to-function coupling): Changes in nuclear body composition and abundance (from proteomics and imaging) are coupled to coherent transcriptomic programs measurable in public RNA-seq/splicing datasets.
Hypothesis 3B (module-specific signatures): Specific compositional modules map to specific functional outputs: speckle remodeling predicts alternative splicing and intron retention patterns; nucleolar remodeling predicts rRNA processing and translation-related gene expression; PML body remodeling predicts interferon-stimulated gene induction and DNA damage response signatures.
Predictions: Joint modeling will identify remodeling signatures that explain variance in transcriptomic outcomes across perturbations beyond what is explained by global stress markers.

Collectively, these hypotheses operationalize emergence: mesoscale assemblies arise from conserved interaction cores plus adaptive peripheral recruitment, with RNA acting as both scaffold and informational substrate, yielding system-level functional consequences. Testing these hypotheses requires synthesis across modalities and thus directly motivates an NCEMS working group.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and design principles. We will conduct a community-scale synthesis using only publicly available data, integrating proteomics, protein–RNA interactions, imaging, and transcriptomics into a unified, queryable Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas and knowledge graph. The approach is organized into four work packages (WPs) with iterative feedback among curation, integration, modeling, and validation.

WP1: Data acquisition, curation, and harmonization. We will systematically identify datasets for nucleoli, speckles, PML bodies, and Cajal bodies from PRIDE (proximity labeling, fractionation, AP-MS), ENCODE eCLIP (protein–RNA binding), RNA interactome capture studies, Human Protein Atlas (IF images and annotations), Image Data Resource (high-content microscopy), and GEO (bulk RNA-seq; perturbations known to remodel nuclear bodies such as heat shock, oxidative stress, DNA damage, interferon, transcriptional inhibition). We will create a controlled vocabulary/ontology for: nuclear body type, marker proteins, assay type, cell line/tissue, perturbation, timepoint, and evidence strength. Mapping will use stable identifiers (UniProt, Ensembl, HGNC) with explicit versioning.

WP2: Evidence integration and meta-analysis for core/periphery. For proteomics, we will reprocess or standardize reported enrichment statistics where possible (e.g., log2 fold-change vs controls, FDR), and otherwise convert to comparable effect sizes using rank-based methods. We will perform random-effects meta-analysis across studies per nuclear body type to estimate membership probability and uncertainty. Imaging-derived evidence will be quantified using available annotations and, where raw images exist, standardized pipelines to compute co-localization with canonical markers, puncta counts, and nuclear intensity distributions. Evidence from multiple modalities will be combined using Bayesian data fusion to yield posterior probabilities for component membership.

WP3: Knowledge graph construction and module discovery. We will build a nuclear body knowledge graph with nodes for proteins, RNAs, perturbations, cell types, assays, and phenotypes; edges will encode protein–protein interactions (e.g., BioGRID/IntAct), protein–RNA edges (eCLIP peaks aggregated to gene-level targets, interactome capture associations), co-localization edges (imaging), and co-enrichment edges (proteomics). We will apply community detection (Leiden/Louvain; multilayer networks by condition) and graph representation learning (node embeddings) to identify conserved cores and condition-specific modules. We will quantify robustness via bootstrapping across studies and sensitivity analyses for assay bias.

WP4: Predictive models and functional coupling. (i) Targeting prediction: supervised models (regularized logistic regression, gradient boosting, and graph neural network baselines) will predict nuclear body association using sequence/structure features (intrinsic disorder predictions, low complexity, domain annotations, prion-like scores, SUMO/SIM motifs, AlphaFold-derived confidence/compactness proxies) plus interaction context features (network centrality, module membership). (ii) RNA feature models: models will predict RNA association using length, k-mer/motif enrichments, repeat content, predicted structure, and binding by core RBPs. (iii) Remodeling-to-function: we will link perturbation-specific remodeling signatures (module activity scores from proteomics/imaging) to transcriptomic outcomes (differential expression; splicing changes via standardized pipelines such as rMATS/MAJIQ where compatible). Multivariate models and causal-inference-inspired sensitivity checks (e.g., controlling for global stress response signatures) will test coupling hypotheses.

Feasibility and coordination. The NCEMS working group structure will include focused sprints for ontology development, curation jamborees, and modeling hackathons. All analyses will be implemented as reproducible workflows (Nextflow/Snakemake) and packaged for reuse. No new experimental data will be generated; all results will derive from integrated public datasets and transparent reanalysis.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary deliverable: the Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas. This open resource will provide (i) curated component lists for nucleoli, speckles, PML bodies, and Cajal bodies with quantitative membership confidence, (ii) condition- and cell-type–specific peripheral recruitment modules, (iii) RNA associations and inferred RNA feature rules, and (iv) remodeling signatures linked to downstream functional programs.

Scientific outcomes. First, we expect to identify high-confidence “core” modules for each nuclear body that are reproducible across proteomic assays and supported by imaging co-localization, resolving inconsistencies among published component lists. Second, we anticipate discovering shared organizational principles across nuclear bodies—e.g., a common architecture of scaffold-like proteins enriched for disorder and multivalency coupled to specialized effector modules—while also defining what is unique to each body (SUMO-centric regulation in PML bodies; rRNA processing machinery in nucleoli; spliceosomal factor reservoirs in speckles). Third, we expect to uncover RNA-centric principles of localization, including RNA classes and sequence/structure features that consistently associate with specific nuclear bodies and the RBP “grammars” that mediate these associations.

Methodological impact. The knowledge-graph framework and probabilistic evidence-fusion strategy will generalize to other mesoscale assemblies (stress granules, centrosomes, synaptic densities), advancing NCEMS’s mission to develop innovative synthesis and analytical strategies for emergent phenomena. Benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for nuclear body targeting prediction will enable fair comparison of future methods.

Community and workforce impact. By engaging multiple labs and trainees in curation, integration, and modeling, the project will broaden participation in data-centric molecular/cellular biology and create reusable training materials. The Atlas will accelerate hypothesis generation for mechanistic studies (outside this project) by highlighting candidate components, RNAs, and perturbations most predictive of functional outcomes, thereby reducing redundancy and guiding more targeted experimentation across the field.
original.budget_and_resources:
This proposal is designed as an NCEMS Working Group that requires coordinated, in-person and virtual collaboration, shared cyberinfrastructure, and dedicated support for cross-domain curation and synthesis beyond a single lab’s capacity.

Requested NCEMS support (cost categories). (1) Working meetings: support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) over 12–18 months, enabling intensive integration sprints across proteomics, RNA, imaging, and modeling. Funds cover travel, lodging, and per diem for a geographically distributed team, with priority for trainees and participants from resource-limited institutions. (2) Personnel support: partial support for a project manager/data curator (coordination, ontology governance, data harmonization), and trainee stipends/salary support (graduate students/postdocs) for curation, pipeline development, and documentation. (3) Computing and storage: NCEMS-managed compute allocations for reprocessing large public datasets (imaging feature extraction; transcriptomic/splicing reanalysis) and persistent storage for intermediate artifacts, containers, and Atlas builds. (4) Dissemination: costs for maintaining the Atlas web presence, DOI-minted releases, and accessibility-compliant training materials.

In-kind contributions. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise and existing open-source code where available (e.g., imaging segmentation notebooks, network analysis utilities), plus mentorship of trainees. Institutions will provide baseline computing and software access for local development.

Resource justification and alignment with NCEMS. The project’s central bottleneck is not data generation but cross-modal synthesis: harmonizing metadata across dozens of studies, building a robust evidence-fusion framework, and maintaining reproducible pipelines and a community resource. NCEMS provides the convening power, neutral coordination, and infrastructure needed to (i) establish shared standards, (ii) run collaborative sprints, (iii) ensure open and reproducible outputs, and (iv) train a cross-disciplinary cohort. These needs exceed what an individual lab or existing bilateral collaboration can realistically sustain.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Cell biology investigates mesoscale nuclear bodies to address the lack of synthesis regarding their composition and cellular function. Current knowledge identifies molecular components but remains fragmented across diverse assays with inconsistent metadata and significant study biases. This project builds a Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas to link nuclear body remodeling to functional outcomes and genome regulation.

The study design employs a community scale synthesis of public data organized into four distinct work packages. Key methods include proximity labeling proteomics and RNA interactome capture alongside Bayesian data fusion and graph neural networks. Results are validated through benchmarking of predictive models for nuclear body targeting and sensitivity analyses via bootstrapping.

The project utilizes datasets from PRIDE and ENCODE eCLIP plus the Human Protein Atlas and GEO databases. These distinct datasets are integrated into a knowledge graph linking proteins and RNAs using standardized ontologies and identifiers. Known data limitations regarding assay bias are mitigated through rank based effect size standardization and Bayesian data fusion.

The project follows an eighteen month timeline covering data curation and the release of the Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to harmonize heterogeneous data types across proteomics and imaging and computational modeling.

All findings and reproducible workflows and training materials will be made publicly available to the scientific community. The team includes experts in proteomics and RNA biology and AI modeling with training opportunities for junior researchers.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the lack of a unified synthesis connecting nuclear body composition and physical properties to cellular functional outcomes. The study employs Bayesian data fusion and multilayer network analysis to integrate fragmented proteomics, transcriptomics, and imaging data into one framework. This project creates a comprehensive knowledge graph that defines conserved core components and predicts how nuclear body remodeling regulates genomes.

title: Emergent Antibiotic Tolerance Mechanisms: Synthesizing Bacterial Single-Cell Physiology, Transcriptomics, and Metabolic Models

original.abstract:
Antibiotic tolerance and persistence are emergent bacterial phenotypes where subpopulations survive lethal drugs without genetic resistance, often via metabolic slowdown, stress responses, and heterogeneous expression. Public datasets include single-cell time-lapse microscopy, transcriptomics under antibiotic stress, and genome-scale metabolic models, yet they remain disconnected. This working group will synthesize these data to uncover general principles of tolerance emergence across species and antibiotics.

We will integrate (i) single-cell imaging datasets tracking growth and survival under antibiotics (public microscopy repositories and supplemental datasets), (ii) bulk and single-cell bacterial transcriptomics under drug exposure (GEO), (iii) proteomics and metabolomics under antibiotic stress (PRIDE, Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) curated regulatory networks and stress response pathways (RegulonDB for E. coli, organism-specific resources), and (v) genome-scale metabolic models (BiGG) and flux data where available. We will standardize antibiotic classes, dosing regimens, growth media, and time points.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved tolerance states characterized by coupled metabolic and regulatory signatures. (2) Determine whether tolerance arises via common dynamical motifs (bet-hedging, bistability, toxin–antitoxin modules) across species. (3) Link emergent single-cell survival distributions to underlying network states and metabolic constraints.

Analytical approach: We will combine stochastic dynamical modeling with data-driven state inference. Single-cell trajectories will be analyzed to infer phenotypic state transitions (growth arrest, recovery) and their rates. Transcriptomics/proteomics will define molecular correlates of these states. Constraint-based metabolic modeling will test whether inferred states correspond to distinct feasible flux regimes, and to predict metabolic interventions that collapse tolerance.

NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis requires coordinated expertise in microbiology, single-cell imaging analysis, systems biology, and stochastic modeling, plus extensive curation of heterogeneous experimental conditions. The working group will create shared standards for reporting tolerance imaging experiments and for mapping them to omics data.

Deliverables will include an open Antibiotic Tolerance Synthesis Atlas with harmonized single-cell and omics datasets, inferred tolerance states, and model-based predictions; reproducible pipelines for analyzing survival time series; and benchmarks for tolerance state classification. Training will include workshops on single-cell bacterial image analysis, metabolic modeling, and open science practices. This synthesis will advance fundamental understanding of how emergent phenotypes arise from molecular networks and may inform strategies to mitigate tolerance using existing data.
original.background_and_significance:
Antibiotic tolerance and persistence are central, unresolved problems in molecular and cellular microbiology. Unlike genetic resistance, tolerance enables bacteria to survive transient antibiotic exposure without heritable increases in MIC, often leading to relapse and providing time for resistance evolution. Tolerance is an emergent phenotype: population-level survival arises from heterogeneous single-cell physiological states shaped by regulatory networks, metabolic constraints, and environmental history. Despite decades of work, the field lacks cross-species, cross-antibiotic principles that explain why survival distributions differ so dramatically among conditions, and which molecular programs reliably produce tolerant states.

Publicly available data relevant to tolerance have expanded rapidly, but remain siloed. First, single-cell time-lapse microscopy and microfluidic “mother machine” studies quantify growth, division, lysis, and recovery under antibiotic exposure with minute-scale resolution, revealing heavy-tailed killing curves and rare persister trajectories. Second, bulk and single-cell transcriptomics datasets capture antibiotic-induced stress responses (e.g., SOS, stringent response, oxidative stress, envelope stress) and shifts in central carbon metabolism, respiration, and translation. Third, proteomics and metabolomics datasets report changes in energy charge, redox state, amino acid pools, and membrane composition under drug stress. Fourth, curated regulatory networks (e.g., RegulonDB and organism-specific resources) and toxin–antitoxin annotations provide mechanistic scaffolds for interpreting expression changes. Fifth, genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) and flux constraints (BiGG and related resources) encode feasible metabolic states and enable hypothesis-driven mapping from omics to physiology.

However, the field lacks a synthesis framework that connects these modalities. Imaging studies often provide exquisite phenotypes but limited molecular readouts; omics studies provide molecular snapshots but rarely link to single-cell survival dynamics; metabolic models are frequently analyzed in isolation from regulatory heterogeneity and antibiotic pharmacodynamics. The result is a fragmented understanding in which proposed mechanisms (e.g., metabolic slowdown, ATP depletion, dormancy, efflux activation, toxin–antitoxin bistability) are supported in specific organisms or drugs but not reconciled into generalizable dynamical motifs.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that targets emergence at the mesoscale: the interface between molecular networks and cellular phenotypes such as growth arrest, recovery competence, and survival time distributions. Tolerance is an ideal NCEMS problem because (i) it is fundamentally about emergent properties of heterogeneous cell populations, (ii) relevant data span molecular to phenotypic scales and are abundant in public repositories, and (iii) progress requires coordinated expertise in microbiology, single-cell image analysis, systems biology, stochastic processes, and metabolic modeling—beyond the capacity of a single laboratory.

This working group will build an integrated, open Antibiotic Tolerance Synthesis Atlas that harmonizes experimental metadata (antibiotic class, dosing regimen, medium, growth phase, temperature, device type, exposure duration) and aligns time-resolved single-cell phenotypes with matched or comparable omics and model contexts. By developing shared standards and reproducible pipelines, we will enable rigorous cross-study comparisons, identify conserved tolerance states, and test whether common network motifs and metabolic constraints generate the observed survival heterogeneity. The resulting synthesis will advance fundamental understanding of how molecular and regulatory programs give rise to emergent survival and will provide a durable community resource for hypothesis generation and method development using only existing public data.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project addresses the overarching question: what general, mechanistic principles explain the emergence of antibiotic tolerance across bacterial species, antibiotic classes, and environments when viewed through integrated single-cell physiology, omics, regulatory networks, and metabolic constraints? We focus on three interlocking sets of questions and falsifiable hypotheses.

RQ1: Are there conserved “tolerance states” that recur across species and antibiotics, and can they be defined by coupled physiological and molecular signatures? Many studies describe persisters as dormant, slow-growing, or stress-activated, but these labels vary by assay. We will test the hypothesis that tolerance is not a single state but a small number of recurring, low-dimensional states characterized by (H1a) reduced biosynthetic flux (translation/replication), (H1b) reprogrammed energy/redox metabolism (ATP maintenance, respiration/fermentation balance), and (H1c) activation of specific stress regulons (e.g., stringent response, SOS, envelope stress) with consistent co-variation patterns. A key prediction is that, after harmonizing metadata, these states will be identifiable via unsupervised integration of single-cell growth trajectories and omics-derived pathway activities, and will generalize across datasets.

RQ2: Do common dynamical motifs generate tolerance across taxa, or are mechanisms idiosyncratic? Competing theories propose bet-hedging (stochastic switching), bistability driven by feedback loops, or discrete modules such as toxin–antitoxin systems. We will test the hypothesis that a limited set of dynamical motifs can explain observed survival distributions across conditions. Specifically, (H2a) heavy-tailed killing curves arise from a mixture of latent phenotypic states with distinct hazard rates; (H2b) transitions into and out of tolerant states follow motif-specific kinetics (e.g., stress-triggered entry vs constitutive switching); and (H2c) regulatory network architectures enriched for positive feedback and slow variables (e.g., ppGpp, ATP, membrane potential) are overrepresented among genes/pathways whose activity correlates with inferred state transitions.

RQ3: How do metabolic constraints and feasible flux regimes shape emergent survival distributions, and can we infer metabolic “choke points” that collapse tolerance across contexts? Antibiotic lethality often depends on growth rate, energy metabolism, and target engagement. We will test the hypothesis that tolerant states correspond to distinct feasible regions of the metabolic solution space rather than simply “lower flux everywhere.” (H3a) Inferred tolerant states map to GEM-predicted flux regimes with increased maintenance-to-growth ratio and altered cofactor balancing; (H3b) cross-condition commonalities exist at the level of flux couplings (e.g., respiration–ROS management, NADH reoxidation, acetate overflow) even when transcript signatures differ; and (H3c) interventions predicted to reduce the size or stability of tolerant flux regimes (e.g., constraining specific ATP-generating routes or redox shunts) will be consistent across multiple organisms/antibiotics in silico.

Cross-cutting methodological questions guide hypothesis testing: (RQ4) can we robustly align time-resolved single-cell phenotypes with time-matched or comparable omics snapshots across heterogeneous experiments? (RQ5) what minimal metadata and reporting standards are required to make tolerance datasets interoperable? We hypothesize (H4) that explicit encoding of antibiotic exposure profiles, growth medium composition, and pre-exposure growth state is sufficient to explain a large fraction of between-study variability and to enable transferable state classifiers.

Together, these questions move beyond cataloging mechanisms toward identifying conserved emergent principles linking molecular networks, metabolic constraints, and single-cell survival dynamics.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. The working group will execute a synthesis-only, multi-lab workflow spanning data acquisition/curation, harmonization, integrative modeling, and validation-by-reanalysis. Participants will include experts in bacterial physiology and antibiotic action, single-cell image analysis, transcriptomics/proteomics/metabolomics, regulatory network biology, constraint-based modeling, and stochastic dynamical systems. All analyses will use publicly available data; no new experiments will be performed.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. (1) Single-cell imaging: time-lapse microscopy and microfluidic datasets with per-cell growth/lineage trajectories under defined antibiotic exposures (from public image repositories, journal supplements, and community-shared archives). (2) Transcriptomics: bulk RNA-seq/microarray and bacterial scRNA-seq where available under antibiotic stress (NCBI GEO/SRA/ArrayExpress). (3) Proteomics/metabolomics: PRIDE and Metabolomics Workbench studies under antibiotic exposure. (4) Regulatory networks: RegulonDB and curated regulons for additional organisms; toxin–antitoxin annotations from public databases. (5) Metabolic models: BiGG GEMs and published condition-specific constraints/flux measurements.

Harmonization and metadata standardization. We will create a tolerance “condition schema” capturing antibiotic class/mechanism, concentration relative to MIC, exposure waveform (step, pulse, ramp), medium composition, carbon source, growth phase, temperature, strain genotype, and assay/device type. Units and ontologies will be normalized (e.g., ChEBI for compounds; OBI/EFO where applicable). Time will be aligned to exposure onset; omics time points will be mapped onto imaging-derived phases (pre-exposure, early stress, growth arrest, recovery) using explicit rules and uncertainty annotations.

Single-cell trajectory analysis and state inference. From imaging, we will extract per-cell features (instantaneous growth rate, division events, elongation, lysis, regrowth lag) and survival outcomes. We will fit hierarchical hidden Markov and semi-Markov models to infer latent phenotypic states and transition rates, allowing condition- and species-specific parameters with shared priors. Survival will be modeled with state-dependent hazard functions to explain killing curves as mixtures of states. We will quantify identifiability and uncertainty via posterior predictive checks and bootstrapping across datasets.

Multi-omics integration to define molecular signatures. For each condition/time window, we will compute pathway/regulon activity scores (e.g., gene set enrichment, regulon inference where feasible) and integrate transcript/protein/metabolite changes using factor models and multi-view methods (e.g., MOFA-style latent factors) constrained by the condition schema. We will link omics factors to inferred phenotypic states using probabilistic regression and mutual information, emphasizing cross-dataset generalization.

Regulatory motif and dynamical analysis. Using curated networks, we will test enrichment of feedback motifs and slow-variable regulators among state-associated genes. We will compare alternative generative models (bet-hedging vs stress-induced switching vs bistability) by fitting model-implied transition structures to inferred state kinetics and selecting via information criteria and predictive performance.

Constraint-based metabolic modeling. We will map omics-derived constraints (e.g., uptake bounds, reaction activity priors) onto GEMs to compute feasible flux spaces for each inferred state/condition using flux balance analysis variants and flux variability analysis. We will identify conserved flux couplings and candidate “collapse points” where constraining a small set of reactions reduces the tolerant feasible region. Predictions will be evaluated internally by consistency across independent datasets and organisms, and by agreement with known tolerance-modulating pathways reported in the literature.

Deliverable pipelines. All steps will be implemented as modular, containerized workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow) with standardized inputs/outputs, enabling community reuse and extension.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcomes. (1) A cross-species taxonomy of antibiotic tolerance states derived from integrated single-cell phenotypes and molecular signatures, including quantitative definitions (state-specific growth distributions, transition rates, and hazard functions). (2) Evidence-based identification of dynamical motifs that best explain emergent survival distributions across antibiotics and environments, clarifying when tolerance is consistent with constitutive switching, stress-induced entry, or bistable modules. (3) A mechanistic bridge between omics signatures and metabolic constraints: mapping tolerance states to feasible flux regimes and identifying conserved flux couplings and candidate metabolic “collapse points” predicted to reduce tolerance in silico.

Community resources. We will produce an open Antibiotic Tolerance Synthesis Atlas containing harmonized metadata, processed single-cell trajectory features, curated links to omics datasets, inferred state models, and metabolic-model mappings. The atlas will include benchmarks for tolerance-state classification and standardized reporting templates for future imaging and omics studies to maximize interoperability.

Methodological impact. The project will deliver reusable, rigorously tested pipelines for (i) extracting and modeling single-cell survival trajectories, (ii) aligning heterogeneous time courses across modalities, and (iii) integrating regulatory-network context with constraint-based models to interpret emergent phenotypes. These methods will generalize to other mesoscale emergence problems (e.g., differentiation, stress adaptation, organelle biogenesis) where heterogeneous single-cell outcomes arise from network–metabolism interactions.

Broader impacts and relevance. By synthesizing existing public data, the project will accelerate understanding of tolerance without new experimentation and will support translational hypothesis generation for combination therapies and dosing strategies. The working group will also expand the data-savvy workforce by training trainees in reproducible single-cell analysis, multi-omics integration, and metabolic modeling, aligned with NCEMS’s mission to catalyze multidisciplinary synthesis teams and open, community-scale resources.
original.budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale aligned to NCEMS working-group needs (synthesis only). The project requires coordinated, in-person and virtual collaboration among multiple labs, intensive data curation, and robust cyberinfrastructure for large-scale image processing and integrative modeling. NCEMS support is essential because the scope (multi-modal harmonization across many studies and organisms) exceeds what any single lab can accomplish and benefits from a neutral synthesis center to convene diverse expertise and enforce open-science standards.

Major cost categories (illustrative, to be adapted to NCEMS guidelines). (1) Working group meetings: support for 2–3 multi-day meetings at NCEMS (or hybrid), including travel, lodging, and per diem for participants across institutions, with explicit allocation for trainees and participants from resource-limited institutions. (2) Personnel support: partial support for a dedicated project/data manager and/or research software engineer to maintain the atlas, implement workflows, manage identifiers/ontologies, and ensure reproducibility; plus limited trainee support (graduate/postdoc) for curation sprints and method benchmarking. (3) Computing and data management: cloud/HPC credits for processing large microscopy datasets, running Bayesian state-inference models, and performing flux-space computations; storage for intermediate artifacts; and DOI-based archival (e.g., Zenodo) preparation. (4) Training and dissemination: costs for running open workshops (captioning, recording, instructional design), and for maintaining a documentation website.

NCEMS resources leveraged. We will use NCEMS convening capacity, facilitation, and community policy frameworks for open team science; access to collaboration tooling; and guidance on data governance. NCEMS-hosted meeting space and staff support will accelerate consensus on metadata standards and deliverable timelines.

Team composition and partnerships. The working group will include multiple labs spanning microbiology, quantitative single-cell analysis, omics, systems biology, and metabolic modeling, with representation across career stages and institution types. Trainees will be integrated into each work package with mentored ownership of specific pipeline modules and atlas components, ensuring workforce development is a core deliverable rather than an add-on.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Molecular and cellular microbiology studies bacterial antibiotic tolerance to address the lack of a unified framework for survival outcomes. Current knowledge identifies metabolic slowdown and stress responses as key factors but remains fragmented across isolated experimental contexts. This project identifies conserved tolerance states and dynamical motifs to establish generalizable principles of survival from molecular networks.

The study design employs a synthesis workflow involving data curation and integrative stochastic modeling of existing public data. Methods include hidden Markov modeling and multi view factor analysis alongside constraint based metabolic modeling to identify choke points. Results are validated by testing consistency across independent datasets and comparing findings against known tolerance pathways in literature.

The project utilizes public repositories including NCBI GEO and PRIDE and Metabolomics Workbench and BiGG for metabolic models. Datasets are integrated by creating a standardized condition schema that aligns metadata and time resolved omics with phenotypes. Data limitations regarding experimental heterogeneity are addressed by developing explicit metadata standards and probabilistic regression models for uncertainty.

The proposal does not address the specific milestones or the overall timeline for the project. Multi lab collaboration is required to integrate diverse expertise in microbiology and systems biology and to manage data curation.

The project will produce an open Antibiotic Tolerance Synthesis Atlas and reproducible containerized analysis pipelines for public access. The team includes experts in microbiology and quantitative analysis across career stages with trainees integrated into work packages.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the lack of a unified framework connecting fragmented molecular data to explain how bacterial networks generate antibiotic tolerance. The study employs integrative stochastic modeling and multi view factor analysis to map heterogeneous survival phenotypes onto conserved metabolic regulatory constraints. This project establishes a comprehensive synthesis atlas that defines generalizable principles of bacterial survival across diverse species and antibiotic classes.

title: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Autophagosome Biogenesis: Integrating Proteomics, Lipid Signatures, and Imaging Dynamics

original.abstract:
Autophagy is a conserved process where emergent mesoscale structures—phagophores and autophagosomes—form, expand, and fuse with lysosomes. While core ATG proteins are known, puzzles remain about how initiation sites are selected, how membrane sources contribute, and how dynamics vary across species and stresses. Public imaging, proteomics, and lipidomics datasets offer a path to a community-scale synthesis.

This working group will integrate (i) live-cell imaging datasets of autophagy markers (LC3/Atg8, WIPI, ATG proteins) under diverse perturbations (IDR), (ii) proteomics of autophagosomes and ATG complexes (PRIDE), (iii) lipidomics datasets capturing PI3P and membrane lipid remodeling under autophagy induction (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) interaction networks and PTM data for autophagy regulators (BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus), and (v) genetic screens for autophagy factors across organisms (yeast, Drosophila, human CRISPR screens). We will curate stressors (starvation, ER stress, infection mimics) and annotate assay types.

Scientific questions: (1) What are conserved versus context-specific modules controlling autophagosome nucleation and expansion? (2) How do lipid remodeling signatures correlate with autophagosome morphology and formation rates? (3) Can we predict emergent autophagy dynamics (bursting vs steady-state) from upstream signaling and membrane source availability?

Analytical approach: We will extract quantitative dynamic features from imaging (puncta initiation rates, growth kinetics, fusion events) using standardized tracking pipelines. Multi-omic integration will link these features to proteomic composition and lipid signatures using latent factor models. Comparative analysis across species will identify conserved emergent behaviors and map divergence to specific regulatory innovations.

NCEMS support is required to coordinate autophagy biologists, lipidomics experts, quantitative imaging scientists, and computational modelers, and to host collaborative curation of heterogeneous datasets. The project’s scale and need for cross-modal harmonization exceed individual lab capabilities.

Deliverables will include an open Autophagosome Biogenesis Atlas with harmonized imaging-derived dynamics, proteomic modules, and lipid signatures; reproducible workflows for autophagy image tracking and omics integration; and a catalog of predicted regulators controlling dynamic regimes. Training will include hands-on workshops on image tracking, lipidomics normalization, and open science, with trainees leading dataset annotation and benchmark creation. The synthesis will yield general principles of how mesoscale autophagic structures emerge from molecular interactions.
original.background_and_significance:
Autophagy is a central homeostatic pathway in eukaryotes that enables cells to survive nutrient limitation, remodel organelles, and respond to infection and proteotoxic stress. Its hallmark is the de novo emergence of a mesoscale membrane structure: a cup-shaped phagophore that expands, closes into a double-membrane autophagosome, and fuses with lysosomes/vacuoles. This transformation is an archetypal “emergence” problem in molecular and cellular biosciences: coordinated molecular interactions (ATG proteins, lipid kinases, tethering factors, cytoskeletal inputs) produce a new functional entity with system-level properties (cargo selectivity, size control, spatial positioning, and temporally patterned flux) that cannot be inferred from any single component.

Despite decades of discoveries—core ATG genes, the PI3K complex, Atg8/LC3 lipidation, WIPI/Atg18 family recruitment, and membrane trafficking contributions—fundamental puzzles remain. First, initiation site selection is incompletely understood. Autophagosomes can nucleate at ER subdomains, ER–mitochondria contacts, Golgi-derived membranes, endosomes, or plasma membrane contributions, depending on cell type and stress. What determines which site becomes productive, and how do upstream signaling and membrane availability bias this choice? Second, membrane source contributions are debated and may differ across species and contexts. The relative roles of ATG9 vesicles, COPII, endosomal recycling, and lipid transfer proteins likely shift with nutrient status, cell cycle, and organismal lineage. Third, autophagy dynamics exhibit distinct regimes: steady-state basal turnover, rapid bursts upon starvation, oscillatory or spatially clustered events, and stress-specific kinetics (e.g., ER stress versus infection mimics). The field lacks a cross-study, quantitative synthesis that connects these dynamic regimes to molecular composition and lipid remodeling.

A key barrier is fragmentation of evidence across modalities and organisms. Live-cell imaging studies quantify puncta formation and lifetimes but often lack matched proteomic/lipidomic context. Proteomics of isolated autophagosomes and ATG complexes reveals compositional diversity but rarely links to dynamics. Lipidomics captures PI3P and remodeling of phospholipids/sphingolipids/sterols, yet is difficult to align with imaging readouts. Genetic screens identify regulators but are hard to interpret mechanistically without integrated network and phenotype mapping. Importantly, these datasets already exist publicly at scale (IDR, PRIDE, Metabolomics Workbench, BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, and multiple CRISPR/RNAi/yeast deletion screens), but have not been harmonized into a coherent mesoscale theory of autophagosome biogenesis.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that is beyond any single lab: (i) cross-species integration (yeast, Drosophila, mammalian systems) to distinguish conserved principles from lineage-specific innovations; (ii) cross-modal harmonization of imaging-derived dynamics with proteomic modules, lipid signatures, and phosphoregulation; and (iii) development of AI-enabled integration strategies that yield mechanistic, testable predictions about emergent mesoscale behavior. This working group will build a unified, open Autophagosome Biogenesis Atlas that enables the community to interrogate how molecular interaction networks and membrane chemistry give rise to reproducible, context-dependent autophagy dynamics. The result will advance fundamental cell biology, inform disease-relevant autophagy dysregulation, and provide generalizable synthesis methods for other mesoscale organelle-like assemblies.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group addresses how emergent mesoscale autophagosome structures arise from coordinated molecular and lipid processes across species and stress contexts. We frame three interconnected research questions, each with explicit hypotheses that can be evaluated using only publicly available data.

Research Question 1: What molecular modules are conserved versus context-specific in controlling autophagosome nucleation and expansion?
Hypothesis 1A (core conserved module): Across eukaryotes, a conserved “nucleation-to-expansion” module—PI3K complex activity (Vps34/Beclin/Atg14), PI3P effectors (WIPI/Atg18), Atg8/LC3 lipidation machinery (Atg7/Atg3/Atg12–5–16), and Atg9 trafficking—will co-vary with imaging-derived initiation rates and growth kinetics, forming a cross-species latent factor that explains a large fraction of dynamic variance.
Hypothesis 1B (context-specific accessory modules): Stressors (starvation, ER stress, infection mimics) recruit distinct accessory modules (e.g., ER-shaping proteins, endosomal tethers, lipid transfer proteins, cytoskeletal regulators) that modulate morphology (size, curvature proxies, closure time) without replacing the conserved core.
Hypothesis 1C (species divergence mapping): Divergence in dynamics between yeast, fly, and mammals will map to expansions/rewiring in regulatory layers (kinases, ubiquitin ligases, selective autophagy receptors) rather than to the core lipidation/nucleation machinery.

Research Question 2: How do lipid remodeling signatures correlate with autophagosome morphology and formation rates?
Hypothesis 2A (PI3P–kinetics coupling): Quantitative PI3P signatures (either direct lipidomics measures or inferred PI3P pathway activity from phosphoproteomics/complex abundance) will positively correlate with initiation frequency and early growth rate, reflecting a rate-limiting role of PI3P microdomain formation.
Hypothesis 2B (lipid composition–morphology coupling): Enrichment of specific lipid classes (e.g., PE availability for LC3/Atg8 conjugation; changes in unsaturation and curvature-prone lipids; sterol/sphingolipid remodeling) will correlate with autophagosome size distributions and closure/fusion timing. Distinct lipid “states” will align with distinct morphological/dynamic regimes.
Hypothesis 2C (membrane source signatures): Lipidomic patterns characteristic of ER, Golgi, endosomal, or mitochondrial-associated membranes will predict which initiation-site-associated protein modules dominate in a given context.

Research Question 3: Can emergent autophagy dynamics (bursting vs steady-state) be predicted from upstream signaling and membrane source availability?
Hypothesis 3A (regime classification): Imaging time series across studies can be classified into a small number of conserved dynamic regimes (basal steady-state, burst-like, oscillatory/clustered, stress-prolonged), and these regimes will be predictable from integrated features of upstream signaling (mTOR/AMPK/ULK1 axis proxies; phosphosite activity signatures) and membrane trafficking capacity (ATG9 cycling, COPII/endosome markers).
Hypothesis 3B (network controllability): Regulators identified in genetic screens will occupy high-control positions in integrated interaction networks (protein–protein and kinase–substrate graphs). Perturbations of these nodes (as represented in existing datasets) will shift regime probability more strongly than perturbations of peripheral nodes.
Hypothesis 3C (cross-species generalization): Models trained in one organism (e.g., yeast) will partially generalize to others when features are mapped to orthologous modules, indicating conserved design principles for mesoscale membrane emergence.

Collectively, these hypotheses convert dispersed public datasets into a unified, falsifiable framework linking molecules and lipids to emergent autophagosome dynamics across biological diversity.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis in four iterative phases: (1) dataset discovery and harmonized metadata; (2) standardized feature extraction within each modality; (3) multi-omic and cross-species integration; and (4) validation-by-consistency and prediction generation. No new experimental data will be produced.

Phase 1: Data inventory, inclusion criteria, and harmonization. We will assemble a curated corpus from: IDR (live-cell imaging of LC3/Atg8, WIPI, ATG proteins), PRIDE (autophagosome/ATG complex proteomics), Metabolomics Workbench (lipidomics under autophagy perturbations), BioGRID (interaction networks), PhosphoSitePlus (PTMs/kinase links), and published genetic screens (yeast deletion, RNAi, CRISPR). Inclusion criteria: public raw or minimally processed data, clear perturbation labels, and sufficient metadata (cell type/organism, markers, imaging modality, time resolution; proteomics acquisition; lipidomics platform). We will create a controlled vocabulary for stressors (starvation, ER stress, infection mimics, proteotoxic stress), assay types, and ortholog mapping (e.g., OrthoDB/Ensembl orthology tables). A data steward team (including trainees) will implement FAIR metadata in a versioned registry.

Phase 2: Imaging-derived dynamic and morphological features. We will standardize image processing using containerized pipelines (e.g., napari/scikit-image + TrackMate/DeepCell alternatives where appropriate) with benchmarked segmentation/tracking. Outputs: puncta initiation rate per cell, puncta lifetime, growth/decay kinetics, spatial clustering metrics, fusion/termination proxies, and morphological descriptors (size/shape, intensity trajectories). We will quantify uncertainty via bootstrapping and propagate quality scores (signal-to-noise, photobleaching indicators, temporal sampling adequacy). Where raw movies are unavailable, we will extract digitized trajectories from provided tables or reanalyze deposited processed images.

Phase 3: Proteomics, lipidomics, PTM, and screen feature extraction. Proteomics: reprocess raw files where possible using consistent search/quantification settings (e.g., standardized FDR, protein inference) or harmonize reported quantifications; derive module scores using complex-aware aggregation (PI3K complex, ATG9 system, lipidation machinery, tethering factors). Lipidomics: normalize across platforms (internal standards when available; batch correction; compositional data approaches), derive lipid class and curvature/unsaturation indices, and compute PI3P-related proxies when direct measurement is lacking. PTM: construct kinase–substrate activity signatures from phosphosite sets and map to upstream pathways (mTOR/AMPK/ULK1 and stress kinases). Screens: encode gene-level effects on autophagy phenotypes; map to orthologous groups and annotate assay endpoints.

Phase 4: Multi-omic integration and cross-species modeling. We will align datasets by organism, stressor class, and comparable readouts using hierarchical models that accommodate missing modalities. Integration methods will include: (i) latent factor models (MOFA-like) to link imaging dynamics with proteomic/lipid states; (ii) graph-based integration combining BioGRID interactions with screen hits and PTM edges to identify conserved control modules; and (iii) regime discovery using time-series clustering (e.g., HMMs or change-point models) to define bursting vs steady-state dynamics. Predictive modeling will use regularized models and interpretable machine learning (e.g., sparse regression, SHAP summaries) with cross-study and cross-species validation.

Rigor and feasibility. We will predefine evaluation metrics: variance explained in imaging dynamics by integrated factors; stability of discovered regimes across datasets; and enrichment of known autophagy regulators among top predictors (as a sanity check, not circular training). Sensitivity analyses will test robustness to metadata uncertainty, platform effects, and orthology mapping ambiguities. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts to adjudicate harmonization decisions, for compute/workflow infrastructure, and for iterative synthesis meetings that ensure biological interpretability of AI-driven outputs.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcomes. (1) A cross-species, quantitative map of autophagosome biogenesis modules, distinguishing a conserved core from stress- and lineage-specific accessory modules. This will address long-standing uncertainty about which steps are universal versus rewired across eukaryotes. (2) A set of lipid remodeling “states” linked to measurable autophagosome dynamics (initiation frequency, growth kinetics, closure timing) and morphology proxies, clarifying how membrane chemistry constrains mesoscale structure emergence. (3) A predictive, mechanistically interpretable model that classifies autophagy into a small number of dynamic regimes (e.g., basal steady-state, burst-like, oscillatory/clustered) and identifies upstream signaling and membrane trafficking features that shift regime probability.

Community resources and deliverables. (1) The Autophagosome Biogenesis Atlas: an openly accessible, harmonized resource connecting imaging-derived dynamic features with proteomic modules, lipid signatures, PTM activity proxies, interaction networks, and genetic screen evidence across yeast, Drosophila, and human systems. (2) Reusable, containerized workflows for autophagy imaging tracking, lipidomics normalization, and multi-omic integration, enabling other labs to reproduce and extend analyses. (3) A prioritized catalog of predicted regulators and module interactions that explain dynamic regime differences, annotated with evidence strength and cross-species conservation.

Impact on NCEMS mission and broader biology. This project directly targets emergent mesoscale behavior—how a membrane-bound organelle-like structure arises and exhibits context-dependent dynamics—from integrated public molecular/cellular data. The synthesis will generate general principles applicable to other mesoscale assemblies (endocytic pits, stress granules, mitochondrial fission sites): how lipid microenvironments, modular protein complexes, and signaling networks jointly produce new structures with distinct dynamical regimes. By training trainees in integrative, open, reproducible synthesis, the working group will expand the data-savvy workforce and establish best practices for community-scale emergence research without new experiments.
original.budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (NCEMS working group model). This project requires NCEMS support to convene a distributed, multidisciplinary team and to provide coordination, compute enablement, and training infrastructure that exceed the capacity of any single lab.

Major cost categories. (1) Working group convenings: funds for 2–3 multi-day meetings (hybrid or in-person) hosted/organized through NCEMS, enabling intensive cross-domain synthesis (autophagy biology, quantitative imaging, lipidomics, proteomics, network science/AI). Travel support will prioritize trainees, early-career investigators, and participants from under-resourced institutions to broaden participation. (2) Personnel time support (as allowed by NCEMS mechanisms): partial support for a project manager/data steward to maintain the dataset registry, metadata standards, and release process; and for a research software engineer to harden pipelines, implement CI testing, and maintain containers/workflows. (3) Compute and storage: cloud or shared compute credits for reprocessing proteomics/lipidomics where permissible, running segmentation/tracking at scale, and training integration models; plus storage for derived products and intermediate artifacts. (4) Training and dissemination: workshop logistics, tutorial development, documentation, and accessibility services (captioning) to maximize community uptake.

Resource commitments and roles. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise and in-kind effort: autophagy experts to define biologically meaningful features and interpret modules; imaging scientists to benchmark tracking; lipidomics/proteomics experts to standardize normalization and reprocessing; computational modelers to develop integrative and comparative methods. Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) will be embedded in curation and reproducibility teams, gaining skills in data stewardship, workflow engineering, and integrative modeling.

Why NCEMS is essential. The key bottleneck is not data availability but coordination and harmonization across heterogeneous public datasets and disciplines. NCEMS provides the neutral convening space, project management scaffolding, and synthesis culture required to align standards, resolve disagreements transparently, and deliver community-grade resources on an accelerated timeline without generating new experimental data.

rephrased.standardized_text:
This project investigates cell biology to understand the biogenesis and dynamics of autophagosomes and phagophores within cellular systems. Current knowledge identifies core proteins and pathways but lacks a unified model for membrane initiation and dynamic regimes. The study integrates molecular data to explain how emergent autophagosome structures arise across species to provide generalizable principles.

The study design employs a four phase community scale synthesis involving data discovery and predictive modeling of existing data. Key methods include latent factor models and standardized image tracking pipelines alongside graph based network analysis and machine learning. Results are validated through consistency checks across datasets and sensitivity analysis regarding metadata and orthology to ensure model accuracy.

The project utilizes public databases including IDR and PRIDE and Metabolomics Workbench and BioGRID and PhosphoSitePlus and genetic screens. Distinct datasets are integrated through controlled vocabularies and ortholog mapping and hierarchical models that align imaging with molecular signatures. Known data limitations regarding fragmentation and platform biases are mitigated through normalization and batch correction and hierarchical modeling techniques.

The proposal does not address the specific project timeline beyond the iterative four phase process described in the methodology. The project scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because harmonizing heterogeneous data exceeds the capacity of any single individual laboratory.

The team will create an open Autophagosome Biogenesis Atlas and release containerized reproducible workflows for all integration methods used. The multidisciplinary team includes biologists and imaging scientists and computational modelers who provide training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the disconnect between molecular components and emergent mesoscale autophagosome dynamics by synthesizing fragmented cross species biological data. The study employs hierarchical latent factor models to integrate disparate proteomic and imaging datasets into a unified quantitative regulatory framework. This project establishes a comprehensive atlas that defines the generalizable principles governing how molecular networks drive organelle biogenesis.

title: Emergent RNA Localization Codes: Synthesizing Subcellular Transcriptomics, RBP Binding Maps, and Imaging to Predict RNA Destinations

original.abstract:
RNA localization creates mesoscale organization of gene expression, enabling local translation and compartment-specific regulation. Although many RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and localization elements are known, a generalizable “localization code” remains elusive. Public datasets now include subcellular fractionation RNA-seq, APEX-seq, spatial transcriptomics, RBP binding maps (eCLIP), and RNA imaging—ideal for synthesis.

This working group will integrate (i) subcellular RNA localization datasets (APEX-seq, fractionation RNA-seq in GEO), (ii) eCLIP and related RBP binding maps (ENCODE), (iii) RNA modification data (m6A and others) where available, (iv) imaging datasets of RNA localization (MERFISH/FISH images in IDR and publications), (v) proteomics/localization for RBPs (HPA, PRIDE), and (vi) perturbation datasets altering RBPs or transport machinery (CRISPR screens, knockdown RNA-seq). We will harmonize compartment definitions (mitochondria, ER, nucleus subdomains, protrusions) and build a standardized annotation schema.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify sequence/structure motifs and RBP combinations that predict RNA localization across compartments and cell types. (2) Determine how localization programs change under stress (e.g., stress granule recruitment, ER stress) and differentiation. (3) Link emergent localization patterns to functional outputs such as localized translation and organelle proteome maintenance.

Analytical approach: We will develop multi-task predictive models that map RNA sequence features (UTR motifs, secondary structure, codon usage) plus RBP binding profiles to localization probabilities. Graph-based models will capture combinatorial RBP interactions. Imaging data will provide validation and refine compartment boundaries. We will also perform meta-analyses to quantify reproducibility and context dependence of localization signals.

NCEMS support is essential because integrating diverse RNA localization assays requires coordinated expertise in RNA biology, spatial transcriptomics, imaging, and machine learning, as well as substantial curation to align compartments and experimental contexts. The working group will establish community standards for reporting localization experiments and derived labels.

Deliverables will include an open RNA Localization Synthesis Database with harmonized labels and features; reproducible pipelines for processing APEX-seq/fractionation datasets; and predictive models with interpretable motif and RBP attributions. Training will include workshops on RNA motif modeling, eCLIP processing, and reproducible ML, with trainees leading curation of specific compartments. The synthesis will advance understanding of emergent spatial gene regulation at the mesoscale.
original.background_and_significance:
Subcellular RNA localization is a central mechanism by which cells create spatially organized gene expression programs. By enriching specific transcripts near organelles, membranes, and cytoskeletal structures, cells enable local translation, compartment-specific regulation, and rapid responses to stimuli without requiring whole-cell transcriptional rewiring. This spatial control is a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon: it emerges from molecular interactions among RNA sequences, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), transport machinery, and local microenvironments, yet it manifests as higher-order organization at the scale of organelles and cellular subdomains. Despite decades of work identifying “zipcodes” in untranslated regions (UTRs), individual RBPs, and transport pathways, the field still lacks a generalizable and predictive “RNA localization code” that can explain and forecast where transcripts accumulate across compartments, cell types, and conditions.

The gap is not primarily due to a lack of data; rather, it stems from fragmentation across assay modalities, cell contexts, and analysis conventions. APEX-seq and related proximity labeling methods provide transcriptome-wide localization to defined subcellular neighborhoods (e.g., mitochondrial outer membrane, ER, nuclear lamina). Biochemical fractionation RNA-seq offers broad compartment enrichment but varies in purity and labeling.
