(4) Computing and data services: cloud credits or NCEMS-provided compute for large-scale image feature extraction and model training; storage for derived, shareable artifacts; DOI minting and repository fees if applicable.

Resource plan and roles. Participating labs will contribute complementary expertise: immune synapse biology and receptor signaling; quantitative imaging and spatial statistics; proteomics/phosphoproteomics interpretation; network biology and causal inference; and multimodal ML. NCEMS will provide facilitation, project management support, and access to collaborative platforms.

Milestones and deliverable-linked spending. Year 1 resources prioritize curation, harmonization, and pipeline prototypes; Year 2 emphasizes modeling, benchmarking, and atlas release; final-quarter resources support documentation, workshops, and archival deposition (Zenodo/OSF/GitHub). All spending is tied to synthesis deliverables, not new data generation, ensuring compliance with NCEMS requirements.

rephrased.standardized_text:
This project investigates the mesoscale spatial organization of the immune synapse within the fields of immunology and cell biology. Current research remains fragmented across cell types and data modalities despite known links between spatial patterning and signaling. The study identifies conserved spatial motifs to determine how architecture constrains signaling thresholds and informs the engineering of therapies.

The project utilizes a synthesis based study design to perform cross modal analysis and causal inference on existing data. Researchers apply spatial statistics and graph based representation learning alongside multimodal machine learning and mechanistic dynamical modeling. Results are validated against held out datasets and cross cell type transfer tests using activation classification and signaling metrics.

The study integrates datasets from the Image Data Resource and proteomics databases like PRIDE and CPTAC and GEO. Integration involves harmonizing metadata with controlled vocabularies and mapping to unified identifiers while modeling batch effects through normalization. Known heterogeneity in imaging modalities is mitigated through standardized pipelines and the propagation of uncertainty into all downstream models.

The project spans two years with the first year dedicated to curation and the second to modeling and release. The scope requires a cross disciplinary team to manage large scale data integration beyond the capacity of one laboratory.

The team will share an open source quantification pipeline and an Immune Synapse Emergence Atlas via public digital repositories. The multidisciplinary group includes experts from various fields and provides training in spatial analysis for students and postdocs.

The study employs graph based representation learning and mechanistic dynamical modeling to integrate fragmented imaging, proteomics, and transcriptomics data modalities. This project establishes a comprehensive atlas of immune synapse design principles to predict cellular decision making and improve therapeutic engineering.

title: Emergent Principles of Protein Allostery at Scale: Integrating Structural Ensembles, Mutational Scans, and Functional Genomics

original.abstract:
Allostery—long-range coupling between sites in proteins—is an emergent property of molecular structure and dynamics. While classic studies focus on individual proteins, public deep mutational scanning (DMS), structural models, and functional genomics now enable a synthesis to identify general rules predicting allosteric coupling and its cellular consequences.

This working group will integrate (i) DMS datasets with publicly available raw/processed scores (MaveDB), (ii) structural data and predicted models (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) molecular dynamics ensemble resources where available, (iv) protein interaction and pathway context (BioGRID, Reactome), and (v) human genetic variation and disease annotations (gnomAD, ClinVar) to connect allosteric sites to phenotypes. We will curate protein families with multiple DMS studies to enable comparative analyses.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify structural and sequence determinants of allosteric sensitivity (e.g., network centrality in residue contact graphs, flexibility, packing frustration). (2) Quantify how allosteric coupling patterns vary across protein classes (enzymes, transcription factors, membrane receptors) and evolutionary distances. (3) Link predicted allosteric sites to cellular phenotypes via pathway integration and genetic dependency data, illuminating why certain distal variants are pathogenic.

Analytical approach: We will compute residue interaction networks from structures and develop models that predict mutational effects at distal sites using graph neural networks and interpretable network metrics. We will meta-analyze DMS across conditions to detect context-dependent allostery. Integrating functional genomics (e.g., dependency scores) will allow prioritization of allosteric sites most relevant to cellular fitness. A methodological deliverable will be an open benchmark suite for allostery prediction using standardized splits across proteins and families.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans structural biology, statistical genetics, ML, and systems biology, and requires coordinated curation of diverse DMS experiments and structural representations. The working group will align on standards for mapping DMS variants to structures and for reporting uncertainty.

Deliverables will include an open Allostery Synthesis Atlas with harmonized DMS-to-structure mappings, predicted allosteric networks, and links to disease variants; reproducible pipelines for feature extraction and modeling; and benchmarks for community method development. Training will include workshops on structural data processing, DMS analysis, and reproducible ML, with trainees leading curation of protein families. The synthesis will uncover general emergent rules of allostery and enable better interpretation of distal variants.
original.background_and_significance:
Allostery—functional coupling between spatially separated sites in a protein—has long served as a paradigm for emergent biological behavior: collective properties arise from networks of interactions that are not obvious from local chemistry alone. Historically, allostery has been elucidated through intensive, protein-by-protein experimentation, yielding canonical examples (e.g., hemoglobin, kinases, GPCRs) and mechanistic models (MWC, KNF, energy landscape perspectives). Yet decades of work have not produced generalizable, quantitative principles that predict (i) which residues participate in long-range coupling, (ii) how coupling depends on structural context and dynamics, and (iii) which distal variants are likely to perturb cellular phenotypes or human disease.

This gap is increasingly consequential. In human genetics, many pathogenic missense variants occur outside active sites or classical binding interfaces, complicating interpretation and therapeutic targeting. In drug discovery, allosteric modulators offer selectivity advantages, but identifying allosteric sites remains difficult. In protein engineering, distal mutations can strongly influence activity, stability, specificity, and regulation, but rules for predicting beneficial distal substitutions are incomplete. These challenges all reflect the same core scientific problem: allostery is an emergent mesoscale phenomenon linking residue-level perturbations to protein-level conformational ensembles and, ultimately, cellular systems.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that converts the recent explosion of public molecular data into broadly applicable allosteric principles. Three public data streams now make this feasible. First, deep mutational scanning (DMS) has produced quantitative, residue-resolved maps of mutational effects across hundreds of proteins and multiple experimental contexts, with many datasets deposited in MaveDB. These maps implicitly contain signatures of long-range coupling: mutations far from an active site can alter function in systematic, nonlocal patterns. Second, structural resources have expanded dramatically, including high-resolution structures (PDB), predicted models at proteome scale (AlphaFold DB), and, for some proteins, ensembles from NMR, cryo-EM heterogeneity analyses, or public molecular dynamics repositories. Third, functional genomics and network biology resources (BioGRID, Reactome, DepMap/CRISPR dependency screens, expression and pathway annotations) connect proteins to cellular phenotypes, while population and clinical genetics (gnomAD, ClinVar) connect variants to organismal outcomes.

Despite these advances, integration remains a bottleneck. DMS measurements are heterogeneous (assay types, selection regimes, score scales), variant annotation and coordinate mapping are inconsistent, and structural representations vary (single structures vs ensembles; resolved vs predicted regions). Moreover, connecting protein-level allosteric sensitivity to cellular phenotype requires careful synthesis across pathway context, genetic dependencies, and disease annotations. No single lab typically spans the necessary expertise in DMS statistics, structural bioinformatics, molecular simulation, machine learning, and systems genetics.

This working group will address this need by building a harmonized, open “Allostery Synthesis Atlas” and an associated benchmark suite for allostery prediction. By integrating DMS, structures/ensembles, interaction networks, and genotype–phenotype evidence, we will identify general, testable rules of allosteric coupling across protein classes and evolutionary distances. The project aligns with NCEMS’s mission by focusing on emergence at the mesoscale—how distributed residue interactions and conformational variability give rise to long-range functional coupling—and by leveraging AI-enabled synthesis of publicly available data to resolve longstanding puzzles in molecular and cellular biosciences.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project centers on the premise that allostery can be quantified as a measurable, distributed sensitivity of protein function to distal perturbations, and that this sensitivity is governed by emergent network- and ensemble-level properties rather than only local chemistry. We will pursue three tightly linked research questions, each with explicit hypotheses that can be evaluated using integrated public datasets.

RQ1: Which structural and sequence features best predict allosteric sensitivity at residue resolution? Allosteric sensitivity here is defined operationally as the degree to which mutations at a residue produce functional effects that cannot be explained by local structural disruption alone (e.g., distance to active site, solvent exposure), and that correlate with changes in activity, regulation, or binding measured by DMS.

H1.1 (network mediation): Residues with high centrality in residue–residue contact graphs (betweenness, current flow, communicability) are enriched for distal DMS sensitivity, reflecting their role as conduits for information/energy propagation.

H1.2 (energetic frustration and packing): Sites with high local packing frustration or heterogeneous contact energies show elevated allosteric sensitivity because they facilitate alternative interaction patterns across the ensemble.

H1.3 (ensemble flexibility): Residues with higher predicted or observed conformational variability (B-factors, AlphaFold pLDDT/PAE proxies, NMR ensembles, MD-derived fluctuations where available) are more likely to participate in context-dependent coupling.

RQ2: How do allosteric coupling patterns vary across protein classes and evolutionary distances, and what constitutes a conserved “allosteric architecture”? We will compare families with multiple DMS datasets (across homologs and/or assay contexts) to quantify conserved vs divergent coupling.

H2.1 (class-specific architectures): Enzymes will display coupling concentrated along catalytic networks and substrate channels; transcription factors will show coupling enriched at DNA-binding and regulatory interfaces; membrane receptors will show coupling aligned with transmembrane helix networks and ligand/effector interfaces.

H2.2 (evolutionary constraint on coupling): Distal sites with strong allosteric sensitivity will be more evolutionarily constrained than matched control sites, but the degree of constraint will depend on whether coupling supports core function (highly conserved) versus regulation/adaptation (more lineage-specific).

H2.3 (epistasis as emergent signature): Proteins with stronger distal coupling will exhibit higher-order epistasis patterns in DMS (non-additive effects across sites), reflecting ensemble redistribution rather than independent local disruptions.

RQ3: When and why do distal variants become pathogenic or phenotypically consequential in cells? We will link predicted allosteric sites to cellular phenotypes through pathway context, interaction networks, and gene dependency data, focusing on human proteins with ClinVar/gnomAD annotations and orthologous DMS where available.

H3.1 (network amplification): Distal variants at allosteric sites are more likely to be pathogenic when the protein occupies a high-control position in cellular networks (e.g., hubs, bottlenecks, pathway gatekeepers), because small functional shifts are amplified.

H3.2 (context dependence): Allosteric variant effects will be more condition-specific (assay/environment dependent in DMS; cell-line dependent in dependency screens) than active-site variants, consistent with regulation via shifting interaction equilibria.

H3.3 (predictive integration): Joint models that combine residue-network/ensemble features with pathway and dependency context will outperform structure-only or genetics-only baselines in prioritizing clinically relevant distal variants.

These questions and hypotheses drive a synthesis agenda that is both mechanistic (mesoscale coupling principles) and translationally relevant (variant interpretation), while remaining fully testable using only existing public data and rigorous benchmarking.
original.methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. We will run an NCEMS-supported working group with coordinated subteams: (A) DMS curation and statistical harmonization, (B) structure/ensemble processing and residue-network feature extraction, (C) predictive modeling and benchmarking, and (D) cellular/clinical integration. The project uses only publicly available datasets and produces no new experimental data.

1) Data acquisition and harmonization (DMS core). We will identify proteins with (i) at least one high-quality DMS dataset in MaveDB and (ii) a mappable structure/model. Priority will be given to families with multiple DMS studies across homologs or conditions (e.g., kinases, nuclear receptors, GPCRs where feasible, transcription factors, metabolic enzymes). For each study, we will extract raw/processed variant scores, uncertainty where available, assay metadata, and selection conditions. We will implement a harmonization framework: (a) map variants to a canonical UniProt sequence; (b) standardize score directionality and scale via robust normalization (e.g., rank-based transforms; z-scoring within study) while preserving interpretability; (c) model measurement error and replicate structure when available; and (d) annotate assay type (activity, binding, abundance, stability proxies) to enable stratified analyses.

2) Mapping variants to structures and ensembles. For each protein, we will map sequence positions to PDB structures and/or AlphaFold DB models using established alignment pipelines (SIFTS where applicable; pairwise alignment with gap handling; isoform resolution). We will annotate structural quality (resolution, missing regions, AlphaFold pLDDT/PAE) and define “analysis-ready” residue sets. Where public ensembles exist (NMR ensembles, multiple PDB conformers, cryo-EM multi-state models, or curated MD trajectories), we will compute ensemble-aware features; otherwise we will use proxies (e.g., AlphaFold confidence, predicted disorder).

3) Residue interaction networks and feature engineering. We will construct residue contact graphs (nodes=residues; edges=contacts weighted by distance, coevolution scores when available, or interaction energy proxies). Features will include classic metrics (degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector centrality), current-flow betweenness, community structure, shortest-path distances to functional sites (active site, ligand-binding residues, interfaces), and measures of local packing/frustration (e.g., contact density, clash/void proxies). Flexibility features will include B-factors, ensemble RMSF, and predicted disorder/confidence. We will also compute evolutionary features (conservation, coevolution couplings from public MSAs where permissible) and biochemical context (secondary structure, solvent accessibility).

4) Defining allosteric sensitivity phenotypes from DMS. We will derive residue-level allosteric sensitivity scores by aggregating mutational effects at each position (robust mean/median of non-synonymous effects), then regressing out local confounders (solvent exposure, proximity to functional sites, predicted stability impact where available) to isolate distal coupling signatures. We will quantify context dependence by comparing DMS conditions within the same protein (when multiple environments/ligands are present) using hierarchical models.

5) Predictive modeling and benchmarking. We will train models to predict residue-level allosteric sensitivity and variant-level effects using (i) interpretable baselines (regularized regression, gradient-boosted trees) and (ii) graph neural networks operating on residue graphs with structural/ensemble features. Benchmarking will use standardized splits designed to test generalization: within-protein (held-out residues), across-protein within family (held-out homolog), and across families (held-out class). We will preregister evaluation metrics (Spearman/Pearson for continuous scores; AUROC/AUPRC for classification of high-sensitivity residues; calibration curves) and compare to simple baselines (distance-to-active-site, solvent exposure only).

6) Cellular and clinical integration. We will map proteins to pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID) and integrate gene dependency data (e.g., DepMap) to quantify cellular essentiality and context specificity. For human proteins, we will overlay gnomAD constraint metrics and ClinVar variant annotations, testing enrichment of pathogenic variants at predicted allosteric sites while controlling for mutability and exposure. We will build integrative models that combine residue-level predictions with network position to prioritize variants likely to have phenotypic impact.

All analyses will be executed via reproducible, containerized workflows and released as an open atlas and benchmark suite.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. The primary scientific outcome will be a quantitative, cross-protein synthesis of how long-range coupling emerges from residue networks and conformational ensembles. We expect to identify a small set of robust predictors of allosteric sensitivity—combining network centrality/communicability, ensemble flexibility proxies, and packing/frustration measures—that generalize across many proteins better than distance-based heuristics. Comparative analyses across protein classes and families will yield “allosteric architectures”: recurring motifs of coupling (e.g., helix networks in receptors, catalytic communication pathways in enzymes, interface-mediated coupling in transcription factors) and their evolutionary conservation patterns.

Methodological outcomes. We will deliver (i) a harmonized dataset linking DMS variant effects to standardized structural coordinates and ensemble-aware features, (ii) an open benchmark suite with clearly defined train/test splits (within protein, across homologs, across families) to enable fair comparison of allostery prediction methods, and (iii) validated modeling pipelines spanning interpretable baselines through graph neural networks. These resources will lower barriers for the community to develop and test new AI methods for mesoscale emergence.

Translational and cellular impact. By integrating predicted allosteric sites with pathway context, interaction networks, and gene dependency, we will produce a principled framework for prioritizing distal variants most likely to alter cellular fitness or cause disease. We anticipate improved interpretation of ClinVar variants of uncertain significance that lie outside active sites, and clearer hypotheses for why certain distal variants are pathogenic (e.g., network amplification in key pathways; context-dependent regulation). The resulting Allostery Synthesis Atlas will be directly useful to researchers studying disease mechanisms, designing allosteric drugs, or engineering proteins.

Workforce and community impact. The working group will train trainees in cross-disciplinary synthesis: DMS statistics, structural bioinformatics, graph learning, and open/reproducible workflows. By convening diverse experts and producing reusable standards for mapping, uncertainty reporting, and benchmarking, the project will create durable community infrastructure aligned with NCEMS goals—enabling future synthesis efforts on other emergent protein phenomena beyond allostery.
original.budget_and_resources:
Budget philosophy and NCEMS need. This is a community-scale synthesis requiring coordinated curation, multi-modal integration, and shared compute/software infrastructure beyond a single lab’s scope. NCEMS support is essential for convening a multidisciplinary team (structural biology, DMS analysis, ML/AI, statistical genetics, systems biology), providing neutral coordination, and enabling intensive, in-person/virtual working sessions that accelerate harmonization standards and joint deliverables.

Requested resources (categories). (1) Working group convenings: support for multiple multi-day meetings (hybrid/in-person) to align standards, conduct hands-on curation/modeling sprints, and run trainee-led tutorials. Costs include travel, lodging, and meeting logistics to ensure participation across institutions, career stages, and geographic regions. (2) Personnel support: partial support for a project coordinator/data curator and/or research software engineer time (distributed across participating labs) to maintain pipelines, manage provenance, and implement the atlas and benchmark infrastructure. Trainee support (graduate/postdoc) will be prioritized for curation, reproducibility checks, and tutorial development. (3) Compute and storage: access to NCEMS-supported compute (CPU/GPU) for graph feature extraction and model training, plus scalable storage for intermediate artifacts (structures, mappings, feature matrices) and public hosting of derived products. (4) Dissemination and training: resources for hosting open workshops, producing documentation, and archiving releases (DOIs).

Feasibility and scope control. To ensure deliverables within the award period, we will phase work: Year 1 focuses on a curated set of protein families with strong DMS coverage and reliable structural mapping; Year 2 expands breadth and refines models/benchmarks and cellular/clinical integration. We will set clear inclusion criteria (data quality thresholds, mapping confidence) to avoid uncontrolled scope.

In-kind contributions. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source tools, and effort for code review and mentoring. NCEMS will provide the convening structure, shared infrastructure, and synthesis-centered project management needed to integrate these contributions into coherent, community-usable outputs.

rephrased.standardized_text:
The field of protein biophysics studies allostery to identify how molecular structure and dynamics drive long range coupling. Current knowledge relies on protein specific models while data from deep mutational scanning and structural databases remain fragmented. This project identifies structural determinants of allosteric sensitivity to improve the interpretation of pathogenic variants and drug discovery.

The study performs a meta analysis of public datasets to build a harmonized Allostery Synthesis Atlas and benchmark. Researchers will apply residue interaction networks and graph neural networks alongside hierarchical modeling to isolate distal coupling signatures. Results will be validated using standardized data splits and compared against baseline heuristics like solvent exposure and distance.

The project utilizes MaveDB and AlphaFold DB alongside BioGRID and DepMap to integrate structural and functional genomics data. Integration involves mapping sequence positions to structural coordinates and overlaying clinical annotations onto residue level interaction networks for analysis. Data heterogeneity and inconsistent mapping will be mitigated through robust normalization and standardized pipelines with explicit uncertainty reporting.

The two year project focuses on data curation in the first year and model refinement during the second year. The scope requires collaboration between structural biology and machine learning experts to establish community wide standards for data synthesis.

All deliverables including the Allostery Synthesis Atlas and reproducible pipelines will be released as open source research resources. The team includes experts in structural bioinformatics and systems genetics who provide training opportunities for students and postdocs.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the lack of predictive principles for long range allosteric coupling by integrating fragmented structural and functional data. The study employs graph neural networks and residue interaction analysis to isolate distal coupling signatures from local structural protein confounders. This project creates a comprehensive allostery synthesis atlas to standardize the interpretation of pathogenic variants and facilitate drug discovery.

title: Deciphering the Sequence-to-Emergent-Property Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates

original.abstract: The emergence of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation represents a paradigm shift in understanding mesoscale cellular organization. Despite extensive single-lab studies, the universal predictive rules governing how diverse protein and RNA sequences encode the physical properties of these condensates remain elusive. This mesoscale phenomenon bridges the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and macroscale cellular functions, such as stress response and gene expression. Understanding this emergence is critical for solving long-standing puzzles in molecular and cellular biosciences, specifically regarding how non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble and disassemble in response to environmental cues. Current research is highly fragmented, lacking a unified framework to explain how local interactions scale up to form functional, mesoscale structures that dictate global cellular outcomes. To address this, our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of phase separation. By integrating publicly available proteomics data, single-molecule biophysics datasets, transcriptomics, and high-throughput imaging repositories from the Protein Data Bank, LLPSDB, and the Image Data Resource, we will employ advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning frameworks to model condensate emergence. Our approach utilizes graph neural networks and deep learning architectures to synthesize these disparate multi-omics and imaging datasets, entirely bypassing the need for new experimental data. This innovative analytical strategy will allow us to map the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, identifying hidden patterns and emergent properties that cannot be observed in isolated datasets. The proposed synthesis goes far beyond the capacity of any individual laboratory, necessitating the dedicated support and resources of NCEMS. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computational scientists, and cell biologists. Our working group is intentionally assembled to reflect diverse scientific perspectives, career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels, ensuring a robust and inclusive approach to this complex problem. This collaborative partnership will break down traditional disciplinary silos, fostering a dynamic environment where diverse new talent can thrive. Crucially, the project serves as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be co-mentored across disciplines, gaining hands-on experience in cloud computing, AI-driven data integration, and collaborative research methodologies. In strict adherence to open science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available to the broader scientific community through open-source repositories like GitHub and Zenodo. Ultimately, this project reveals how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale influences higher-order cellular functions.
original.background_and_significance: The emergence of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represents one of the most profound paradigm shifts in modern molecular and cellular biology. For decades, the organization of the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm was largely understood through the lens of membrane-bound organelles. However, the discovery that proteins and nucleic acids can spontaneously demix into liquid-like, non-membrane-bound droplets has revolutionized our understanding of mesoscale cellular architecture. This phenomenon bridges the critical gap between nanoscale molecular interactions, such as transient multivalent contacts between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and macroscale cellular functions, including stress response, chromatin organization, and gene expression. Despite the explosion of research in this area, the field remains highly fragmented. Individual laboratories have generated vast amounts of specialized data, ranging from single-molecule biophysics and proteomics to high-throughput cellular imaging. Yet, a fundamental puzzle remains unsolved: What are the universal predictive rules, or the 'sequence-to-emergent-property grammar,' that dictate how specific biomolecular sequences encode the physical and functional properties of these condensates? Currently, we lack a unified framework to explain how local, nanoscale interactions scale up to form functional, mesoscale structures that dictate global cellular outcomes. The complexity of these mesoscale phenomena, coupled with the sheer volume of publicly available, yet siloed, datasets, makes this a challenge that cannot be solved by any single laboratory. It requires a community-scale synthesis approach. The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) is uniquely positioned to support this endeavor. By synthesizing distinct, publicly available datasets from repositories such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB), LLPSDB, and the Image Data Resource (IDR), our proposed working group will leverage advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies to uncover the hidden rules of condensate emergence. This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale, specifically focusing on the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The lack of a predictive grammar currently hinders both basic biological understanding and therapeutic design, particularly for neurodegenerative diseases where condensate dynamics are dysregulated. By integrating vast, disparate data sources without generating new experimental data, we will transition the field from descriptive, single-gene studies to a predictive, systems-level understanding of mesoscale emergence. This synthesis will solve a long-standing mystery in the molecular and cellular biosciences, illuminating how spatial, temporal, and informational complexities arise in biological systems.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: The proposed synthesis project is driven by three compelling, interconnected research questions designed to uncover the fundamental rules governing mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. Question 1: What constitutes the universal sequence-to-emergent-property grammar that dictates the material state and physical properties of biomolecular condensates? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that a decipherable, universal grammar exists within the primary sequences of proteins and RNAs, specifically within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent structured domains, that predictably scales from nanoscale molecular interactions to mesoscale physical properties such as viscosity, surface tension, and network connectivity. By synthesizing biophysical data from LLPSDB with structural data from the PDB, we anticipate identifying hidden sequence motifs, charge patterning, and spacer lengths that act as the fundamental syntax for condensate formation. Question 2: How do emergent condensate properties dynamically adapt to complex, multifactorial environmental cues across different cellular contexts? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the phase separation threshold and subsequent material properties of condensates are not static, but are dynamically tuned by environmental factors (e.g., pH, temperature, ion concentration, and molecular crowding) in a manner that can be predicted by integrating multi-omics data. By synthesizing transcriptomic and proteomic datasets with biophysical phase diagrams, we expect to reveal how cellular states modulate the physical chemistry of the cytoplasm to trigger or dissolve condensates. This will explain how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale is dynamically regulated by the cellular environment. Question 3: How do the mesoscale material properties of condensates dictate higher-order, macroscale cellular functions and phenotypic outcomes? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the material properties of biomolecular condensates (e.g., liquid-like vs. gel-like states) act as non-linear signal amplifiers that couple local sequence composition to global cellular responses, such as stress granule assembly during environmental stress or transcriptional bursting in the nucleus. By integrating high-throughput imaging data from the Image Data Resource (IDR) with functional genomic datasets, we will map the causal relationships between mesoscale condensate dynamics and macroscale cellular phenotypes. Addressing these questions requires the integration of vastly different data types, ranging from one-dimensional sequence data to multidimensional imaging and multi-omics datasets. These questions are entirely novel in their scope and scale, moving beyond the traditional single-protein focus to establish a generalized, predictive model for phase separation. By answering these questions, this working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble and disassemble, providing a unified framework for understanding mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
original.methods_and_approach: To decipher the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of biomolecular condensates, our working group will employ a community-scale synthesis approach, relying exclusively on existing, publicly available data. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, our methodological innovation lies in the integration of disparate datasets using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) frameworks. Data Ingestion and Harmonization: The first phase involves the systematic aggregation and curation of heterogeneous datasets. We will extract sequence, biophysical, and phase diagram data from LLPSDB and PhaSePro. Structural features, including AlphaFold-predicted intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent contact points, will be sourced from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and UniProt. High-throughput cellular imaging data capturing condensate dynamics will be retrieved from the Image Data Resource (IDR), while corresponding cellular state information will be drawn from public transcriptomic and proteomic repositories (e.g., GEO, PRIDE). Harmonizing these multiscale datasets, spanning 1D sequences, 3D structures, and 4D imaging, will require the development of novel data ontologies to ensure interoperability. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks: Once harmonized, we will utilize state-of-the-art AI architectures to model condensate emergence. We will deploy Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to represent multivalent molecular interactions, where nodes represent interaction domains (e.g., RNA-binding domains, charged motifs) and edges represent transient physical contacts. GNNs are uniquely suited to capture the complex, non-linear network topologies that give rise to mesoscale phase separation. To predict continuous physical properties such as critical concentration, viscosity, and surface tension, we will utilize deep learning regression models and transformer-based architectures trained on the harmonized biophysical datasets. Image Analysis and Multi-Omics Integration: To bridge the gap between in vitro biophysics and in vivo cellular outcomes, we will apply convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract quantitative features from IDR imaging data, such as condensate size, number, and dissolution rates. These imaging features will be correlated with transcriptomic profiles using multi-omics integration algorithms to identify how cellular stress states dictate condensate behavior. Transdisciplinary Collaboration: This methodological approach is beyond the capabilities of any individual research lab. It requires the convergence of diverse scientific perspectives. Our working group will consist of structural biologists to guide feature engineering, biophysicists to validate the physical plausibility of AI predictions, computational scientists to architect the deep learning models, and cell biologists to contextualize the findings within macroscale cellular functions. Through iterative, cross-disciplinary feedback loops, the team will refine the AI models, ensuring they are biologically interpretable and mathematically robust. This synthesis strategy will map the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, extracting hidden patterns that isolated single-lab datasets cannot reveal.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will deliver the first unified, AI-driven predictive model capable of decoding the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of biomolecular condensates. This model will allow researchers to input any protein or RNA sequence and accurately predict its propensity to phase separate, its resulting material properties, and its sensitivity to environmental cues. This directly solves a long-standing mystery regarding how mesoscale non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble. Second, by mapping the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, we will uncover novel biological insights into how mesoscale emergence influences higher-order cellular functions, such as stress responses and gene regulation. This predictive capability has profound implications beyond basic science, offering new avenues for biotechnology and therapeutic interventions targeting condensate dysregulation in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Crucially, this project will have a massive impact on workforce development. It will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be cross-trained in molecular biology, cloud computing, and advanced AI methodologies, breaking down traditional disciplinary silos. By convening a transdisciplinary team reflecting diverse scientific perspectives, career stages, geographic locations, and institutional levels, we will tap into diverse new talent and foster a highly collaborative, inclusive research community. Ultimately, the synthesis of these vast, disparate datasets will generate innovative analytical strategies that the broader scientific community can adopt to study other complex emergence phenomena, solidifying NCEMS's vision of understanding mesoscale biological complexity.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed community-scale synthesis project demonstrates a clear and compelling need for NCEMS support, as the required integration of massive, multi-modal datasets and the convening of a transdisciplinary team far exceed the resources and capabilities of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. The requested budget is meticulously aligned with the goals of catalyzing team science, leveraging AI, and training the next-generation workforce. A significant portion of the budget will be allocated to support Working Group convenings. Funds will cover travel, lodging, and logistical expenses for intensive, multi-day collaborative meetings at the NCEMS facility. These face-to-face interactions are critical for breaking down disciplinary silos among our diverse team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computational scientists, and cell biologists, fostering the deep intellectual integration necessary to tackle mesoscale emergence. To execute the computationally intensive AI and machine learning workflows, funds are requested for robust cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud). Training complex Graph Neural Networks and deep learning models on vast proteomics, transcriptomics, and high-throughput imaging datasets requires scalable GPU infrastructure that goes beyond standard institutional clusters. Crucially, the budget includes dedicated support for trainees. Stipends and travel allowances will be provided for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, ensuring they can fully participate in working group meetings and cross-disciplinary co-mentoring activities. This investment is vital for fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train a future data-savvy workforce proficient in both molecular biosciences and advanced data science. Finally, funds are allocated for open science dissemination, including open-access publication fees and data storage costs, ensuring all synthesized datasets and analytical pipelines remain freely accessible to the global scientific community.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Molecular and cellular biology investigates biomolecular condensates formed via liquid liquid phase separation to address missing predictive frameworks. Current research remains fragmented across single lab studies while universal rules governing sequence to emergent property relationships stay unknown. This project develops a predictive systems level model to decipher the grammar of condensates for understanding cellular organization.

The study employs a community scale synthesis project that integrates existing multi omics and imaging datasets using artificial intelligence. The team applies graph neural networks and deep learning regression models alongside convolutional neural networks for image feature extraction. rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the missing predictive framework for how nanoscale molecular interactions scale to form functional mesoscale biomolecular condensate structures. The study employs graph neural networks and deep learning to synthesize heterogeneous multi omics and imaging data into a unified model. This project provides the first comprehensive grammar of sequence to emergent property relationships to explain cellular organization and disease.

title: Emergence of Cellular Morphology from Cytoskeletal Crosstalk and Motor Protein Dynamics

original.abstract: The dynamic interplay between actin filaments and microtubules drives the emergence of complex cellular morphologies, representing a fundamental example of mesoscale biological organization. While the individual components of the cytoskeleton have been studied exhaustively, the emergent properties arising from their large-scale crosstalk remain a critical puzzle in cellular biomechanics. This mesoscale emergence dictates essential cellular outcomes, including directed migration, division, and mechanosensing. Understanding how these distinct biopolymer networks coordinate via crosslinking proteins and molecular motors to generate global cellular forces is essential for advancing our knowledge of cellular emergence. Currently, the field lacks a comprehensive model that integrates molecular-level motor kinetics with whole-cell morphological changes. To bridge this gap, our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent mechanics of cytoskeletal crosstalk. We will aggregate and synthesize publicly available cryo-electron tomography datasets, live-cell super-resolution microscopy archives, and biophysical force-measurement databases from repositories such as EMPIAR and the Cell Image Library. By leveraging topological data analysis and agent-based machine learning models, we will simulate and analyze the emergent network topologies without generating any new experimental data. This data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local cytoskeletal interactions produce global, mesoscale cellular architectures. Addressing this multi-scale problem requires resources and collaborative infrastructure that far exceed the capabilities of a single research group, making NCEMS support indispensable. Our working group will unite a diverse cohort of polymer physicists, structural biologists, computational mechanobiologists, and live-cell imaging experts. We have specifically recruited team members from various geographic locations and institutional backgrounds to ensure a wide range of scientific perspectives. This diversity will stimulate cross-disciplinary innovation, allowing us to tackle this long-standing puzzle from multiple angles. Furthermore, this project is deeply committed to training the next generation of researchers. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive unparalleled cross-training in computational modeling, big data synthesis, and complex systems theory. By working in a highly collaborative team, trainees will develop the skills necessary to lead the future of data-savvy biological research. We are fully committed to gold-standard open science practices; all integrated datasets, simulation codebases, and analytical workflows will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. Through this synthesis, we will illuminate how nanoscale molecular motors and biopolymers orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale forces, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to uncover the fundamental rules of biological emergence.
original.background_and_significance: The spatial and temporal organization of the cytoskeleton is a quintessential example of mesoscale biological emergence. At the fundamental level, individual biopolymers—primarily actin filaments and microtubules—and their associated motor proteins operate through well-defined thermodynamic and kinetic principles. However, when these nanoscale components interact en masse, they give rise to highly complex, unexpected global properties that govern whole-cell morphology, directed migration, mechanosensing, and cell division. This leap from molecular interactions to cellular-scale architecture represents a critical frontier in the molecular and cellular biosciences. While decades of reductionist studies have exhaustively characterized the isolated mechanics of actin and microtubules, the synergistic crosstalk between these two distinct networks remains a profound puzzle. Crosslinking proteins and molecular motors physically and biochemically couple these networks, creating a dynamic, force-generating composite material. Understanding how local, transient interactions within this composite drive the emergence of global cellular forces and architectures is essential for decoding the physical rules of life. Currently, the field suffers from a profound fragmentation of knowledge. Structural biologists generate high-resolution cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) maps of cytoskeletal intersections; biophysicists measure localized traction forces; and cell biologists capture dynamic morphological changes using live-cell super-resolution microscopy. These datasets are siloed across distinct repositories and disciplines. Consequently, we lack a comprehensive, predictive model that bridges the gap between nanoscale molecular motor kinetics and mesoscale cytoskeletal network topologies. This fragmentation hinders our ability to answer fundamental questions about how cellular morphology emerges and adapts to environmental mechanical cues. The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) is uniquely positioned to address this grand challenge. We propose a community-scale synthesis project that leverages the unprecedented volume of publicly available data to decode the emergent mechanics of cytoskeletal crosstalk. By integrating structural, dynamic, and biophysical datasets, we will uncover the universal principles governing mesoscale cytoskeletal emergence. This project is highly significant for several reasons. First, it addresses a long-standing mystery in cellular biomechanics by shifting the focus from individual filaments to emergent network properties. Second, it develops innovative analytical strategies, specifically bridging topological data analysis with agent-based machine learning, to synthesize disparate multiscale data types. Third, it directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale. This synthesis cannot be achieved by a single laboratory; it requires the concerted effort of a transdisciplinary team capable of managing massive datasets, developing novel computational frameworks, and interpreting complex biological phenomena. By synthesizing existing knowledge, we will catalyze a paradigm shift in how we understand the emergence of cellular form and function, providing a foundational framework for future research in mechanobiology, developmental biology, and synthetic biology.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our proposed synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective to understand how nanoscale interactions between actin filaments, microtubules, and motor proteins coordinate to produce the mesoscale emergent property of whole-cell morphology. To achieve this, our transdisciplinary working group will address three compelling, interrelated research questions, each accompanied by specific, testable hypotheses derived from the synthesis of existing publicly available datasets.

Question 1: What are the universal topological motifs that define actin-microtubule crosstalk, and how do they scale to determine global cellular architecture?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that despite the vast diversity of cellular morphologies, actin-microtubule intersections organize into a finite set of conserved, mesoscale topological motifs. Furthermore, we posit that the frequency and spatial distribution of these motifs act as the primary determinants of global cytoskeletal network architecture, dictating whether a cell adopts a polarized (migratory) or symmetric (stationary) morphology. By applying topological data analysis (TDA) to aggregated cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and super-resolution microscopy datasets, we expect to identify and classify these emergent structural motifs across diverse cell types.

Question 2: How do the kinetic parameters of molecular motors and crosslinking proteins govern the emergence of mesoscale force generation and tension distribution within the composite cytoskeletal network?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the non-linear emergence of whole-cell mechanical forces is driven by the collective, cooperative kinetics of motor proteins acting at actin-microtubule intersections, rather than the simple additive forces of individual motors. We predict that specific kinetic thresholds of motor activity trigger phase transitions in the network, shifting it from a fluid-like, disorganized state to a solid-like, force-transmitting state. By synthesizing biophysical force-measurement databases with live-cell imaging archives, and utilizing agent-based machine learning models, we will test how varying motor kinetics predict these emergent mechanical phase transitions.

Question 3: In what ways do external spatial constraints and mechanical boundaries influence the emergent self-organization of the cytoskeletal composite?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the mesoscale emergence of cytoskeletal crosstalk is highly sensitive to external boundary conditions, such that identical molecular components will self-organize into distinctly different macroscopic architectures depending on the geometric constraints of the cellular microenvironment. We anticipate that machine learning models trained on datasets of cells in various micro-patterned environments will reveal a predictable relationship between external geometry and the emergent internal topology of the actin-microtubule network.

By addressing these questions, our working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how cells reliably generate complex, robust shapes from highly dynamic, stochastic molecular components. These questions deliberately avoid generating new experimental data, focusing instead on extracting deeper, broader insights from the wealth of fragmented data already available. The answers will illuminate the fundamental rules of biological emergence at the mesoscale, providing a predictive understanding of how molecular-level alterations—such as mutations in motor proteins or crosslinkers—propagate upward to cause catastrophic failures in cellular morphology and function.
original.methods_and_approach:
This project strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of utilizing only existing, publicly available data. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, our methodological innovation lies in the community-scale synthesis and integration of distinct, multiscale datasets to uncover emergent mesoscale phenomena. Our transdisciplinary approach combines advanced data harvesting, topological data analysis (TDA), and agent-based machine learning (ML).

Data Aggregation and Curation: We will systematically mine, aggregate, and standardize datasets from major public repositories. High-resolution structural data of cytoskeletal intersections will be sourced from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Mesoscale dynamic imaging of actin and microtubule networks will be harvested from the Cell Image Library, the Allen Cell Explorer, and the BioImage Archive. Biophysical traction force microscopy and optical tweezer datasets will be compiled from published supplementary materials and data repositories like Zenodo and Dryad. A dedicated team of data scientists and structural biologists will develop automated pipelines to standardize metadata, harmonize spatial resolutions, and align temporal scales across these diverse data types, creating a unified, queryable database of cytoskeletal crosstalk.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA): To extract meaningful structural motifs from noisy, complex cryo-ET and super-resolution datasets, we will employ TDA, specifically persistent homology. TDA is uniquely suited for biological mesoscale synthesis because it identifies robust geometric and topological features—such as loops, voids, and connected components—that persist across different spatial scales. By applying TDA to our synthesized structural database, we will quantify the connectivity and topology of actin-microtubule networks, identifying the conserved mesoscale motifs proposed in our hypotheses. This approach translates qualitative images into rigorous, quantifiable topological landscapes.

Agent-Based Machine Learning Models: To understand the dynamic emergence of cellular forces, we will develop spatially explicit, agent-based ML models. In these models, actin filaments, microtubules, crosslinkers, and motor proteins will act as individual agents governed by rules derived from the synthesized biophysical and kinetic data. We will use reinforcement learning algorithms to train these models on the live-cell imaging and traction force datasets. The ML models will simulate how local interactions (agent behaviors) self-organize to produce the global network topologies identified by TDA. By perturbing in silico motor kinetics or crosslinker densities, we can predict the resulting changes in mesoscale morphology and force generation, validating our hypotheses regarding mechanical phase transitions.

Working Group Structure and Collaboration: The complexity of this synthesis requires diverse scientific perspectives. Our working group consists of polymer physicists, structural biologists, computational mechanobiologists, and live-cell imaging experts from diverse geographic locations and institutional tiers (including R1 and primarily undergraduate institutions). We will convene for biannual in-person synthesis meetings at NCEMS, supplemented by bi-weekly virtual sprints. Sub-teams will be formed to tackle specific data integration tasks, ensuring cross-pollination of expertise. This transdisciplinary framework ensures that our analytical strategies remain biologically grounded while pushing the boundaries of computational data science, ultimately yielding insights far beyond the reach of any single laboratory.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that significantly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will produce the first comprehensive, multiscale predictive model of cytoskeletal crosstalk. By identifying the universal topological motifs and kinetic thresholds that govern actin-microtubule interactions, we will solve a major, long-standing puzzle regarding the mesoscale emergence of cellular morphology and force generation. This model will allow researchers to predict how molecular-level perturbations—such as those occurring in neurodegenerative diseases or cancer metastasis—cascade into global cellular dysfunction.

Second, we will generate a massive, harmonized, and publicly accessible database of cytoskeletal structural and biophysical data. This resource, alongside our novel analytical pipelines combining Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and agent-based machine learning, will provide the broader scientific community with innovative tools to investigate other complex, emergent mesoscale phenomena.

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact on human capital and workforce development will be profound. Our working group places a premium on training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will be fully integrated into the project, receiving cross-disciplinary mentorship from leading experts in polymer physics, structural biology, and computational data science. Trainees will acquire highly transferable skills in big data synthesis, machine learning, and complex systems modeling—expertise that is critically needed in the modern biological workforce. By intentionally recruiting diverse talent from various institutional backgrounds, including underrepresented groups in STEM, we will tap into diverse new talent pools and foster a more inclusive scientific community. Ultimately, this project will catalyze a paradigm shift, demonstrating the immense power of community-scale data synthesis to answer fundamental biological questions without generating a single new experimental data point, perfectly fulfilling the NCEMS mission.
original.budget_and_resources:
The proposed synthesis project requires a scale of collaborative infrastructure, computational power, and transdisciplinary coordination that fundamentally exceeds the capabilities and resources of any single research laboratory. Therefore, NCEMS support is indispensable for our success.

The requested budget is meticulously aligned with the goals of community-scale synthesis and workforce training. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to supporting the personnel essential for this work, specifically funding full-time postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. These trainees will serve as the engine of our data aggregation and computational modeling efforts, receiving unparalleled cross-training in biological data science.

To stimulate robust cross-disciplinary collaboration, funds are requested to support biannual, intensive in-person working group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These face-to-face synthesis sessions are critical for bridging disciplinary vocabularies, aligning analytical strategies between structural biologists and polymer physicists, and fostering team cohesion. Additionally, we budget for virtual collaboration tools and platforms to maintain momentum during bi-weekly remote sprints.

Given the massive volume of cryo-ET, super-resolution microscopy, and biophysical datasets we will synthesize, substantial resources are allocated for high-performance cloud computing and scalable data storage. These computational resources are necessary to train our agent-based machine learning models and execute computationally heavy topological data analyses on large-scale topological landscapes.

Finally, the budget includes allocations for open access publication fees and costs associated with hosting our harmonized databases on open-access repositories. We also request travel funds for trainees to present our synthesized findings at major national and international conferences, ensuring the broad dissemination of our novel analytical strategies and biological insights. By providing the necessary financial and logistical framework, NCEMS will enable our diverse team to successfully tackle this complex, multiscale puzzle and train the future data-savvy scientific workforce.

Current knowledge characterizes individual filaments well but fails to explain the emergent properties arising from their synergistic crosstalk. The study design aggregates and analyzes existing public data through computational modeling without generating any new experimental data. Key methods include topological data analysis to identify structural motifs and agent based machine learning models for simulations. Results are validated by predicting how perturbations in motor kinetics or crosslinker densities affect mesoscale morphology and force.
