rephrased.main_idea: This research investigates how molecular interactions within the cytoskeleton generate emergent cellular architectures to address the lack of multiscale models. The study employs topological data analysis and agent based machine learning to synthesize fragmented biological data into coherent mechanical frameworks. This project provides a novel computational resource that maps universal topological motifs governing the transition from molecular kinetics to morphology.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Properties of Chromatin Topology and Epigenetic Memory

original.abstract: The three-dimensional folding of the genome into topologically associating domains represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence that fundamentally regulates gene expression and cellular identity. While one-dimensional epigenetic marks and isolated chromatin looping events are well-documented, the rules governing how these local interactions scale up to form stable, mesoscale chromatin architectures remain a major unresolved puzzle. This emergence of higher-order chromatin structure from linear DNA sequences and localized protein binding dictates critical subcellular outcomes, including cell fate determination and epigenetic memory. The lack of a unified understanding of this mesoscale phenomenon stems from the historical siloing of genomic, structural, and transcriptomic data. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis initiative to resolve the emergent properties of chromatin topology. We will systematically integrate massive volumes of publicly available Hi-C, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq data from international consortia such as ENCODE, the 4D Nucleome Project, and the Gene Expression Omnibus. By employing advanced transformer-based deep learning models and graph convolutional networks, we will synthesize these distinct, multi-omics datasets to predict the emergence of 3D chromatin structures from 1D sequence data, entirely utilizing existing public data. This innovative analytical strategy will uncover the hidden grammar of mesoscale genome organization. The sheer volume and complexity of this multi-omics integration necessitate the unique collaborative environment and computational resources provided by NCEMS. No single laboratory possesses the interdisciplinary expertise required to bridge genomics, polymer physics, and advanced artificial intelligence. Our team brings together computational genomicists, biophysicists, machine learning engineers, and developmental biologists from diverse institutions and career stages. This collaborative partnership will tap into diverse new talent, fostering an inclusive environment that drives novel scientific insights. A core component of our proposal is the rigorous training of the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a transdisciplinary mentoring network, acquiring highly sought-after skills in deep learning, genomic data science, and reproducible research workflows. We will strictly adhere to community-created policies on open science, ensuring that all code, trained AI models, and synthesized chromatin interaction maps are freely accessible via public repositories. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our working group will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale chromatin domains influences global transcriptional programs, thereby answering long-standing questions about the physical basis of epigenetic memory and cellular emergence.
original.background_and_significance: The spatial organization of the genome is a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. While linear DNA sequences provide the fundamental blueprint of life, it is the three-dimensional folding of the genome into topologically associating domains (TADs) and higher-order chromatin architectures that dictates gene expression, cellular identity, and epigenetic memory. At the nanoscale, individual transcription factors, histones, and epigenetic modifications interact with DNA. However, the unexpected appearance of stable, megabase-scale chromatin topologies from these localized, nanoscale interactions remains a profound and unresolved mystery in the molecular and cellular biosciences. This mesoscale architecture serves as the physical basis for epigenetic memory, ensuring that cell-type-specific transcriptional programs are faithfully maintained across cell divisions. Historically, the molecular and cellular sciences have approached this complexity by siloing genomic, transcriptomic, and structural data. While international consortia such as ENCODE, the 4D Nucleome Project, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) have generated massive, publicly available datasets detailing one-dimensional epigenetic marks (ChIP-seq), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), gene expression (RNA-seq), and three-dimensional chromatin interactions (Hi-C), these distinct data modalities have rarely been integrated at a community scale. Consequently, we lack a unified, predictive understanding of the 'hidden grammar' governing how 1D sequence and epigenetic features coalesce into 3D mesoscale structures. This gap in knowledge is not due to a lack of data, but rather a lack of transdisciplinary synthesis. Addressing this challenge requires an approach that transcends the capabilities of any single research laboratory. It necessitates the convergence of computational genomics, polymer physics, developmental biology, and advanced artificial intelligence to synthesize disparate datasets into a cohesive model of chromatin emergence. The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) is uniquely positioned to catalyze this initiative. By leveraging NCEMS's resources, our working group will conduct a community-scale synthesis project that relies entirely on existing, publicly available data. We will move beyond isolated, single-assay analyses to uncover the fundamental rules of chromatin topology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is highly significant; it will not only solve long-standing puzzles regarding the physical mechanisms of epigenetic memory but also provide a predictive framework for how sequence variations and epigenetic perturbations cascade into altered 3D topologies and aberrant cellular phenotypes. Ultimately, this synthesis will transform our conceptual understanding of the genome from a static linear sequence into a dynamic, emergent mesoscale machine, driving novel discoveries in cellular biology and answering compelling questions about the fundamental nature of cellular emergence and identity.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our proposed working group will tackle fundamental mysteries surrounding the emergent properties of chromatin topology and epigenetic memory through the synthesis of multi-omics data. The overarching objective is to decode the rules by which 1D genomic and epigenomic features scale up to form 3D mesoscale chromatin architectures, and how these structures dictate global transcriptional outcomes. To achieve this, we have formulated three primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses. Question 1: What is the underlying 'hidden grammar' that dictates the emergence of topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops from linear DNA sequences and localized epigenetic marks? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the emergence of stable mesoscale chromatin topology is governed by a complex, non-linear combinatorial code of transcription factor binding motifs, histone modifications, and DNA accessibility patterns. By synthesizing ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and Hi-C data using advanced deep learning models, we predict that distinct, quantifiable combinations of these 1D features are sufficient to accurately predict 3D chromatin folding patterns across diverse cell types. Question 2: How do dynamic changes in this mesoscale chromatin architecture facilitate the establishment and maintenance of epigenetic memory during cell fate determination? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that epigenetic memory is physically encoded within the stability and persistence of specific TAD boundaries and intra-TAD interactions. We postulate that during cellular differentiation, transient changes in 1D epigenetic marks trigger localized phase separations and polymer restructuring, which subsequently lock into stable 3D conformations. Through the longitudinal synthesis of time-course RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and Hi-C datasets from public repositories, we expect to demonstrate that the maintenance of these emergent 3D structures is the primary driver of sustained cell-type-specific transcriptional programs across cell divisions. Question 3: Can artificial intelligence and graph-based models uncover previously unrecognized, higher-order principles of chromatin organization that are conserved across different biological scales and species? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the structural rules governing mesoscale chromatin emergence are evolutionarily conserved and can be mathematically represented as interconnected networks. We predict that by employing graph convolutional networks to model chromatin interactions as complex systems, we will identify universal topological motifs—analogous to structural domains in proteins—that are fundamental to genome organization but remain undetected by traditional pairwise interaction analyses. These questions align perfectly with the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale. By addressing these questions, our collaborative working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the physical and informational basis of the genome. We are not generating new experimental data; rather, we are asking novel, transformative questions that can only be answered through the community-scale synthesis of vast, previously siloed datasets. This inquiry will fundamentally shift the paradigm of molecular biology from a reductionist view of isolated genomic elements to a holistic understanding of the genome as a complex, emergent mesoscale system.
original.methods_and_approach: This community-scale synthesis project relies exclusively on the integration and analysis of existing, publicly available data, adhering strictly to NCEMS guidelines. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, our approach leverages massive volumes of multi-omics data sourced from premier international repositories, including the ENCODE Consortium, the 4D Nucleome Project, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The core datasets will comprise Hi-C (for 3D chromatin interactions), ChIP-seq (for histone modifications and transcription factor binding), ATAC-seq (for chromatin accessibility), and RNA-seq (for transcriptomic output) across a diverse array of human and murine cell lines and developmental stages. Our methodological framework is divided into three integrated phases: Data Harmonization, Deep Learning Synthesis, and Topological Network Analysis. In the Data Harmonization phase, we will develop a standardized computational pipeline to process, normalize, and align disparate multi-omics datasets into a unified coordinate system. Given the inherent noise and batch effects in public data, this phase requires the combined expertise of our computational genomicists and biophysicists to ensure that the integrated data accurately reflects biological reality rather than technical artifacts. The Deep Learning Synthesis phase represents the analytical core of our project. We will employ advanced transformer-based deep learning models, originally designed for natural language processing, to decipher the 'hidden grammar' of the genome. These models will be trained to treat the 1D genome (sequence, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq peaks) as a sequence of 'words' and predict the resulting 3D Hi-C contact matrices as the emergent 'sentences' or mesoscale structures. The self-attention mechanisms inherent in transformer architectures are uniquely suited to capture long-range genomic dependencies, allowing us to model how distant regulatory elements interact in three-dimensional space. In the Topological Network Analysis phase, we will utilize Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). By representing the genome as a massive spatial graph—where genomic bins are nodes and 3D interactions are edges—GCNs will enable us to identify higher-order topological motifs and community structures that define epigenetic memory. Our machine learning engineers will collaborate closely with developmental biologists to map these emergent graph structures onto cellular phenotypes and gene expression profiles derived from the RNA-seq data. This ambitious analytical strategy is beyond the capabilities of most individual research labs and necessitates the transdisciplinary collaboration fostered by NCEMS. Our team bridges the gap between biological theory and computational execution. Through regular working group meetings, hackathons, and virtual collaborations, we will iteratively refine our models. Furthermore, this approach provides an unparalleled training environment. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in this multi-disciplinary matrix, gaining hands-on, highly sought-after expertise in genomic data science, AI model training, and the synthesis of complex mesoscale biological systems, thereby cultivating the next generation of data-savvy molecular bioscience researchers.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. First, we will produce a unified, predictive AI model capable of accurately generating 3D chromatin interaction maps from widely available 1D genomic and epigenomic data. This tool will democratize 3D genomics, allowing researchers worldwide to infer complex chromatin topologies without the need for costly and technically demanding Hi-C experiments. Second, our synthesis will yield a comprehensive atlas of emergent topological motifs that govern epigenetic memory across various cell types and developmental stages. By mapping the 'hidden grammar' of the genome, we will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how linear DNA sequences dictate complex subcellular outcomes and cellular identities. Beyond scientific discovery, the impact of this project extends to methodological innovation and workforce development. We will pioneer the application of transformer-based architectures and Graph Convolutional Networks in the context of multi-omics data synthesis, establishing new analytical standards for the field. Furthermore, the insights gained into the physical basis of epigenetic memory will have broad implications for understanding cellular reprogramming, developmental disorders, and diseases characterized by topological dysfunction, such as cancer. By providing a predictive framework for chromatin folding, our work will empower the broader scientific community to formulate novel hypotheses regarding genome regulation. Crucially, this working group will serve as a premier training incubator. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers within a transdisciplinary, multi-institutional team, we will cultivate a diverse, new generation of data-savvy scientists. These trainees will emerge with dual expertise in deep learning and molecular biology, perfectly positioned to lead the future of computational biosciences. Ultimately, by leveraging the unique collaborative environment of NCEMS to synthesize existing public data, our project will catalyze a paradigm shift, illuminating how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale chromatin domains drives the fundamental mechanics of life.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project demonstrates a clear and absolute need for NCEMS support, as the scale of data integration and the required transdisciplinary collaboration far exceed the resources of any single laboratory. Since our research relies entirely on existing publicly available data, our budget includes zero capital for wet-lab equipment, reagents, or new data generation. Instead, the budget is strategically allocated toward computational infrastructure, human capital, and fostering collaborative partnerships. The primary resource requirement is high-performance computing (HPC). Training advanced transformer models and Graph Convolutional Networks on massive, multi-omics datasets (terabytes of Hi-C, ChIP-seq, and RNA-seq data) necessitates significant GPU and CPU resources. We request funding for cloud computing credits and access to NCEMS-affiliated supercomputing clusters to facilitate rapid model iteration and data storage. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to training the future data-savvy workforce. We request stipend and tuition support for three graduate students and salary support for two postdoctoral researchers. These trainees represent diverse geographic locations and institutional research levels, ensuring we tap into diverse new talent. Their funding is critical, as they will be the primary engines of data synthesis, code development, and model evaluation under the mentorship of our cross-disciplinary principal investigators. Finally, we request resources to support the collaborative infrastructure of the Working Group. This includes travel and accommodation funds for bi-annual, in-person synthesis meetings at the NCEMS facility, which are essential for deep, cross-disciplinary brainstorming between our biophysicists, computational genomicists, and developmental biologists. Additional funds are allocated for open-access publication fees and the hosting of virtual workshops to disseminate our open-source tools, ensuring our findings achieve maximum reach and impact within the molecular and cellular biosciences community.

title: Emergence of Metabolic Adaptation through Mitochondrial Reticular Network Dynamics

original.abstract: Mitochondria are not isolated organelles but exist as dynamic, interconnected reticular networks whose emergent properties dictate cellular metabolism, apoptosis, and stress resistance. The continuous cycle of mitochondrial fusion and fission creates a mesoscale network that is highly responsive to environmental cues. However, the exact mechanisms by which localized protein interactions at the mitochondrial membrane scale up to alter the global topology and metabolic output of the entire network remain a fundamental mystery in cellular biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is crucial for deciphering how cells dynamically adapt their energy production to meet fluctuating demands. Our working group aims to solve this long-standing puzzle through a community-scale synthesis of mitochondrial dynamics. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including high-resolution volumetric electron microscopy from the OpenOrganelle database, live-cell fluorescence imaging from the Image Data Resource, and comprehensive metabolomics profiles from the Metabolomics Workbench. To analyze this complex, multi-modal data without generating new experiments, we will develop novel computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools. Using reinforcement learning and deep neural networks, we will model how local fusion and fission events cascade to produce emergent, cell-wide metabolic states. This project requires the integration of structural imaging with functional metabolomics at a scale that is impossible for a single research lab, making the support of NCEMS absolutely vital. We will assemble a transdisciplinary team comprising cell biologists, network theorists, computer vision experts, and metabolic modelers. Our working group is structured to promote collaborative partnerships across different geographic locations and institutional research levels, ensuring a rich diversity of scientific thought. This environment will be instrumental in stimulating the cross-disciplinary collaboration necessary to tackle complex mesoscale phenomena. Furthermore, our project places a strong emphasis on training the next generation of scientists. Trainees, including graduate students and postdocs, will be cross-trained in advanced image processing, network theory, and multi-omics integration, preparing them to be leaders in data-intensive biology. In alignment with gold-standard open science practices, all synthesized network topologies, AI algorithms, and metabolic models will be distributed through open-source platforms like GitHub. By illuminating the relationship between mesoscale network architecture and macroscale cellular metabolism, this synthesis project will directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
original.background_and_significance: Mitochondria have traditionally been depicted as isolated, static organelles, often colloquially referred to as the powerhouses of the cell. However, contemporary molecular and cellular biology reveals a starkly different reality: mitochondria exist as highly dynamic, interconnected reticular networks. This complex architecture undergoes continuous remodeling through coordinated cycles of membrane fusion and fission, driven by specialized dynamin-related GTPases. These localized, nanoscale protein interactions at the mitochondrial membrane scale up to dictate the global topology of the mitochondrial network. This topological configuration is a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where the collective behavior of molecular components generates a higher-order structural and functional state intermediate between individual biomolecules and the entire cell. The emergent properties of this mesoscale network are profoundly significant, as they dictate critical cellular outcomes, including metabolic efficiency, apoptosis, and stress resistance. Despite the availability of vast amounts of data, the precise mechanistic rules governing how localized fusion and fission events cascade to alter the global network topology, and subsequently, the metabolic output of the cell, remain a fundamental mystery. Resolving this long-standing puzzle requires a conceptual shift from reductionist single-protein studies to a systems-level understanding of mesoscale network dynamics. Currently, the scientific community possesses a wealth of publicly available, high-quality data spanning multiple modalities. High-resolution volumetric electron microscopy datasets, such as those housed in the OpenOrganelle database, provide unprecedented ultrastructural detail of mitochondrial networks. Concurrently, repositories like the Image Data Resource offer extensive live-cell fluorescence imaging, capturing the temporal dynamics of mitochondrial remodeling. Furthermore, the Metabolomics Workbench contains comprehensive profiles of cellular metabolic states under various physiological and pathological conditions. However, these rich datasets remain largely siloed. No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, diverse biological expertise, and methodological breadth required to integrate these disparate data types into a cohesive model of mesoscale emergence. This fragmentation represents a critical bottleneck in our understanding of cellular bioenergetics. Our proposed synthesis project directly addresses this gap by leveraging the unique support and resources of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). By synthesizing these existing, multimodal datasets without generating new experimental data, we aim to uncover the hidden rules of mitochondrial network emergence. This project is highly significant because it will not only elucidate the fundamental principles of metabolic adaptation but also pioneer innovative analytical strategies for integrating structural, temporal, and functional data. The insights gained will transform our understanding of how cells dynamically adapt their energy production to meet fluctuating environmental demands, with broad implications for aging, neurodegeneration, and metabolic diseases. By catalyzing a transdisciplinary collaboration among cell biologists, network theorists, computer vision experts, and metabolic modelers, this synthesis effort will push the boundaries of molecular and cellular biosciences, firmly establishing the mesoscale as a critical frontier for biological discovery and fulfilling the core mission of NCEMS.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective to understand how local molecular interactions at the mitochondrial membrane generate emergent mesoscale network topologies that dictate cellular metabolic states. To achieve this, we have formulated three compelling, interconnected research questions and corresponding hypotheses that can be rigorously tested through the synthesis and integration of publicly available structural, dynamic, and metabolic datasets. Question 1: What are the quantitative topological signatures of mitochondrial reticular networks that reliably predict distinct cellular metabolic states? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that mitochondrial networks exhibit specific, quantifiable mesoscale topological motifs, such as varying degrees of branching, node connectivity, and spatial clustering, that directly correlate with specific metabolic profiles. By synthesizing volumetric electron microscopy data from OpenOrganelle with corresponding metabolomics data from the Metabolomics Workbench, we expect to identify emergent structural phenotypes that serve as physical manifestations of metabolic adaptation. Question 2: How do localized, nanoscale fusion and fission events cascade through the mitochondrial network to induce global, mesoscale topological transitions? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that mitochondrial network remodeling is not a random process but follows principles of self-organized criticality, where local fission or fusion events alter the membrane tension and biochemical signaling of adjacent network nodes, triggering a cascading effect. By applying advanced spatial network analysis and computer vision algorithms to live-cell fluorescence imaging from the Image Data Resource, we predict that we can map these temporal cascades. We anticipate discovering that specific environmental stressors or metabolic demands lower the activation energy for these cascades, driving the network toward a hyper-fused or fragmented emergent state to optimize energy distribution or isolate damaged components. Question 3: Can the emergent metabolic output of a cell be accurately predicted based solely on the dynamic restructuring of its mitochondrial mesoscale network? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the relationship between mitochondrial network dynamics and cellular metabolism is deterministic and can be modeled using advanced artificial intelligence. Specifically, we posit that deep neural networks and reinforcement learning algorithms, trained on our synthesized multimodal datasets, can decode the complex mapping between mesoscale architectural changes and macroscale metabolic shifts. We expect these models to demonstrate that the emergent properties of the network, rather than the absolute abundance of metabolic enzymes, are the primary drivers of metabolic plasticity. By addressing these novel questions, our working group aims to solve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences: the mechanistic link between organelle form and cellular function. The synthesis of disparate datasets will allow us to test these hypotheses at a scale and depth previously unattainable. Exploring these questions requires a departure from traditional, isolated experimental approaches, demanding instead a community-scale synthesis effort. The resulting answers will not only elucidate the fundamental rules of mitochondrial emergence but also establish a new paradigm for understanding how mesoscale physical architectures govern biochemical processes, directly aligning with the NCEMS mission to uncover unexpected biological system properties.
original.methods_and_approach: To investigate the emergent properties of mitochondrial reticular networks, our working group will execute a community-scale synthesis project relying exclusively on existing, publicly available datasets. Our approach integrates multimodal data through a novel computational pipeline, requiring zero new experimental data generation, thereby strictly adhering to NCEMS funding requirements. The methodology is structured around three integrated analytical pillars executed by a transdisciplinary team of cell biologists, network theorists, computer vision experts, and metabolic modelers. Data Acquisition and Curation: We will systematically harvest and curate data from three primary repositories. First, we will extract high-resolution, three-dimensional volumetric electron microscopy datasets from the OpenOrganelle database to capture the precise ultrastructural topology of mitochondrial networks across diverse cell types. Second, we will mine the Image Data Resource for high-frequency, live-cell fluorescence microscopy time-lapses to capture the temporal dynamics of mitochondrial fusion and fission. Third, we will retrieve steady-state and fluxomics data from the Metabolomics Workbench, focusing on datasets derived from cell lines and conditions matching our imaging data. Computational Vision and Spatial Network Extraction: To translate raw imaging data into quantifiable mesoscale architectures, our computer vision experts will develop and deploy advanced deep learning segmentation models. Once segmented, the mitochondrial networks will be skeletonized and converted into spatial graphs. In these graphs, nodes will represent mitochondrial junctions or endpoints, and edges will represent the connecting tubules. Network theorists will then compute a comprehensive suite of topological metrics, including degree distribution, betweenness centrality, clustering coefficients, and spatial reach, effectively digitizing the mesoscale architecture of the mitochondria into mathematically rigorous formats. AI-Driven Multimodal Synthesis and Modeling: The core of our synthesis effort lies in linking these topological graphs to metabolic outputs using artificial intelligence. We will utilize deep neural networks to perform canonical correlation analysis, bridging the structural features extracted from OpenOrganelle and the Image Data Resource with the biochemical profiles from the Metabolomics Workbench. To model the temporal emergence of these networks, we will employ reinforcement learning frameworks. The reinforcement learning agents will be trained to simulate localized fusion and fission events, learning the rules of network remodeling by optimizing for the observed global topological states found in the live-cell time-lapses. This will allow us to model how local perturbations cascade into cell-wide metabolic adaptations. Working Group Structure and Collaboration: This ambitious synthesis is beyond the capabilities of any single research lab. We will assemble a geographically diverse working group comprising principal investigators and trainees from research-intensive institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and computational research centers. The team will meet bi-weekly virtually and convene for bi-annual intensive hackathons at the NCEMS headquarters. This collaborative structure ensures a rich diversity of scientific perspectives, fostering the cross-pollination of ideas necessary to develop these innovative analytical strategies. Trainees will be deeply embedded in this process, receiving hands-on cross-training in multi-omics integration, graph theory, and deep learning, thereby cultivating the next generation of data-savvy biological scientists.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to illuminate mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. Scientifically, we will solve a long-standing puzzle by mapping the precise mechanistic relationship between localized mitochondrial membrane dynamics, global network topology, and cellular metabolic states. By defining the topological signatures of metabolic adaptation, we will provide a novel conceptual framework that shifts the paradigm from organelle-as-entity to organelle-as-network. Methodologically, we will deliver a suite of innovative, validated analytical strategies. Our project will produce novel computer vision algorithms optimized for three-dimensional organelle segmentation and spatial network extraction, alongside pioneering reinforcement learning models capable of simulating mesoscale biological cascades. These tools will be adaptable for studying other reticular organelles, such as the endoplasmic reticulum, broadly impacting the field of systems biology. The impact on the scientific workforce will be equally profound. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers within a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary working group, we will explicitly train the future data-savvy workforce. Trainees will gain rare, dual expertise in cellular biology and advanced computational data science, positioning them as future leaders in data-intensive biological research. Furthermore, this project demonstrates the immense, untapped potential of synthesizing existing, siloed public data. By successfully integrating structural imaging from OpenOrganelle, temporal dynamics from the Image Data Resource, and biochemical data from Metabolomics Workbench, we will showcase a cost-effective, high-impact model for biological discovery. Ultimately, the insights generated into how cells dynamically adapt their energy production will provide foundational knowledge with long-term translational potential for understanding metabolic diseases, aging, and neurodegeneration, solidifying the critical role of mesoscale emergence in health and disease.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project requires specific, targeted resources that go far beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory or traditional collaborative grant, making NCEMS support absolutely vital. Because this project relies entirely on synthesizing existing publicly available data, exactly zero percent of the budget will be allocated to experimental reagents, laboratory equipment, or new data generation. The primary budget allocation will support the human capital and collaborative infrastructure necessary for transdisciplinary synthesis. Funds will be dedicated to supporting our trainees, graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, who will be the primary drivers of data integration and algorithm development. This investment directly fulfills the NCEMS mandate to train the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. A significant portion of the budget is requested to facilitate the Working Group collaborative activities. This includes travel, lodging, and logistical support for bi-annual, intensive, multi-day hackathons and synthesis meetings held at the NCEMS headquarters. These in-person convenings are critical for bridging the disciplinary languages of cell biologists, network theorists, and artificial intelligence experts, fostering the deep intellectual integration required to solve complex mesoscale puzzles. Finally, we request funds for essential computational resources. While the data is publicly available, the synthesis, storage, and processing of massive volumetric electron microscopy datasets and the training of deep neural networks require substantial computational power. The budget will cover cloud computing instances equipped with high-performance graphics processing units necessary for computer vision and reinforcement learning tasks. Funds will also support open science publication fees and the long-term hosting of our interactive data portals. This resource allocation ensures our diverse team has the exact collaborative and computational infrastructure needed to successfully elucidate the emergent properties of mitochondrial networks.

rephrased.standardized_text:

Mitochondria form dynamic networks through fusion and fission but the rules governing how local events influence metabolic states remain unknown. The study determines how local molecular interactions generate emergent network topologies to provide a systems level understanding of energy production.

The study design employs a community scale synthesis of multi modal public datasets using a computational pipeline for modeling. The approach applies computer vision algorithms for image segmentation and spatial network analysis alongside deep neural networks and reinforcement learning. Results are validated by testing the predictive accuracy of the models against the synthesized multi modal datasets.

The project utilizes OpenOrganelle for electron microscopy and Image Data Resource for fluorescence imaging and Metabolomics Workbench for profiles. Data integration occurs by mapping structural features from imaging to biochemical profiles using deep learning based canonical correlation analysis. The proposal does not address the specific milestones or the overall timeline for the completion of this research project. The project scope requires expertise in cell biology and network theory and computer vision and metabolic modeling for success.

All synthesized network topologies and algorithms and metabolic models will be released via open source platforms such as GitHub. The team includes principal investigators and trainees from cell biology and network theory and computer vision and metabolic modeling.
rephrased.main_idea: This research investigates how local molecular interactions at mitochondrial membranes scale to determine emergent network topologies and cellular metabolic states. The study employs a computational pipeline that integrates multi modal public datasets through deep learning and spatial graph theory analysis. This project establishes a novel systems level framework for predicting how mitochondrial network dynamics adapt to regulate global energy production.

title: Decoding the Mesoscale Emergence of Lipid Raft Clustering and Transmembrane Signaling

original.abstract: The plasma membrane is a highly complex, heterogeneous environment where the dynamic clustering of sphingolipids, cholesterol, and specific proteins forms mesoscale domains known as lipid rafts. These transient structures are critical for the emergence of robust transmembrane signaling cascades, yet the biophysical rules governing their assembly and their role in signal amplification remain highly controversial and poorly understood. The transition from chaotic, nanoscale lipid interactions to ordered, mesoscale signaling platforms represents a classic example of biological emergence that dictates higher-order cellular responses to external stimuli. To resolve this long-standing debate, our working group proposes a comprehensive data synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of lipid raft clustering. We will leverage publicly available molecular dynamics simulation trajectories, single-particle tracking datasets, and super-resolution microscopy archives from repositories such as the SRA, PRIDE, and specific biophysical databases. By applying advanced spatio-temporal data mining and unsupervised machine learning algorithms, we will integrate these distinct datasets to identify the universal principles of mesoscale domain formation. This approach relies entirely on existing data, utilizing AI to extract novel insights regarding how local lipid-protein affinities scale up to create functional signaling hubs. The complexity of membrane biophysics combined with the necessity for advanced data science makes this project uniquely suited for NCEMS support. A single laboratory cannot effectively bridge the gap between atomistic simulations and cellular-scale imaging. Therefore, we have assembled a diverse team of computational biophysicists, membrane biologists, data scientists, and systems biologists. Our team composition reflects a commitment to diverse scientific perspectives, incorporating researchers from various career stages and institutional backgrounds to foster innovative problem-solving. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a central pillar of our proposal. Postdocs and graduate students will engage in collaborative research, mastering techniques in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and reproducible scientific programming. We are deeply committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science. All analytical workflows, synthesized datasets, and predictive models will be made publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub, providing the broader community with invaluable tools for membrane research. Ultimately, this project will synthesize disparate biophysical and cellular data to reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale lipid domains drives the emergence of complex cellular signaling networks, fulfilling the core scientific vision of NCEMS.
original.background_and_significance:
The plasma membrane is not merely a passive barrier but a highly dynamic, heterogeneous landscape essential for cellular communication and survival. Central to this dynamism is the concept of lipid rafts—transient, nanoscale assemblies of sphingolipids, cholesterol, and specific membrane proteins. These structures are hypothesized to coalesce into larger, mesoscale domains upon cellular stimulation, serving as critical platforms for the emergence of robust transmembrane signaling cascades. Despite decades of intense study, the biophysical rules governing the assembly of these domains and their precise role in signal amplification remain highly controversial. This controversy stems largely from the methodological limitations of individual disciplines; atomistic molecular dynamics simulations provide high temporal and spatial resolution but are limited to nanoscale phenomena over microseconds, whereas super-resolution microscopy and single-particle tracking offer cellular-scale insights but often lack atomistic detail. Consequently, the transition from chaotic, nanoscale lipid interactions to ordered, mesoscale signaling platforms represents a classic example of biological emergence that has remained fundamentally elusive.

This project directly addresses this long-standing puzzle by proposing a comprehensive, community-scale data synthesis initiative. We argue that the answers to lipid raft emergence do not require new experimental data but rather the intelligent integration of existing, disparate datasets. By synthesizing publicly available molecular dynamics trajectories, single-particle tracking datasets, and super-resolution microscopy archives, we can bridge the spatio-temporal gap that currently divides membrane biophysics. This approach aligns perfectly with the scientific vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We focus squarely on the mesoscale—the critical nexus between individual biomolecules and higher-order subcellular outcomes. Understanding how local lipid-protein affinities scale up to create functional signaling hubs is not just a question of membrane biophysics; it is a fundamental inquiry into how biological systems leverage physical properties to transmit information.

The significance of this work extends beyond resolving a specific biological debate. By establishing a unified framework for mesoscale domain formation, we will provide a predictive model for how diverse external stimuli trigger coordinated cellular responses, which is vital for understanding disease states like cancer and neurodegeneration where signaling is dysregulated. Furthermore, this project pioneers a novel analytical strategy, demonstrating how artificial intelligence and advanced spatio-temporal data mining can synthesize multiscale data. The sheer complexity of membrane biophysics, combined with the massive volume of available data, necessitates a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that goes far beyond the capabilities of a single laboratory. By bringing together computational biophysicists, membrane biologists, data scientists, and systems biologists, we will catalyze the cross-pollination of ideas required to decode the emergent properties of lipid rafts, ultimately advancing our understanding of cellular signaling and establishing a new paradigm for synthesis research in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
To decode the emergent properties of lipid raft clustering and its role in transmembrane signaling, our working group has formulated a series of interconnected research questions and hypotheses that span the nano-to-mesoscale continuum. These questions are designed to be answered exclusively through the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets, leveraging AI to uncover patterns invisible to isolated analyses.

Question 1: What are the universal biophysical rules governing the transition of nanoscale lipid assemblies into stable mesoscale domains? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that mesoscale emergence is not driven by a single lipid-protein interaction but by a cooperative, non-linear scaling of local affinities. Specifically, we posit that critical fluctuations in membrane thickness and local curvature, driven by cholesterol and sphingolipid packing, create energetic funnels that stabilize transient protein clusters. By synthesizing molecular dynamics simulations with super-resolution microscopy data, we expect to identify a critical threshold of local lipid concentration required to trigger spontaneous mesoscale domain formation.

Question 2: How do distinct transmembrane signaling receptors exploit mesoscale lipid domains for signal amplification? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that lipid rafts function as selective allosteric modulators for signaling receptors. Rather than simply concentrating reactants, the unique viscoelastic properties of the mesoscale domain alter the conformational dynamics of embedded kinases and receptors, significantly lowering the activation energy for downstream signaling cascades. We will test this by correlating single-particle tracking data of receptor mobility with structural data from proteomic databases, predicting that receptor dwell times within synthesized raft environments positively correlate with known signal amplification metrics.

Question 3: Can artificial intelligence identify hidden spatio-temporal motifs across disparate experimental modalities that predict functional raft formation? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that unsupervised machine learning algorithms can extract universal 'signatures of emergence'—spatio-temporal patterns of lipid and protein behavior that are conserved across different cell types and experimental techniques. By training AI models on a synthesized dataset comprising molecular dynamics trajectories, single-particle tracking, and super-resolution imaging, we anticipate uncovering previously unrecognized kinetic motifs that dictate whether a nanoscale cluster will dissolve or mature into a functional mesoscale signaling hub.

Question 4: How does the complexity of the surrounding lipidome influence the stability and lifetime of emergent mesoscale structures? 
Hypothesis 4: We hypothesize that the broader lipidomic context acts as a rheostat for mesoscale emergence. Utilizing publicly available lipidomics databases alongside biophysical tracking data, we propose that variations in the saturation index of bulk membrane phospholipids dictate the phase boundary conditions of lipid rafts, thereby controlling their size, lifetime, and signaling capacity. 

This comprehensive framework of questions and hypotheses directly addresses the NCEMS mandate to tackle compelling scientific questions regarding mesoscale emergence. By interrogating these specific areas, our transdisciplinary team will synthesize a cohesive, multiscale model of lipid raft dynamics, transforming our understanding of how cellular membranes process and amplify complex biological information.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach is entirely computational and synthesis-driven, adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. We will execute a comprehensive data synthesis pipeline that integrates atomistic, molecular, and cellular-scale datasets to decode mesoscale emergence. The project is structured into three distinct phases: Data Aggregation, Multiscale Integration, and AI-Driven Pattern Recognition.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will source high-fidelity datasets from established public repositories. Atomistic and coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories of lipid bilayers and membrane proteins will be retrieved from MemProtMD, the ATB, and Zenodo. Single-particle tracking (SPT) datasets capturing receptor diffusion dynamics will be sourced from the SRA and specialized biophysical databases. Super-resolution microscopy archives (e.g., STORM, PALM) detailing protein clustering will be extracted from the BioImage Archive. A dedicated team of data scientists will harmonize these disparate data types, standardizing metadata, spatial coordinates, and temporal resolutions into a unified, cloud-based data lake optimized for high-throughput querying.

Phase 2: Multiscale Spatio-Temporal Integration. Bridging the gap between microsecond MD simulations and millisecond SPT/microscopy data requires innovative analytical strategies. Our computational biophysicists will develop a novel mathematical framework based on hidden Markov models and anomalous diffusion theories. We will extract fundamental biophysical parameters (e.g., lipid packing defects, local curvature, diffusion coefficients) from the MD trajectories and use them to parameterize coarse-grained kinetic models. These models will then be validated against the macroscopic clustering behaviors observed in the SPT and super-resolution datasets. This synthesis will allow us to map nanoscale molecular interactions directly onto mesoscale domain formation, creating a continuous spatio-temporal continuum.

Phase 3: AI-Driven Pattern Recognition and Modeling. To identify the universal principles of mesoscale emergence, we will deploy advanced artificial intelligence algorithms. Unsupervised machine learning, specifically spatio-temporal graph neural networks (ST-GNNs) and deep autoencoders, will be trained on the integrated data lake. These algorithms are uniquely suited to detect hidden, non-linear correlations between lipid composition, protein mobility, and domain clustering across different experimental modalities. The AI models will search for 'signatures of emergence'—specific kinetic and structural motifs that predict the transition from chaotic nanoscale interactions to ordered mesoscale signaling hubs.

Team Composition and Collaboration: This ambitious synthesis requires a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary approach. Our Working Group comprises computational biophysicists (experts in MD and statistical mechanics), membrane biologists (experts in receptor signaling), data scientists (experts in AI and database architecture), and systems biologists. Regular virtual workshops and biannual in-person hackathons will facilitate cross-disciplinary knowledge transfer. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be embedded within these cross-functional teams, receiving hands-on training in big data integration, machine learning, and reproducible scientific programming, thereby cultivating the next generation of data-savvy biological scientists. This robust, multidisciplinary methodology ensures a rigorous investigation of emergent membrane phenomena.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. Primarily, we expect to resolve the long-standing controversy surrounding lipid raft existence and function. By integrating disparate multiscale data, we will deliver the first comprehensive, empirically validated model of mesoscale domain emergence in the plasma membrane. This model will elucidate the precise biophysical rules governing how local lipid-protein affinities scale up to create functional signaling hubs, directly answering a fundamental question of biological emergence.

Beyond the specific biological insights, a major outcome of this project will be the development and release of a novel, AI-driven analytical framework for multiscale data integration. The spatio-temporal graph neural networks and kinetic mapping algorithms we develop will be adaptable to a wide range of other biological systems, providing the broader scientific community with innovative tools to investigate mesoscale phenomena in different cellular contexts.

The impact of this project extends significantly into workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees into our transdisciplinary Working Group, we will train a cohort of graduate students and postdocs who are uniquely fluent in both membrane biophysics and advanced data science. These trainees will emerge as leaders in the future data-savvy workforce, equipped to tackle complex biological puzzles using AI and big data synthesis.

Finally, the insights gained regarding transmembrane signaling amplification will have profound broader impacts on human health. Understanding the emergent properties of signaling platforms is crucial for deciphering the molecular basis of numerous diseases, including cancer and neurodegeneration, where membrane signaling is frequently dysregulated. By fulfilling the core scientific vision of NCEMS, this project will catalyze a paradigm shift in how we understand and analyze complex, emergent biological systems.
original.budget_and_resources:
The proposed synthesis project requires NCEMS funding because the sheer scale and multidisciplinary nature of the work far exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory or traditional grant mechanism. The budget is strategically designed to support the collaborative infrastructure, computational resources, and workforce training essential for this community-scale endeavor. We are not requesting any funds for experimental equipment or laboratory supplies, strictly adhering to the synthesis mandate.

The primary budget allocation will support personnel, specifically focusing on the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We request funding for two full-time postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These trainees will be cross-mentored by our diverse team of principal investigators, ensuring they gain expertise spanning computational biophysics, AI, and membrane biology. Their salaries and stipends represent an investment in the future workforce.

A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to facilitating transdisciplinary collaboration. We request funds to support biannual, multi-day, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These intensive hackathons are critical for brainstorming, troubleshooting complex integration challenges, and fostering the deep collaborative bonds necessary for synthesis research. Additionally, funds are allocated for ongoing virtual collaboration tools and open-science publication fees.

Finally, we require robust computational resources to handle the massive volumes of synthesized data and train advanced AI models. The budget includes allocations for high-performance cloud computing instances (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) and substantial cloud storage for our unified data lakes. This infrastructure is vital for the spatio-temporal data mining and unsupervised machine learning algorithms central to our methodology. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will assemble the necessary human and computational capital to decode mesoscale emergence, delivering high-impact scientific discoveries and invaluable open-source tools to the broader biological community.

title: Uncovering the Rules of Nucleolar Assembly and Ribosome Biogenesis Emergence

original.abstract: The nucleolus is the most prominent mesoscale condensate within the eukaryotic nucleus, serving as the primary site for ribosome biogenesis. Its assembly from individual ribosomal RNAs and hundreds of distinct proteins is a quintessential example of multi-component, multi-phase biological emergence. Despite its critical role in cellular growth and stress response, the physical principles that dictate how disparate molecular components self-organize into the distinct fibrillar and granular sub-compartments of the nucleolus remain an unsolved puzzle. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is essential for deciphering how cells coordinate massive macromolecular assembly lines. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to uncover the physical and genetic rules governing nucleolar emergence. We will integrate a vast array of publicly available datasets, including nucleolar proteomics, CLIP-seq data for RNA-protein interactions, and super-resolution imaging from the Human Protein Atlas and the PRIDE database. By utilizing generative AI models and multi-layer network analysis, we will synthesize these complex datasets to map the sequence-to-structure relationships that drive nucleolar phase separation. This project will not generate new experimental data but will instead rely on data science to extract novel, deeper insights into mesoscale organelle assembly. The scope of integrating multi-omics data with complex phase-separation physics requires the extensive collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. This project is far beyond the capabilities of an individual lab. We have formed a transdisciplinary working group that includes RNA biologists, soft matter physicists, computational biologists, and bioinformaticians. Our team is carefully curated to include diverse perspectives, spanning multiple geographic regions and incorporating early-career researchers alongside established experts. This diversity is crucial for developing innovative analytical strategies to tackle complex emergence phenomena. A key objective of our working group is to train the next generation of data-savvy molecular biologists. Trainees will gain hands-on experience in integrating heterogeneous datasets, applying generative AI to biological problems, and navigating the complexities of open science. We pledge to make all findings, integrated databases, and AI analysis pipelines publicly available through community-standard repositories, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how local molecular interactions drive the unexpected appearance of complex, multiphase mesoscale architectures, directly advancing the NCEMS objective of understanding subcellular emergence.
original.background_and_significance: The transition from nanometer-scale macromolecules to micrometer-scale cellular structures represents a profound frontier in the molecular and cellular biosciences. This phenomenon, defined as mesoscale emergence, is characterized by the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties that cannot be predicted merely by cataloging individual molecular parts. The nucleolus stands as the quintessential and most prominent example of mesoscale emergence within the eukaryotic nucleus. Operating as a membraneless organelle, the nucleolus is the primary site for ribosome biogenesis, a massive macromolecular assembly line essential for cellular growth, proliferation, and stress response. Structurally, the nucleolus is not a homogenous droplet but rather a highly organized, multi-phase condensate comprising three distinct sub-compartments: the fibrillar center (FC), the dense fibrillar component (DFC), and the granular component (GC). The assembly of these nested compartments from individual ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and hundreds of distinct proteins is driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). However, the specific physical, thermodynamic, and genetic rules that dictate how these disparate molecular components reliably self-organize into a functional, multi-phase architecture remain a major unsolved puzzle in cellular biology. While reductionist approaches have identified many key nucleolar proteins and RNAs, they have failed to explain the emergent properties of the system as a whole. Conversely, macroscopic observations of nucleolar morphology often lack molecular-level resolution. Currently, a vast and unprecedented amount of publicly available data exists spanning these scales, including high-throughput nucleolar proteomics, CLIP-seq datasets mapping RNA-protein interactions, and super-resolution spatial imaging from repositories like the Human Protein Atlas. Unfortunately, these datasets remain siloed across different sub-disciplines. No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, transdisciplinary expertise, or mandate to synthesize this disparate data into a cohesive, predictive model of nucleolar emergence. This fragmentation represents a critical missed opportunity. Our proposed community-scale synthesis project directly addresses this gap by leveraging the collaborative framework of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). By synthesizing existing multi-omics and imaging data, we will bridge the gap between molecular interactions and mesoscale architecture. The significance of this work extends far beyond the nucleolus; it will establish a pioneering methodological blueprint for understanding multi-phase condensate emergence across all biological systems. Furthermore, deciphering the rules of nucleolar assembly has profound implications for understanding cellular stress responses and pathologies where ribosome biogenesis is dysregulated, such as ribosomopathies and cancer. By integrating soft matter physics, generative artificial intelligence, and RNA biology without generating new experimental data, this project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to catalyze multidisciplinary teams to answer fundamental questions of emergence. It will not only solve long-standing mysteries of nucleolar architecture but also train a new generation of scientists capable of navigating and synthesizing the massive, complex datasets that define modern biology.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
To unravel the complexities of nucleolar emergence, our working group has formulated three compelling, interconnected research questions that can only be addressed through the community-scale synthesis of existing, publicly available data. 

Question 1: What is the 'molecular grammar'—the specific sequence-level and structural determinants—of the RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions that drive the initial phase separation of the nucleolus? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that specific intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in nucleolar proteins, acting in concert with highly structured, multivalent motifs in ribosomal RNA, form a predictable interaction network. By synthesizing PRIDE proteomics data with ENCODE CLIP-seq datasets using generative AI, we expect to identify a universal molecular grammar where sequence charge distribution, hydrophobicity, and RNA secondary structure quantitatively predict the propensity for nucleolar condensate formation. 

Question 2: How do these local, molecular-scale interactions thermodynamically dictate the emergent, mesoscale multi-phase architecture (the nested FC, DFC, and GC sub-compartments) of the nucleolus? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the spatial segregation of the nucleolus into distinct fibrillar and granular components is driven by a thermodynamic gradient of binding affinities and RNA processing states. We propose that as pre-rRNA is transcribed and processed, its interaction valency dynamically changes, altering the local viscoelasticity and driving the sequential phase separation of the DFC and GC. We will test this by integrating multi-layer network analysis of molecular interactions with soft matter physics models (e.g., Flory-Huggins theory), validated against super-resolution spatial data from the Human Protein Atlas. 

Question 3: Can we computationally predict nucleolar structural alterations and emergent phenotypic properties under various cellular stress conditions using solely our synthesized baseline data models? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that cellular stress (such as heat shock or nutrient deprivation) perturbs specific nodes within the nucleolar interaction network, leading to predictable, emergent structural phenotypes, such as nucleolar fragmentation or the formation of nucleolar caps. By utilizing graph neural networks trained on our synthesized multi-omics database, we will simulate how alterations in protein abundance or RNA transcription rates propagate through the network to alter mesoscale architecture. 

Addressing these questions requires a paradigm shift from traditional, single-lab experimental biology to a transdisciplinary, data-synthesis approach. None of these questions can be answered by examining a single dataset in isolation. Instead, they require the integration of sequence data, interaction maps, and spatial imaging. By answering these questions, we will transition the field from a descriptive understanding of the nucleolus to a predictive, quantitative framework of mesoscale emergence. This will fulfill the NCEMS objective of solving long-standing puzzles regarding how local molecular rules generate unexpected, higher-order cellular outcomes, all while exclusively utilizing and recombining existing public data sources.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodology is strictly computational and synthesis-driven, relying entirely on existing publicly available data, thereby adhering to the core NCEMS mandate. The approach is divided into three integrated phases: Data Acquisition and Harmonization, Generative AI and Network Modeling, and Physics-Based Validation. 

Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Harmonization. We will systematically mine and integrate three primary data modalities. First, we will extract nucleolar proteomic profiles from the PRIDE database, focusing on protein abundance, post-translational modifications, and IDR mapping across various cell lines. Second, we will acquire RNA-protein interaction data from CLIP-seq, eCLIP, and PAR-CLIP datasets available via ENCODE and GEO, specifically targeting interactions involving ribosomal RNA and snoRNAs. Third, we will pull super-resolution imaging data and spatial proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas to define the localization of proteins within the FC, DFC, and GC. The major challenge—and a key training opportunity—will be harmonizing these heterogeneous datasets. We will develop a standardized ontology and automated bioinformatic pipelines to resolve batch effects, normalize expression values, and map all data to a unified multi-omics reference genome. 

Phase 2: Generative AI and Multi-Layer Network Modeling. To synthesize this harmonized data, we will construct a multi-layer interaction network. Layer 1 will represent protein-protein interactions; Layer 2 will map RNA-protein interactions; Layer 3 will encode spatial localization. We will deploy Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to identify emergent topological features within this multi-layer graph that correspond to phase separation drivers. Furthermore, we will utilize Transformer-based generative AI models (similar to AlphaFold, but adapted for multi-component condensates) to predict the 'molecular grammar' of interactions. By feeding the AI with paired sequence (protein IDRs and RNA motifs) and spatial data, the model will learn the sequence-to-structure relationships that govern valency and affinity in the nucleolus. 

Phase 3: Physics-Based Validation of Emergence. To ensure our AI models reflect biological reality, our soft matter physicists will integrate the AI-derived interaction affinities into thermodynamic models of liquid-liquid phase separation. We will utilize Cahn-Hilliard equations and multi-component Flory-Huggins theory to simulate the mesoscale phase behavior of the virtual nucleolus. If the AI-predicted interaction network is accurate, the physics simulations should spontaneously yield the nested, three-phase architecture (FC, DFC, GC) observed in the Human Protein Atlas imaging data. 

Working Group Dynamics: This approach requires profound transdisciplinary collaboration. RNA biologists will guide the biological relevance of the interaction networks; bioinformaticians will handle data harmonization; computational biologists will train the AI models; and soft matter physicists will execute the thermodynamic simulations. The NCEMS infrastructure will provide the essential collaborative nexus, cloud computing resources, and meeting frameworks necessary to integrate these diverse scientific perspectives into a unified analytical strategy.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission of understanding mesoscale emergence. Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the first comprehensive, quantitative model of nucleolar assembly that bridges the gap between molecular sequence grammar and multi-phase mesoscale architecture. By solving this long-standing puzzle, we will establish a predictive framework applicable not only to the nucleolus but to the emergence of other membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates across eukaryotic biology. 

A major tangible outcome will be the creation of the 'Nucleolar Emergence Atlas' (NEA), a unified, publicly accessible database integrating harmonized proteomics, CLIP-seq, and spatial imaging data. Alongside the database, we will release our trained Generative AI models and multi-layer network algorithms as open-source software tools, enabling the broader scientific community to simulate condensate dynamics and predict the impact of genetic mutations on organelle structure. 

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact on workforce development will be profound. This project will directly support and train four postdoctoral researchers and six graduate students. These trainees will be uniquely positioned at the intersection of RNA biology, soft matter physics, and advanced data science. They will gain invaluable, hands-on experience in cloud computing, AI application in biology, and open science practices, directly addressing the critical need for a next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce. 

Finally, the project will demonstrate the immense, untapped value of synthesizing existing public data. By showing that fundamental, paradigm-shifting discoveries can be made without generating a single new experimental data point, we will validate the NCEMS synthesis model, stimulating further cross-disciplinary collaborations and maximizing the return on investment of previously funded experimental research.
original.budget_and_resources:

The budget is strategically allocated to support transdisciplinary collaboration, computational resources, and workforce training. 

Personnel (45%): The largest portion of the budget is dedicated to training the next-generation workforce. We request stipend and salary support for four postdoctoral fellows and six graduate students. These trainees will be co-mentored by PIs from different disciplines (e.g., a physics PI and a biology PI), ensuring true cross-training in data science, AI, and molecular biology. 

Working Group Meetings and Collaboration (30%): To foster deep transdisciplinary integration, we request travel and lodging funds for four intensive, in-person working group meetings at the NCEMS facility over the project period. These multi-day hackathons and synthesis sessions are critical for aligning the RNA biologists, physicists, and computational scientists. Funds are also allocated for virtual collaboration tools and administrative support to maintain momentum between in-person meetings. 

Computational Resources (20%): Synthesizing massive multi-omics datasets and training generative AI models requires significant computational power. We request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or GCP) and access to high-performance GPU clusters. While we will leverage existing NCEMS computing infrastructure where possible, dedicated cloud budgets will ensure agile development and deployment of our AI models and thermodynamic simulations. 

Open Science and Publication (5%): Funds are allocated to cover article processing charges (APCs) for open-access journals and costs associated with hosting the 'Nucleolar Emergence Atlas' database and Docker containers on robust, long-term cloud storage platforms. 

This budget directly supports the NCEMS mandate by investing in people, collaborative infrastructure, and open-source computational tools rather than wet-lab equipment or new data generation.
