title: Emergent Cargo Sorting Dynamics in Extracellular Vesicle Biogenesis

original.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes and microvesicles, are mesoscale lipid-bound particles that mediate critical intercellular communication. The biogenesis of EVs involves the highly selective sorting of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids into budding membranes. However, the physical and molecular rules governing how local, nanoscale clustering of specific cargoes drives the emergent macroscopic budding and release of these vesicles remain poorly understood. Deciphering this mesoscale emergence is crucial for understanding how cells package complex molecular information for systemic delivery. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of EV cargo sorting and biogenesis. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including EV proteomics, transcriptomics, and high-resolution imaging data from specialized repositories like Vesiclepedia, EVpedia, and the PRIDE database. By employing advanced graph neural networks and multi-modal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic networks of cargo-lipid interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local molecular crowding leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional extracellular vesicles. The complexity of EV biogenesis requires the integration of multi-omics data with membrane biophysics, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites exosome biologists, computational systems biologists, lipidomics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular communication networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale transport vehicles, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.
original.background_and_significance: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), encompassing exosomes and microvesicles, represent a fundamental paradigm of intercellular communication, orchestrating complex physiological and pathological processes across diverse biological systems, from immune modulation to cancer metastasis and neurodegenerative disease spread. Operating precisely at the mesoscale—the critical nexus between individual biomolecular interactions and macroscopic cellular behavior—EVs are lipid-bound nanoparticles that encapsulate a highly curated repertoire of proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids. Despite their ubiquitous biological importance, the biogenesis of EVs remains a profound enigma. Specifically, the field lacks a mechanistic understanding of how local, nanoscale clustering of specific molecular cargoes spontaneously drives the emergent macroscopic budding, membrane curvature, and subsequent release of these vesicles. This phenomenon is a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence: the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties (a functional transport vehicle) arising from the complex interplay of lower-scale components (lipid-protein networks, molecular crowding, and membrane biophysics). Currently, the molecular and cellular biosciences are experiencing an unprecedented explosion of data. Specialized repositories such as Vesiclepedia, EVpedia, ExoCarta, and the PRIDE database house massive, publicly available multi-omics datasets detailing the proteomic, transcriptomic, and lipidomic profiles of EVs across varied cell types and conditions. Concurrently, high-resolution imaging repositories offer structural insights into membrane dynamics. However, these datasets remain highly fragmented, siloed by discipline, and underutilized for cross-scale synthesis. Individual laboratories typically lack the computational infrastructure and diverse expertise required to integrate multi-omics data with membrane biophysics to extract universal rules of emergence. Our proposed working group directly addresses this critical gap by initiating a community-scale data synthesis project that aligns perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We hypothesize that the rules governing EV biogenesis are not dictated by a single master regulator but emerge from dynamic, distributed networks of cargo-lipid interactions. By synthesizing these disparate, publicly available datasets without generating any new experimental data, we aim to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how cells package complex molecular information. The significance of this project is twofold. First, it will fundamentally transform our understanding of mesoscale biological emergence, shifting the paradigm from reductionist views of single-molecule sorting to a holistic, systems-level understanding of molecular crowding, phase separation, and membrane physics. Second, it will pioneer innovative analytical strategies, utilizing advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning architectures to bridge biological scales. This transdisciplinary approach is beyond the capacity of any single lab, requiring the collaborative, multi-institutional infrastructure provided by NCEMS. By uniting computational systems biologists, exosome biologists, lipidomics experts, and machine learning engineers, our working group will catalyze transformative discoveries, recruit and tap into diverse new talent, and establish a gold-standard framework for data synthesis in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: To unravel the emergent properties of EV cargo sorting and biogenesis, our working group will address a series of compelling, well-defined scientific questions. These questions are designed to bridge the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and mesoscale vesicular emergence, relying entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data. Question 1: What are the universal, cross-cell-type molecular interaction networks that dictate the selective sorting of cargo into nascent extracellular vesicles? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that EV cargo sorting is not governed by isolated, independent targeting sequences, but rather emerges from conserved, highly connected 'hub-and-spoke' network motifs. We posit that specific lipid-protein interaction hubs act as nanoscale nucleation points, driving biomolecular condensates and phase separations that obligatorily recruit secondary and tertiary cargoes. By synthesizing EV proteomic and lipidomic data across diverse cell types from Vesiclepedia and PRIDE, we expect to identify these universal network topologies that are otherwise obscured in single-study datasets. Question 2: How does the local stoichiometry and nanoscale crowding of sorted biomolecules drive the emergent mesoscale membrane curvature required for vesicle budding? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the macroscopic budding of EVs is a non-linear, emergent physical property dictated by a critical threshold of molecular crowding and lipid packing defects. We predict that the aggregation of specific high-density cargo networks induces localized biophysical stress on the plasma or endosomal membrane, spontaneously lowering the energetic barrier for membrane invagination. By integrating high-resolution imaging data (e.g., from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive) with structural proteomics, our graph neural networks will model the spatial constraints and biophysical forces generated by cargo clustering. Question 3: Can multi-modal deep learning architectures predict the emergent cargo profile of an extracellular vesicle based solely on the parent cell’s multi-omic state? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the emergent composition of EVs is highly deterministic and can be accurately predicted by mapping the parent cell's transcriptomic and proteomic landscapes through multi-modal deep learning. We posit that by training advanced AI models on paired cellular and EV multi-omics datasets, we can decode the hidden 'sorting syntax'—the complex, multi-variable rules that cells use to package molecular information. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how diverse cellular states (e.g., stress, malignancy, senescence) dynamically alter EV communication payloads. Question 4: Are there distinct, identifiable trajectories of mesoscale emergence that differentiate exosome biogenesis (endosomal origin) from microvesicle biogenesis (plasma membrane origin)? Hypothesis 4: Despite originating from different subcellular compartments, we hypothesize that exosomes and microvesicles share convergent biophysical mechanisms of mesoscale emergence. By synthesizing spatially resolved transcriptomics, subcellular proteomics, and EV composition data, we expect to uncover shared biophysical principles of membrane deformation that operate independently of the specific subcellular origin, thereby unifying fragmented theories in the EV field. These hypotheses will guide our data synthesis efforts, leveraging AI to extract profound biological insights from existing public resources.
original.methods_and_approach: Our methodological approach is strictly computational and synthetic, generating no new experimental data, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mandate. We will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available data through a rigorous, multi-phased computational pipeline. Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Harmonization. We will systematically harvest multi-omics data from established public repositories, including Vesiclepedia, EVpedia, ExoCarta, the PRIDE database, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). This dataset will encompass EV and parent-cell proteomics, transcriptomics, and lipidomics across diverse species and cell types. Simultaneously, we will extract spatial and structural data from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The primary challenge in community-scale synthesis is data heterogeneity. We will develop a standardized, open-source harmonization pipeline to normalize disparate data formats, correct for batch effects using advanced empirical Bayes frameworks, and map all molecular entities to a unified multi-omic ontology. Phase 2: Network Modeling via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To address the physical and molecular rules of cargo clustering, we will construct massive, multi-layered heterogeneous networks. Nodes will represent proteins, transcripts, and lipids, while edges will represent known physical interactions, co-expression dynamics, and spatial proximities derived from the harmonized data. We will employ Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Graph Attention Networks (GATs) to identify emergent clustering patterns. These GNNs will be trained to detect topological motifs that are highly enriched in EVs compared to parent cells, identifying the nanoscale 'nucleation hubs' responsible for cargo sorting. Phase 3: Multi-Modal Deep Learning for Emergent Predictions. To predict EV cargo profiles from parent cell states, we will design a multi-modal deep learning architecture, such as a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) coupled with transformer-based attention mechanisms. This model will integrate the harmonized transcriptomic, proteomic, and lipidomic datasets, learning the high-dimensional, non-linear mappings between the intracellular environment and the emergent EV payload. Attention weights will be extracted to interpret the biological rules driving these predictions, ensuring the model acts as an engine for biological discovery rather than a 'black box.' Phase 4: Biophysical Constraint Modeling. To link molecular crowding with mesoscale membrane budding, we will integrate structural data into our network models. We will utilize coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, parameterized entirely by our synthesized structural and lipidomic data, to model the biophysical consequences of the identified cargo clusters on membrane curvature. This will mathematically bridge the gap between nanoscale clustering and mesoscale vesicle emergence. Phase 5: Collaborative Synthesis and Evaluation. This transdisciplinary approach requires the synergistic expertise of our diverse working group. Computational biologists will lead the AI development, exosome biologists will provide domain-specific validation of the extracted sorting rules, and lipidomics experts will refine the biophysical models. We will host bi-monthly virtual synthesis workshops and bi-annual in-person hackathons at the NCEMS facility to iteratively evaluate model outputs, refine algorithms, and synthesize findings into novel biological paradigms.

First, by decoding the universal rules of EV cargo sorting, we will solve a major, long-standing puzzle in cell biology, explaining how nanoscale molecular interactions precipitate the emergent mesoscale formation of extracellular vesicles. We expect to identify the specific protein-lipid network motifs that drive membrane budding, providing a comprehensive map of intercellular communication packaging. This mechanistic understanding will have profound downstream impacts on deciphering how diseases like cancer and neurodegeneration hijack these pathways for systemic spread. Second, we will deliver a suite of innovative, AI-driven analytical strategies. The multi-modal deep learning architectures and Graph Neural Networks developed here will establish a new methodological gold standard for integrating heterogeneous biological data. These predictive models will allow researchers worldwide to input a cell's transcriptomic state and accurately predict its emergent EV cargo profile, accelerating research in diagnostics, therapeutics, and synthetic biology. Furthermore, the impact of this project extends deeply into workforce development and community building. By actively recruiting a diverse team of researchers spanning various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds, we will tap into diverse new talent. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive unparalleled cross-disciplinary training at the intersection of membrane biophysics, machine learning, and big data integration. They will emerge as leaders in the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the profound power of data synthesis. Data heterogeneity and fragmentation will be addressed through a standardized and open source harmonization pipeline.

The timeline includes bi-monthly virtual workshops and bi-annual in-person hackathons while the specific project duration is not specified. Multi-lab collaboration is required to integrate diverse expertise and access infrastructure provided by the National Synthesis Center for Emergence.

All analytical pipelines and synthesized datasets and predictive models will be made publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub. The team includes biologists and computational experts and engineers who provide cross disciplinary training for postdoctoral fellows and students.
rephrased.main_idea: This research investigates how nanoscale molecular clustering drives the emergent budding of extracellular vesicles to address current gaps in biogenesis. title: Decoding the Emergence of Viral Inclusion Bodies and Host Cell Hijacking

original.abstract: During infection, many viruses induce the formation of specialized mesoscale structures known as viral inclusion bodies or 'viral factories.' These membrane-less or membrane-associated compartments emerge from the complex interplay between viral components and hijacked host cellular machinery. Understanding how a minimal set of viral proteins can rapidly reorganize the host cytoplasm to create these emergent mesoscale structures is a fundamental puzzle in virology and cell biology. This emergence dictates the efficiency of viral replication and the suppression of host immune responses. Our working group proposes a comprehensive data synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of viral inclusion body formation. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including host-pathogen interactomes, spatial transcriptomics, and high-throughput cellular imaging from repositories such as BioGRID, the Gene Expression Omnibus, and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced network theory and spatio-temporal machine learning models, we will synthesize these multi-omics datasets to reconstruct the dynamic assembly of viral factories. This approach relies entirely on existing public data, leveraging AI to uncover the hidden rules of how local viral-host interactions scale up to produce global cellular subversion. The multifaceted nature of viral hijacking requires a collaborative partnership that transcends individual lab capabilities, making NCEMS support essential. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of virologists, structural biologists, computational network theorists, and data scientists. Our working group is structured to promote diverse scientific perspectives, incorporating researchers from various geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this critical biological mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in multi-omics integration, AI-driven network analysis, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of viral mesoscale structures influences higher-order cellular outcomes, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.
original.background_and_significance: Viruses are master manipulators of cellular architecture. Upon infection, many viruses induce the formation of specialized mesoscale structures, commonly referred to as viral inclusion bodies (VIBs) or viral factories. These structures, which can be membrane-less or membrane-associated compartments, serve as the primary sites for viral genome replication, transcription, and assembly, while simultaneously shielding viral components from host innate immune sensors. The formation of these factories represents a classic and highly significant example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. A relatively small number of viral proteins interact with the highly complex, crowded environment of the host cytoplasm, leading to the rapid, unexpected appearance of novel structural properties that fundamentally alter subcellular and cellular outcomes. Despite decades of research detailing individual viral proteins and specific host-pathogen interactions, a unified understanding of the physical and network-driven rules governing the emergence of VIBs remains a major puzzle in virology and cell biology. Currently, the molecular and cellular biosciences are experiencing an unprecedented explosion of publicly available data. Repositories such as BioGRID, the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), and the Image Data Resource (IDR) house vast amounts of host-pathogen interactome data, spatial transcriptomics, and high-throughput cellular imaging, respectively. However, these datasets remain largely siloed. Individual research laboratories typically lack the computational infrastructure, diverse expertise, and resources required to integrate multi-omics and multidimensional imaging data at a scale necessary to uncover the universal principles of viral factory emergence. This fragmentation represents a critical missed opportunity. Our proposed working group will address this gap by leveraging data synthesis and artificial intelligence to decode the emergent properties of VIB formation. This project aligns perfectly with the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission. By synthesizing existing, publicly available datasets, we will investigate how local, microscale interactions between viral and host proteins scale up to produce mesoscale functional compartments. Understanding this process is not only crucial for fundamental cell biology—revealing how organelles and liquid-liquid phase separation can be rapidly induced and controlled—but also holds profound implications for human health. Decoding the universal rules of host cell hijacking could identify novel, broad-spectrum therapeutic targets that disrupt the emergent properties of viral factories rather than targeting easily mutable individual viral proteins. Furthermore, the transdisciplinary nature of this synthesis will stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration, bringing together structural biologists, virologists, and computational scientists to establish new analytical paradigms. By integrating diverse perspectives, we will move beyond reductionist models and embrace a systems-level view of viral infection, paving the way for next-generation discoveries in cellular organization and host-pathogen dynamics.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective to understand how local molecular interactions between viral and host components give rise to emergent mesoscale viral factories. To achieve this, our working group will address three compelling, interconnected scientific questions, each accompanied by specific hypotheses testable through the integration of publicly available datasets. Question 1: What are the conserved network topological features of host-pathogen interactomes that drive the nucleation and assembly of viral inclusion bodies across different viral families? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that diverse viruses, regardless of their specific genome type or entry mechanism, converge on a shared set of host cellular hub proteins and interaction motifs to induce mesoscale compartmentalization. By synthesizing interactome data from BioGRID and IntAct across multiple virus families (e.g., Flaviviridae, Coronaviridae, Filoviridae), we expect to identify conserved network signatures—such as high-degree nodes and specific bottleneck interactions—that act as universal scaffolds for viral factory emergence. We anticipate that these conserved hubs are disproportionately involved in cellular processes related to liquid-liquid phase separation and cytoskeletal remodeling. Question 2: How do the spatio-temporal dynamics of host gene expression correlate with the physical emergence and maturation of viral mesoscale structures? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the physical expansion of viral inclusion bodies drives a localized, emergent reprogramming of the host transcriptome, characterized by the spatial sequestration of specific host mRNAs and the exclusion of innate immune transcripts. By integrating spatial transcriptomics and single-cell RNA-sequencing data from GEO with corresponding temporal imaging data, we will test the prediction that viral factories create distinct functional microenvironments. We expect to find that the mesoscale physical properties of these factories directly correlate with the localized suppression of host antiviral signaling pathways, thereby linking structural emergence to functional cellular outcomes. Question 3: Can machine learning models trained on integrated multi-omics and imaging datasets predict the emergent morphological properties of viral inclusion bodies based solely on the primary sequences of the interacting viral-host proteins? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the physical characteristics of viral factories—such as their size, membrane association, and intracellular localization—are encoded within the biophysical properties of the underlying viral-host protein interaction networks. By employing spatio-temporal machine learning and graph neural networks on combined structural (PDB), interactomic, and imaging (IDR) data, we predict that we can map molecular-level biophysical features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency) to mesoscale morphological phenotypes. These questions directly address long-standing puzzles in molecular and cellular sciences. They shift the paradigm from studying single viral proteins to understanding the collective, emergent behaviors of complex biomolecular networks. By exclusively utilizing public data, we will test these hypotheses at a scale previously unattainable, generating novel insights into the fundamental principles of biological emergence and cellular subversion.
original.methods_and_approach: To decode the emergent properties of viral inclusion bodies, our working group will employ a purely computational, community-scale data synthesis approach. We will generate no new experimental data, instead relying entirely on the integration, curation, and advanced analysis of existing, publicly available datasets. Our methodology is structured around a pipeline of data acquisition, multi-omics integration, and AI-driven predictive modeling, requiring the collaborative expertise of our transdisciplinary team. Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Harmonization. We will systematically mine and curate data from major public repositories. Host-pathogen protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks will be extracted from BioGRID, IntAct, and STRING. Transcriptomic data, including bulk, single-cell, and spatial RNA-seq related to viral infection time-courses, will be sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress. High-resolution cellular imaging and microscopy metadata, capturing the spatio-temporal dynamics of viral factories, will be acquired from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR). A critical first step will be standardizing these heterogeneous data types into a unified, machine-readable graph database framework (e.g., Neo4j), ensuring interoperability and facilitating complex queries across modalities. Phase 2: Advanced Network Theory and Multi-Omics Integration. With the harmonized database, our computational network theorists will apply advanced graph algorithms to analyze the topological properties of the integrated viral-host interactome. We will utilize network propagation and community detection algorithms to identify conserved host subnetworks targeted by multiple viral families. To bridge the gap between molecular interactions and mesoscale emergence, we will map transcriptomic profiles onto these interactomes. This integration will allow us to track how the functional state of the host cell network evolves in tandem with the physical assembly of viral factories, identifying key molecular drivers of mesoscale organization, such as proteins with high intrinsic disorder propensity (analyzed via DisProt and MobiDB) that facilitate liquid-liquid phase separation. Phase 3: Spatio-Temporal Machine Learning and AI Modeling. The core of our synthesis effort involves leveraging artificial intelligence to uncover hidden rules of emergence. Our data scientists will develop Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on the integrated multi-omics and structural data to predict host-pathogen interaction strengths and complex formations. Furthermore, we will employ computer vision models (e.g., convolutional neural networks) to extract quantitative morphological features from the IDR imaging data. By coupling the GNN outputs with these imaging features using multimodal deep learning architectures, we will model the spatio-temporal scaling from microscale protein interactions to mesoscale factory emergence. This comprehensive approach requires a transdisciplinary team spanning virology, structural biology, computer science, and bioinformatics. The complexity of integrating such diverse data streams to model emergent phenomena far exceeds the capabilities of any single research lab, making the collaborative environment and resources of NCEMS absolutely indispensable for the success of this project.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission of understanding mesoscale emergence in biological systems. Scientifically, we will deliver the first comprehensive, cross-viral family map of the emergent rules governing viral inclusion body formation. By identifying the conserved network topologies and biophysical drivers that dictate host cell hijacking, we will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how minimal viral genomes can so profoundly reorganize the complex host cytoplasm. This knowledge will establish a new paradigm in virology, shifting focus from individual viral targets to the emergent properties of infection, potentially uncovering novel, broad-spectrum therapeutic vulnerabilities. Methodologically, we will develop and release an innovative, multimodal AI framework capable of linking molecular interaction networks to mesoscale morphological phenotypes. This analytical strategy will be highly adaptable, providing the broader molecular and cellular biology community with powerful new tools to study other emergent phenomena, such as the formation of endogenous membraneless organelles and stress granules. Crucially, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development and community building. By bringing together a diverse, transdisciplinary working group of virologists, structural biologists, and data scientists across various career stages and geographic locations, we will foster a new collaborative ecosystem. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers embedded in this project will receive unparalleled, hands-on training in multi-omics integration, advanced AI modeling, and team science. They will emerge as leaders in the future data-savvy workforce, equipped with the unique skill sets required to tackle the next generation of complex, big-data challenges in the biological sciences.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed community-scale synthesis project requires resources and collaborative infrastructure that fundamentally exceed the capacity of any single laboratory or traditional grant mechanism, necessitating the unique support of NCEMS. Our budget is strategically designed to facilitate transdisciplinary team science, support computational infrastructure, and train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. The primary budget allocation will support the convening of our working group. We request funds for travel, accommodation, and per diem expenses to host four intensive, in-person synthesis meetings over the two-year project period at the NCEMS facility. These face-to-face meetings are critical for bridging disciplinary divides, brainstorming analytical strategies, and fostering the deep collaborative partnerships required to tackle the complexities of mesoscale emergence. Between in-person meetings, funds will support virtual collaboration tools and platforms to maintain continuous project momentum. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to workforce training and human capital. We request salary and stipend support for two dedicated postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students. These trainees will be co-mentored by working group members across different institutions, receiving cross-disciplinary training in virology, network theory, and AI. They will serve as the primary engines of data integration and model development. Finally, we request resources for advanced computational infrastructure. While we will leverage existing university high-performance computing clusters where possible, we require dedicated cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) to support the storage of massive, harmonized imaging and omics datasets, and to train computationally intensive multimodal deep learning models. Additional funds are allocated for open-access publication fees and the hosting costs associated with our interactive, public-facing data portals, ensuring our adherence to strict open science mandates.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Biophysics of Centrosome Maturation and Spindle Bipolarity

original.abstract: The centrosome is the primary microtubule-organizing center in animal cells, undergoing a dramatic mesoscale maturation process prior to mitosis to ensure the formation of a bipolar spindle. This maturation involves the massive, dynamic recruitment of pericentriolar material (PCM), driven by phase separation and intricate protein scaffolding. However, the precise biophysical rules governing how nanoscale molecular interactions within the PCM scale up to generate the emergent property of robust spindle bipolarity remain a significant, unsolved puzzle. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is vital for deciphering how cells prevent aneuploidy and ensure faithful genome segregation. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of centrosome maturation. We will systematically integrate publicly available high-resolution proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, and live-cell spindle dynamics datasets from the PRIDE database, EMPIAR, and the Cell Image Library. By deploying advanced 3D spatial modeling and generative AI frameworks, we will synthesize these diverse data types to construct predictive models of PCM condensation and microtubule nucleation. This project relies entirely on leveraging existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies, bypassing the need for new experimental interventions. The multi-scale nature of centrosome biology necessitates a collaborative partnership that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, requiring the unique support of NCEMS. We have assembled a transdisciplinary team of cell division biologists, soft matter physicists, computational modelers, and machine learning experts. Our working group is intentionally diverse, bringing together researchers from different institutional tiers and geographic locations to ensure a rich variety of scientific perspectives. This collaborative environment will be instrumental in solving long-standing puzzles regarding mitotic emergence. Furthermore, this project is designed to be a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will be co-mentored in a highly interactive setting, acquiring critical skills in 3D data synthesis, AI-driven modeling, and open science methodologies. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, spatial models, and analytical code will be released to the public domain via GitHub and dedicated repositories. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale PCM condensates influences higher-order cellular division, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission.
original.background_and_significance: The centrosome is the primary microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells, playing an indispensable role in orchestrating the formation of a bipolar mitotic spindle. Prior to mitosis, the centrosome undergoes a dramatic, dynamic structural transition known as centrosome maturation. This process is characterized by the massive recruitment and assembly of pericentriolar material (PCM) around the centrioles. The PCM acts as a dense, micron-scale scaffold that nucleates and anchors microtubules. Recent experimental breakthroughs have revealed that PCM assembly is driven by a combination of intricate protein scaffolding and liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), creating a mesoscale condensate with unique biophysical properties. However, a fundamental gap exists in our understanding of the emergent biophysics governing this process. Specifically, it remains a long-standing puzzle how nanoscale molecular interactions among individual PCM components—such as SPD-5, PLK-1, Aurora A, and gamma-tubulin—scale up to generate the mesoscale architecture of the mature centrosome, and how this mesoscale architecture robustly ensures the macroscale emergent property of spindle bipolarity. Understanding this cross-scale emergence is not merely an academic exercise; it is vital for deciphering how cells prevent chromosomal instability and aneuploidy, which are hallmarks of oncogenesis and developmental disorders. The complexity of PCM maturation, operating at the critical mesoscale between individual biomolecules and whole organelles, makes it a quintessential system for studying emergent phenomena in molecular and cellular biosciences. Despite the wealth of publicly available data on centrosome biology, including high-resolution proteomics, cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), and live-cell imaging, these datasets remain siloed within distinct disciplinary domains. Proteomic datasets capture compositional dynamics, structural data reveal nanoscale architectures, and optical imaging tracks macroscale spindle behaviors. To date, no concerted effort has synthesized these disparate data streams into a cohesive, predictive model of centrosome emergence. This fragmentation precludes a holistic understanding of how physical rules at the molecular level dictate cellular-scale outcomes. Our proposed synthesis project addresses this critical bottleneck by leveraging the unique support structure of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We will catalyze a multidisciplinary scientific team to synthesize existing, publicly available datasets, bypassing the need for de novo experimental data generation. By integrating structural, compositional, and dynamic data across spatial and temporal scales, we aim to uncover the fundamental biophysical rules of PCM condensation and microtubule nucleation. This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to explore emergent properties at the mesoscale. By translating isolated datasets into a unified mechanistic framework, we will solve a major puzzle in cell division biology, providing unprecedented insights into the robust, emergent self-organization of the mitotic spindle.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: To unravel the emergent biophysics of centrosome maturation and its role in ensuring spindle bipolarity, our working group has formulated a series of compelling, interconnected research questions and hypotheses. These questions are specifically designed to be answered through the synthesis of disparate, publicly available datasets, spanning nanoscale proteomics to macroscale cellular dynamics. Question 1: What are the stoichiometric and spatial rules governing the transition of PCM proteins from soluble monomers to mesoscale phase-separated condensates? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that PCM condensation is driven by a precise, threshold-dependent stoichiometry of core scaffolding proteins (e.g., SPD-5/CDK5RAP2) and regulatory kinases (e.g., PLK1), which collectively encode a biophysical switch for liquid-liquid phase separation. By synthesizing quantitative proteomics data from the PRIDE database with structural constraints derived from EMPIAR cryo-ET maps, we predict the emergence of distinct, concentration-dependent phase boundaries that dictate the onset of PCM assembly prior to mitosis. Question 2: How does the nanoscale structural organization within the PCM condensate dictate the spatial distribution and efficiency of microtubule nucleation? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the PCM is not a homogenous liquid, but rather a highly organized mesoscale material exhibiting spatial gradients of gamma-tubulin ring complexes. We posit that these gradients are an emergent property of the differential binding affinities and diffusion rates of PCM components. By integrating 3D cryo-ET structural maps with live-cell fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) data from the Cell Image Library, we expect to demonstrate that internal PCM scaffolding creates localized hotspots of microtubule nucleation, optimizing the radial array necessary for robust spindle capture. Question 3: How do variations in mesoscale PCM biophysics predict the macroscale success or failure of bipolar spindle formation? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the emergent mechanical properties of the matured centrosome—specifically its viscoelasticity and surface tension, derived from the collective interactions of its constituent proteins—are the primary determinants of spindle pole stability under microtubule-generated forces. We predict that in silico perturbations of these mesoscale properties, modeled using generative AI and trained on synthesized multi-omic and imaging datasets, will accurately predict the transition from bipolar to multipolar spindles, a major driver of aneuploidy. Synthesis Strategy: These questions represent a fundamental shift from reductionist biology to systems-level biophysics. Answering them is beyond the capability of any single experimental laboratory, as it requires the simultaneous integration of molecular composition, structural architecture, and cellular dynamics. By leveraging advanced data science and AI-driven spatial modeling, our transdisciplinary team will synthesize these varied data streams to test our hypotheses. This approach will not only answer long-standing mysteries regarding the mechanics of cell division but will also establish a novel analytical paradigm for studying mesoscale emergent phenomena in cellular biology.
original.methods_and_approach: Our methodology strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of utilizing only existing publicly available data, employing a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary approach to achieve community-scale synthesis. We will integrate three primary data modalities: high-resolution proteomics (PRIDE database), cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) structural maps (EMPIAR), and live-cell imaging of spindle dynamics (Cell Image Library). The project is structured into three integrated phases: Data Harmonization, AI-Driven Spatial Modeling, and Predictive Simulation. Phase 1: Multi-Scale Data Harmonization. The first major hurdle in our synthesis is reconciling the disparate formats, resolutions, and metadata of the selected datasets. Our data science experts will develop automated pipelines to extract and normalize quantitative protein abundance and interaction data from PRIDE, focusing on known PCM components and regulatory kinases across various cell cycle stages. Concurrently, structural biologists in our working group will segment and annotate cryo-ET volumes from EMPIAR to extract the 3D spatial coordinates and densities of centrioles and surrounding PCM scaffolds. Finally, kinetic parameters such as microtubule growth rates and PCM recruitment kinetics will be extracted from the Cell Image Library using automated computer vision algorithms. All harmonized data will be mapped onto a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. Phase 2: Generative AI and 3D Spatial Modeling. To bridge the gap between nanoscale composition and mesoscale architecture, we will employ generative AI frameworks, specifically Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The GNNs will be trained on the harmonized proteomic interactome data to predict the interaction strengths and valencies of PCM proteins. These molecular parameters will then feed into a 3D spatial modeling environment utilizing coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo simulations. The generative AI will iteratively propose mesoscale PCM architectures, which will be validated against the empirical cryo-ET density maps. This synthesis will generate the first high-resolution, data-driven 3D models of PCM condensates, revealing the emergent spatial organization of microtubule nucleation sites. Phase 3: Predictive Simulation of Spindle Bipolarity. To link the emergent mesoscale properties of our PCM models to macroscale cellular outcomes, we will utilize agent-based modeling (ABM). The ABM will simulate the dynamic interactions between the synthesized PCM models and dynamic microtubules under varying cellular constraints. We will use the kinetic data extracted from live-cell imaging to calibrate the forces generated by microtubule polymerization and motor protein activity. By perturbing the biophysical parameters of the PCM within the simulation, we will predict the conditions that lead to robust bipolar spindle formation versus aberrant multipolar states. Team and Collaboration: This approach necessitates a profound integration of disciplines. Cell division biologists will provide biological constraints and contextualize findings; soft matter physicists will guide the thermodynamic modeling of phase separation; computational modelers will build the MD and ABM simulations; and machine learning experts will develop the generative AI architectures. Through regular, structured Working Group meetings supported by NCEMS, this diverse team will synthesize these methods into a cohesive analytical strategy, driving novel insights into mitotic emergence.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences, directly addressing the NCEMS mission to illuminate mesoscale emergent properties. First, we will solve a long-standing puzzle in cell biology by defining the precise biophysical rules that govern centrosome maturation. By mapping the transition from nanoscale molecular interactions to mesoscale PCM condensation, we will provide a mechanistic explanation for how cells ensure robust spindle bipolarity, offering critical new insights into the etiology of aneuploidy and cancer. Second, the project will yield an innovative, open-source analytical strategy. The integration pipelines, 3D spatial models, and generative AI frameworks developed here will establish a new paradigm for synthesizing multi-modal biological data. These tools will be adaptable to other membrane-less organelles and mesoscale assemblies, catalyzing discovery across the broader scientific community. Third, the project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into this transdisciplinary working group, we will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, acquiring highly sought-after skills in machine learning, computational biophysics, and big data harmonization. Finally, this project will demonstrate the untapped power of publicly available data. By generating novel, deep insights without the need for de novo experimental data, we will highlight the immense value of data synthesis, encouraging the community to maximize the utility of existing repositories. Ultimately, our findings will bridge the conceptual gap between molecular composition and cellular phenotype, fundamentally advancing our understanding of emergence in biological systems.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed budget and resource allocation are explicitly tailored to support a collaborative, community-scale synthesis project, strictly excluding any costs associated with de novo experimental data generation. We request NCEMS support primarily to facilitate the intensive, transdisciplinary collaboration required to execute this ambitious vision. The core of the budget is allocated to support the Working Group meetings. We request funding for travel, lodging, and per diem expenses for our geographically diverse team of cell biologists, physicists, and data scientists to convene at the NCEMS facility for three week-long, intensive synthesis summits over the two-year project period. These in-person meetings are critical for overcoming disciplinary language barriers, integrating complex methodologies, and fostering team cohesion. Additionally, a significant portion of the budget is dedicated to training the future data-savvy workforce. We request stipend and tuition support for two graduate students and salary support for one postdoctoral fellow. These trainees will serve as the primary engines of data harmonization and model development, benefiting from the co-mentorship of the working group's senior investigators. To support the heavy computational demands of our AI-driven spatial modeling and predictive simulations, we request resources for cloud computing infrastructure. This will provide the necessary GPU acceleration for training our generative AI models and running large-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Finally, we request a modest allocation for open-access publication fees to ensure our findings are freely available to the global scientific community. The unique resources and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS are absolutely essential for this project; the required synthesis of disparate data types and the integration of highly specialized computational and biological expertise far exceed the capabilities and resources of any single laboratory or traditional collaborative grant.

title: Emergence of Secretory Flux from Golgi Cisternal Stacking Dynamics

original.abstract: The Golgi apparatus is a highly organized mesoscale organelle characterized by its distinct architecture of stacked, flattened cisternae. This unique structural emergence is essential for the sequential processing and sorting of cellular cargo. Despite decades of morphological studies, the biophysical mechanisms by which dynamic membrane tethering and localized lipid sorting drive the self-organization of these stacks—and how this architecture dictates the emergent property of efficient secretory flux—remain fundamentally unresolved. Understanding this mesoscale phenomenon is crucial for explaining how cells manage massive intracellular transport networks. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent dynamics of Golgi stacking and secretory flux. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including spatial proteomics, high-resolution 3D electron microscopy, and lipidomics from repositories such as the Human Protein Atlas, EMPIAR, and the Metabolomics Workbench. By employing advanced topological data analysis and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic network of membrane interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local molecular tethering leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional Golgi architecture. The complexity of Golgi biophysics requires the integration of structural imaging with multi-omics data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites membrane traffic biologists, computational biophysicists, lipidomics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular transport networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale transport hubs, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.
original.background_and_significance:
The Golgi apparatus represents one of the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. Bridging the nanometer scale of individual biomolecules and the micrometer scale of whole-cell physiology, the Golgi organizes into a highly ordered, polarized stack of flattened membrane cisternae. This sophisticated architecture is not hard-wired by a rigid cytoskeletal scaffold; rather, it emerges dynamically through the continuous, self-organizing interactions of membrane lipids, tethering proteins (such as GRASPs and golgins), and SNARE complexes. While the fundamental molecular components of the Golgi have been extensively cataloged over the past several decades, a critical knowledge gap remains: we do not understand the biophysical rules and quantitative thresholds that drive these individual components to spontaneously self-assemble into stacked, flattened structures, nor do we understand how this specific mesoscale architecture gives rise to the emergent property of highly efficient, directional secretory flux. 

Traditionally, the study of Golgi architecture has been hindered by a reductionist approach, with individual laboratories focusing on single proteins, specific lipid classes, or static morphological snapshots. This fragmented approach has generated an immense volume of publicly available data—ranging from high-resolution 3D electron cryo-tomography (cryo-ET) maps to comprehensive spatial proteomics and lipidomics—yet these datasets remain largely siloed. The true complexity of mesoscale phenomena cannot be decoded by analyzing these isolated data streams. Instead, it requires a community-scale synthesis that integrates structural, proteomic, and lipidomic data to reveal the hidden, non-linear interactions that govern organelle emergence.

This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by leveraging data science and artificial intelligence to synthesize existing, diverse datasets, thereby solving a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences. By shifting the paradigm from descriptive molecular biology to predictive, systems-level biophysics, our transdisciplinary working group will elucidate the universal principles of mesoscale self-organization. Understanding the emergence of Golgi architecture is not merely an academic exercise; it is fundamentally significant for comprehending how cells manage massive intracellular transport networks under varying physiological loads. Furthermore, because Golgi fragmentation is a hallmark of numerous human pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases and cancer, uncovering the rules of its structural emergence and maintenance will provide critical insights into cellular failure. By executing this synthesis project entirely through the integration of publicly available data, we will demonstrate the untapped power of data-driven biology to answer novel, compelling questions about how unexpected biological system properties appear at the mesoscale.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project is driven by three interconnected research questions that explore the mechanistic link between molecular interactions, mesoscale structural emergence, and cellular function. 

Question 1: What are the universal topological rules governing the transition from disordered vesicular networks to highly ordered, flattened cisternal stacks? 
We hypothesize that the emergence of stacked cisternae is driven by a critical phase transition dependent on specific stoichiometric ratios of sphingolipids, cholesterol, and tethering proteins (e.g., GRASP55/65). We predict that by integrating 3D structural data from EMPIAR with spatial lipidomics, our models will reveal that localized lipid phase separation creates thermodynamically stable membrane microdomains. These microdomains constrain the degrees of freedom of tethering proteins, forcing an emergent transition from a highly curved tubular network to flattened, stacked sheets. We will test this by utilizing topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify the geometric features (Betti numbers, curvature distributions) of Golgi structures across different cellular states and correlating these with multi-omics abundance data.

Question 2: How does the mesoscale architecture of cisternal stacking dictate the emergent property of efficient, polarized secretory flux? 
While it is widely accepted that stacking is important for function, the quantitative relationship between architecture and transport efficiency remains a mystery. We hypothesize that cisternal stacking optimizes secretory flux by minimizing the 3D spatial diffusion distances for transient cargo carriers while simultaneously maximizing the local concentration of processing enzymes. We postulate that this architecture acts as a biophysical 'funnel,' creating a non-linear acceleration of cargo transit times that cannot be achieved in unstacked networks. By synthesizing spatial proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas with dynamic live-cell imaging datasets available in public repositories, we will train spatio-temporal deep learning models to simulate cargo flux. We predict these models will demonstrate that variations in inter-cisternal distance and stack number directly dictate the kinetic efficiency of glycosylation and sorting.

Question 3: How do mesoscale Golgi structures maintain robustness and homeostatic elasticity under fluctuating secretory loads? 
The Golgi must accommodate massive variations in cargo volume without losing its structural integrity. We hypothesize that the Golgi stack possesses an emergent 'homeostatic elasticity,' allowing it to dynamically adjust cisternal volume, spacing, and fenestration in response to lipidomic shifts without undergoing catastrophic disassembly. We propose that specific golgin networks act as shock absorbers. By synthesizing data from cells under varied physiological stress conditions (available via the Metabolomics Workbench and PRIDE), our machine learning models will identify the critical threshold at which this homeostatic elasticity fails, leading to organelle fragmentation. Answering these questions requires no new experimental data but relies entirely on the novel integration of existing multi-modal datasets, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to tackle compelling scientific questions through data synthesis.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our approach relies entirely on the community-scale synthesis of publicly available data, utilizing advanced computational techniques to extract novel biological insights. The project is divided into three integrated methodological phases: Data Aggregation, Multi-Modal Harmonization, and AI-Driven Predictive Modeling.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will systematically mine, curate, and aggregate large-scale datasets from established public repositories. High-resolution 3D structural data (FIB-SEM and cryo-ET) will be sourced from EMPIAR to capture the morphological diversity of the Golgi apparatus across different cell types and states. Spatial proteomics and transcriptomics data will be retrieved from the Human Protein Atlas and the PRIDE database, providing the molecular coordinates of Golgi-resident enzymes, tethers, and SNAREs. Finally, lipidomic profiles corresponding to various secretory states will be extracted from the Metabolomics Workbench. A dedicated team of data scientists and membrane biologists will rigorously quality-control these datasets, standardizing metadata to ensure interoperability.

Phase 2: Multi-Modal Data Harmonization via Topological Data Analysis (TDA). The primary challenge in synthesis research is integrating disparate data types. We will employ TDA, specifically persistent homology, to bridge the gap between 3D morphology and molecular composition. TDA will allow us to quantify the complex geometry of the Golgi—extracting topological invariants such as connected components, holes, and voids—independent of the specific coordinate system. These topological features will serve as a common mathematical scaffold. We will utilize manifold alignment techniques to map the high-dimensional omics data onto these topological scaffolds, creating a unified, multi-modal meta-dataset. This harmonized dataset will represent the first comprehensive spatial-molecular map of the Golgi mesoscale.

Phase 3: Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning Architectures. To model the emergent dynamics of Golgi stacking and secretory flux, we will develop novel Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The Golgi will be represented as a dynamic spatial graph, where nodes represent membrane microdomains (annotated with localized proteomic/lipidomic features) and edges represent physical tethers or vesicular flux pathways. We will train these GNNs to predict the structural evolution of the Golgi graph under varying molecular conditions. To ensure our models are biologically plausible, we will implement Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), which constrain the AI's learning process using known biophysical laws of membrane elasticity and thermodynamics. 

Collaboration and Expertise: This methodology is beyond the capability of any single laboratory. It requires the transdisciplinary synergy of our working group. Cell biologists will guide feature selection and biological interpretation; computational biophysicists will design the PINN constraints; lipidomics experts will curate the metabolic data; and machine learning engineers will build and optimize the GNN architectures. Through intensive, collaborative synthesis, we will transform static, siloed datasets into a dynamic, predictive model of mesoscale organelle emergence.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that significantly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will produce the first multi-scale, predictive computational model of Golgi apparatus emergence. This model will resolve long-standing puzzles regarding how local molecular tethering and lipid sorting drive the self-organization of mesoscale organelle architecture, fundamentally shifting the field from descriptive observation to predictive biophysics. 

Second, we will generate a massive, harmonized meta-dataset that seamlessly integrates 3D electron microscopy, spatial proteomics, and lipidomics. This unprecedented resource will be invaluable to the broader scientific community, providing a foundational scaffold for future research into cellular transport, organelle biogenesis, and membrane dynamics. 

Third, the methodological innovations developed here—specifically the integration of Topological Data Analysis with Physics-Informed Graph Neural Networks for organelle modeling—will establish a new analytical paradigm. These tools can be readily adapted by other researchers to study the emergence of different mesoscale structures, such as the endoplasmic reticulum network or mitochondrial cristae.

Beyond scientific discovery, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mission. Our working group will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous, hands-on cross-training at the intersection of membrane biology, artificial intelligence, and big data management. By bringing together diverse talent from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds, we will foster an inclusive scientific culture that champions transdisciplinary collaboration. Ultimately, our findings will illuminate the fundamental rules of cellular emergence, providing critical insights that could eventually inform therapeutic strategies for diseases characterized by secretory dysfunction and Golgi fragmentation.
original.budget_and_resources:
The proposed synthesis project requires the unique collaborative infrastructure, computational resources, and logistical support provided by NCEMS, which far exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory or standard grant mechanism. 

Personnel (45%): The majority of the budget will support the primary drivers of data synthesis: two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students. These trainees will be co-mentored by our transdisciplinary leadership team, receiving unparalleled training in AI and big data integration. Their funding is critical for the rigorous curation, harmonization, and modeling of the massive datasets required for this project.

Working Group Meetings and Travel (30%): Deep, transdisciplinary synthesis requires dedicated, face-to-face collaboration. We request funds to support three intensive, week-long working group meetings per year at the NCEMS facility. These meetings will bring together our diverse team of membrane biologists, biophysicists, and ML engineers from their respective geographic locations. NCEMS’s specialized collaborative spaces and facilitation expertise are essential for overcoming disciplinary language barriers and driving conceptual breakthroughs.

Computational Resources (15%): While we will leverage institutional resources where possible, the training of Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks on massive 3D EM and omics datasets requires significant computational power. We request funds for dedicated cloud computing time (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) and access to high-performance GPU clusters to ensure rapid model iteration and testing.

Open Science and Publication (10%): Funds are allocated for open-access publication fees, cloud storage costs for hosting our large harmonized datasets on public repositories, and the development/maintenance of our interactive web portal.

By utilizing exclusively publicly available data, this budget requests zero funds for expensive wet-lab equipment, reagents, or data generation. This ensures an exceptionally high return on investment, with all resources directed entirely toward community-scale synthesis, computational innovation, and workforce training.
