title: Decoding the Emergent Assembly of Plant Cell Wall Cellulose Synthase Rosettes

original.abstract: The plant cell wall is a massive, extracellular mesoscale matrix that dictates cellular shape, growth, and defense. The fundamental building blocks of this wall, cellulose microfibrils, are synthesized by highly organized, hexameric protein complexes known as cellulose synthase (CESA) rosettes. The dynamic assembly of these mesoscale rosettes at the plasma membrane and their collective movement driven by the underlying cytoskeleton represent a profound example of biological emergence. However, the precise rules governing how individual CESA proteins self-assemble and coordinate to produce highly ordered cellulose microfibrils remain a long-standing puzzle. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of CESA rosette assembly and function. We will integrate publicly available transcriptomics, proteomics, and high-resolution live-cell imaging datasets from repositories such as the Arabidopsis Information Resource, PRIDE, and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced graph neural networks and particle-tracking machine learning algorithms, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to model the dynamic spatio-temporal assembly of rosettes without generating new experimental data. This AI-driven synthesis will reveal the hidden biophysical rules that govern how nanoscale protein interactions scale up to produce mesoscale extracellular matrices. The integration of complex biomechanical data with plant multi-omics requires a level of transdisciplinary collaboration that can only be supported by NCEMS. Our working group brings together plant cell biologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from varying career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity is essential for fostering the innovative analytical strategies required to tackle plant mechanobiological emergence. A major focus of our initiative is to train the next generation of researchers in data-intensive biology. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, machine learning, and collaborative software development. We are fully committed to gold-standard open science practices; all synthesized datasets, AI models, and codebases will be made publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing existing structural and molecular data, this project will answer long-standing questions about how plant cells process physical information, revealing the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
original.background_and_significance: The plant cell wall is an intricate, extracellular mesoscale matrix that fundamentally dictates cellular shape, directional growth, and defense mechanisms against environmental stresses. The primary load-bearing components of this matrix are cellulose microfibrils, which are synthesized at the plasma membrane by highly organized, hexameric protein complexes known as cellulose synthase (CESA) rosettes. The dynamic assembly of these mesoscale rosettes and their collective, directed movement driven by the underlying cortical microtubule cytoskeleton represent a profound and classic example of biological emergence. Specifically, it illustrates how nanoscale protein-protein interactions scale up to generate highly ordered, mesoscale macromolecular structures that ultimately define macroscopic plant phenotypes. The mesoscale—the critical nexus between individual biomolecules and functional organelles—is where the unpredictability of biological systems often manifests. In the context of CESA rosettes, the emergent property is not just the physical hexameric ring, but the synchronized, dynamic behavior of these complexes as they extrude cellulose while navigating the crowded environment of the plasma membrane. Understanding this requires moving beyond reductionist single-gene approaches. Despite decades of intense study, the precise biophysical and molecular rules governing how individual CESA proteins self-assemble, traffic to the plasma membrane, and coordinate to produce cellulose microfibrils remain a long-standing puzzle in plant mechanobiology. Historically, research has been siloed, with molecular biologists focusing on CESA genetics and biophysicists studying cell wall mechanics independently. However, the modern era of biological research has yielded vast repositories of publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and high-resolution live-cell imaging data. Repositories such as the Arabidopsis Information Resource (TAIR), the PRIDE database for proteomics, and the Image Data Resource (IDR) house petabytes of untapped, multi-modal information. Synthesizing these disparate datasets presents an unprecedented opportunity to uncover the hidden rules of CESA rosette assembly. This proposed community-scale data synthesis project aligns perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We aim to leverage AI and data science to synthesize these publicly available datasets, avoiding the generation of any new experimental data. The complexity of mesoscale phenomena—specifically the transition from individual CESA monomers to functional, moving rosettes—demands a transdisciplinary approach that transcends the capabilities of any single research laboratory. By integrating complex biomechanical data with plant multi-omics, our working group will address fundamental questions regarding emergence in molecular and cellular biology. The significance of this work extends beyond plant biology; understanding the emergent properties of multiprotein complex assembly at the plasma membrane will provide foundational insights applicable to other biological systems where mesoscale organization dictates cellular outcomes. Furthermore, this project will stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration by uniting plant cell biologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists. By prioritizing diverse scientific perspectives across varying career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds, we will foster the innovative analytical strategies required to tackle plant mechanobiological emergence. Ultimately, decoding the emergent assembly of CESA rosettes will solve a long-standing mystery in molecular sciences, establishing a new paradigm for how public data can be synthesized to reveal the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our proposed working group will tackle fundamental mysteries surrounding the mesoscale emergence of CESA rosettes by synthesizing vast amounts of publicly available multi-omics and imaging data. The core objective is to decode the biophysical and molecular rules that govern how nanoscale CESA monomers self-assemble into functional hexameric rosettes and coordinate their activity at the plasma membrane. To achieve this, we have formulated three primary research questions, each paired with specific, testable hypotheses that leverage our AI-driven data synthesis approach. Research Question 1: What are the precise stoichiometric requirements and temporal interaction networks that govern the initial assembly of CESA complexes in the Golgi apparatus prior to their secretion to the plasma membrane? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the assembly of functional CESA rosettes is dictated by a strict, temporally regulated sequence of protein-protein interactions that can be predicted through the synthesis of time-course transcriptomic and proteomic data. By utilizing advanced graph neural networks to model these interactions, we expect to identify previously unrecognized accessory proteins and chaperone networks that act as essential catalysts for hexamer formation, representing an emergent property of the secretory pathway. Research Question 2: How do environmental and developmental signals alter the spatio-temporal dynamics of CESA rosette insertion, movement, and degradation at the plasma membrane? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the dynamic behavior of CESA rosettes—including their insertion rates, velocity along microtubule tracks, and lifetime at the membrane—exhibits emergent, non-linear responses to specific cellular stress signals. By synthesizing high-resolution live-cell imaging datasets from the Image Data Resource (IDR) using particle-tracking machine learning algorithms, we predict that rosette velocity and clustering are highly coordinated behaviors dependent on membrane lipid composition and localized mechanosensory feedback loops, rather than isolated, independent events. Research Question 3: What are the fundamental biophysical rules that scale nanoscale CESA protein interactions into the mesoscale structural integrity of the extracellular plant cell wall? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the macroscopic mechanical properties of the plant cell wall are an emergent outcome of the coordinated, collective movement of multiple CESA rosettes, rather than the simple additive effect of individual cellulose microfibrils. We will test this by integrating multi-modal datasets—correlating proteomic abundance with imaging-derived movement metrics—to construct a unified predictive model. We anticipate that this model will reveal critical density thresholds of CESA rosettes required to trigger phase transitions in cell wall elasticity and strength. These questions are uniquely suited for the NCEMS framework because they cannot be answered by a single laboratory generating new experimental data. Instead, they require the community-scale synthesis of distinct, previously unlinked datasets. By addressing these questions, our working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding plant cell wall biosynthesis. Furthermore, the hypotheses challenge traditional reductionist views, proposing instead that the functional capacity of the plant cell wall is a classic emergent phenomenon arising from the complex, predictable integration of mesoscale components across space, time, and varying environmental conditions.
original.methods_and_approach: To unravel the emergent properties of CESA rosette assembly and function, our working group will employ a community-scale data synthesis approach, strictly utilizing existing, publicly available datasets. Our methodology is designed to integrate disparate multi-omics and high-resolution imaging data through advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning frameworks, without generating any new experimental data. This transdisciplinary approach requires the combined expertise of plant cell biologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists. Data Acquisition and Curation: We will source massive datasets from established public repositories. Transcriptomic and genomic data will be retrieved from the Arabidopsis Information Resource (TAIR) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Mass spectrometry-based proteomics data, including protein-protein interaction networks and post-translational modification profiles, will be extracted from the PRIDE database. For spatial and temporal dynamics, we will mine the Image Data Resource (IDR) and other open-access bioimaging archives for high-resolution, time-lapse live-cell imaging datasets of fluorescently tagged CESA proteins and associated cytoskeletal markers. A dedicated sub-team of data scientists and plant biologists will collaboratively curate, standardize, and clean these multi-modal datasets to ensure high-quality inputs for our analytical pipelines. Multi-Omics Synthesis via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs): To address the stoichiometry and molecular assembly of CESA rosettes (Research Question 1), we will develop specialized Graph Neural Networks. GNNs are highly adept at modeling complex relational data. We will construct multi-layered graphs where nodes represent genes, proteins, and metabolites, and edges represent temporal co-expression or physical interactions derived from the synthesized TAIR and PRIDE datasets. By applying graph representation learning, we will uncover hidden, high-dimensional interaction motifs and predict the emergent chaperone networks required for proper hexameric assembly in the Golgi apparatus. Spatio-Temporal Modeling via Machine Learning Particle Tracking: To analyze the dynamics of CESA rosettes at the plasma membrane (Research Question 2), we will deploy advanced computer vision and machine learning-based particle tracking algorithms on the curated live-cell imaging datasets. Utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) combined with recurrent architectures (e.g., LSTMs), we will extract quantitative metrics such as rosette insertion rates, track velocities, trajectory linearity, and membrane lifetimes. This AI-driven synthesis will allow us to detect subtle, emergent patterns in collective rosette behavior under varying environmental conditions that traditional, manual analyses have missed. Transdisciplinary Integration and Predictive Modeling: To answer Research Question 3, we will fuse the outputs of the GNNs and the particle-tracking algorithms into a unified, multi-scale predictive model. This integration will map the molecular states of CESA proteins (e.g., phosphorylation status from proteomics) directly onto their mesoscale behavioral phenotypes (e.g., movement velocity from imaging). Our computational biophysicists will utilize these integrated parameters to simulate the biophysical rules governing cellulose microfibril extrusion and cell wall mechanics. By operating entirely in the computational space, our methodology leverages the power of community-scale synthesis. The project relies on the diverse scientific perspectives of our team to iteratively refine these AI models, ensuring that our analytical strategies remain biologically grounded while pushing the boundaries of data-intensive discovery in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that significantly advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. By decoding the assembly and dynamics of CESA rosettes, we expect to reveal the hidden biophysical rules that govern how nanoscale protein interactions scale up to produce functional, mesoscale extracellular matrices. This will solve a long-standing puzzle in plant mechanobiology, providing a definitive model for cellulose biosynthesis that has eluded the scientific community for decades. Beyond plant biology, the discovery of these emergent rules will offer foundational insights applicable to other complex multiprotein systems at the plasma membrane across various taxa. Methodologically, this project will yield innovative analytical strategies. The custom Graph Neural Networks and machine learning-based particle-tracking pipelines developed to synthesize multi-modal omics and imaging data will be highly adaptable. These tools will empower the broader scientific community to extract new value from existing public databases, accelerating discoveries in other areas of cellular emergence. Crucially, this initiative will have a profound impact on workforce development, directly aligning with the NCEMS mandate to train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students integrated into our working group will receive rigorous, transdisciplinary cross-training. They will bridge the gap between biological theory and computational application, gaining highly sought-after skills in big data integration, AI/ML deployment, and collaborative software engineering. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the immense power of community-scale data synthesis. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives and leveraging NCEMS resources, we will catalyze a paradigm shift in how researchers approach complex biological questions, proving that profound novel insights can be achieved by synthesizing the wealth of publicly available data without the need for new experimental generation.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed community-scale synthesis project requires NCEMS support and resources that far exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. Because this project strictly utilizes existing publicly available data and does not involve the generation of new experimental data, our budget is strategically allocated toward facilitating transdisciplinary collaboration, computational infrastructure, and workforce training, rather than wet-lab supplies or equipment. A primary component of the budget is dedicated to supporting the Working Group's collaborative infrastructure. We request funds to host bi-annual, intensive in-person synthesis meetings at the NCEMS facility. These gatherings are critical for fostering deep, cross-disciplinary integration among our diverse team of plant cell biologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists. Funds will cover travel, lodging, and per diem expenses for all members, ensuring equitable participation across varying geographic locations, institutional research levels, and career stages. Crucially, a significant portion of the budget will directly support the training of the next-generation workforce. We request funding for two postdoctoral fellowships and three graduate student stipends. These trainees will be the engine of our data synthesis efforts, receiving unparalleled cross-training in machine learning, big data integration, and collaborative software development. Additionally, we require resources for advanced computational infrastructure. While we will leverage institutional high-performance computing clusters, we request funds for cloud computing services (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) to handle the massive storage requirements of high-resolution imaging datasets (IDR) and to train our computationally intensive Graph Neural Networks and particle-tracking models. Finally, a small allocation is requested for open-access publication fees to ensure our findings remain freely accessible. This budget perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission, prioritizing collaborative human capital and cutting-edge computational resources to unlock the emergent properties of molecular and cellular systems.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Assembly of Bacterial Microcompartments

original.abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), such as carboxysomes, are highly sophisticated, mesoscale proteinaceous organelles that encapsulate specific metabolic pathways to enhance efficiency and prevent the release of toxic intermediates. The self-assembly of thousands of shell proteins and internal enzymes into a geometrically precise, functional polyhedral structure is a spectacular example of biological emergence. Despite detailed structural knowledge of individual BMC components, the predictive rules governing how these parts dynamically self-organize into functional mesoscale compartments across diverse bacterial species remain elusive. Understanding this emergence is critical for advancing synthetic biology and understanding microbial ecology. Our working group proposes a large-scale data synthesis project to decode the emergent assembly pathways of BMCs. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including comparative genomics, structural data, and proteomics from repositories such as the NCBI, the Protein Data Bank, and PRIDE. By leveraging advanced structural bioinformatics, AlphaFold-multimer predictions, and deep learning-based kinetic modeling, we will synthesize these datasets to predict BMC assembly pathways. This project relies entirely on existing data, using innovative AI strategies to map the complex network of interactions that drive mesoscale protein condensation and shell formation. The multifaceted nature of BMC biology requires a transdisciplinary approach that exceeds the capacity of any single lab, making NCEMS support critical. We will convene a diverse team of structural biologists, microbiologists, computational biophysicists, and machine learning engineers. Our working group is structured to promote collaborative partnerships across diverse geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages, ensuring a broad range of scientific perspectives. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this long-standing microbial mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in structural data integration, AI-driven modeling, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale protein organelles influences higher-order metabolic outcomes, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.
original.background_and_significance: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), exemplified by carboxysomes and metabolosomes, represent a pinnacle of evolutionary engineering. These mesoscale, proteinaceous organelles are ubiquitous across diverse bacterial phyla, serving to encapsulate sensitive or toxic metabolic pathways, thereby enhancing catalytic efficiency and protecting the cellular environment. Composed of thousands of individual shell proteins—hexamers, pentamers, and trimers—that self-assemble around a condensed enzymatic core, BMCs form geometrically precise polyhedral structures. The spontaneous organization of these macromolecular components into a functional, spatially defined compartment is a paradigmatic example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. Despite decades of research yielding high-resolution structural data for individual BMC components, a fundamental mystery remains: what are the predictive rules governing the dynamic self-organization of these disparate parts into functional mesoscale compartments? Currently, our understanding is fragmented. Structural biologists have deposited thousands of protein structures into the Protein Data Bank (PDB), microbiologists have sequenced countless bacterial genomes housed in NCBI, and biochemists have generated extensive interactome data available in PRIDE. However, these datasets remain siloed. The lack of a unified, synthesized perspective limits our ability to predict assembly pathways, understand the evolutionary trajectory of BMCs, or rationally design synthetic microcompartments for bioengineering applications. This project addresses this critical knowledge gap by proposing a massive, community-scale data synthesis initiative. Aligning directly with the U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mandate, we will leverage existing, publicly available data to decode the emergent properties of BMC assembly. By integrating comparative genomics, structural biology, and proteomics, we will move beyond reductionist views of individual proteins to understand the system-level phenomena that dictate mesoscale organelle formation. The significance of this work is twofold. First, it will solve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology regarding how transient, weak protein-protein interactions collectively drive the robust, deterministic assembly of complex biological architectures. Second, it will establish a novel computational paradigm for studying mesoscale emergence, utilizing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning-based kinetic modeling. This transdisciplinary approach—requiring the combined expertise of structural biologists, microbiologists, computational biophysicists, and machine learning engineers—exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory. By synthesizing these diverse data streams, we will elucidate how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale influences higher-order subcellular and cellular metabolic outcomes. Furthermore, this project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, equipping them with the skills necessary to navigate and synthesize vast biological datasets. Ultimately, unlocking the design principles of BMCs will not only deepen our fundamental understanding of microbial ecology and cellular organization but will also catalyze breakthroughs in synthetic biology, enabling the development of custom nanoreactors for sustainable biomanufacturing, carbon fixation, and targeted drug delivery.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: To decode the emergent assembly of Bacterial Microcompartments (BMCs), our working group will focus on three primary research questions, each addressing a critical facet of mesoscale biological emergence. These questions are designed to be answered exclusively through the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets, utilizing advanced AI and computational modeling. Question 1: What are the universal sequence-to-structure-to-assembly rules that govern the formation of diverse BMC classes across different bacterial phyla? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that despite significant sequence divergence among shell proteins across evolutionary lineages, a conserved set of geometric and thermodynamic interaction motifs dictates the emergent assembly of the polyhedral shell. By synthesizing genomic data (NCBI) with structural databases (PDB) and utilizing AlphaFold-multimer predictions, we expect to identify cryptic, pan-BMC interaction interfaces that drive the initial nucleation and subsequent propagation of the protein shell. We postulate that specific, identifiable amino acid co-evolutionary networks act as thermodynamic switches that guide the system toward a closed polyhedral state rather than an open-ended aggregate. Question 2: How do the kinetic pathways of core enzyme condensation and shell encapsulation coordinate to prevent misassembly and the formation of kinetic traps? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the emergent assembly of BMCs relies on a tightly regulated, hierarchical kinetic pathway where the liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) or condensation of core enzymes acts as a necessary scaffold for the ordered recruitment and multimerization of shell proteins. By integrating proteomics and interactomics data (PRIDE) with deep learning-based kinetic modeling, we predict that the interaction affinities between core enzymes and specific shell proteins are evolutionarily tuned to synchronize condensation and encapsulation. We anticipate that synthesizing these datasets will reveal distinct kinetic checkpoints that prevent the premature closure of empty shells or the failure to encapsulate critical metabolic intermediates. Question 3: Can we predict the emergent mesoscale properties (e.g., shell permeability, stability, and size) of uncharacterized BMCs based solely on their genomic operon architecture and predicted protein interactomes? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the higher-order structural and functional properties of BMCs are encoded not just in individual protein sequences, but in the stoichiometric ratios and interaction networks of the entire BMC operon. By training machine learning models on synthesized multi-omics datasets, we expect to develop a predictive framework that links operon architecture to the physical properties of the assembled organelle. We hypothesize that variations in the ratio of hexameric to pentameric shell proteins, driven by differential expression patterns inferred from transcriptomic data, directly modulate the emergent size and permeability of the microcompartment. Addressing these questions will solve long-standing mysteries regarding how molecular parts dynamically self-organize into functional mesoscale compartments. By answering these questions through a purely synthetic, data-driven approach, our working group will establish new methodological standards for investigating biological emergence. This transdisciplinary inquiry will yield profound insights into the physical principles of self-assembly, providing a comprehensive blueprint of how molecular interactions scale up to produce complex, functional cellular subsystems.
original.methods_and_approach: Our methodological approach is rooted in the large-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. Our workflow is divided into three interconnected phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, AI-Driven Structural Synthesis, and Deep Learning-Based Kinetic Modeling. Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will construct a comprehensive, unified database of BMC components by mining existing repositories. Genomic data and operon architectures will be extracted from the NCBI RefSeq database. High-resolution structural data for individual BMC proteins will be sourced from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Furthermore, we will integrate mass spectrometry-based proteomics and protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from the PRIDE database to establish empirical baselines for protein abundances and interaction networks. This phase requires rigorous data harmonization, utilizing automated pipelines to standardize metadata, resolve nomenclature inconsistencies, and map genomic sequences to structural models. Phase 2: AI-Driven Structural Synthesis. To bridge the gap between individual protein structures and mesoscale assemblies, we will employ advanced AI-driven structural bioinformatics. We will utilize AlphaFold-Multimer and RoseTTAFold to predict the structures of multi-protein complexes and interaction interfaces that have not been experimentally resolved. By running massive, parallelized structure predictions on high-performance computing clusters, we will map the complete interactome of BMC shell and core proteins. We will apply Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to analyze these predicted interaction networks, identifying conserved structural motifs and co-evolutionary patterns across thousands of diverse bacterial species. This will allow us to synthesize a comprehensive atlas of the structural rules governing BMC facet formation and vertex closure. Phase 3: Deep Learning-Based Kinetic Modeling. To understand the dynamic emergence of BMCs, we will transition from static structural models to dynamic kinetic simulations. We will synthesize our structural interactome data with empirical proteomics data to parameterize deep learning-based kinetic models. Utilizing frameworks like reinforcement learning, we will simulate the assembly pathways of BMCs under varying stoichiometric and thermodynamic conditions. These models will explore the massive phase space of possible assembly trajectories, identifying the most probable pathways that lead to functional, closed polyhedra while avoiding kinetic traps. We will specifically model the interplay between core enzyme condensation (using predictive phase-separation algorithms) and shell protein encapsulation. Transdisciplinary Collaboration: This ambitious synthesis requires a diverse working group. Our team integrates structural biologists (to validate AI structural predictions), microbiologists (to provide ecological and evolutionary context), computational biophysicists (to design kinetic models), and machine learning engineers (to optimize deep learning pipelines). We will host bi-monthly virtual synthesis sessions and bi-annual in-person hackathons at the NCEMS facility to foster intensive cross-disciplinary collaboration. By combining these diverse perspectives and utilizing cutting-edge AI to synthesize disparate datasets, our approach will transcend traditional reductionist methodologies, providing a holistic, systems-level understanding of mesoscale biological emergence that is impossible to achieve within a single laboratory setting.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale biological emergence. First, we will produce the 'BMC-SynthAtlas', the first comprehensive, publicly accessible database integrating genomic, structural, and interactomic data for thousands of bacterial microcompartments across diverse phyla. This resource will serve as a foundational tool for the global molecular and cellular biology community. Second, we will deliver a validated suite of AI-driven predictive models capable of mapping the assembly pathways and emergent physical properties of BMCs based solely on genomic sequence data. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how complex, multi-protein organelles self-assemble with high fidelity. The impact of these outcomes extends far beyond basic science. By elucidating the design principles of BMCs, this project will catalyze significant advancements in synthetic biology. Researchers will be able to leverage our predictive rules to engineer bespoke nanoreactors for targeted drug delivery, enhanced carbon fixation, and the sustainable biomanufacturing of high-value chemicals. Furthermore, understanding BMC emergence will provide deeper insights into microbial ecology, particularly how bacteria adapt to specific metabolic niches through subcellular compartmentalization. Crucially, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers within a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary network, we will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. These trainees will gain invaluable, hands-on experience in structural data integration, advanced machine learning, and collaborative coding. Ultimately, by successfully synthesizing disparate public datasets to reveal the mechanisms of mesoscale emergence, this project will strongly validate the NCEMS vision, demonstrating the immense power of community-scale data synthesis to answer the most fundamental and complex questions in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

title: Emergence of Lipid Homeostasis through Peroxisome Biogenesis Networks

original.abstract: Peroxisomes are highly dynamic mesoscale organelles essential for cellular lipid metabolism and reactive oxygen species detoxification. Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes can form de novo from the endoplasmic reticulum or multiply by fission, creating a highly adaptable, emergent metabolic network. The precise molecular rules governing how local protein import and membrane lipid sorting dictate the global abundance, size, and metabolic capacity of the peroxisomal compartment remain a major unresolved puzzle in cell biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is vital for deciphering how cells maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental stresses. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis. We will systematically integrate publicly available lipidomics data, high-throughput fluorescence microscopy, and interactomic datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench, the Image Data Resource, and BioGRID. By employing advanced computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools powered by machine learning, we will synthesize these disparate datasets to model the dynamic state of the peroxisome network. This approach utilizes only existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies that reveal the physical rules of mesoscale metabolic emergence. The sheer scale and complexity of integrating spatial imaging with functional lipidomics require the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary team brings together cell biologists, lipid biochemists, computational data scientists, and systems biologists. We have intentionally assembled a working group that reflects diverse scientific perspectives, including researchers from various career stages and geographic locations. This diversity is essential for breaking down disciplinary silos and fostering novel insights into complex biological phenomena. Training the next generation of researchers is a fundamental aspect of our proposal. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, developing critical skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative open science. In strict adherence to community policies on reproducible science, all integrated datasets, network models, and analytical code will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale organelle networks influences higher-order cellular metabolism, perfectly aligning with the overarching goals of NCEMS.
original.background_and_significance: Peroxisomes represent a quintessential example of mesoscale biological emergence. Unlike mitochondria, which only divide from pre-existing organelles, peroxisomes possess the remarkable ability to form de novo from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or multiply via fission. This duality allows cells to rapidly and dynamically scale their peroxisomal networks in response to metabolic demands, environmental stresses, and developmental cues. As crucial hubs for cellular lipid metabolism—particularly the beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids—and the detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis are foundational to cellular homeostasis. Despite decades of study, the precise molecular rules governing how local events, such as peroxisomal membrane protein (PMP) import and lipid sorting at the ER, dictate the global abundance, spatial distribution, size, and metabolic capacity of the peroxisomal compartment remain a major unresolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is vital for deciphering how cells maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental stresses and why peroxisome biogenesis disorders are so devastating. Currently, the field is rich with publicly available but isolated datasets. The Metabolomics Workbench houses extensive functional lipidomics data detailing metabolic states across various cell types and conditions. The Image Data Resource (IDR) contains massive repositories of high-throughput fluorescence microscopy images capturing the spatial distribution and morphological dynamics of peroxisomes. BioGRID and other interaction databases catalog the complex protein-protein interactomes underlying peroxisome assembly and fission. However, these datasets have never been systematically integrated to model the emergent properties of the peroxisome network. This fragmentation represents a critical missed opportunity. By synthesizing these disparate data streams, we can bridge the gap between molecular interactions (nanoscale) and cellular metabolic states (microscale), focusing precisely on the mesoscale organelle network. This proposed community-scale synthesis project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission. It addresses a fundamental question of emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences by leveraging only existing, publicly available data. It moves beyond the capabilities of a single laboratory by demanding a convergence of expertise in cell biology, lipid biochemistry, computational data science, and systems biology. By integrating spatial imaging with functional lipidomics and interactomic data, we will elucidate the physical and molecular rules of mesoscale metabolic emergence. This synthesis will not only solve long-standing puzzles regarding peroxisome network scaling but will also develop innovative computational strategies for multi-omics and spatial data integration. Furthermore, this project addresses the critical need to understand how mesoscale structures decouple or couple with other cellular networks, such as the ER and mitochondria, during metabolic stress. The dynamic interplay between these organelles forms a meta-network essential for cellular survival. By utilizing advanced machine learning and network analysis, we will map these interactions, providing a holistic view of cellular lipid homeostasis. This synthesis will catalyze a new era of organelle biology, shifting the focus from isolated components to emergent, system-wide properties, thereby fulfilling the core vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our synthesis project is driven by three overarching research questions that aim to decode the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis networks. By integrating multi-modal public datasets, we will test specific hypotheses regarding the mesoscale organization and metabolic capacity of these organelles. Question 1: How do local protein-protein interaction networks at the ER-peroxisome interface dictate the global spatial distribution and morphological heterogeneity of the peroxisome network? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the topology of the peroxisome interactome, specifically the abundance and connectivity of Pex3/Pex19 docking complexes and fission factors (e.g., Fis1/Mff), serves as a predictive blueprint for the emergent spatial architecture of the peroxisome network. We expect that specific interactomic signatures will correlate with distinct morphological states (e.g., hyper-fission vs. de novo biogenesis dominance) captured in high-throughput imaging datasets. By mapping interactomic data from BioGRID onto spatial features extracted from the Image Data Resource (IDR), we anticipate identifying critical network nodes that act as master regulators of mesoscale organelle emergence. Question 2: What are the mathematical rules governing the scaling relationship between peroxisome network morphology (size, number, distribution) and global cellular lipid homeostasis? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that peroxisome networks do not scale linearly with cellular lipid load; rather, they exhibit non-linear, emergent scaling behaviors optimized for specific metabolic stress states. We predict that integrating spatial network metrics (derived from computer vision analysis of microscopy data) with functional lipidomics profiles (from the Metabolomics Workbench) will reveal distinct 'metabolic-morphological attractors.' For instance, conditions characterized by high very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation will correspond to highly specific, emergent spatial configurations of peroxisomes that maximize membrane contact sites with lipid droplets and mitochondria, thereby optimizing metabolic flux. Question 3: Can machine learning models trained on integrated multi-omics and spatial datasets accurately predict the emergent metabolic state of a cell based solely on the structural dynamics of its peroxisome network? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the structural configuration of the mesoscale peroxisome network is fundamentally deterministic of its metabolic output. Therefore, AI-driven spatial network analysis tools can be trained to predict complex lipidomic profiles from fluorescence microscopy images alone. We posit that by synthesizing these diverse datasets, we can develop a robust computational framework that uncovers the hidden physical rules linking organelle architecture to metabolic function. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells dynamically balance de novo biogenesis and fission to maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental conditions. Together, these questions challenge the traditional, reductionist view of organelle biology. Instead of studying individual peroxisomal proteins in isolation, our hypotheses focus on the emergent properties that arise when these components interact at the mesoscale. By answering these questions through data synthesis, we will establish a new paradigm for understanding how dynamic, highly adaptable organelle networks self-organize to regulate cellular metabolism, directly addressing the NCEMS call for transdisciplinary research into molecular and cellular emergence.
original.methods_and_approach: To investigate the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis, our working group will employ a purely data-driven, synthesis-based approach, rigorously adhering to the constraint of generating no new experimental data. Our methodology relies on the systematic integration of three distinct, publicly available data streams: functional lipidomics (Metabolomics Workbench), high-throughput fluorescence microscopy (Image Data Resource, IDR), and protein-protein interactions (BioGRID and STRING). Phase 1: Data Curation and Harmonization. The first major hurdle in community-scale synthesis is standardizing disparate datasets. Our computational data scientists will develop automated pipelines to extract and curate lipidomic profiles of wild-type and peroxisome-deficient/stressed cell lines from the Metabolomics Workbench. Concurrently, we will retrieve corresponding high-throughput imaging datasets from the IDR that feature fluorescently tagged peroxisomal markers (e.g., PMP70, GFP-SKL). Interactomic data detailing peroxisome biogenesis factors will be pulled from BioGRID. We will utilize semantic web technologies and biological ontologies to create a unified, harmonized meta-database linking specific cellular conditions across these three modalities. Phase 2: Computer Vision and Spatial Feature Extraction. To quantify the mesoscale emergence of peroxisome networks, we will apply advanced computer vision algorithms to the IDR imaging datasets. Using deep learning-based segmentation models (e.g., Cellpose adapted for organelle detection), we will extract highly granular spatial features for millions of individual cells. These features will include peroxisome count, volume, spatial distribution (e.g., clustering vs. dispersion), and proximity to the nucleus or other organelles. This will transform qualitative image data into quantitative, high-dimensional structural profiles representing the emergent physical state of the network. Phase 3: Spatial Network Analysis and Interactome Mapping. We will construct spatial network models where individual peroxisomes are treated as nodes, and their spatial proximities are treated as edges. By integrating BioGRID interactomic data, we will overlay molecular interaction probabilities onto these spatial networks. This will allow us to model how local protein complex formations (e.g., at the ER) propagate to influence global network topology. We will utilize graph neural networks (GNNs) to identify emergent structural motifs within these spatial interactomes. Phase 4: Multi-Modal Synthesis and Machine Learning. The final phase involves synthesizing the structural profiles (Phase 2 & 3) with the functional lipidomic data (Phase 1). We will employ multi-omics integration frameworks, such as Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA), to identify latent factors that drive the co-variation between peroxisome network architecture and cellular lipid homeostasis. Furthermore, we will train predictive machine learning models (e.g., Random Forests, Gradient Boosting) to forecast lipidomic states based entirely on spatial network metrics. This transdisciplinary approach requires the collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. The sheer computational scale of processing IDR images, combined with the biochemical expertise needed to interpret complex lipidomic shifts, is beyond any single laboratory. By leveraging diverse scientific perspectives, we will develop innovative analytical strategies that synthesize existing data into a cohesive model of mesoscale organelle emergence, solving long-standing puzzles in cellular metabolism.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mission. Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the first comprehensive, multi-scale model of peroxisome biogenesis as an emergent network. By elucidating the mathematical rules that link local protein interactions to mesoscale organelle architecture and macroscale cellular lipid homeostasis, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells dynamically scale their metabolic compartments. This will provide unprecedented insights into cellular adaptation, aging, and the etiology of peroxisomal biogenesis disorders. Methodologically, we will deliver a suite of innovative, open-source analytical strategies and computational pipelines. Our novel application of graph neural networks and computer vision to integrate spatial imaging with functional lipidomics will establish a new gold standard for multi-modal data synthesis. These tools will be broadly applicable to other researchers studying emergent phenomena in different organelle systems, thereby amplifying the impact of our work across the biological sciences. Crucially, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By bringing together a transdisciplinary team of cell biologists, lipid biochemists, and computational scientists across various career stages and geographic locations, we will break down traditional academic silos. Our working group will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will receive intensive, cross-disciplinary mentorship, acquiring highly sought-after skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative data synthesis. The resulting predictive models will not only advance basic science but also offer potential new avenues for identifying therapeutic targets in metabolic diseases characterized by lipid dysregulation, ensuring a lasting legacy for this NCEMS-funded initiative. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the immense untapped potential of publicly available data, proving that community-scale synthesis is a powerful engine for discovery.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project requires the unique collaborative infrastructure and resources provided by NCEMS, as it significantly exceeds the capabilities and funding scope of any single laboratory. Crucially, in accordance with NCEMS guidelines, no funds are requested for the generation of new experimental data. The primary budget allocation will support the convening of our transdisciplinary working group. We request funding for four in-person, multi-day synthesis meetings to be held at the NCEMS facility over the two-year project period. These intensive collaborative sessions are essential for bridging disciplinary vocabularies, integrating diverse scientific perspectives, and driving the conceptual synthesis of our data. The budget will cover travel, lodging, and per diem expenses for all working group members, ensuring equitable participation across different geographic locations and career stages. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to training and workforce development. We request stipend and tuition support for two graduate students and partial salary support for one postdoctoral fellow. These trainees will be the primary engines of data integration and will benefit immensely from the cross-disciplinary mentorship network established by the working group. To support the heavy computational demands of processing high-throughput IDR imaging data and training machine learning models, we request resources for secure, high-performance cloud computing infrastructure (e.g., AWS or similar platforms). This includes costs for data storage, GPU-accelerated computing instances, and software licensing necessary for advanced computer vision and spatial network analysis. Finally, funds are requested for open science dissemination, including open-access publication fees and costs associated with hosting our harmonized datasets and Docker containers on public repositories. This budget directly empowers our team to leverage existing public data, develop innovative analytical strategies, and foster the transdisciplinary collaboration required to unravel the emergent properties of mesoscale organelle networks.

title: Decoding the Emergent Membrane Scission Dynamics of the ESCRT Machinery

original.abstract: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery is a highly conserved set of proteins that drive membrane remodeling and scission away from the cytoplasm. This machinery functions in diverse cellular processes, including multivesicular body biogenesis, viral budding, and cytokinesis. The sequential assembly of ESCRT components into mesoscale helical filaments that constrict and cleave membranes represents a profound example of biophysical emergence. However, the universal rules governing how local, nanoscale protein-lipid interactions translate into the generation of massive, mesoscale mechanical forces for membrane scission remain highly contested. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent biophysics of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including cryo-electron microscopy structures, single-molecule biophysics data, and cellular imaging from repositories such as the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced molecular dynamics simulations guided by machine learning and topological data analysis, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to reconstruct the spatio-temporal dynamics of membrane constriction. This project relies entirely on existing public data, utilizing AI to extract novel insights into how local molecular interactions dictate the emergence of complex mesoscale forces. The integration of structural biophysics with cellular imaging requires a collaborative effort that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory, necessitating the support of NCEMS. We have assembled a diverse team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computer vision experts, and cellular ultrastructure specialists. Our working group is intentionally curated to include diverse scientific perspectives, bridging researchers from different institutional tiers and geographic locations. This collaborative environment will drive the innovative analytical strategies needed to solve this long-standing biological mystery. Furthermore, this project serves as a vital training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will gain hands-on experience in structural data integration, advanced image analysis, and open science practices. We are fully committed to making all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines freely available to the scientific community through open-source platforms like GitHub. By illuminating the relationship between protein assembly and membrane scission, this synthesis project will directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
original.background_and_significance: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery is a highly conserved biological apparatus responsible for driving topologically unique membrane remodeling and scission events away from the cytoplasm. This machinery is indispensable for a myriad of critical cellular processes, including multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis, the budding of enveloped viruses such as HIV-1, and the final abscission step of cytokinesis. The sequential recruitment and assembly of ESCRT-I, -II, and -III complexes, culminating in the polymerization of ESCRT-III into mesoscale helical filaments, represents a profound and elegant example of biophysical emergence. At the nanoscale, individual ESCRT-III monomers interact with specific lipid geometries; however, it is the collective, higher-order assembly and subsequent ATP-dependent remodeling by the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 that generates the massive, mesoscale mechanical forces required to constrict and cleave the membrane neck. Despite decades of intense study, the universal rules governing this emergent translation of local protein-lipid interactions into mesoscale force generation remain highly contested. Current models debate whether scission is driven by a buckling spring mechanism, a sliding filament mechanism, or a dome-like structural collapse. This fundamental knowledge gap persists largely because traditional, single-laboratory experimental approaches are limited in their spatial and temporal resolution, often capturing only static snapshots or isolated in vitro phenomena. The complexity of this mesoscale phenomenon necessitates a community-scale synthesis approach, perfectly aligned with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). Over the past decade, an unprecedented volume of structural and cellular data has been deposited into public repositories. High-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of ESCRT filaments are available in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB), while dynamic, single-molecule biophysics trajectories and live-cell imaging datasets reside in repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive. However, these multi-modal datasets remain siloed. Our proposed synthesis project will aggregate, integrate, and synthesize these massive, publicly available datasets to decode the emergent biophysics of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. By leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and data science, our transdisciplinary working group will bridge the gap between structural biophysics and cellular ultrastructure. This project does not seek to generate new experimental data; rather, it harnesses the untapped potential of existing data to solve a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular sciences. The synthesis of such disparate data types—ranging from sub-nanometer structural coordinates to micron-scale cellular phenotypes—far exceeds the computational and analytical capabilities of any single research group. It requires the convergence of structural biologists, biophysicists, computer vision experts, and cellular ultrastructure specialists. By illuminating the relationship between ESCRT protein assembly and membrane scission, this project will directly advance the NCEMS vision of understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale, ultimately providing a predictive framework for emergent mechanobiology that can be applied to other complex macromolecular machines.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
To unravel the emergent biophysics of the ESCRT machinery, our working group has formulated a series of interconnected research questions and hypotheses that can only be addressed through the systematic synthesis of existing multi-modal data. Our inquiry is guided by the overarching premise that the mesoscale mechanical forces required for membrane scission are not inherent to any single ESCRT component, but rather emerge dynamically from the spatiotemporal integration of nanoscale protein-protein and protein-lipid interactions.

Question 1: What are the universal geometric and thermodynamic rules governing the transition of ESCRT-III filaments from flat spirals to 3D helical funnels across different cellular contexts?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that a conserved, sequence-independent topological mechanism drives ESCRT-III filament buckling. By synthesizing static cryo-EM structures with dynamic single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) data, we predict that the emergence of mesoscale buckling is dictated by a critical threshold of membrane curvature and specific electrostatic lipid interactions, which will be universally identifiable across MVB biogenesis, viral budding, and cytokinesis datasets.

Question 2: How does the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 coordinate the continuous turnover of ESCRT-III subunits to generate the mechanical work required for membrane constriction and ultimate scission?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that Vps4 does not act merely as a disassembly factor, but functions as an active mechanochemical motor that drives a "sliding filament" mechanism within the ESCRT-III polymer. By integrating existing high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) datasets with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we expect to reveal that Vps4-mediated extraction of specific ESCRT-III subunits induces a global, emergent conformational change in the filament network, constricting the membrane neck to the critical hemifission radius.

Question 3: In what ways do local membrane lipid compositions (e.g., PI(3)P, cholesterol, and ceramide) modulate the emergent mechanical properties of the ESCRT-III/Vps4 complex?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that local lipid sorting acts as an allosteric regulator of mesoscale ESCRT assembly. By synthesizing lipidomics data with cellular imaging and structural models, we anticipate finding that specific lipid microdomains lower the activation energy barrier for filament buckling, thereby dictating the spatial precision and timing of scission.

Question 4: Can machine learning models predict the emergent scission efficiency of novel or mutant ESCRT assemblies based solely on their nanoscale structural parameters?
Hypothesis 4: We hypothesize that artificial intelligence, specifically graph neural networks (GNNs) trained on synthesized structural and phenotypic data, can accurately predict mesoscale scission outcomes. We expect that topological data analysis of the ESCRT-membrane interface will identify a minimal set of geometric features that define the "scission-competent" state.

Addressing these questions perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mandate to tackle compelling scientific questions using publicly available data. By testing these hypotheses through data synthesis, we will resolve long-standing debates regarding the ESCRT mechanism. Furthermore, answering these questions requires the cross-disciplinary expertise of our team, combining structural biology, computational biophysics, and AI, to acquire novel, deeper, and broader insights into how complex mesoscale forces emerge in cellular biology.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our transdisciplinary working group will employ a purely computational, data-driven synthesis approach to decode ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. In strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines, this project will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, we will aggregate, harmonize, and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets from diverse repositories, utilizing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and computational biophysics to extract novel mesoscale insights.

Data Aggregation and Harmonization: We will systematically mine the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) for all available high-resolution structures of ESCRT-III and Vps4 complexes. Concurrently, we will extract dynamic single-molecule biophysics data (smFRET, HS-AFM) from the BioImage Archive and cellular imaging datasets (live-cell fluorescence, electron tomography) from the Image Data Resource (IDR). Because these datasets exist in disparate formats and spatiotemporal scales, our first critical step is data harmonization. We will develop automated, open-source Python pipelines to standardize coordinate frames, normalize intensity values, and annotate metadata using standardized biological ontologies.

AI-Guided Structural Synthesis and Topological Data Analysis (TDA): To bridge the gap between static nanoscale structures and dynamic mesoscale assemblies, we will employ Topological Data Analysis (TDA). TDA will allow us to extract shape-based, scale-invariant features from the aggregated cryo-EM and electron tomography datasets. We will train Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on these topological features to predict intermediate conformational states of the ESCRT-III filament that have not been experimentally captured. The GNNs will map the trajectory of filament buckling, identifying the structural transition states that define the emergence of mechanical force.

Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CG-MD) Simulations: To test our hypotheses regarding force generation and lipid interactions, we will integrate our AI-predicted intermediate structures into highly scalable Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CG-MD) simulations using the Martini 3 force field. By parameterizing these simulations with aggregated lipidomics data, we will model the mesoscale dynamics of the entire ESCRT-membrane scission neck (comprising millions of particles) over microsecond timescales. This will allow us to calculate the mechanical work generated by Vps4-mediated subunit turnover and observe the emergent membrane constriction forces in silico.

Cross-Disciplinary Collaborative Workflow: The complexity of synthesizing structural biophysics, computer vision, and cellular ultrastructure requires a robust collaborative framework. Our working group will utilize cloud-based computational infrastructure to enable real-time, multi-institutional data sharing and analysis. Bi-weekly virtual synthesis meetings and bi-annual in-person hackathons will ensure continuous cross-pollination of ideas between our structural biologists, biophysicists, and AI experts.

Training the Data-Savvy Workforce: This project is designed as a premier training ground. Graduate students and postdocs will be co-mentored by PIs from different disciplines, gaining hands-on expertise in multi-modal data integration, machine learning, and advanced MD simulations. Trainees will lead the development of the data harmonization pipelines and AI models, equipping them with highly sought-after skills in the modern, data-driven biological sciences. This comprehensive approach ensures that we not only solve a fundamental biological puzzle but also build the collaborative and analytical infrastructure necessary for future mesoscale synthesis research.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission of understanding mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will deliver a unified, spatiotemporally resolved model of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. By resolving the long-standing debate over the biophysical mechanisms of filament buckling and Vps4-driven force generation, this project will fundamentally rewrite our understanding of how nanoscale protein interactions translate into massive, mesoscale mechanical forces. This predictive framework will have broad implications, potentially illuminating the mechanics of other complex macromolecular machines.

Second, we will produce a suite of innovative, open-source analytical tools. The Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Topological Data Analysis (TDA) pipelines developed to integrate multi-modal structural and cellular data will be packaged into user-friendly software libraries. These tools will empower the broader scientific community to conduct their own synthesis research, enabling the analysis of diverse emergent phenomena beyond the ESCRT machinery.

Third, our project will generate a highly curated, harmonized meta-database of ESCRT structural, biophysical, and cellular imaging data. This resource will serve as a permanent community asset, facilitating future data-mining and machine-learning applications.

Finally, the impact on human capital will be profound. By training a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs in advanced data synthesis, AI, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, we will directly contribute to the development of the future data-savvy scientific workforce. The collaborative partnerships forged across different institutional tiers and geographic locations will stimulate new avenues of transdisciplinary research, proving that community-scale synthesis of publicly available data can rival, and often exceed, the insights generated by isolated experimental approaches. Ultimately, this project will catalyze a paradigm shift in how we study emergent mechanobiology.
