title: Synthesizing the Emergent Architecture of the Cellular Glycocalyx Meshwork

original.abstract: The glycocalyx is a dense, mesoscale meshwork of glycoproteins and glycolipids that coats the surface of nearly all eukaryotic cells. This complex sugar barrier mediates critical cellular outcomes, including immune recognition, mechanotransduction, and pathogen entry. Despite its importance, the glycocalyx remains one of the least understood cellular structures due to its immense structural complexity. How the nanoscale biosynthesis of diverse glycan chains scales up to produce the emergent, biophysical properties of this mesoscale meshwork is a major unsolved puzzle in glycobiology. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of glycocalyx architecture. We will integrate publicly available glycomics, spatial transcriptomics, and super-resolution imaging datasets from specialized repositories like GlyTouCan, the Gene Expression Omnibus, and the Image Data Resource. By employing advanced graph neural networks and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic network of glycan interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local sugar biosynthesis leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional cellular barriers. The complexity of glycobiology requires the integration of chemical biology with multi-omics data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites glycobiologists, computational biophysicists, multi-omics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular surface networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale surface barriers, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.
original.background_and_significance:
The cellular glycocalyx represents one of the most compelling and enigmatic examples of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Coating the surface of nearly all eukaryotic cells, this dense meshwork of glycoproteins, glycolipids, and proteoglycans serves as the primary interface between the cell and its environment. It mediates highly critical cellular outcomes, including immune system recognition, cellular mechanotransduction, and the entry of viral and bacterial pathogens. Despite its undeniable biological significance, the glycocalyx remains one of the least understood cellular structures. This knowledge gap is primarily driven by the immense structural complexity and dynamic nature of glycan networks, which cannot be fully captured by traditional, single-discipline experimental approaches. The fundamental mystery lies in emergence: how does the nanoscale biosynthesis of diverse, localized glycan chains scale up to produce the highly organized, biophysical properties of a mesoscale meshwork? 

Currently, the molecular and cellular sciences are rich with isolated datasets that capture fragments of this process. Repositories such as GlyTouCan house vast amounts of structural glycomics data; the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) contains extensive spatial transcriptomic profiles of glycosyltransferases and related enzymes; and the Image Data Resource (IDR) archives high-fidelity super-resolution imaging of cellular surfaces. However, these datasets exist in silos. The lack of integration across scales—from the molecular sequence of sugars to the spatial organization of the cellular surface—has prevented a holistic understanding of glycocalyx architecture. 

This proposal directly addresses the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) call by executing a community-scale data synthesis project that requires no new experimental data generation. We propose to synthesize these disparate, publicly available datasets to uncover the rules governing the mesoscale emergence of the glycocalyx. This synthesis is beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory; it requires a transdisciplinary approach that merges chemical biology, computational biophysics, and advanced artificial intelligence. By leveraging this wealth of untapped data, our working group will solve a long-standing puzzle in glycobiology: the translation of molecular-level sugar modifications into cellular-level barrier functions. 

Furthermore, this project aligns seamlessly with the NCEMS vision of understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at different scales of composition and space. The mesoscale—the critical nexus between individual biomolecules and whole organelles—is precisely where the glycocalyx operates. By integrating AI and data science with molecular biology, we will catalyze multidisciplinary scientific discovery, stimulate novel questions regarding cellular surface dynamics, and recruit and train a new generation of data-savvy scientists. Ultimately, this research will transform our understanding of cellular barriers, providing foundational insights that will impact fields ranging from developmental biology to immunology and infectious disease, all while adhering strictly to the highest standards of open and reproducible science.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions that seek to decode the emergent properties of the glycocalyx. These questions are designed to bridge the gap between nanoscale molecular data and mesoscale cellular phenomena, relying entirely on the computational synthesis of existing public datasets. 

Question 1: How do nanoscale glycan linkages and chemical modifications scale to dictate the emergent mesoscale properties (e.g., thickness, density, and charge) of the glycocalyx? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that specific, identifiable combinatorial patterns of nanoscale glycan structures act as 'molecular blueprints' that predictably generate distinct mesoscale biophysical states. Rather than a random assortment of sugars, the glycocalyx architecture is governed by emergent topological rules where localized clustering of specific glycoproteins (e.g., heavily sialylated mucins) disproportionately drives the macroscopic rigidity and porosity of the cellular barrier. 

Question 2: What are the universal emergent topological motifs of the glycocalyx meshwork across diverse eukaryotic cell types, and how do these motifs reorganize during pathogenic transitions? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that emergent topological motifs within the glycocalyx are evolutionarily conserved across diverse cell types to maintain baseline barrier integrity, but undergo predictable, systemic reorganization during disease states (such as viral infection or malignant transformation). By synthesizing super-resolution imaging with glycomic profiles, we expect to identify 'glyco-architectural signatures'—mesoscale structural shifts that correlate with cellular vulnerability or resilience to external pathogens. 

Question 3: How can spatial transcriptomic profiles of the cellular biosynthetic machinery predict the emergent biophysical properties of the surface barrier? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the spatial co-expression networks of glycosyltransferases and glycosidases within the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum directly correlate with the localized emergent architecture of the glycocalyx. We predict that by mapping transcriptomic data to surface imaging data, we can build a predictive AI model that accurately forecasts the mesoscale physical properties of the glycocalyx based solely on the transcriptional state of the cell. 

These research questions are highly novel because they shift the focus of glycobiology from the mere cataloging of sugar structures to the understanding of systemic, emergent physical properties. By addressing these questions, our working group will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells dynamically tune their surface barriers in response to environmental cues. The hypotheses challenge the traditional, linear view of glycan biosynthesis, proposing instead a complex systems perspective where non-linear interactions between diverse molecules give rise to entirely new physical properties at the mesoscale. Testing these hypotheses requires the integration of multi-modal omics and imaging data, demanding a sophisticated data science approach that perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to foster deep, transdisciplinary insights into molecular and cellular emergence.
original.methods_and_approach:
To answer our research questions without generating new experimental data, our working group will employ a robust, multi-phased computational methodology centered on data harmonization, advanced machine learning, and collaborative synthesis. 

Phase 1: Multi-Modal Data Acquisition and Harmonization 
We will systematically mine publicly available repositories to construct a unified meta-database. Structural glycomics data will be extracted from GlyTouCan and UniCarbKB. Spatial transcriptomics targeting the cellular biosynthetic machinery will be sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Super-resolution microscopy and cryo-electron tomography images of cellular surfaces will be aggregated from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR). Our multi-omics experts will develop standardized pipelines to harmonize these disparate data types, mapping transcriptomic identifiers to glycan structures and correlating these with morphological features extracted from imaging datasets. 

Phase 2: AI-Driven Feature Extraction and Synthesis 
To bridge the molecular and mesoscale levels, our machine learning engineers will deploy spatio-temporal deep learning architectures. We will utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract quantitative, mesoscale topological features (e.g., mesh density, filament length, spatial clustering) from the super-resolution imaging data. Concurrently, we will implement Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the nanoscale interactions between diverse glycan chains. GNNs are uniquely suited for this task, as they can represent glycans as nodes and their chemical linkages as edges, capturing the complex, non-linear topology of the sugar networks. 

Phase 3: Modeling Mesoscale Emergence 
The core synthesis will involve fusing the GNN-derived molecular models with the CNN-derived mesoscale imaging features. We will train multi-modal transformer models to identify correlations between the transcriptomic expression of glyco-enzymes, the predicted nanoscale glycan structures, and the observed mesoscale architecture of the glycocalyx. This AI-driven approach will allow us to reverse-engineer the universal principles of glycocalyx emergence, testing our hypotheses by predicting macroscopic barrier properties based on localized molecular inputs. 

Phase 4: Working Group Dynamics and Training 
This project is fundamentally beyond the scope of a single lab. Our transdisciplinary working group—comprising glycobiologists, computational biophysicists, and AI researchers—will meet bi-weekly virtually and convene for three intensive, in-person synthesis hackathons over the grant period. We have strategically recruited members from diverse geographic locations, career stages, and institutional research levels to ensure a rich variety of scientific perspectives. A critical component of our approach is the cross-training of the future data-savvy workforce. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will be embedded in all phases of the project. Through structured mentorship and hands-on workshops during our hackathons, trainees with biological backgrounds will learn advanced AI and data integration techniques, while computational trainees will gain deep domain expertise in molecular and cellular biophysics. This methodology ensures scientific rigor while fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for collaborative, transdisciplinary synthesis.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to decode emergent phenomena in the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, by identifying the universal rules that govern how nanoscale glycan biosynthesis scales into mesoscale barrier properties, we will solve a major, long-standing puzzle in glycobiology. This will fundamentally shift the paradigm from viewing the glycocalyx as a static coating to understanding it as a dynamic, emergent system. 

Second, the project will yield highly innovative analytical strategies. The multi-modal AI architectures—specifically the integration of Graph Neural Networks with spatio-temporal deep learning to bridge omics and imaging data—will establish a new methodological gold standard for mesoscale biology. These computational pipelines will be adaptable to other complex cellular networks, amplifying the project's impact far beyond glycobiology. 

Third, the insights generated will have profound implications for human health. Understanding the emergent architecture of the glycocalyx will uncover new mechanisms of viral entry, cancer metastasis, and immune evasion, providing a foundational biophysical context for future therapeutic interventions. 

Finally, the impact on workforce development will be substantial. By bringing together a diverse, transdisciplinary working group, we will tap into diverse new talent across geographic and institutional boundaries. Our rigorous cross-training program will produce a cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral fellows uniquely equipped to navigate the intersection of big data, artificial intelligence, and cellular biology. These newly trained, data-savvy scientists will be perfectly positioned to lead the next generation of synthesis research, ensuring a lasting legacy of multidisciplinary collaboration and innovation in the molecular sciences.

The budget is specifically designed to facilitate transdisciplinary integration, large-scale data synthesis, and workforce training, with absolutely no funds allocated for experimental data generation. 

Personnel costs represent the core of our budget. We request stipend and tuition support for two graduate students and salary for two postdoctoral fellows. These trainees are the engine of the synthesis project and the focus of our workforce development goals. They will conduct the day-to-day data harmonization and machine learning tasks while receiving invaluable cross-disciplinary training. 

Travel and meeting logistics are critical for our transdisciplinary working group. We request funds to support three intensive, in-person 'synthesis hackathons' over the funding period. These funds will cover travel, lodging, and hosting expenses for our diverse team of researchers, ensuring that members from various geographic locations and institutional backgrounds can collaborate effectively, build trust, and integrate their distinct expertise. 

Cloud computing and data storage resources are essential for handling the massive volume of multi-omics and super-resolution imaging data. We request funding for cloud infrastructure (e.g., AWS or Azure) to train our computationally intensive Graph Neural Networks and deep learning models, as well as to host our synthesized meta-databases for public access. 

Finally, we have allocated funds for Open Science and Publication fees to ensure that all manuscripts are published in high-impact, open-access journals. title: Emergent Contractility from Myosin II Thick Filament Assembly in Non-Muscle Cells

original.abstract: In non-muscle cells, the dynamic assembly of non-muscle myosin II into mesoscale bipolar thick filaments is essential for generating the contractile forces that drive cell migration, adhesion, and cytokinesis. The transition from individual, auto-inhibited myosin motors to highly ordered, force-generating mesoscale ensembles represents a classic example of biophysical emergence. However, the precise spatio-temporal rules governing how localized phosphorylation events and actin network architecture coordinate to drive this large-scale filament assembly remain a highly debated puzzle in mechanobiology. Understanding this emergence is vital for deciphering how cells dynamically alter their shape and exert physical force. Our working group proposes a comprehensive data synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of myosin filament assembly. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including live-cell super-resolution microscopy, biophysical force measurements, and phosphoproteomics from repositories such as the Cell Image Library, PRIDE, and specific mechanobiology databases. By utilizing advanced spatio-temporal data mining and unsupervised machine learning algorithms, we will synthesize these distinct datasets to identify the universal principles of mesoscale contractility. This approach relies entirely on existing data, leveraging AI to uncover the hidden rules of how local molecular motors scale up to produce global cellular forces. The multifaceted nature of cellular biomechanics requires a collaborative partnership that transcends individual lab capabilities, making NCEMS support essential. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of mechanobiologists, structural biophysicists, computational modelers, and data scientists. Our working group is structured to promote diverse scientific perspectives, incorporating researchers from various geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this critical biological mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in multi-modal data integration, AI-driven network analysis, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale contractile structures influences higher-order cellular morphology, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.
original.background_and_significance: Non-muscle myosin II (NMII) is a fundamental molecular motor responsible for generating contractile forces in non-muscle cells, driving essential processes such as cell migration, adhesion, tissue morphogenesis, and cytokinesis. At the core of these dynamic cellular behaviors lies a classic, yet poorly understood, example of biophysical emergence: the transition of individual, auto-inhibited NMII molecules into highly ordered, force-generating mesoscale ensembles known as bipolar thick filaments. While the structural biology of the myosin motor domain is well characterized at the nanoscale, and the macroscopic consequences of cellular contractility are observable at the phenotypic level, the mesoscale dynamics bridging these scales remain a profound mystery. Specifically, the spatio-temporal rules governing how localized phosphorylation events, biochemical signaling cascades, and the physical architecture of the surrounding actin network coordinate to drive large-scale filament assembly are highly debated. Understanding this emergence is critical, as it dictates how cells dynamically alter their morphology and exert physical force on their microenvironment. Currently, the field of mechanobiology is rich with disparate datasets spanning multiple scales. High-throughput phosphoproteomics capture the biochemical states of regulatory light chains; live-cell super-resolution microscopy provides spatial snapshots of filament assembly; and traction force microscopy (TFM) quantifies the resulting macroscopic mechanical outputs. However, these data are highly siloed. The complexity of mesoscale phenomena requires a paradigm shift from isolated, single-lab experimental approaches to community-scale synthesis. This project directly addresses the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission by leveraging existing, publicly available data to solve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. By synthesizing proteomics, advanced imaging, and biophysical force measurements, we aim to uncover the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties, specifically, how local molecular interactions scale up to produce global cellular forces. The mesoscale, defined here as the scale between individual myosin biomolecules and higher-order subcellular contractile networks, is exactly where this emergent property manifests. Our transdisciplinary working group will bridge the gap between structural biophysics, cell biology, and computational data science. We will utilize advanced AI and unsupervised machine learning to mine repositories such as the Cell Image Library, PRIDE, and mechanobiology-specific databases. This synthesis will not generate new experimental data but will extract unprecedented value from existing resources, answering fundamental questions about the rules of emergent contractility. The significance of this work extends beyond basic cell biology; it provides a foundational understanding of mechanotransduction that is applicable to cancer metastasis, developmental disorders, and cardiovascular diseases. By mapping the mesoscale emergence of NMII filaments, this project will catalyze novel research strategies, establish new analytical methodologies for multi-modal data integration, and set a gold standard for transdisciplinary synthesis in the molecular and cellular sciences.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses: To decode the emergent properties of non-muscle myosin II (NMII) thick filament assembly, our working group will address three compelling, interconnected scientific questions. These questions are specifically designed to be answered through the synthesis of existing, multi-modal datasets, moving beyond the capabilities of any single experimental approach to reveal the hidden rules of mesoscale contractility. Question 1: What are the spatio-temporal thresholds of NMII regulatory light chain (RLC) phosphorylation required to trigger the emergent assembly of mesoscale bipolar thick filaments? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that NMII filament assembly is not a linear response to kinase activity but rather a highly cooperative, threshold-driven emergent phenomenon. By synthesizing phosphoproteomic time-series data from the PRIDE database with live-cell super-resolution imaging from the Cell Image Library, we predict the identification of specific, localized phosphorylation density thresholds that serve as nucleation points. We expect machine learning models to reveal that cooperative phosphorylation kinetics, previously masked in bulk assays, dictate the sudden appearance of ordered mesoscale ensembles. Question 2: How does the pre-existing topological architecture of the actin cytoskeleton constrain or facilitate the spatial organization and scaling of NMII thick filaments? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the actin network acts as a physical template that dictates the emergent scaling of NMII filaments, where specific actin geometries (e.g., anti-parallel bundles versus branched networks) lower the energetic barrier for myosin ensemble formation. By integrating super-resolution structural datasets with biophysical modeling, we anticipate uncovering a set of geometric rules governing how local actin topologies guide the spatial distribution and maximum size of NMII bipolar filaments. We predict that AI-driven spatial point pattern analysis of synthesized imaging data will demonstrate that mesoscale filament emergence is strictly dependent on cross-linker-mediated actin architecture. Question 3: What are the quantitative transfer functions that map the structural parameters of mesoscale NMII assemblies to the macroscopic generation of cellular traction forces? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the macroscopic traction forces exerted by a cell are not simply the sum of individual motor forces, but are an emergent property dictated by the higher-order spatial arrangement and connectivity of the mesoscale NMII filaments. By coupling structural imaging datasets with corresponding Traction Force Microscopy (TFM) data available in mechanobiology repositories, we aim to train deep learning algorithms to predict cellular force outputs solely from the topological features of the NMII mesoscale network. We expect to find that specific mesoscale network configurations exhibit non-linear force amplification, representing a true emergent property of the cellular system. These questions directly align with the NCEMS objective to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties across scales of space, time, and motion. By framing our hypotheses around the integration of distinct data types, we ensure that our synthesis project will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how local molecular inputs are translated into global cellular mechanics.
original.methods_and_approach: Our approach is strictly computational and synthesis-driven, adhering to the NCEMS mandate of utilizing only existing, publicly available data without generating new experimental results. The complexity of integrating multi-modal datasets spanning biochemistry, structure, and mechanics necessitates a transdisciplinary working group comprising mechanobiologists, structural biophysicists, computational modelers, and data scientists. Our methodology is divided into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, AI-Driven Spatio-Temporal Synthesis, and Predictive Mechanistic Modeling. Phase 1: Data Aggregation, Standardization, and Curation. We will systematically mine disparate public repositories to build a unified, multi-scale database of NMII dynamics. Phosphoproteomic data detailing NMII regulatory light chain states will be sourced from the PRIDE archive and PeptideAtlas. High-resolution spatial data, including live-cell super-resolution microscopy and electron microscopy of actin-myosin networks, will be extracted from the Cell Image Library, BioImage Archive, and EMPIAR. Cellular force measurements, specifically Traction Force Microscopy (TFM) maps, will be gathered from specialized mechanobiology databases and published supplementary datasets. A significant methodological innovation of our working group will be the development of a standardized metadata ontology to align these diverse data types across common temporal and spatial coordinates, enabling cross-modal synthesis. Phase 2: AI-Driven Spatio-Temporal Synthesis. To uncover the rules of mesoscale emergence, we will employ advanced data science and artificial intelligence techniques. We will utilize unsupervised machine learning, specifically spatial clustering algorithms and topological data analysis (TDA), to identify hidden structural patterns in super-resolution imaging data. TDA is particularly suited for detecting emergent mesoscale structures, such as filament nodes and bundles, that are not apparent at the single-molecule level. To link phosphorylation kinetics with structural assembly, we will develop spatio-temporal data mining pipelines that map temporal proteomic profiles onto spatial assembly rates using dynamic time warping and cross-correlation analyses. This will allow us to test our hypothesis regarding cooperative phosphorylation thresholds driving emergent assembly. Phase 3: Predictive Mechanistic Modeling. To bridge the gap between mesoscale structure and macroscopic force, we will implement deep learning frameworks. We will train Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on paired structural and mechanical datasets. The GNNs will represent the actin-myosin network as a mathematical graph, where nodes are NMII filaments and edges are actin cross-links. By training these models to predict traction forces based on network topology, we will extract the quantitative transfer functions that define emergent contractility. To ensure biological interpretability, we will employ Explainable AI (XAI) techniques to identify which specific mesoscale architectural features most significantly contribute to force generation. Throughout this process, our working group will utilize collaborative cloud computing environments to facilitate seamless data sharing and model development among our geographically diverse team members, developing innovative analytical strategies broadly applicable to the wider biosciences community.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand biological emergence at the mesoscale. First, we will deliver a paradigm-shifting mechanistic understanding of non-muscle myosin II (NMII) thick filament assembly. By identifying the precise spatio-temporal phosphorylation thresholds and actin topological constraints that govern this process, we will solve a long-standing puzzle in mechanobiology, explaining how local molecular interactions scale up to produce global cellular forces. Second, we will produce a highly curated, integrated, and standardized multi-modal database linking phosphoproteomics, super-resolution microscopy, and cellular biomechanics. This unprecedented resource will overcome current data silos, providing the broader scientific community with a powerful tool for future mechanobiological research. Third, we will develop and validate novel, open-source AI and machine learning pipelines specifically designed for cross-modal data synthesis and the detection of emergent topological features in biological networks. These analytical strategies will be highly transferable, enabling researchers to investigate mesoscale emergence in other complex macromolecular systems. Beyond scientific discovery, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative, geographically diverse, and transdisciplinary working group, we will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will gain invaluable, hands-on experience in cloud computing, multi-modal data integration, advanced AI techniques, and open science practices. Ultimately, by decoding the emergent properties of cellular contractility, our findings will provide crucial insights into the physical mechanisms underlying cell migration and tissue morphogenesis, offering new theoretical frameworks that could eventually inform therapeutic strategies for diseases characterized by aberrant mechanotransduction, such as cancer metastasis and fibrotic disorders.
original.budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project requires a level of collaborative infrastructure and computational power that significantly exceeds the capabilities of any individual research laboratory, making NCEMS support absolutely essential. The budget is strategically designed to facilitate transdisciplinary collaboration, support intensive data synthesis, and prioritize the training of the next-generation workforce, with zero funds allocated for new experimental data generation. A primary component of the budget will support the convening of our working group. Funds are requested for bi-annual, in-person collaborative synthesis meetings at the NCEMS facility, bringing together our geographically diverse team of mechanobiologists, biophysicists, and data scientists. These intensive sessions are critical for cross-pollinating ideas, refining AI models, and ensuring cohesive project integration. Between in-person meetings, resources will be allocated for advanced virtual collaboration platforms to maintain continuous, seamless teamwork. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to computational resources. We request funding for high-performance cloud computing instances necessary for processing massive super-resolution image datasets, training deep learning algorithms, and hosting our integrated multi-modal databases. This centralized computational infrastructure is vital for enabling all team members, regardless of their home institution's resources, to actively participate in the data synthesis. Crucially, the budget includes robust support for workforce training. We are requesting dedicated funding for graduate student and postdoctoral fellowships. These trainees will be the primary drivers of the data integration and AI pipeline development, gaining unparalleled experience in data-savvy research. Finally, funds are allocated for open-science dissemination, including open-access publication fees, data storage costs on persistent repositories, and the hosting of virtual workshops to train the broader community on our developed methodologies, ensuring our findings and tools achieve maximum impact.

Mechanobiology studies the assembly of non muscle myosin II into mesoscale bipolar thick filaments within non muscle cells. Structural biology of the motor domain is known but the bridging mesoscale dynamics remain largely uncharacterized today. This project decodes emergent properties of filament assembly to explain how molecular interactions scale to produce cellular forces.

The study uses a computational design to integrate existing datasets for spatio temporal data mining and predictive modeling. title: Decoding the Emergent Dynamics of Proteasome Clustering and Localized Degradation

original.abstract: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the primary mechanism for targeted protein degradation in eukaryotic cells. Recent evidence suggests that under certain conditions, proteasomes dynamically cluster into mesoscale condensates to efficiently process high localized concentrations of ubiquitinated substrates. This emergent spatial organization represents a paradigm shift from the traditional view of freely diffusing proteasomes. However, the biophysical drivers of this mesoscale clustering and how it dictates the global efficiency of cellular protein quality control remain a fundamental, unsolved puzzle. Understanding this emergence is crucial for explaining how cells maintain proteostasis during stress and aging. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent properties of proteasome clustering. We will systematically integrate publicly available spatial proteomics data, live-cell fluorescence imaging, and interactomic datasets from the PRIDE database, the Image Data Resource, and BioGRID. By employing advanced computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools powered by machine learning, we will synthesize these disparate datasets to model the dynamic state of the proteasome network. This approach utilizes only existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies that reveal the physical rules of mesoscale degradation emergence. The sheer scale and complexity of integrating spatial imaging with functional proteomics require the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary team brings together cell biologists, protein biochemists, computational data scientists, and systems biologists. We have intentionally assembled a working group that reflects diverse scientific perspectives, including researchers from various career stages and geographic locations. This diversity is essential for breaking down disciplinary silos and fostering novel insights into complex biological phenomena. Training the next generation of researchers is a fundamental aspect of our proposal. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, developing critical skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative open science. In strict adherence to community policies on reproducible science, all integrated datasets, network models, and analytical code will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale organelle networks influences higher-order cellular proteostasis, perfectly aligning with the overarching goals of NCEMS.
original.background_and_significance: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is the central pillar of protein quality control in eukaryotic cells, responsible for the targeted degradation of misfolded, damaged, or obsolete proteins. For decades, the prevailing model of the UPS posited that proteasomes function primarily as freely diffusing enzymatic complexes distributed relatively uniformly throughout the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm. However, recent sporadic but compelling lines of evidence have initiated a paradigm shift, suggesting that under specific physiological conditions—such as acute cellular stress, aging, or localized proteotoxic insults—proteasomes dynamically reorganize. They cluster into membrane-less mesoscale condensates, fundamentally altering their spatial distribution to efficiently process high localized concentrations of ubiquitinated substrates. This dynamic reorganization is a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence. It bridges the gap between individual biomolecular interactions (ubiquitin-binding and proteasomal degradation) and higher-order cellular outcomes (global proteostasis and stress resilience). Despite the profound implications of this phenomenon, the biophysical drivers that precipitate this mesoscale clustering, and the precise mathematical rules governing how this spatial organization dictates global degradation efficiency, remain a fundamental, unsolved puzzle in molecular biology. Individual research laboratories have generated vast, disparate datasets touching upon this phenomenon, including high-resolution live-cell imaging of proteasome dynamics, extensive interactomic maps of the ubiquitination cascade, and quantitative spatial proteomics. Yet, these datasets exist in profound isolation. The complexity of mesoscale phenomena cannot be unraveled by any single experimental approach or isolated dataset. It requires a community-scale synthesis project to integrate these multidimensional data streams. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by leveraging AI and advanced data science to synthesize publicly available data, aiming to decode the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale. By integrating structural, spatial, and functional data, our working group will transform isolated observations into a comprehensive, predictive model of emergent proteasome dynamics. The significance of this work extends far beyond basic cell biology; understanding how cells naturally optimize protein degradation through spatial organization provides critical insights into the etiology of protein-misfolding diseases, such as neurodegeneration and various cancers. Furthermore, this project will pioneer novel analytical strategies for fusing imaging and proteomics data, establishing a methodological blueprint for future investigations into other emergent mesoscale condensates. Ultimately, this research will solve a long-standing mystery regarding cellular stress responses, recruit diverse scientific talent, and train a new generation of data-savvy bioscientists equipped to tackle the complexities of emergent biological systems.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our transdisciplinary synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions, each designed to interrogate the emergent properties of proteasome clustering through the integration of publicly available datasets. 

Question 1: What are the fundamental interactomic and biophysical drivers that trigger the phase separation and mesoscale clustering of proteasomes under varied cellular states? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that proteasome clustering is not a random aggregation but a highly regulated emergent process driven by specific, multivalent interactions between polyubiquitinated substrates, ubiquitin-binding shuttle factors (such as RAD23B and ubiquilins), and intrinsic scaffolding regions within the 19S regulatory particle. By synthesizing interactomic data from BioGRID with quantitative mass spectrometry data from the PRIDE database, we expect to identify a conserved network of 'driver' proteins whose expression and interaction topologies reliably predict the onset of mesoscale proteasome condensation across different eukaryotic lineages.

Question 2: How does the spatial organization of these mesoscale proteasome clusters dictate the kinetics, selectivity, and global efficiency of targeted protein degradation? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that mesoscale clustering creates localized, high-density degradation 'hubs' that non-linearly accelerate substrate turnover compared to freely diffusing proteasomes. This represents a true emergent property where the spatial arrangement at the mesoscale optimizes the biochemical kinetics at the molecular scale. To test this, we will synthesize live-cell fluorescence imaging from the Image Data Resource (IDR) with functional proteomics data. We anticipate that mathematical modeling of these integrated datasets will reveal that clustered states exhibit enhanced degradation kinetics specifically for complex, aggregation-prone substrates, thereby conferring a distinct survival advantage during proteotoxic stress.

Question 3: Can artificial intelligence and spatial network models accurately predict the formation, spatial distribution, and dissolution of proteasome condensates based solely on the cellular ubiquitin landscape and transcriptomic stress markers? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that AI-driven spatial network models can capture the underlying physical rules governing mesoscale degradation emergence. By training advanced machine learning algorithms on our harmonized datasets, we will demonstrate that the spatial dynamics of the proteasome network can be predicted from upstream signaling and ubiquitination profiles. This predictive capability will validate our synthesized model of emergence, proving that the macroscopic behavior of the proteasome network is a deterministic outcome of specific, identifiable molecular and mesoscale interactions. Addressing these questions will solve long-standing puzzles regarding cellular proteostasis and fulfill the NCEMS mandate to answer novel questions through data synthesis.
original.methods_and_approach:
To decode the emergent dynamics of proteasome clustering, our working group will execute a highly structured, purely computational synthesis of existing publicly available data, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate against generating new experimental data. Our approach is divided into three integrated phases: Data Acquisition and Harmonization, AI-Driven Spatial and Interactomic Analysis, and Predictive Systems Modeling.

Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Harmonization. We will systematically harvest and curate datasets from three primary repositories. First, we will extract high-resolution, time-lapse fluorescence microscopy data from the Image Data Resource (IDR), focusing on experiments tracking fluorescently tagged proteasome subunits (e.g., PSMD11, PSMB5) and ubiquitin under baseline and stress conditions. Second, we will mine the PRIDE database for quantitative spatial proteomics and ubiquitinome datasets to quantify the abundance and localization of substrates and shuttle factors. Third, we will utilize BioGRID and IntAct to map the comprehensive protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks of the ubiquitin-proteasome system. A critical first step will be standardizing metadata and harmonizing these disparate data types into a unified, queryable graph database architecture, enabling seamless cross-referencing between spatial coordinates, protein abundance, and interaction topologies.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Spatial and Interactomic Analysis. To extract meaningful spatial features from the IDR imaging data, we will deploy advanced computer vision algorithms. We will adapt deep learning-based segmentation models, such as Cellpose and StarDist, specifically trained to identify and quantify membrane-less condensates. This will yield quantitative metrics of proteasome clusters, including volume, density, sphericity, and dissolution rates. Concurrently, we will apply network science methodologies to the interactomic data, identifying highly connected hubs and multivalent nodes that correlate with phase separation. 

Phase 3: Predictive Systems Modeling via Synthesis. The core synthesis will be achieved by fusing the spatial metrics with the interactomic networks using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In these models, nodes will represent proteins or complexes, and edges will represent interactions weighted by their spatial proximity and co-localization probabilities derived from the imaging data. We will use these GNNs to model the dynamic state of the proteasome network, utilizing machine learning to uncover the hidden biophysical rules that govern the transition from a diffuse to a clustered state.

Transdisciplinary Collaboration and Training: This project is fundamentally beyond the scope of a single laboratory. Our working group comprises cell biologists to ensure physiological relevance, computational data scientists to lead AI development, and protein biochemists to validate interactomic assumptions. We will hold bi-weekly virtual meetings and three intensive, in-person synthesis hackathons hosted at NCEMS. Furthermore, graduate students and postdocs will be integrated into every phase, receiving dual mentorship across disciplines to build a critical, data-savvy workforce capable of leading future synthesis research.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences while fulfilling the core objectives of NCEMS. 

Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the first unified, predictive model of mesoscale proteasome emergence. By deciphering the biophysical rules that govern proteasome clustering, we will solve a long-standing puzzle regarding how eukaryotic cells efficiently manage localized proteotoxic stress. This model will provide a paradigm-shifting framework for understanding protein quality control, demonstrating precisely how emergent spatial organization at the mesoscale dictates higher-order cellular survival. This foundational knowledge has profound broader impacts, offering critical theoretical groundwork for future translational research into protein-misfolding diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, where proteasome dynamics are fundamentally impaired.

Methodologically, we will develop and validate innovative analytical strategies for integrating high-dimensional spatial imaging with quantitative proteomics and interactomics. The AI-driven spatial network models and adapted computer vision pipelines created during this project will be highly generalizable. They will provide the broader scientific community with robust computational tools to investigate other instances of mesoscale emergence and liquid-liquid phase separation across different biological systems.

Crucially, this project will have a lasting impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees into our transdisciplinary working group, we will cultivate a new generation of scientists who are entirely fluent in both molecular biology and advanced data science. These trainees will gain invaluable, hands-on experience in community-scale synthesis, machine learning, and collaborative research methodologies. Ultimately, the successful execution of this proposal will demonstrate the immense power of synthesizing publicly available data, cementing the role of NCEMS as a critical catalyst for driving novel discoveries and shaping the future of biological research.
original.budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we require the robust collaborative infrastructure and financial support uniquely provided by NCEMS. The requested budget is strictly allocated to support human capital, computational resources, and collaborative activities, with zero funds directed toward new experimental data generation.

Personnel Support: The majority of the budget is dedicated to training and workforce development. We request funding to support two full-time postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These trainees will serve as the primary data scientists and bioinformaticians executing the data harmonization and machine learning pipelines. Their stipends and tuition represent a direct investment in the future data-savvy scientific workforce.

Collaborative Meetings and Travel: A critical component of this transdisciplinary project is breaking down disciplinary silos. We request funds for travel and lodging to support three intensive, multi-day Working Group synthesis hackathons to be held at the NCEMS headquarters. These in-person meetings are essential for aligning biological interpretations with computational models, fostering deep collaboration among our geographically distributed team members across various career stages.

Computational Resources: Synthesizing massive spatial proteomics and high-resolution imaging datasets requires significant computational power. We request funds for secure, high-performance cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or GCP) to train our deep learning computer vision models and Graph Neural Networks. If NCEMS provides internal high-performance computing clusters, these funds will be reallocated to support additional trainee involvement.

Open Science and Dissemination: Finally, we request funds to cover Article Processing Charges (APCs) for open-access publications and costs associated with long-term data storage and hosting on platforms like Zenodo. 

This budget demonstrates a clear need for NCEMS support that goes far beyond the capabilities of any single lab, providing the essential resources required to synthesize existing data into groundbreaking insights on mesoscale emergence.

The study employs a graph neural network framework to integrate disparate proteomics and imaging data into a unified predictive model.
