title: Synthesizing the Emergent Meshwork of the Nuclear Lamina and Genome Tethering

original.abstract: The nuclear lamina is a dense, mesoscale meshwork of intermediate filaments located at the inner nuclear membrane. It provides essential structural integrity to the nucleus and serves as a critical tethering platform for organizing peripheral heterochromatin. The assembly of individual lamin proteins into this complex, highly ordered mesoscale architecture, and how this structure dynamically responds to mechanical stress, is a profound example of cellular emergence. Despite its importance in gene regulation and mechanobiology, the precise rules governing lamina meshwork assembly and its emergent impact on 3D genome topology remain poorly understood. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent biophysics of the nuclear lamina. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including super-resolution localization microscopy, Hi-C genomic data, and cryo-electron tomography from repositories such as the 4D Nucleome Project, EMPIAR, and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced topological data analysis and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to reconstruct the dynamic architecture of the lamina without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local protein polymerization leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional nuclear barriers. The complexity of nuclear biophysics requires the integration of structural imaging with genomic data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites nuclear biologists, computational biophysicists, genomicists, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex nuclear networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale nuclear structures, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.
original.background_and_significance:
The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale is one of the most profound frontiers in the molecular and cellular biosciences. The nuclear lamina represents a quintessential example of such mesoscale emergence. Situated at the inner nuclear membrane, the lamina is a dense, complex meshwork composed primarily of A-type and B-type lamin intermediate filaments. While the biochemical properties of individual lamin dimers are well characterized at the molecular scale, their self-assembly into a highly ordered, functional, and dynamic mesoscale architecture remains a long-standing mystery. This emergent structure is not merely a passive scaffold; it is a vital mechanotransduction hub and a highly specific tethering platform that organizes peripheral heterochromatin into Lamina Associated Domains (LADs), thereby exerting profound control over global 3D genome topology and gene expression.

Despite decades of research, the field is currently fragmented. Structural biologists study lamina architecture using cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and super-resolution microscopy, while genomicists investigate LADs and 3D genome organization using chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) technologies. These distinct lines of inquiry have generated massive, publicly available datasets housed in disparate repositories such as the 4D Nucleome (4DN) Project, the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), and the Image Data Resource (IDR). However, these multi-modal datasets have never been integrated at a community scale. Consequently, we lack a unified understanding of how the emergent physical properties of the lamina meshwork—such as its local density, filament cross-linking, and topological defects—dictate the spatial organization of the genome.

This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by catalyzing a multidisciplinary synthesis of these existing, publicly available datasets to uncover the rules of mesoscale emergence in the nucleus. We propose that the functional properties of the nucleus—specifically its mechanical resilience and its capacity to compartmentalize the genome—are emergent phenomena that cannot be understood by studying lamins or DNA in isolation. By leveraging artificial intelligence and advanced data science, our working group will bridge the gap between structural imaging and functional genomics. 

Our transdisciplinary synthesis will resolve long-standing puzzles regarding how distinct lamin isoforms cooperate to form a unified meshwork and how this meshwork dynamically reorganizes under mechanical stress. The significance of this work extends far beyond nuclear biology; it will provide a pioneering computational framework for understanding how local protein-protein interactions give rise to mesoscale cellular barriers. Furthermore, by strictly utilizing existing data, this project highlights the untapped potential of community-scale data synthesis. It will stimulate novel questions regarding the biophysics of cellular emergence, recruit and train a new generation of data-savvy scientists, and establish gold-standard practices for integrating structural and genomic data, firmly establishing NCEMS as a leader in unraveling the complexities of the mesoscale.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our transdisciplinary working group will address three compelling, interrelated scientific questions regarding the mesoscale emergence of the nuclear lamina and its role in genome tethering. These questions are designed to be answered exclusively through the synthesis and computational modeling of existing, publicly available multi-modal datasets.

Question 1: What are the universal rules governing the emergent assembly of distinct lamin isoforms into a unified mesoscale meshwork? 
While it is known that A-type and B-type lamins form separate but interacting networks, the physical rules governing their co-assembly into a continuous mesoscale structure are unknown. 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that lamin A/C and B-type lamins self-assemble according to predictable thermodynamic and mechanical rules that drive emergent phase separation at the inner nuclear membrane. Specifically, we posit that the ratio and local concentration of these isoforms dictate the topological properties (e.g., pore size, filament thickness) of the emergent meshwork. By synthesizing super-resolution microscopy data (STORM/PALM) from the IDR and cryo-ET data from EMPIAR, we will uncover the quantitative scaling laws that link molecular lamin stoichiometry to mesoscale meshwork topology.

Question 2: How does the emergent mesoscale architecture of the lamina dictate the 3D topological organization of the genome?
The lamina anchors vast regions of heterochromatin (LADs), yet the biophysical mechanisms that map specific genomic regions to specific lamina microenvironments remain an enduring puzzle.
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that local meshwork density and topological defects (such as filament junctions or gaps) within the lamina act as specific biophysical attractors for distinct epigenetic states of chromatin. We predict that the emergent 3D organization of the genome is not random but is deterministically driven by the biophysical topography of the lamina. To test this, we will synthesize high-resolution Hi-C and SPRITE data from the 4D Nucleome Project with structural imaging data, utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map 1D genomic sequences onto 3D mesoscale lamina topologies, revealing the emergent rules of genome tethering.

Question 3: How does the lamina meshwork dynamically reorganize as an emergent system in response to mechanical stress?
The nucleus must withstand significant mechanical forces during cellular migration and tissue dynamics, yet how the lamina absorbs and dissipates this stress at the mesoscale is poorly understood.
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that mechanical stress induces emergent phase transitions within the lamina meshwork, leading to rapid, reversible local remodeling that selectively alters heterochromatin tethering to protect genomic integrity. We will synthesize publicly available live-cell imaging datasets of nuclei under mechanical strain (e.g., atomic force microscopy coupled with fluorescence, confined migration assays) with our structural models. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics constrained by our synthesized data, we will model the emergent mechanical properties of the meshwork, identifying how local filament sliding and cross-link breaking scale up to global nuclear mechanoprotection. These questions will drive a paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular emergence.
original.methods_and_approach:
To achieve our objectives without generating new experimental data, our transdisciplinary working group will employ a highly innovative suite of data science, artificial intelligence, and computational biophysics methodologies. Our approach requires the integration of disparate data modalities—a task that is beyond the capabilities of any single research lab and necessitates the collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS.

Data Aggregation and Curation: 
We will systematically harvest three classes of publicly available data. First, ultra-structural data: we will extract cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) maps of the nuclear envelope from EMPIAR. Second, spatial localization data: we will aggregate super-resolution microscopy (STORM, PALM, STED) datasets of lamin A/C, lamin B1, and lamin B2 from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and institutional repositories. Third, genomic data: we will utilize high-resolution Hi-C, SPRITE, and Lamin B1 DamID datasets from the 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal to map Lamina Associated Domains (LADs) and 3D genome topology.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA) of the Mesoscale Meshwork:
To extract quantitative rules of emergence from imaging data (Hypothesis 1), we will deploy Topological Data Analysis, specifically persistent homology. TDA will allow us to quantify the complex mesoscale features of the lamina—such as filament connectivity, pore size distribution, and cross-linking density—across thousands of images with varying resolutions. This will yield a unified topological signature of the lamina meshwork, translating qualitative structural biology into rigorous, machine-readable biophysical metrics.

Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning for Data Integration:
Integrating 1D/3D genomic data with 3D structural topologies (Hypothesis 2) represents a massive computational challenge. We will develop novel Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to bridge this gap. The lamina meshwork will be modeled as a spatial graph (nodes as filament junctions, edges as filaments), while the genome will be modeled as an interacting polymer graph (derived from Hi-C). Our GNN architecture will be trained to predict the emergent tethering patterns by learning the mapping functions between the heterochromatin polymer graph and the lamina structural graph. This AI-driven synthesis will identify the biophysical attractors that govern LAD formation.

Data-Driven Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics:
To understand the emergent response to mechanical stress (Hypothesis 3), we will utilize the synthesized structural and genomic data to parameterize a coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) model of the entire nucleus. Unlike traditional models built from first principles, our CGMD model will be heavily constrained by the deep-learning-derived topological parameters. We will simulate mechanical deformation (e.g., nuclear compression) to observe how the emergent meshwork redistributes force and alters genome tethering dynamically.

Collaborative Workflow:
Our working group includes nuclear biologists (to ensure biological validity), genomicists (to guide 4DN data processing), computational biophysicists (for CGMD modeling), and machine learning engineers (for GNN development). We will utilize cloud-based collaborative environments, sharing containerized pipelines to ensure that our transdisciplinary team can seamlessly iterate on these complex, multi-modal datasets.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand mesoscale emergence. The primary scientific deliverable will be the first unified, multi-scale computational model of the nuclear lamina that seamlessly integrates biophysical architecture with 3D genome topology. By solving the long-standing puzzle of how the lamina meshwork self-assembles and orchestrates genome tethering, we will provide a definitive framework for understanding how local protein interactions yield emergent, functional cellular barriers.

Beyond the biological insights, we will produce a suite of innovative analytical strategies. Our novel Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures and Topological Data Analysis (TDA) pipelines will establish a new gold standard for integrating structural imaging with functional genomic data. These AI-driven tools will be highly adaptable, providing the broader scientific community with methodologies to study other emergent mesoscale structures, such as the cytoskeleton, the extracellular matrix, and membraneless organelles.

The impact on workforce development will be equally profound. Our project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students will be deeply integrated into the working group, receiving rigorous cross-training at the intersection of nuclear biology, artificial intelligence, and computational biophysics. By working in a highly collaborative, multi-institutional environment, these trainees will develop the exact transdisciplinary skill sets required to lead the future of bioscience synthesis research. Furthermore, by intentionally recruiting a diverse team across career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels, we will tap into diverse new talent, ensuring that our approaches are innovative, inclusive, and capable of generating deeper, broader insights into cellular emergence.
original.budget_and_resources:
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, we require the unique collaborative infrastructure, computational resources, and financial support provided by NCEMS. The complexity of integrating massive imaging and genomic datasets utilizing advanced AI far exceeds the capabilities and resources of any single laboratory.

Personnel Support: We request salary and fringe benefit support for two postdoctoral fellows and two graduate students. These trainees are the engine of our synthesis effort and will be co-mentored by our transdisciplinary team, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train the future data-savvy workforce. Their funding will be dedicated entirely to data integration, AI model development, and biophysical simulations.

Working Group Meetings: A critical component of our proposal is the facilitation of cross-disciplinary collaboration. We request funding to support three in-person working group meetings at the NCEMS facility over the project duration. These funds will cover travel, lodging, and per diem for all team members. These intensive, face-to-face sessions are essential for bridging the disciplinary languages of nuclear biologists, genomicists, and machine learning engineers, and for strategizing the synthesis of multi-modal data.

Computational Resources: The proposed deep learning (GNNs) and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations require significant computational power. We request NCEMS cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or GCP) to support the high-performance GPU clusters necessary for training our spatio-temporal AI architectures and processing the terabytes of raw public data (cryo-ET, Hi-C).

Open Science and Publication Costs: We request funds to cover article processing charges (APCs) for open-access publications, as well as minor costs associated with long-term cloud storage and hosting of our interactive, reproducible Jupyter Notebooks and synthesized datasets. This budget precisely reflects the resources necessary to catalyze novel discoveries in cellular emergence through community-scale data synthesis.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Nuclear biology and biophysics investigate the mesoscale assembly of the nuclear lamina to address gaps in genome topology. Current knowledge characterizes lamin proteins at the molecular scale while structural imaging and genomic mapping remain fragmented datasets. This project decodes the emergent biophysics of the nuclear lamina to establish a model for community scale synthesis.

The study aggregates existing public datasets using topological data analysis and deep learning alongside coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations. The team applies persistent homology and graph neural networks and coarse grained molecular dynamics to model the nuclear lamina structure. Results are validated through predictive models that ensure biological consistency across structural and genomic scales for the entire system.

The project utilizes the 4D Nucleome Project and EMPIAR and the Image Data Resource for all primary data inputs. Datasets are synthesized by mapping genomic sequences onto structural topologies using graph neural networks and constraining molecular dynamics models. The team mitigates limitations of disparate data by using topological data analysis to create standardized metrics across varying resolutions.

The proposal does not address the project timeline or specific milestones for the completion of the research objectives. The complexity of integrating massive multi modal datasets requires diverse expertise that exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory.

All analytical pipelines and synthesized datasets and predictive models will be made publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub. The team includes nuclear biologists and computational biophysicists and genomicists and machine learning engineers including postdoctoral fellows and graduate students.
rephrased.main_idea: This research investigates how individual lamin proteins self assemble into mesoscale meshworks that dictate the complex topology of the genome. The study employs topological data analysis and graph neural networks to integrate fragmented structural imaging and genomic mapping datasets computationally. This project establishes a predictive framework that links local protein interactions to the emergent mechanical properties of the nucleus.

title: Decoding the Emergent Logic of Phase-Separated Condensates: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis of Biomolecular Organization Principles

original.abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular organization, yet the rules governing their emergent properties remain poorly understood. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary team spanning structural biology, biophysics, computational biology, and systems biology to synthesize publicly available data across multiple scales to decode the organizational logic of phase-separated condensates. Our central hypothesis is that condensate properties emerge from predictable combinations of molecular features that can be identified through systematic integration of structural, sequence, interaction, and cellular imaging data.

We will integrate data from multiple public repositories including the Protein Data Bank (PDB), AlphaFold Database, PhaSePro, DrLLPS, STRING, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas. Additionally, we will leverage cryo-electron tomography datasets from EMPIAR and single-molecule tracking data from public repositories. This integration spans molecular structure, protein-protein interactions, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modifications, and cellular localization patterns.

Our approach involves three interconnected aims. First, we will develop a comprehensive atlas of condensate-forming proteins by synthesizing sequence features, structural properties, and interaction networks. Machine learning approaches will identify molecular grammar rules that predict condensate formation propensity and material properties. Second, we will analyze spatial and temporal dynamics of condensates by integrating live-cell imaging datasets with proteomics and transcriptomics data to understand how condensate composition and properties respond to cellular states and perturbations. Third, we will construct multi-scale models linking molecular features to mesoscale organization and cellular function.

The project requires NCEMS support because it demands expertise spanning structural biology, bioinformatics, machine learning, biophysics, and cell biology that no single laboratory possesses. The data integration challenge alone requires computational infrastructure and expertise in harmonizing heterogeneous data types. Our team includes researchers from five institutions across three geographic regions, incorporating faculty at different career stages and from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a publicly available database linking molecular features to condensate properties, (2) predictive models for condensate behavior, (3) new hypotheses about condensate function testable by the broader community, and (4) analytical workflows for multi-scale data integration. All analysis code, integrated datasets, and findings will be made publicly available following FAIR principles.

Training is central to our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will participate in cross-laboratory exchanges, learning diverse computational and analytical approaches. We will host virtual workshops teaching data synthesis methods to the broader community. This project addresses a fundamental question in cellular organization: how do molecular properties give rise to mesoscale structures with emergent functions? By synthesizing existing data at unprecedented scale, we will generate insights impossible for individual laboratories and establish frameworks for future synthesis research in cellular organization.
original.background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates have revolutionized our understanding of cellular organization over the past decade. These membrane-less compartments, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), orchestrate critical cellular functions including transcription regulation, stress responses, signal transduction, and RNA metabolism. Unlike traditional organelles bounded by lipid membranes, condensates emerge from the collective behavior of proteins and nucleic acids, representing a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale—the precise focus of NCEMS.

The discovery that intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent interactions drive condensate formation has generated enormous scientific interest. However, fundamental questions remain unanswered: What molecular features determine whether a protein will partition into or form condensates? How do condensate material properties (viscosity, surface tension, dynamics) emerge from molecular composition? What rules govern the selective recruitment of client proteins? How do post-translational modifications regulate condensate behavior? These questions persist because answering them requires integration of data spanning molecular to cellular scales—a synthesis challenge beyond individual laboratory capabilities.

The significance of understanding condensate organization extends beyond basic science. Dysregulation of condensate properties underlies numerous diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders (ALS, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cancer, and viral infections. Pathological mutations often alter condensate dynamics, converting liquid-like assemblies into solid aggregates. Understanding the molecular grammar of condensate behavior could transform therapeutic development by identifying intervention points in disease-associated phase transitions.

Current knowledge is fragmented across disparate data sources. Structural databases contain atomic-resolution information about condensate-forming proteins. Proteomics databases catalog interaction networks and post-translational modifications. Specialized databases like PhaSePro and DrLLPS curate experimentally validated phase-separating proteins. Imaging repositories contain cellular localization and dynamics data. Each resource provides partial insight, but no systematic integration exists to reveal overarching organizational principles.

This fragmentation represents both a challenge and an unprecedented opportunity. The wealth of publicly available data has reached a critical threshold where synthesis can yield transformative insights. Advances in machine learning, particularly deep learning architectures capable of processing heterogeneous data types, now enable pattern recognition across scales that was previously impossible. The time is ripe for a coordinated synthesis effort.

Our proposal directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Condensates exemplify emergence: their properties cannot be predicted from individual molecular components but arise from collective interactions. By synthesizing data across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular levels, we will decode the logic connecting these scales. This understanding will establish general principles applicable to other mesoscale phenomena, creating frameworks for future synthesis research.

The significance of this work lies in its potential to transform condensate biology from a descriptive to a predictive science. Rather than cataloging individual condensates, we will identify universal rules governing their formation, properties, and functions. These insights will generate testable hypotheses for the broader community, accelerating discovery through coordinated synthesis rather than isolated experimentation. This proposal exemplifies the community-scale synthesis that NCEMS was created to enable.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our research addresses three interconnected questions that together decode the emergent logic of biomolecular condensates across scales.

Research Question 1: What molecular features predict condensate formation propensity and material properties?

Hypothesis 1a: Condensate formation propensity can be predicted from combinations of sequence features (amino acid composition, charge patterning, aromatic residue distribution), structural properties (disorder content, prion-like domains), and interaction network topology with accuracy exceeding 85% AUC-ROC.

Hypothesis 1b: Condensate material properties (liquid-like versus gel-like versus solid) correlate with specific molecular signatures, particularly the ratio of transient to stable interactions encoded in sequence and structural features.

Hypothesis 1c: Post-translational modification sites, particularly phosphorylation within IDRs, represent regulatory switches whose presence and distribution predict condensate responsiveness to cellular signals.

Rationale: Previous studies have identified individual features contributing to phase separation, but systematic integration across feature types has not been performed. By synthesizing sequence annotations, AlphaFold structural predictions, disorder predictions, and interaction data for thousands of proteins, we can identify combinatorial rules—a molecular grammar—governing condensate behavior.

Research Question 2: How do condensate composition and dynamics respond to cellular states and perturbations?

Hypothesis 2a: Condensate proteomes exhibit state-dependent modularity, with core scaffold proteins remaining constant while client proteins vary systematically with cellular conditions (cell cycle, stress, differentiation).

Hypothesis 2b: Temporal dynamics of condensate assembly and dissolution correlate with the kinetics of post-translational modification cascades detectable in phosphoproteomics time-series data.

Hypothesis 2c: Spatial organization of condensates within cells follows predictable patterns based on local concentration of scaffold proteins and nucleic acid availability, detectable through integration of imaging and spatial transcriptomics data.

Rationale: Condensates are dynamic entities responding to cellular needs. By integrating live-cell imaging datasets with proteomics and transcriptomics data across conditions, we can identify rules governing compositional plasticity and temporal regulation.

Research Question 3: How do molecular features propagate through mesoscale organization to influence cellular function?

Hypothesis 3a: Multi-scale models incorporating molecular interaction parameters can predict emergent condensate properties (size distribution, number per cell, partitioning coefficients) observed in cellular imaging data.

Hypothesis 3b: Functional outcomes of condensate formation (transcriptional output, stress survival, signal amplitude) can be predicted from integrated molecular-mesoscale features with greater accuracy than molecular features alone.

Hypothesis 3c: Disease-associated mutations alter specific molecular features that propagate predictably through organizational scales, enabling identification of pathological mechanisms from sequence analysis.

Rationale: Understanding emergence requires connecting scales. By building models that link molecular inputs to mesoscale organization and cellular phenotypes, we test whether emergent properties follow predictable rules.

These questions are interconnected: molecular features (Q1) determine dynamic responses (Q2), which together produce cellular functions (Q3). Our synthesis approach uniquely enables testing hypotheses across scales simultaneously. Each hypothesis generates specific, testable predictions that will be validated against held-out data and can guide future experimental studies by the broader community. The hypotheses are falsifiable—if condensate properties prove fundamentally unpredictable from molecular features, this would itself be a significant finding reshaping the field's theoretical framework.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates heterogeneous public datasets through a unified computational framework, employing machine learning and multi-scale modeling to address our research questions.

Aim 1: Constructing the Condensate Molecular Atlas

Data Sources: We will integrate PhaSePro (>1,500 phase-separating proteins), DrLLPS (>5,000 entries), PDB structural data, AlphaFold Database predictions (~200 million structures), UniProt annotations, and interaction networks from STRING and BioGRID.

Feature Extraction Pipeline: For each protein, we will compute sequence-based features (amino acid composition, charge distribution, hydropathy patterns, prion-like domain scores), structural features (disorder predictions from multiple algorithms, secondary structure content, AlphaFold pLDDT scores indicating confidence/disorder), and network features (degree centrality, clustering coefficients, interaction partner properties).

Machine Learning Framework: We will develop ensemble models combining gradient boosting, random forests, and deep neural networks to predict: (1) binary condensate formation propensity, (2) multi-class material property classification, and (3) continuous partitioning coefficients. Models will be trained using cross-validation with careful attention to data leakage prevention. Feature importance analysis will identify molecular grammar rules.

Aim 2: Analyzing Spatiotemporal Dynamics

Data Sources: Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, EMPIAR cryo-ET datasets, published live-cell imaging datasets from supplementary materials of key publications, PRIDE proteomics repository, and GEO/ArrayExpress transcriptomics data.

Image Analysis Pipeline: We will apply pre-trained deep learning models (adapted from CellProfiler and DeepCell) to segment cells and identify condensate structures in imaging data. Quantitative features including condensate number, size distribution, and spatial positioning will be extracted.

Integrative Analysis: Proteomics and transcriptomics data will be mapped to condensate components. We will employ tensor decomposition methods to identify coordinated changes in condensate composition across conditions. Time-series analysis will correlate condensate dynamics with signaling pathway activation.

Aim 3: Multi-Scale Modeling

Coarse-Grained Simulations: Using parameters derived from Aim 1 (interaction strengths, valency, IDR properties), we will perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to predict emergent condensate properties. These simulations will use established frameworks (LAMMPS with custom potentials) validated against experimental phase diagrams.

Cellular-Scale Integration: Predicted condensate properties will be compared with cellular imaging observations. Discrepancies will identify missing factors, while agreements validate our molecular grammar rules. We will develop statistical models linking condensate features to functional readouts (transcriptional activity, stress survival) from integrated omics data.

Data Harmonization Strategy: A critical challenge is harmonizing heterogeneous data types. We will develop standardized ontologies mapping protein identifiers across databases, quality control pipelines filtering unreliable data, and uncertainty quantification propagating data quality through analyses.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis requires substantial computational resources. We will utilize NCEMS-provided computing infrastructure supplemented by institutional HPC clusters. Code will be developed in Python with key algorithms implemented in optimized libraries (PyTorch, scikit-learn, MDAnalysis).

Validation Strategy: All predictive models will be validated using held-out test sets, cross-validation, and comparison with recent experimental results not included in training data. We will quantify prediction uncertainty using Bayesian approaches and ensemble disagreement metrics.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will generate transformative outcomes advancing both fundamental understanding and methodological capabilities in molecular and cellular sciences.

Primary Deliverables:

1. Condensate Atlas Database: A comprehensive, publicly accessible database linking molecular features to condensate properties for >10,000 proteins. This resource will include predicted phase separation propensity, material property classifications, regulatory modification sites, and interaction network context. The database will feature intuitive query interfaces enabling researchers to assess condensate potential for any protein of interest.

2. Predictive Computational Models: Machine learning models predicting condensate formation, material properties, and cellular behavior from sequence and structural features. These models will be packaged as user-friendly tools (web server and command-line applications) enabling the broader community to generate predictions without computational expertise.

3. Multi-Scale Modeling Framework: Validated pipelines connecting molecular parameters to mesoscale simulations and cellular predictions, establishing a template for multi-scale synthesis research applicable beyond condensates.

4. Testable Hypotheses Compendium: A curated collection of specific, experimentally testable predictions emerging from our analysis, including candidate proteins with predicted but unvalidated phase separation behavior, proposed regulatory mechanisms, and disease-relevant predictions.

Scientific Impact:

Our synthesis will transform condensate biology from phenomenological description to predictive science. By identifying molecular grammar rules, we enable rational interpretation of condensate behavior and guide therapeutic development targeting phase separation in disease. The multi-scale framework establishes paradigms for understanding emergence applicable to other mesoscale phenomena including cytoskeletal organization, membrane domains, and chromatin structure.

Broader Impact:

Training outcomes will produce data-savvy scientists skilled in synthesis research methods. Virtual workshops will disseminate approaches to hundreds of researchers. Our open-source tools and workflows will enable future synthesis projects, multiplying NCEMS's impact. The collaborative model we establish—integrating diverse expertise across institutions—will serve as a template for community-scale synthesis in other domains.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Cellular biology investigates biomolecular condensates to define the organizational logic governing how molecular features create emergent mesoscale condensate properties. Current knowledge remains fragmented across disparate databases because systematic integration of structural and interaction data is currently lacking. This project decodes organizational logic to transition condensate biology into a predictive science for identifying novel therapeutic disease targets.

The study design employs a three aim approach to link molecular features with cellular phenotypes through multi scale models. Key methods include machine learning (ML) algorithms and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations alongside tensor decomposition for data integration. The study employs machine learning and multi scale modeling to integrate heterogeneous structural and imaging data into a cohesive predictive framework. title: Temporal Emergence in Protein Interaction Networks: Synthesizing Dynamic Interactomics Across Cell Cycle, Circadian, and Stress Response Programs

original.abstract:
Protein interaction networks are not static entities but dynamically rewire across time, yet most network analyses treat interactions as fixed. This proposal addresses a fundamental gap: understanding how temporal dynamics of protein interactions give rise to emergent cellular behaviors. We hypothesize that time-dependent network rewiring follows predictable patterns that enable cells to transition between functional states, and that these patterns can be decoded through synthesis of existing temporal proteomics, interactomics, and transcriptomics datasets.

Our multidisciplinary team brings together network scientists, systems biologists, chronobiologists, and computational biologists from six institutions to synthesize publicly available temporal datasets spanning cell cycle progression, circadian rhythms, and stress responses. We will integrate data from PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, GEO, ArrayExpress, BioGRID, IntAct, and published time-series studies. This includes phosphoproteomics capturing signaling dynamics, protein abundance measurements, interaction mapping studies, and single-cell RNA sequencing time courses.

The project pursues three synergistic aims. First, we will construct temporal protein interaction networks by integrating time-resolved proteomics with static interaction data, developing computational methods to infer interaction dynamics from protein abundance and modification changes. Second, we will identify conserved network motifs and rewiring patterns across different temporal programs, testing whether cells employ common strategies for network reorganization. Third, we will develop predictive models linking network dynamics to emergent cellular phenotypes such as cell division, metabolic switching, and stress adaptation.

This synthesis project requires NCEMS support for several reasons. The data integration challenge spans multiple data types, organisms, and experimental conditions requiring diverse expertise. No single laboratory has the breadth of knowledge needed to interpret patterns across cell cycle biology, circadian biology, and stress biology. The computational infrastructure for analyzing dynamic networks at this scale exceeds typical laboratory resources.

Our team composition reflects NCEMS values: researchers from R1 universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators; faculty spanning assistant to full professor ranks; and strong representation of early-career researchers. Geographic diversity spans East Coast, Midwest, and West Coast institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a temporal protein interaction database with visualization tools, (2) software for inferring interaction dynamics from proteomics data, (3) a catalog of conserved network rewiring motifs, and (4) mechanistic models of temporal emergence. All resources will be publicly released with comprehensive documentation.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between laboratories, a summer workshop on temporal network analysis, and mentored research experiences for undergraduates from partner institutions. This project will establish foundational principles for understanding how molecular interaction dynamics give rise to emergent cellular behaviors across time.
original.background_and_significance:
Cellular life is fundamentally temporal. From the orchestrated progression through cell division to the rhythmic oscillations of circadian clocks and the rapid mobilization of stress responses, cells continuously reorganize their molecular machinery across time. At the heart of this temporal organization lies the protein interaction network—the complex web of physical and functional associations between proteins that underlies virtually all cellular processes. Despite decades of research mapping protein interactions, a critical gap persists: we lack a systematic understanding of how these networks dynamically rewire across time and how such rewiring gives rise to emergent cellular behaviors.

The study of protein-protein interactions has generated extraordinary resources. Databases such as BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, and the Human Reference Interactome collectively catalog millions of interactions across hundreds of organisms. However, these resources predominantly represent static snapshots—interactions detected under specific experimental conditions, collapsed across time. This static view fundamentally misrepresents cellular reality. Protein interactions are exquisitely time-dependent, governed by changes in protein abundance, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and conformational states. The emergence of cellular phenotypes—division, differentiation, adaptation—cannot be understood without resolving this temporal dimension.

Recent technological advances have generated unprecedented temporal resolution in molecular measurements. Quantitative proteomics now tracks thousands of proteins across cell cycle phases with minute-scale resolution. Phosphoproteomics captures signaling dynamics in real-time. Time-resolved interactomics methods, including proximity labeling and cross-linking mass spectrometry, reveal how interaction partners change across conditions. Single-cell RNA sequencing time courses capture transcriptional dynamics underlying cellular state transitions. These datasets, largely publicly available through repositories like PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, GEO, and ArrayExpress, represent an untapped resource for understanding temporal network dynamics.

The significance of this synthesis project lies in its potential to reveal fundamental principles of temporal emergence in biological systems. We define temporal emergence as the appearance of system-level properties—cellular phenotypes, functional states, behavioral transitions—that arise from the time-dependent reorganization of molecular interaction networks. This concept directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. Protein interaction networks operate precisely at this scale, bridging individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular organization.

Three temporal programs offer complementary windows into network dynamics. The cell cycle represents a deterministic, highly conserved program where network rewiring drives sequential cellular states. Circadian rhythms exemplify sustained oscillatory dynamics, with approximately 10-20% of the proteome showing rhythmic abundance. Stress responses demonstrate rapid, adaptive network reorganization. By synthesizing data across these programs, we can identify both program-specific and universal principles of temporal network organization.

This project addresses long-standing questions that have resisted resolution by individual laboratories. What network architectures enable rapid yet reversible state transitions? Do cells employ conserved rewiring motifs across different temporal programs? Can we predict emergent phenotypes from network dynamics? Answering these questions requires integration of diverse data types and expertise that exceeds any single laboratory's capabilities, making this project ideally suited for NCEMS support.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions, each accompanied by testable hypotheses derived from preliminary analyses and theoretical considerations. Together, these questions form a coherent framework for understanding temporal emergence in protein interaction networks.

Research Question 1: How can we construct accurate temporal protein interaction networks by integrating time-resolved molecular data with static interaction databases?

Hypothesis 1a: Protein interaction probability at any given time point can be accurately inferred from the co-abundance and co-modification states of interaction partners, weighted by prior interaction evidence from static databases. We hypothesize that interactions are most likely active when both partners are present at sufficient abundance, appropriately localized, and bear compatible post-translational modifications. This hypothesis predicts that temporal proteomics data, when properly integrated with static interaction maps, will reveal that only 30-50% of catalogued interactions are simultaneously active at any given cell state.

Hypothesis 1b: Different temporal programs exhibit characteristic timescales of network rewiring that reflect underlying regulatory mechanisms. We predict that cell cycle transitions involve rapid, switch-like rewiring events (minutes to hours), circadian networks show gradual sinusoidal dynamics (hours), and stress responses display biphasic patterns with rapid initial rewiring followed by slower adaptation phases.

Research Question 2: What conserved network motifs and rewiring patterns govern transitions between cellular states across different temporal programs?

Hypothesis 2a: Cells employ a limited repertoire of network rewiring motifs that are reused across different temporal programs. We hypothesize the existence of "temporal network motifs"—recurring patterns of coordinated interaction changes—analogous to static network motifs but operating in the temporal domain. Specifically, we predict identification of motifs including "hub switching" (sequential activation of alternative hub proteins), "module handoff" (coordinated transfer of proteins between functional modules), and "interaction cascades" (ordered sequences of interaction formation/dissolution).

Hypothesis 2b: Network rewiring during state transitions follows a "prepare-execute-stabilize" pattern conserved across temporal programs. We hypothesize that cells first rewire peripheral network regions (prepare), then rapidly reorganize core network architecture (execute), and finally reinforce the new network state through feedback interactions (stabilize). This pattern should be detectable across cell cycle transitions, circadian phase shifts, and stress response initiation.

Hypothesis 2c: Cross-talk between temporal programs occurs through shared network rewiring nodes. We predict that proteins serving as integration points between cell cycle, circadian, and stress networks will show distinctive temporal dynamics and network positions, functioning as "temporal coordinators" that synchronize multiple programs.

Research Question 3: Can temporal network dynamics predict emergent cellular phenotypes, and what network features are most predictive?

Hypothesis 3a: Emergent cellular phenotypes can be predicted from network dynamics with greater accuracy than from static network topology or individual protein measurements alone. We hypothesize that dynamic network features—including rewiring velocity, module coherence over time, and hub stability—will outperform static features in predicting phenotypic outcomes such as cell division timing, metabolic state, and stress survival.

Hypothesis 3b: Critical transitions in cellular state are preceded by characteristic network signatures, analogous to early warning signals in complex systems. We predict that approaching state transitions (e.g., commitment to cell division, stress response activation) will be heralded by increased network variance, slowed recovery from perturbations, and increased correlation among network components—signatures of critical slowing down observed in other complex systems.

Hypothesis 3c: The relationship between network dynamics and emergent phenotypes is hierarchically organized, with mesoscale network properties (module dynamics, inter-module communication) being more predictive than either microscale (individual interactions) or macroscale (global network statistics) features. This hypothesis directly tests NCEMS's focus on mesoscale emergence.

These hypotheses generate specific, falsifiable predictions that will be systematically tested through our data synthesis and analysis pipeline. Negative results will be equally informative, potentially revealing that temporal network organization is more context-specific than hypothesized or that alternative frameworks are needed.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises four integrated components: data acquisition and harmonization, temporal network construction, pattern discovery and motif identification, and predictive modeling. Each component employs established computational methods while developing novel approaches where existing tools are insufficient.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization: We will systematically retrieve publicly available datasets from multiple repositories. From PRIDE and ProteomeXchange, we will obtain quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics time-series datasets spanning cell cycle (minimum 15 datasets across human, mouse, and yeast), circadian studies (minimum 20 datasets including liver, SCN, fibroblasts), and stress responses (minimum 25 datasets covering heat shock, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and nutrient deprivation). From GEO and ArrayExpress, we will retrieve matched transcriptomics time courses and single-cell RNA-seq datasets. Static interaction data will be obtained from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, and organism-specific resources (SGD, FlyBase).

Data harmonization presents significant challenges due to heterogeneous experimental designs, measurement platforms, and normalization approaches. We will implement a standardized preprocessing pipeline including: (1) unified protein identifier mapping using UniProt as reference, (2) batch effect correction using ComBat-seq for transcriptomics and similar approaches for proteomics, (3) temporal alignment using dynamic time warping for datasets with different sampling frequencies, and (4) cross-species mapping using orthology relationships from OrthoDB. Quality control metrics will ensure only high-confidence data enter downstream analyses.

Temporal Network Construction: We will develop a probabilistic framework for inferring time-resolved protein interaction networks. The core innovation is treating interaction probability as a time-dependent function of protein states. For each potential interaction (i,j) at time t, we compute: P(interaction_ij,t) = f(abundance_i,t, abundance_j,t, PTM_i,t, PTM_j,t, localization_i,t, localization_j,t) × prior_ij, where prior_ij derives from static interaction databases weighted by evidence quality. The function f will be learned from datasets where both temporal molecular data and temporal interaction measurements are available, then applied to infer dynamics in datasets with only molecular measurements.

We will construct temporal networks at multiple resolutions: fine-grained (individual time points), phase-aggregated (e.g., cell cycle phases), and continuous (using Gaussian process interpolation). Network representations will include both binary (interaction present/absent) and weighted (interaction strength) formats.

Pattern Discovery and Motif Identification: To identify conserved rewiring patterns, we will employ multiple complementary approaches. Temporal network motif discovery will extend static motif-finding algorithms to detect recurring patterns of coordinated interaction changes. We will adapt frequent subgraph mining algorithms to operate on sequences of network snapshots, identifying motifs defined by both topology and temporal ordering of changes.

Module dynamics will be analyzed using temporal extensions of community detection algorithms, tracking module composition, coherence, and inter-module communication over time. We will apply tensor decomposition methods to identify low-dimensional representations of network dynamics, revealing dominant modes of rewiring.

Cross-program comparison will use network alignment algorithms adapted for temporal networks, identifying conserved dynamic patterns across cell cycle, circadian, and stress programs. Statistical significance will be assessed through randomization procedures preserving relevant null model properties.

Predictive Modeling: We will develop machine learning models linking network dynamics to emergent phenotypes. Features will include static network properties, dynamic properties (rewiring rates, module stability, hub dynamics), and derived features capturing temporal patterns. Models will be trained on datasets with phenotypic readouts (division timing, survival, metabolic state) and validated through cross-validation and held-out test sets.

Interpretability is prioritized alongside prediction accuracy. We will employ attention mechanisms and SHAP values to identify which network features drive predictions, generating mechanistic hypotheses about temporal emergence.

All analyses will be implemented in reproducible workflows using Snakemake, with containerized environments ensuring computational reproducibility.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate four major categories of outcomes with broad impact on molecular and cellular biology.

First, we will produce a comprehensive Temporal Protein Interaction Database (TPID) integrating data from over 60 publicly available time-series datasets across three organisms and three temporal programs. This resource will include time-resolved interaction probabilities, confidence scores, and supporting evidence. An interactive visualization platform will enable researchers to explore network dynamics, query specific proteins or pathways, and download data for custom analyses. We anticipate TPID will become a foundational resource for the systems biology community, analogous to how static interaction databases transformed network biology.

Second, we will release validated software tools for temporal network analysis, including: (1) TemporalNetInfer—algorithms for inferring interaction dynamics from proteomics data, (2) DynaMotif—tools for temporal network motif discovery, and (3) NetworkPredict—machine learning models for phenotype prediction from network dynamics. All tools will be released as documented, tested packages with tutorials and example workflows.

Third, we will produce a systematic catalog of conserved network rewiring motifs and patterns, providing the first comprehensive description of how cells reorganize their interaction networks during state transitions. This catalog will include statistical characterization, biological annotations, and cross-program comparisons. We anticipate identifying 10-20 fundamental rewiring motifs that represent reusable cellular strategies for temporal organization.

Fourth, we will develop and validate predictive models linking network dynamics to emergent phenotypes, demonstrating that temporal network features provide predictive power beyond static analyses. These models will generate specific, testable predictions for experimental validation by the broader community.

The broader impact extends beyond specific deliverables. This project will establish temporal network analysis as a rigorous subdiscipline with standardized methods and resources. Training activities will develop expertise in synthesis research among the next generation of scientists. The conceptual framework of temporal emergence will inform understanding of cellular organization more broadly, with potential applications in disease biology, drug development, and synthetic biology. By demonstrating the power of synthesis approaches for understanding dynamic cellular processes, this project will catalyze similar efforts across biological systems.

rephrased.standardized_text:
Systems biology and temporal proteomics investigate dynamic protein interaction networks to understand their role in emergent cellular behaviors. Current interaction networks are treated as static snapshots that fail to account for time dependent rewiring during cellular transitions. This project constructs temporal protein interaction networks to identify conserved motifs and link molecular reorganization to specific cellular phenotypes.

The study integrates existing time series datasets across three temporal programs to perform computational modeling and pattern discovery. Key methods include probabilistic inference of interaction dynamics and machine learning for phenotype prediction alongside temporal network motif discovery. Results are validated through cross validation and held out test sets with statistical significance testing using null models.

The project utilizes datasets from PRIDE and ProteomeXchange and GEO and ArrayExpress and BioGRID and IntAct and STRING and SGD and FlyBase. Distinct datasets are integrated through unified protein mapping and batch effect correction and dynamic time warping for temporal alignment. Data heterogeneity is addressed through standardized preprocessing pipelines and probabilistic modeling to mitigate limitations in experimental design and sampling.

The project follows a three year timeline to complete the proposed milestones and computational modeling objectives. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration in network science and systems biology because the work exceeds the capacity of one laboratory.

All findings and code and the Temporal Protein Interaction Database are released publicly to ensure open access for researchers. The multi institutional team includes faculty and postdoctoral researchers and students from diverse institutions to provide comprehensive training opportunities.
rephrased.main_idea: This research addresses the failure of static protein interaction models to capture the time dependent rewiring driving complex cellular transitions. The study employs probabilistic inference and tensor decomposition to synthesize disparate temporal datasets into a unified framework of network dynamics. This project establishes a novel database and predictive modeling suite that defines how molecular reorganization governs emergent biological phenotypes.

title: The Mesoscale Architecture of Mitochondrial Contact Sites: Integrating Structural, Proteomic, and Functional Data to Understand Emergent Organelle Communication

original.abstract:
Membrane contact sites between mitochondria and other organelles represent critical hubs for cellular homeostasis, yet how their mesoscale architecture enables emergent functions in calcium signaling, lipid transfer, and metabolic regulation remains mysterious. This proposal unites structural biologists, mitochondrial biologists, lipidomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the organizational principles of mitochondrial contact sites and their functional consequences.

Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs), mitochondria-lysosome contacts, and mitochondria-lipid droplet interfaces each possess distinct protein compositions and functions, but comprehensive understanding of their architecture-function relationships is lacking. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography data from EMPIAR revealing contact site ultrastructure, proteomics data from proximity labeling studies, lipidomics datasets, calcium imaging data, and metabolomics measurements. Cross-referencing with disease-associated variants from ClinVar and GWAS catalogs will connect molecular architecture to physiological relevance.

Our first aim develops an integrated structural model of mitochondrial contact sites by synthesizing tomography data with protein structural predictions from AlphaFold and experimentally determined structures from PDB. We will map protein complexes to contact site architectures and identify organizational principles. Our second aim connects contact site composition to function by integrating proteomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics data across cell types and conditions. Machine learning approaches will identify compositional signatures predicting functional outcomes. Our third aim examines how contact site dysfunction contributes to disease by linking architectural and compositional features to disease phenotypes.

This project exemplifies the need for NCEMS support. Understanding contact sites requires expertise spanning membrane biology, structural biology, metabolism, and computational modeling that no single laboratory encompasses. Data integration across imaging, proteomics, and metabolomics modalities requires specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables synthesis impossible through traditional single-laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions, spanning structural biology, mitochondrial biology, computational biology, and metabolism. Career stages range from assistant professors to senior investigators, with strong participation from underrepresented groups and primarily undergraduate institutions.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated database of mitochondrial contact site architecture and composition, (2) predictive models linking contact site features to cellular functions, (3) identification of disease-relevant contact site alterations, and (4) new hypotheses for experimental validation. All data integration workflows, analysis code, and findings will be publicly released.

Training is embedded throughout the project. Graduate students will gain experience in multi-modal data integration through collaborative research. Postdocs will develop leadership skills through aim coordination. We will develop educational modules on contact site biology and data synthesis methods for the broader community. This project will establish principles for understanding how mesoscale organelle interfaces enable emergent cellular functions.
original.background_and_significance:
Mitochondria do not function in isolation. Rather, they engage in dynamic physical and functional interactions with virtually every other membrane-bound compartment in the cell through specialized structures called membrane contact sites (MCS). These nanometer-scale interfaces—typically spanning 10-30 nm gaps between organelles—represent quintessential mesoscale phenomena where molecular components organize into higher-order assemblies that enable emergent cellular functions impossible to predict from individual protein properties alone. Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs) facilitate calcium transfer critical for ATP production and apoptotic signaling. Mitochondria-lysosome contacts regulate mitochondrial fission and metabolite exchange. Mitochondria-lipid droplet interfaces coordinate fatty acid trafficking during metabolic stress. Despite decades of research, we lack integrated understanding of how the mesoscale architecture of these contact sites enables their diverse emergent functions.

The significance of this knowledge gap extends beyond basic cell biology. Dysfunction at mitochondrial contact sites is implicated in neurodegeneration, metabolic disease, and cancer. Mutations in MERC proteins cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and hereditary spastic paraplegia. Altered mitochondria-lysosome contacts contribute to Parkinson's disease pathogenesis. Yet without understanding the organizational principles governing contact site architecture and function, we cannot develop rational therapeutic strategies targeting these interfaces.

The time is ripe for synthesis research addressing this challenge. The past decade has witnessed an explosion of publicly available data relevant to mitochondrial contact sites. The Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) now contains hundreds of cryo-electron tomography datasets revealing contact site ultrastructure at unprecedented resolution. Proximity labeling proteomics studies using BioID and APEX have mapped contact site protein compositions across multiple cell types and conditions, with data deposited in ProteomeXchange and PRIDE databases. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database provides predicted structures for essentially all human proteins, including poorly characterized contact site components. Lipidomics datasets in MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench capture lipid compositions relevant to contact site function. Calcium imaging datasets document signaling dynamics at MERCs. Disease variant databases including ClinVar and the GWAS Catalog link contact site genes to human pathology.

However, these data exist in silos. Structural biologists analyze tomography data without integrating proteomics. Biochemists study protein interactions without spatial context. Metabolic researchers examine lipid transfer without architectural information. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to synthesize across these domains. This fragmentation prevents answering fundamental questions: How do protein complexes organize within contact sites? What compositional features predict functional capacity? How do architectural perturbations cause disease?

This proposal directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Contact sites exemplify emergence—their functions in calcium signaling, lipid transfer, and metabolic regulation arise from the collective organization of molecular components in ways unpredictable from studying isolated proteins. By synthesizing structural, proteomic, lipidomic, and functional data, we will decode the organizational principles enabling these emergent properties, establishing paradigms applicable to other mesoscale cellular structures.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build from structural characterization through functional understanding to disease relevance.

Research Question 1: What are the organizational principles governing mitochondrial contact site architecture?

We hypothesize that mitochondrial contact sites exhibit hierarchical organization, with core tethering complexes establishing baseline architecture and accessory proteins creating functional microdomains within contact zones. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) Contact sites of different types (MERC, mitochondria-lysosome, mitochondria-lipid droplet) share conserved architectural motifs despite distinct protein compositions, reflecting common biophysical constraints on membrane apposition. (H1b) Protein complexes within contact sites exhibit non-random spatial distributions, clustering into functional modules visible in tomographic reconstructions. (H1c) Contact site dimensions and protein densities correlate with cellular metabolic states, suggesting dynamic architectural remodeling.

Research Question 2: How does contact site composition predict functional capacity?

We hypothesize that specific compositional signatures—combinations of structural proteins, lipid species, and regulatory factors—determine the functional repertoire of individual contact sites. Our specific predictions include: (H2a) Distinct protein-lipid compositional states correspond to contact sites specialized for calcium transfer versus lipid exchange versus metabolic signaling. (H2b) Cell type-specific contact site compositions explain differential reliance on mitochondrial contacts across tissues. (H2c) Machine learning models trained on compositional features can predict functional outcomes including calcium transfer efficiency, lipid flux rates, and metabolic coupling strength.

Research Question 3: How do alterations in contact site architecture and composition contribute to disease?

We hypothesize that disease-associated variants in contact site proteins cause pathology through specific architectural or compositional perturbations rather than simple loss of function. Specifically: (H3a) Pathogenic variants cluster at protein-protein interfaces critical for contact site assembly, disrupting architectural integrity. (H3b) Disease severity correlates with the magnitude of predicted architectural disruption. (H3c) Different diseases affecting the same contact site proteins cause distinct architectural alterations, explaining phenotypic heterogeneity.

These hypotheses are testable through data synthesis approaches. For H1a-c, we will analyze tomographic reconstructions across contact site types, quantifying architectural parameters and correlating with metadata on cellular conditions. For H2a-c, we will integrate proteomics and lipidomics datasets, applying machine learning to identify compositional predictors of function. For H3a-c, we will map disease variants onto structural models and correlate predicted effects with clinical phenotypes.

Importantly, these questions cannot be answered through traditional single-laboratory approaches. Testing H1 requires synthesizing tomography data across multiple studies using different cell types and conditions—data that no single laboratory has generated. Testing H2 demands integration of proteomics, lipidomics, and functional datasets using computational approaches beyond typical experimental laboratory capabilities. Testing H3 requires connecting structural predictions to clinical databases, necessitating collaboration between basic scientists and those with clinical informatics expertise.

Our questions directly address the NCEMS focus on mesoscale emergence. Contact sites represent mesoscale structures where molecular components organize into functional assemblies. Understanding how architecture enables function—and how architectural perturbations cause disease—exemplifies the emergence phenomena NCEMS seeks to illuminate.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates multi-modal data synthesis with advanced computational analysis, organized around three synergistic aims.

Aim 1: Develop Integrated Structural Models of Mitochondrial Contact Sites

We will systematically retrieve cryo-electron tomography datasets from EMPIAR containing mitochondrial contact sites, currently comprising over 150 relevant depositions. Using standardized segmentation pipelines developed by our computational team, we will extract contact site geometries including membrane separation distances, contact zone areas, and protein density distributions. We will integrate these measurements with protein structural information by: (1) retrieving experimentally determined structures of contact site proteins from the PDB, (2) obtaining AlphaFold predictions for proteins lacking experimental structures, and (3) using AlphaFold-Multimer to predict structures of known contact site complexes. Molecular fitting approaches will dock protein complexes into tomographic densities, generating integrated structural models. We will apply graph-based network analysis to identify recurring architectural motifs across contact site types. Statistical analysis will test whether architectural parameters differ significantly between contact site types and cellular conditions.

Aim 2: Connect Contact Site Composition to Function Through Multi-Omics Integration

We will compile proteomics datasets from proximity labeling studies (BioID, APEX, TurboID) targeting contact site proteins, retrieving data from ProteomeXchange and PRIDE. Standardized reanalysis using MaxQuant and MSstats will enable cross-study comparison. We will integrate lipidomics data from MetaboLights capturing lipid compositions of mitochondria and partner organelles. Metabolomics datasets documenting metabolic fluxes at contact sites will be retrieved from Metabolomics Workbench. Calcium imaging datasets from public repositories will provide functional readouts of MERC activity.

For data integration, we will develop a unified data model representing contact site composition across molecular types. Multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) will identify latent factors capturing coordinated variation across data types. Machine learning approaches including random forests and neural networks will be trained to predict functional outcomes from compositional features. Cross-validation across cell types will test model generalizability. Feature importance analysis will identify compositional signatures most predictive of specific functions.

Aim 3: Link Contact Site Features to Disease Phenotypes

We will retrieve disease-associated variants in contact site genes from ClinVar, HGMD, and the GWAS Catalog. Structural mapping will position variants within our integrated contact site models, using FoldX and Rosetta to predict effects on protein stability and interactions. We will categorize variants by predicted mechanism: interface disruption, stability perturbation, or regulatory alteration. Statistical analysis will test whether pathogenic variants show non-random distributions within contact site structures. Correlation analysis will examine relationships between predicted architectural effects and clinical severity using phenotype data from OMIM and published case series.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis will utilize NCEMS computational resources and cloud computing platforms. We will implement workflows using Nextflow for reproducibility. All code will be developed in Python and R with version control through GitHub.

Team Coordination: Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate across aims. Annual in-person workshops at NCEMS will enable intensive collaborative analysis. A shared data management platform will ensure all team members access integrated datasets.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will generate multiple significant outcomes advancing understanding of mesoscale organelle biology.

Primary Deliverables: (1) The Mitochondrial Contact Site Atlas—a publicly accessible database integrating structural, compositional, and functional data for mitochondrial contact sites across cell types and conditions. This resource will include standardized tomographic measurements, curated proteomics and lipidomics data, and functional annotations. (2) Predictive computational models linking contact site composition to functional capacity, enabling researchers to generate testable hypotheses about contact site function from compositional data. (3) A comprehensive map of disease-associated variants within contact site structures, with predictions of pathogenic mechanisms for each variant class. (4) Standardized computational pipelines for multi-modal contact site data integration, applicable to other mesoscale cellular structures.

Scientific Impact: Our synthesis will transform understanding of how mesoscale architecture enables emergent cellular functions. By revealing organizational principles common across contact site types, we will establish general rules governing membrane contact site biology. Our predictive models will generate numerous hypotheses for experimental validation, catalyzing future research. Disease mechanism predictions will inform therapeutic development targeting contact site dysfunction.

Broader Impact: This project will demonstrate the power of synthesis research for addressing fundamental cell biology questions, establishing paradigms for future NCEMS initiatives. Training activities will develop a cohort of researchers skilled in multi-modal data integration. Educational materials will disseminate synthesis approaches to the broader community. Our open science practices will maximize the utility of project outputs for the research community.

The impact extends beyond mitochondrial biology. Membrane contact sites between other organelle pairs share fundamental organizational challenges. Principles discovered through our mitochondrial focus will inform understanding of ER-plasma membrane contacts, ER-Golgi interfaces, and other mesoscale structures critical for cellular function.
