title: The Emergence of Ribosome Heterogeneity: Synthesizing Structural, Compositional, and Translational Data to Understand Specialized Ribosomes

original.abstract:
Ribosomes were long considered uniform molecular machines, but emerging evidence suggests compositional heterogeneity enabling specialized translation, yet the principles governing ribosome specialization and its functional consequences remain poorly understood. This proposal assembles structural biologists, translation biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode ribosome heterogeneity and its emergent effects on gene expression.

Ribosome heterogeneity arises from differential incorporation of ribosomal protein paralogs, ribosomal RNA modifications, and associated factors. We will integrate structural data from PDB and EMDB, ribosome profiling data from GEO, proteomics data on ribosome composition, RNA modification data, and translation efficiency measurements. Cross-species and cross-tissue comparisons will reveal conserved and specialized features.

Our first aim maps ribosome compositional diversity by synthesizing proteomics data on ribosomal protein composition across cell types, tissues, and conditions. We will identify patterns of paralog usage and associated factors. Our second aim examines structural consequences of compositional variation by integrating structural data with compositional information to understand how heterogeneity affects ribosome architecture. Our third aim connects ribosome heterogeneity to emergent translational properties by integrating compositional data with ribosome profiling and translation efficiency measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding ribosome heterogeneity requires expertise spanning structural biology, translation biology, and systems biology. Data integration across structural, proteomic, and functional data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning structural biology, translation biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a comprehensive ribosome heterogeneity database, (2) models linking composition to structure, (3) predictions connecting ribosome variants to translational outcomes, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between laboratories, workshops on ribosome biology and data synthesis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about translation: how does ribosome heterogeneity arise, and how does this compositional diversity produce emergent effects on gene expression?
original.background_and_significance:
The ribosome represents one of biology's most ancient and essential molecular machines, responsible for translating genetic information into functional proteins across all domains of life. For decades, ribosomes were conceptualized as homogeneous entities—identical molecular factories producing proteins with uniform efficiency regardless of cellular context. This paradigm has been fundamentally challenged by accumulating evidence demonstrating that ribosomes exhibit remarkable compositional heterogeneity, with profound implications for understanding gene expression regulation and cellular adaptation.

Ribosome heterogeneity manifests through multiple mechanisms operating at the mesoscale—precisely the scale where NCEMS seeks to understand emergent biological properties. First, ribosomal protein paralogs, arising from gene duplication events, show differential expression across tissues, developmental stages, and physiological conditions. In mammals, approximately 20% of ribosomal proteins have expressed paralogs with distinct incorporation patterns. Second, ribosomal RNA undergoes extensive post-transcriptional modifications, including 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation at over 200 sites, with modification patterns varying between cell types. Third, ribosome-associated factors, including regulatory proteins and small RNAs, dynamically associate with ribosomes to modulate translation. These compositional variations create a diverse population of "specialized ribosomes" with potentially distinct translational properties.

The functional consequences of ribosome heterogeneity represent a fundamental gap in our understanding of gene expression. Emerging evidence suggests that specialized ribosomes preferentially translate specific mRNA subsets, potentially through recognition of particular sequence or structural features. This "ribosome code" hypothesis proposes that ribosome composition provides an additional layer of translational regulation beyond mRNA abundance and codon usage. However, the principles governing how compositional heterogeneity produces emergent translational specificity remain poorly understood.

This knowledge gap persists because understanding ribosome heterogeneity requires integration across traditionally separate disciplines and data types. Structural biologists have determined thousands of ribosome structures, revealing conformational dynamics and factor binding. Translation biologists have generated extensive ribosome profiling datasets measuring translation genome-wide. Proteomics researchers have quantified ribosomal protein composition across conditions. RNA biologists have mapped ribosomal RNA modifications. Yet these datasets remain largely siloed, preventing comprehensive understanding of how compositional variation produces functional consequences.

The significance of this problem extends beyond basic biology. Ribosome dysfunction underlies numerous human diseases, collectively termed "ribosomopathies," including Diamond-Blackfan anemia, Treacher Collins syndrome, and certain cancers. Understanding how ribosome heterogeneity contributes to normal cellular function and disease pathogenesis has direct translational implications. Furthermore, ribosomes represent major targets for antibiotics, and understanding structural heterogeneity could inform drug development strategies.

This project addresses a compelling scientific question ideally suited for NCEMS: how does ribosome compositional heterogeneity at the mesoscale produce emergent effects on translation? The question is unanswerable by individual laboratories because it requires synthesis across structural, proteomic, and functional data types, demanding expertise spanning multiple disciplines. The vast publicly available data—thousands of structures, hundreds of ribosome profiling datasets, extensive proteomics measurements—makes synthesis research both feasible and necessary. Our collaborative, transdisciplinary approach will generate insights impossible through traditional single-laboratory investigations.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build understanding of ribosome heterogeneity from composition to structure to function, ultimately revealing emergent principles governing specialized translation.

Research Question 1: What is the landscape of ribosome compositional heterogeneity across cell types, tissues, developmental stages, and species?

Hypothesis 1a: Ribosomal protein paralog usage follows tissue-specific patterns conserved across mammals, reflecting functional specialization requirements of different cell types. We predict that metabolically active tissues (liver, muscle) will show distinct paralog signatures compared to proliferative tissues (bone marrow, intestinal epithelium).

Hypothesis 1b: Ribosome-associated factors exhibit condition-dependent association patterns that correlate with cellular stress responses and metabolic states. We hypothesize that specific factors associate with ribosomes under nutrient limitation, oxidative stress, or developmental transitions, creating functionally distinct ribosome populations.

Hypothesis 1c: Ribosomal RNA modification patterns show hierarchical organization, with a conserved "core" modification set essential for basic function and a "variable" modification set conferring specialized properties. Cross-species comparison will distinguish conserved from lineage-specific modifications.

Research Question 2: How does compositional heterogeneity affect ribosome structure and dynamics at the mesoscale?

Hypothesis 2a: Ribosomal protein paralogs with sequence differences in functionally important regions (mRNA channel, peptide exit tunnel, factor binding sites) produce measurable structural alterations detectable through comparative cryo-EM analysis. We predict that paralogs with >15% sequence divergence will show distinct local conformations.

Hypothesis 2b: Ribosomal RNA modifications cluster in structurally and functionally important regions, with modification patterns affecting local RNA flexibility and ribosome conformational dynamics. Integration of modification maps with structural data will reveal modification "hotspots" at functionally critical sites.

Hypothesis 2c: Compositional variants exhibit distinct conformational ensembles, with heterogeneous ribosomes sampling different functional states with altered probabilities. This hypothesis predicts that ribosome heterogeneity affects not just static structure but dynamic properties relevant to translation mechanism.

Research Question 3: How does ribosome heterogeneity produce emergent effects on translation, and can we predict translational outcomes from ribosome composition?

Hypothesis 3a: Specific ribosome compositions preferentially translate mRNAs with particular sequence or structural features, creating a predictable "ribosome code." We hypothesize that mRNA 5'UTR structure, upstream open reading frames, and codon usage patterns determine sensitivity to ribosome composition.

Hypothesis 3b: Ribosome heterogeneity affects translation fidelity, elongation rate, and co-translational protein folding in mRNA-specific ways. We predict that compositional variants show distinct error rates and elongation kinetics detectable through ribosome profiling analysis.

Hypothesis 3c: The relationship between ribosome composition and translational output follows emergent, non-linear principles where combinations of compositional features produce effects not predictable from individual components. This hypothesis addresses the core NCEMS focus on emergence at the mesoscale.

These hypotheses are testable through synthesis of existing data and generate specific predictions for experimental validation. Our approach explicitly addresses emergence—how molecular-level compositional differences produce system-level translational properties through mesoscale structural organization. The hypotheses span scales from individual modifications to genome-wide translation patterns, requiring the transdisciplinary expertise assembled in our working group.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a coordinated analysis framework, leveraging AI and machine learning to extract patterns impossible to discern through traditional approaches.

Aim 1: Mapping Ribosome Compositional Diversity

Data Sources: We will systematically compile ribosomal protein quantification data from PRIDE and MassIVE proteomics repositories, focusing on studies using quantitative methods (TMT, SILAC, label-free quantification). We estimate >200 relevant datasets spanning human, mouse, and other model organisms. RNA modification data will be obtained from RMBase and MODOMICS databases, supplemented by published modification mapping studies using techniques including Pseudo-seq, RiboMeth-seq, and mass spectrometry.

Analytical Approach: We will develop standardized pipelines for cross-study normalization of proteomics data, accounting for technical variation while preserving biological signal. Machine learning approaches (random forests, gradient boosting) will identify tissue-specific and condition-dependent compositional signatures. Dimensionality reduction (UMAP, t-SNE) will visualize the compositional landscape, revealing clusters of similar ribosome populations. Phylogenetic analysis across species will distinguish conserved from variable features.

Aim 2: Structural Consequences of Compositional Variation

Data Sources: We will analyze ribosome structures from the Protein Data Bank (>1,500 ribosome entries) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (>500 ribosome maps). Structures span multiple organisms, functional states, and compositional variants, providing unprecedented opportunity for comparative analysis.

Analytical Approach: Automated structural alignment and comparison pipelines will identify regions showing compositional-dependent structural variation. We will employ molecular dynamics simulations using publicly available force fields to model how compositional changes affect ribosome dynamics. AlphaFold2 predictions for ribosomal protein paralogs will enable structural comparison where experimental structures are unavailable. Integration with compositional data from Aim 1 will link specific compositions to structural features. Network analysis will identify allosteric communication pathways potentially affected by compositional variation.

Aim 3: Connecting Heterogeneity to Translational Outcomes

Data Sources: Ribosome profiling datasets from GEO and SRA repositories (>1,000 datasets) provide genome-wide translation measurements. We will integrate these with matched RNA-seq data, proteomics measurements of protein output, and mRNA structural predictions from computational tools.

Analytical Approach: We will develop integrative models connecting ribosome composition (Aim 1) to translational efficiency measurements. Deep learning approaches (transformers, graph neural networks) will learn relationships between mRNA features and sensitivity to ribosome composition. Causal inference methods will distinguish direct effects of ribosome heterogeneity from confounding factors. Cross-validation across independent datasets will ensure generalizability.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis requires substantial computational resources for processing large structural datasets, running molecular dynamics simulations, and training machine learning models. NCEMS computational resources are essential for this community-scale synthesis.

Integration Strategy: Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate analysis across aims. A shared data infrastructure using FAIR principles will enable seamless integration. Quarterly in-person workshops at NCEMS will facilitate intensive collaborative analysis sessions, ensuring that insights from each aim inform others.

Validation Approach: Predictions will be validated against held-out datasets and published experimental results. We will generate specific, testable hypotheses for experimental validation by the broader community.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will generate transformative resources and insights advancing understanding of ribosome heterogeneity and its emergent effects on gene expression.

Primary Outcomes:

1. Ribosome Heterogeneity Atlas: A comprehensive, publicly accessible database cataloging ribosome compositional diversity across cell types, tissues, conditions, and species. This resource will include standardized proteomics data on ribosomal protein composition, curated RNA modification maps, and ribosome-associated factor inventories. The atlas will serve as an essential reference for the translation biology community.

2. Structure-Composition Models: Computational models linking ribosome composition to structural features, enabling prediction of how compositional changes affect ribosome architecture and dynamics. These models will incorporate machine learning approaches trained on integrated structural and compositional data.

3. Translational Outcome Predictors: Predictive frameworks connecting ribosome composition to translational efficiency, accuracy, and mRNA selectivity. These tools will enable researchers to predict how ribosome heterogeneity affects translation of specific genes.

4. Testable Hypotheses: Specific, experimentally testable predictions about ribosome specialization mechanisms, providing roadmap for future experimental studies by the broader community.

Broader Impact:

This project addresses fundamental questions about translation regulation with implications spanning basic biology to human health. Understanding ribosome heterogeneity will illuminate mechanisms underlying ribosomopathies and inform therapeutic development. Our open resources will accelerate research across the translation biology community.

The project exemplifies NCEMS goals by demonstrating how synthesis research reveals emergent properties at the mesoscale. Our transdisciplinary approach—integrating structural biology, translation biology, and computational science—provides a model for future synthesis projects. Training activities will develop the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of conducting community-scale synthesis research.

All outcomes directly address the NCEMS mission: understanding emergent properties through synthesis of publicly available data, requiring collaboration beyond individual laboratory capabilities, and following gold-standard open science practices.

title: Emergent Properties of the Nuclear Pore Complex: Integrating Structural, Transport, and Regulatory Data Across Scales

original.abstract:
The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is one of the largest molecular machines in cells, mediating nucleocytoplasmic transport, yet how its mesoscale architecture enables emergent transport selectivity and regulatory functions remains incompletely understood. This proposal unites structural biologists, transport biologists, computational scientists, and systems biologists to synthesize publicly available data to decode NPC organization and function.

The NPC comprises approximately 30 different nucleoporins (Nups) in multiple copies, creating a selective barrier that enables regulated transport. We will integrate structural data from cryo-EM and cryo-ET studies, protein interaction data, transport kinetics measurements, Nup localization data, and disease-associated variant information. Cross-species comparisons will identify conserved principles and evolutionary adaptations.

Our first aim constructs an integrated structural model of the NPC by synthesizing cryo-EM structures, AlphaFold predictions, and crosslinking mass spectrometry data. We will map the organization of intrinsically disordered FG-Nups that create the transport barrier. Our second aim examines transport selectivity by integrating cargo identification data, transport rate measurements, and FG-Nup interaction data to understand how the NPC achieves selective permeability. Our third aim connects NPC organization to emergent regulatory functions including gene expression control and chromatin organization.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding NPC function requires expertise spanning structural biology, transport biology, and gene regulation. Data integration across structural, kinetic, and functional data types requires diverse approaches. The computational requirements for modeling NPC behavior exceed typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning structural biology, transport biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) an integrated NPC structural database, (2) models of transport selectivity, (3) predictions linking NPC organization to regulatory functions, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations, workshops on NPC biology, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about nuclear organization: how does NPC architecture enable emergent transport selectivity and regulatory functions?
original.background_and_significance:
The nuclear pore complex (NPC) represents one of the most sophisticated molecular machines in eukaryotic cells, serving as the exclusive gateway for macromolecular transport between the nucleus and cytoplasm. With an estimated molecular mass of approximately 120 MDa in humans, the NPC exemplifies mesoscale biology—operating at the critical interface between individual biomolecules and organelle-level organization. Despite decades of research, fundamental questions persist about how the NPC's architecture enables its remarkable emergent properties: exquisite transport selectivity, rapid throughput of thousands of molecules per second, and integration with chromatin organization and gene regulation.

The NPC consists of approximately 30 distinct nucleoporins (Nups), each present in multiple copies arranged with eight-fold rotational symmetry. The scaffold Nups form the structural framework, while intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeat-containing Nups create the selective permeability barrier within the central channel. This barrier permits passive diffusion of small molecules while requiring active, signal-mediated transport for larger cargoes. The mechanisms underlying this selectivity—whether through selective phase separation, virtual gating, or polymer brush models—remain actively debated, representing a long-standing puzzle in cell biology.

Recent advances have generated unprecedented volumes of publicly available data relevant to NPC structure and function. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) studies have resolved NPC architecture at near-atomic resolution across multiple species. The AlphaFold database provides predicted structures for all Nups, including previously uncharacterized regions. Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) datasets reveal proximity relationships between Nup domains. Proteomics studies have catalogued transport cargoes and their kinetics, while genome-wide association studies and clinical databases document disease-associated NPC variants.

Critically, these data exist in isolation across disparate repositories, formats, and analytical frameworks. No comprehensive effort has integrated structural data with transport kinetics, regulatory functions, and evolutionary conservation to develop unified models of NPC emergence. This fragmentation represents both a challenge and an opportunity perfectly suited for NCEMS-supported synthesis research.

The significance of understanding NPC emergent properties extends beyond fundamental cell biology. NPC dysfunction is implicated in numerous human diseases, including certain cancers, viral infections, and neurodegenerative disorders. Mutations in Nups cause developmental syndromes and premature aging. Understanding how NPC architecture enables function will illuminate disease mechanisms and potentially reveal therapeutic targets.

This project addresses NCEMS's core mission by tackling mesoscale emergence—how the collective behavior of NPC components produces transport selectivity and regulatory functions that cannot be predicted from individual Nup properties alone. The NPC exemplifies emergence across scales of composition (multiple Nup copies), space (nanometer to hundred-nanometer organization), time (millisecond transport events to cell-cycle-dependent regulation), and information (signal-mediated cargo recognition). Our synthesis approach will reveal principles of mesoscale organization applicable beyond the NPC to other large molecular assemblies.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that probe emergent properties of the NPC across structural, functional, and regulatory scales.

Research Question 1: How does the mesoscale organization of FG-Nups within the NPC central channel create the emergent property of selective permeability?

Hypothesis 1a: FG-Nup organization follows predictable principles based on amino acid composition, anchor positions, and interaction propensities that can be modeled by integrating structural constraints with biophysical parameters derived from published studies.

Hypothesis 1b: Transport selectivity emerges from the collective behavior of FG-Nups creating distinct microenvironments within the central channel, with different regions preferentially accommodating different cargo classes based on size, surface properties, and transport receptor interactions.

Hypothesis 1c: Cross-species comparison will reveal conserved organizational principles of FG-Nups despite sequence divergence, indicating that emergent selectivity depends on physical properties rather than specific sequences.

Research Question 2: What quantitative relationships govern the emergent transport kinetics of the NPC, and how do these relationships constrain NPC architecture?

Hypothesis 2a: Transport rates for different cargo classes follow predictable scaling relationships based on cargo size, transport receptor affinity, and FG-Nup interaction strength that can be derived from synthesizing published kinetic measurements.

Hypothesis 2b: The NPC operates near optimal efficiency for its primary transport functions, with architectural features representing evolutionary solutions to competing demands of selectivity, speed, and energy consumption.

Hypothesis 2c: Disease-associated Nup variants that affect transport can be classified into mechanistic categories based on their predicted effects on FG-Nup organization, cargo binding, or scaffold integrity, enabling genotype-phenotype predictions.

Research Question 3: How does NPC organization enable emergent regulatory functions beyond transport, including chromatin organization and gene expression control?

Hypothesis 3a: Specific Nups mediate NPC-chromatin interactions through defined protein-protein and protein-DNA contacts that can be predicted by integrating ChIP-seq data, proximity labeling datasets, and structural information.

Hypothesis 3b: NPC-associated gene regulation represents an emergent property arising from the spatial organization of NPCs within the nuclear envelope, with NPC clustering creating regulatory microdomains.

Hypothesis 3c: The dual functions of NPCs in transport and gene regulation are mechanistically coupled, with transport activity influencing local chromatin states through cargo-dependent or transport-receptor-dependent mechanisms.

These hypotheses are testable through data synthesis and generate specific predictions for experimental validation. For example, Hypothesis 1c predicts that FG-Nup organization models trained on yeast data should predict human FG-Nup behavior despite low sequence identity. Hypothesis 2c predicts that disease variants can be grouped by mechanism, with each group showing distinct phenotypic signatures. Hypothesis 3c predicts correlations between transport activity and chromatin accessibility at NPC-proximal genomic regions.

Our hypotheses specifically address emergence by focusing on collective behaviors and system-level properties. We do not simply catalog NPC components but ask how their organization produces functions exceeding the sum of parts. This framework aligns with NCEMS's emphasis on understanding unexpected biological system properties arising at the mesoscale.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through computational pipelines designed for reproducibility and extensibility.

Aim 1: Integrated Structural Modeling of NPC Architecture

We will compile structural data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB), Protein Data Bank (PDB), and AlphaFold Database. Our team will develop automated pipelines to extract Nup coordinates from published cryo-EM/ET structures across species (human, yeast, Xenopus, Trypanosoma). We will integrate XL-MS distance constraints from published datasets using the XlinkDB repository and primary literature. For FG-Nup modeling, we will apply coarse-grained molecular dynamics parameterized by published biophysical measurements (Stokes radii, persistence lengths, interaction strengths). The integrative modeling platform (IMP) will combine these heterogeneous data types into ensemble structural models with quantified uncertainties. Machine learning approaches will predict FG-Nup conformational preferences from sequence features trained on published NMR and single-molecule data.

Aim 2: Transport Selectivity Analysis

We will compile transport cargo datasets from published proteomics studies, including nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation experiments and proximity labeling studies. Transport kinetics data will be extracted from single-molecule tracking studies, FRAP experiments, and in vitro reconstitution measurements available in primary literature. We will construct a comprehensive database of nuclear localization signals (NLS) and nuclear export signals (NES) from UniProt annotations and published experimental validations. Statistical modeling will identify quantitative relationships between cargo properties (size, charge, signal strength) and transport parameters. Network analysis will map cargo-transport receptor-FG-Nup interaction networks using published binding data. We will apply Bayesian inference to estimate transport parameters from heterogeneous kinetic measurements.

Aim 3: Regulatory Function Integration

We will obtain NPC-chromatin interaction data from published ChIP-seq experiments for Nups and associated factors, available through GEO and ENCODE. Gene expression datasets from Nup perturbation studies will be systematically compiled and reanalyzed using standardized pipelines. We will integrate NPC localization data with chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and histone modification datasets. Network inference methods will identify regulatory relationships between NPC components and gene expression programs. Disease variant data from ClinVar, gnomAD, and published studies will be mapped onto structural models to predict functional consequences.

Computational Infrastructure

All analyses will utilize containerized workflows (Docker/Singularity) ensuring reproducibility. We will leverage NCEMS computational resources for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations and machine learning model training. Data integration will employ standardized ontologies (Gene Ontology, Sequence Ontology) and identifiers (UniProt, PDB) enabling interoperability. Version-controlled repositories will track all code and analysis pipelines.

Team Coordination

Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate cross-institutional efforts. Quarterly in-person workshops at NCEMS will enable intensive collaborative analysis sessions. Shared cloud infrastructure will facilitate real-time data and code sharing. Each aim involves investigators from multiple institutions ensuring diverse perspectives.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will generate multiple deliverables with broad impact on molecular and cellular biology.

Primary Deliverables:

1. The NPC Integrated Structure Database (NPC-ISD): A comprehensive, queryable resource containing harmonized structural data across species, including ensemble models of FG-Nup organization with uncertainty quantification. This database will serve as the definitive structural resource for the NPC research community.

2. Quantitative Transport Models: Mathematical frameworks relating cargo properties to transport kinetics, enabling prediction of transport behavior for uncharacterized cargoes. These models will include parameter estimates with confidence intervals derived from data synthesis.

3. NPC-Chromatin Regulatory Maps: Genome-wide predictions of NPC-mediated gene regulation, identifying candidate genes and regulatory elements influenced by NPC proximity and composition.

4. Disease Variant Classification System: A mechanistically-grounded classification of disease-associated Nup variants with predictions for functional consequences, prioritizing variants for experimental investigation.

5. Testable Hypotheses: Specific, experimentally addressable predictions emerging from our synthesis, provided with proposed validation strategies for the broader community.

Broader Impact:

Our work establishes a paradigm for studying mesoscale emergence in large molecular machines. The analytical frameworks developed for NPC data integration will be applicable to other complex assemblies (ribosomes, proteasomes, spliceosomes). By demonstrating successful synthesis across structural, kinetic, and regulatory data types, we provide templates for similar efforts.

The project addresses long-standing questions about selective transport mechanisms with implications for understanding nuclear organization, gene regulation, and disease. Our disease variant predictions may inform clinical interpretation of genetic findings.

Training outcomes include development of data-savvy researchers capable of cross-disciplinary synthesis. Workshop materials and tutorials will extend training impact beyond direct participants. The project demonstrates collaborative, open science practices as a model for the field.

title: The Emergence of Cellular Memory: Synthesizing Epigenetic, Transcriptional, and Chromatin Data to Understand Heritable Cell States

original.abstract:
Cells maintain stable identities across divisions despite identical genomes, yet how molecular mechanisms produce emergent cellular memory remains poorly understood. This proposal assembles epigeneticists, chromatin biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the principles underlying cellular memory and identity maintenance.

Cellular memory involves coordinated action of transcription factors, chromatin modifications, and three-dimensional genome organization, but how these mechanisms integrate to produce stable yet flexible cell states is unclear. We will integrate ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics, Hi-C and chromatin conformation data, single-cell transcriptomics from Human Cell Atlas, DNA methylation data, and cell lineage tracing datasets.

Our first aim maps the epigenetic landscape of cellular identity by synthesizing chromatin modification data across cell types and developmental stages. We will identify modification patterns associated with stable versus plastic cell states. Our second aim examines chromatin organization's role in cellular memory by integrating 3D genome data with epigenetic and transcriptional information. Our third aim develops predictive models of cellular memory by integrating multi-omic data to understand how molecular features combine to produce emergent cell state stability.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding cellular memory requires expertise spanning epigenetics, chromatin biology, and systems biology. Data integration across epigenomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin conformation data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from eight institutions spanning epigenetics, chromatin biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated cellular memory database, (2) models predicting cell state stability, (3) identification of key memory mechanisms, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges, workshops on epigenetic data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about cellular identity: how do molecular mechanisms produce emergent cellular memory enabling stable cell states?
original.background_and_significance:
Cellular memory represents one of the most profound examples of emergence in biology: the ability of cells to maintain stable identities across multiple divisions despite possessing identical genetic information. A hepatocyte remains a hepatocyte, and a neuron remains a neuron, even as both undergo mitosis and environmental perturbations. This stability emerges from the coordinated interaction of multiple molecular systems operating at the mesoscale—precisely the domain that NCEMS prioritizes for synthesis research. Understanding how molecular mechanisms produce emergent cellular memory addresses fundamental questions about biological organization and has profound implications for regenerative medicine, cancer biology, and developmental disorders.

The molecular basis of cellular memory involves three interconnected systems operating between the biomolecular and organellar scales. First, epigenetic modifications including DNA methylation and histone post-translational modifications create heritable chemical marks that influence gene accessibility. Second, transcription factor networks establish self-reinforcing regulatory circuits that maintain gene expression programs. Third, three-dimensional chromatin organization positions genes within nuclear space, influencing their transcriptional potential. While each system has been studied extensively in isolation, how they integrate to produce emergent cellular memory remains a central unsolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology.

The scientific significance of this question extends across multiple domains. In developmental biology, understanding cellular memory explains how transient developmental signals produce permanent cell fate decisions. In cancer biology, aberrant cellular memory underlies both oncogenic transformation and therapeutic resistance. In regenerative medicine, manipulating cellular memory could enable directed differentiation and cellular reprogramming. Despite decades of research, we lack predictive frameworks explaining why some cell states are highly stable while others remain plastic, or how molecular perturbations propagate to alter cellular identity.

This synthesis project is timely because unprecedented amounts of publicly available data now exist across all three molecular systems underlying cellular memory. The ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics consortia have generated thousands of ChIP-seq datasets mapping histone modifications and transcription factor binding across hundreds of cell types. The Human Cell Atlas and related single-cell initiatives provide transcriptomic profiles capturing cellular heterogeneity and state transitions. Hi-C and related chromosome conformation capture techniques have mapped three-dimensional genome organization across developmental contexts. DNA methylation atlases document this critical epigenetic mark across tissues and disease states. Crucially, cell lineage tracing datasets now enable tracking of cellular identity maintenance and transitions in vivo.

Despite this data abundance, no comprehensive synthesis has integrated these diverse datasets to understand emergent cellular memory. Individual laboratories typically specialize in one data type or molecular system, lacking the computational infrastructure and disciplinary breadth required for integration. This project directly addresses this gap by assembling a transdisciplinary team with complementary expertise to synthesize publicly available data across epigenomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin conformation domains. The collaborative framework enabled by NCEMS support will generate insights impossible for individual laboratories, advancing our fundamental understanding of how molecular mechanisms produce emergent cellular properties at the mesoscale.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions examining how molecular mechanisms integrate to produce emergent cellular memory. Each question is accompanied by testable hypotheses that will guide our synthesis analyses and generate predictions for future experimental validation.

Research Question 1: What epigenetic signatures distinguish stable cell states from plastic or transitional states?

We hypothesize that stable cell states are characterized by specific combinatorial patterns of chromatin modifications that create self-reinforcing epigenetic domains, whereas plastic states exhibit more heterogeneous or intermediate modification patterns. Specifically, we predict that (H1a) stable cell identities correlate with broader domains of concordant histone modifications spanning multiple genes, while plastic states show more localized, gene-specific modifications; (H1b) the ratio of activating to repressive modifications at lineage-specific genes predicts cell state stability, with extreme ratios indicating committed states and intermediate ratios indicating plasticity; and (H1c) DNA methylation patterns at specific genomic features (enhancers, promoters, gene bodies) differentially contribute to cellular memory, with enhancer methylation being particularly predictive of stable identity maintenance.

Research Question 2: How does three-dimensional chromatin organization contribute to cellular memory, and what is its relationship to epigenetic modifications?

We hypothesize that chromatin topology creates spatial constraints that reinforce epigenetic states, producing emergent stability greater than either mechanism alone. Our specific predictions include: (H2a) topologically associating domains (TADs) containing identity genes show increased boundary strength in committed versus plastic cell states; (H2b) chromatin compartmentalization (A/B compartments) correlates with but temporally precedes establishment of stable epigenetic modifications during differentiation; and (H2c) long-range chromatin interactions between enhancers and promoters of identity genes are more conserved across cell divisions in stable versus transitional states. We further hypothesize that the integration of chromatin topology with epigenetic modifications creates synergistic memory systems where perturbation of either component destabilizes cellular identity.

Research Question 3: Can we develop predictive models that integrate multi-omic features to explain emergent cell state stability?

We hypothesize that cellular memory emerges from the nonlinear integration of multiple molecular features, and that machine learning approaches can identify the combinatorial rules governing this emergence. Specific hypotheses include: (H3a) models incorporating features from all three molecular systems (epigenetic modifications, transcription factor binding, chromatin organization) will outperform single-system models in predicting cell state stability; (H3b) feature importance analysis will reveal hierarchical relationships among molecular systems, identifying which features are necessary versus sufficient for cellular memory; and (H3c) the transition between stable cell states follows predictable trajectories through multi-dimensional epigenetic space, with specific intermediate states representing obligate transition points.

These research questions directly address the emergence of cellular memory at the mesoscale—the interface between individual biomolecules and cellular-level phenotypes. By synthesizing data across molecular systems, we will identify principles governing how local molecular interactions produce global cell state stability. Our hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions that will advance understanding regardless of whether they are confirmed or refuted. Confirmation would establish predictive frameworks for cellular memory, while refutation would reveal unexpected complexity requiring alternative models. This hypothesis-driven approach ensures that our synthesis research produces actionable scientific insights rather than purely descriptive catalogs.

The questions are designed to build upon each other: Question 1 establishes the epigenetic correlates of cellular memory, Question 2 examines how chromatin organization interacts with these correlates, and Question 3 integrates findings into predictive frameworks. This logical progression ensures coherent synthesis while allowing parallel investigation by different team members with complementary expertise.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates publicly available datasets across epigenomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin conformation domains using standardized computational pipelines and machine learning frameworks. The project proceeds through three interconnected aims corresponding to our research questions.

Aim 1: Mapping the Epigenetic Landscape of Cellular Identity

We will systematically download and harmonize ChIP-seq data from ENCODE (>10,000 datasets) and Roadmap Epigenomics (>2,800 datasets) covering histone modifications (H3K4me1/3, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K9me3, H3K36me3) and transcription factor binding across >100 cell types. DNA methylation data from TCGA, Roadmap, and GEO repositories will be integrated using standardized processing pipelines. We will develop a unified annotation framework mapping modifications to genomic features (promoters, enhancers, gene bodies, intergenic regions) using established databases (GENCODE, FANTOM5).

Analytical approaches include: (1) dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP, diffusion maps) to visualize epigenetic state space and identify clusters corresponding to stable versus plastic states; (2) chromatin state modeling using ChromHMM and Segway to define combinatorial modification patterns; (3) differential analysis comparing modification breadth, intensity, and co-occurrence between committed and transitional cell types; and (4) trajectory analysis using pseudotime methods adapted from single-cell analysis to order cell types along differentiation continua.

Aim 2: Integrating Chromatin Organization with Epigenetic States

We will compile Hi-C and related chromosome conformation data from 4D Nucleome, ENCODE, and published studies, encompassing >50 cell types. Data processing will use established pipelines (HiC-Pro, Juicer, cooler) with standardized normalization (ICE, KR). We will integrate these with Aim 1 epigenetic data using matched cell types and genomic coordinates.

Analytical approaches include: (1) TAD boundary strength quantification using insulation scores and correlation with epigenetic features; (2) A/B compartment calling and comparison with chromatin modification distributions; (3) significant chromatin interaction identification using methods like HOMER, HiCCUPS, and FitHiC; (4) integration of chromatin loops with enhancer-promoter pairs defined by epigenetic marks; and (5) network analysis examining relationships between topological features and gene expression stability using single-cell RNA-seq data from Human Cell Atlas.

Aim 3: Predictive Modeling of Cellular Memory

We will develop machine learning models integrating features from Aims 1-2 to predict cell state stability. Training data will derive from cell lineage tracing datasets and single-cell transcriptomics capturing state transitions. Feature engineering will extract quantitative metrics from epigenetic modifications (breadth, intensity, combinatorial patterns), chromatin organization (TAD strength, compartment scores, loop density), and transcription factor binding (network connectivity, binding site accessibility).

Modeling approaches include: (1) gradient boosting methods (XGBoost, LightGBM) for interpretable feature importance; (2) deep learning architectures (graph neural networks, transformers) capturing complex nonlinear relationships; (3) ensemble methods combining multiple model types; and (4) explainability analysis using SHAP values and attention mechanisms to identify key predictive features.

Model validation will employ cross-validation across cell types, temporal validation using developmental time-series, and external validation using held-out datasets. We will specifically test whether models trained on one developmental system generalize to others, assessing the universality of cellular memory principles.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis requires substantial computational resources including high-memory computing for Hi-C processing, GPU clusters for deep learning, and distributed storage for integrated datasets. NCEMS support provides essential infrastructure beyond individual laboratory capabilities.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate four major outcomes advancing our understanding of emergent cellular memory while providing resources enabling future research.

First, we will create the Integrated Cellular Memory Database (ICMD), a publicly accessible resource harmonizing epigenomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin conformation data across >100 cell types. This database will include standardized processing, unified annotations, and queryable interfaces enabling researchers to explore relationships between molecular features and cellular identity. The ICMD addresses a critical gap: while individual datasets exist across repositories, no integrated resource currently enables systematic cross-modal analysis of cellular memory mechanisms.

Second, we will develop and validate predictive models of cell state stability. These models will quantify the relative contributions of epigenetic modifications, chromatin organization, and transcription factor networks to cellular memory. Beyond academic interest, such models have practical applications in predicting cellular reprogramming efficiency, identifying cancer cells vulnerable to identity disruption, and designing differentiation protocols for regenerative medicine.

Third, our synthesis will identify key mechanisms underlying cellular memory, distinguishing features that are necessary, sufficient, or modulatory for stable cell states. We will generate ranked lists of genomic loci, chromatin features, and regulatory networks most critical for identity maintenance across cell types. These findings will focus experimental efforts on high-priority targets.

Fourth, we will produce specific, testable hypotheses for experimental validation by the broader community. These hypotheses will emerge from unexpected patterns in our synthesis analyses and model predictions, representing novel insights impossible to generate from single-dataset studies.

The broader impact extends across molecular and cellular biology. Understanding cellular memory principles informs developmental biology, cancer research, and regenerative medicine. Our open resources enable researchers worldwide to build upon our findings. Training activities develop the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of synthesis research. The collaborative framework demonstrates how transdisciplinary teams can address questions beyond individual laboratory capabilities, establishing a model for future NCEMS working groups addressing emergence phenomena at the mesoscale.

NCEMS provides essential coordination, computational resources, and collaborative frameworks enabling this community-scale synthesis project. title: Decoding the Emergent Logic of Protein Quality Control Networks: Multi-Scale Synthesis of Chaperone, Degradation, and Aggregation Data

original.abstract:
Protein quality control systems maintain proteome integrity through coordinated action of chaperones, degradation machinery, and sequestration mechanisms, yet how these components integrate to produce emergent proteostasis remains poorly understood. This proposal unites protein folding experts, proteomics specialists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode proteostasis network organization and function.

Proteostasis involves hundreds of chaperones, co-chaperones, and degradation factors working in concert, but comprehensive understanding of their coordination is lacking. We will integrate protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data on chaperone-client complexes, aggregation propensity predictions, proteomics data on protein stability, and disease-associated variant information from ClinVar.

Our first aim maps the proteostasis interaction network by synthesizing chaperone-client interactions, co-chaperone networks, and connections to degradation machinery. We will identify network modules and regulatory hubs. Our second aim examines client triage decisions by integrating client properties, chaperone interactions, and fate data to understand how the network decides between folding, degradation, and sequestration. Our third aim connects proteostasis network organization to emergent cellular outcomes including stress resistance and aging.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding proteostasis requires expertise spanning protein folding, proteomics, and systems biology. Data integration across interaction, structural, and functional data types requires diverse approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning protein folding, proteomics, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a comprehensive proteostasis network database, (2) models of client triage decisions, (3) predictions linking network properties to cellular outcomes, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations, workshops on proteostasis analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about protein homeostasis: how do quality control components integrate to produce emergent proteome maintenance?
original.background_and_significance:
Protein homeostasis, or proteostasis, represents one of the most fundamental challenges in cellular biology. Every cell must continuously synthesize, fold, maintain, and degrade thousands of distinct protein species while preventing the accumulation of misfolded or aggregated proteins that can cause cellular dysfunction and disease. The proteostasis network encompasses approximately 2,000 proteins in human cells, including molecular chaperones (Hsp70, Hsp90, Hsp60 families), co-chaperones, the ubiquitin-proteasome system, autophagy machinery, and specialized sequestration factors. Despite decades of research on individual components, we lack a systems-level understanding of how these components coordinate to produce the emergent property of proteome maintenance.

The significance of this knowledge gap extends across basic biology and medicine. Proteostasis failure underlies numerous age-related diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Cancer cells exploit proteostasis networks to survive proteotoxic stress, making these pathways therapeutic targets. Aging itself is characterized by progressive proteostasis decline. Yet we cannot predict how perturbations to specific network components will affect overall proteome integrity, nor can we explain why certain proteins are particularly vulnerable to aggregation while others remain stable throughout life.

The central mystery lies in understanding emergence within the proteostasis network. Individual chaperones have modest effects on protein folding, yet the integrated network maintains thousands of client proteins across diverse conditions. The network exhibits remarkable properties: it can triage clients toward appropriate fates (refolding, degradation, or sequestration), adapt to stress conditions, and maintain function despite component fluctuations. These emergent properties arise from network organization and dynamics that remain poorly characterized.

This project is timely because the data landscape has transformed dramatically. Comprehensive protein-protein interaction databases (BioGRID contains over 2 million interactions; IntAct over 1 million) now capture extensive chaperone-client and chaperone-cochaperone relationships. Structural biology has revealed atomic-level details of chaperone-client complexes through cryo-EM and crystallography, deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Large-scale proteomics studies have quantified protein stability, abundance, and turnover across conditions, available through PRIDE and ProteomeXchange. Aggregation propensity algorithms trained on experimental data enable proteome-wide predictions. ClinVar and gnomAD document disease-associated variants affecting proteostasis components and their clients. However, these data remain siloed within their respective communities.

The mesoscale focus of NCEMS aligns perfectly with proteostasis biology. Chaperone-client complexes, protein aggregates, and quality control compartments (such as aggresomes and stress granules) operate precisely at the mesoscale between individual molecules and organelles. Understanding how molecular interactions produce mesoscale assemblies that influence cellular outcomes represents a paradigm case of emergence in biology.

No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate structural, interaction, proteomics, and computational data into a unified framework. This synthesis project will transform our understanding of proteostasis by revealing the organizational principles that enable emergent proteome maintenance, with implications spanning basic cell biology, aging research, and therapeutic development for protein misfolding diseases.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that probe emergent properties of the proteostasis network at increasing scales of biological organization.

Research Question 1: What is the organizational architecture of the proteostasis network, and how do network properties enable robust proteome maintenance?

We hypothesize that the proteostasis network exhibits modular organization with specialized modules handling distinct client classes, connected through regulatory hubs that coordinate responses. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) Chaperone-client interactions partition into modules corresponding to client structural features (beta-sheet rich, intrinsically disordered, membrane-associated); (H1b) Co-chaperone networks function as specificity determinants that route clients to appropriate modules; (H1c) Network topology features including redundancy, feedback loops, and hub connectivity explain the robustness of proteostasis to single-component perturbations. These hypotheses will be tested by constructing comprehensive network maps from interaction databases and analyzing their topological properties using graph-theoretic approaches.

Research Question 2: How does the proteostasis network make triage decisions that determine whether a client protein is refolded, degraded, or sequestered?

We hypothesize that client fate emerges from the integration of multiple client properties and network states rather than simple decision rules. Specifically: (H2a) Client intrinsic properties (aggregation propensity, thermodynamic stability, structural features) establish baseline fate probabilities; (H2b) Chaperone binding kinetics and cochaperone recruitment modify these probabilities through competitive interactions; (H2c) Cellular state variables (ATP levels, chaperone availability, stress status) shift the decision landscape globally. We will test these hypotheses by integrating client property databases with fate outcome data to build predictive models of triage decisions, then validating predictions against independent datasets.

Research Question 3: How does proteostasis network organization produce emergent cellular phenotypes including stress resistance, proteome stability during aging, and disease susceptibility?

We hypothesize that emergent cellular outcomes depend on network-level properties rather than individual component activities. Specifically: (H3a) Stress resistance correlates with network properties including connectivity, redundancy, and adaptive capacity rather than expression levels of individual chaperones; (H3b) Age-related proteostasis decline reflects network fragmentation and loss of coordination before individual component failure; (H3c) Disease-associated variants in proteostasis components cause pathology through network perturbation effects that extend beyond direct interaction partners. These hypotheses will be tested by correlating network metrics with phenotypic data from stress response studies, aging datasets, and disease variant databases.

These questions address the NCEMS mission by focusing on emergence—how molecular-level interactions produce mesoscale organization that generates cellular-level outcomes. The proteostasis network exemplifies emergence: individual chaperone-client interactions are relatively weak and transient, yet the integrated network produces robust proteome maintenance across the cellular lifetime. Understanding this emergence requires the multi-scale data integration that defines synthesis science.

Our hypotheses are falsifiable through specific predictions. If H1a is correct, client structural features will predict chaperone module assignment with high accuracy. If H2c is correct, models incorporating cellular state will outperform client-property-only models. If H3b is correct, network fragmentation metrics will precede individual component changes in aging datasets. Negative results would redirect our understanding toward alternative organizational principles.

These questions cannot be answered by individual laboratories because they require integration across data types (interactions, structures, proteomics, phenotypes) that span multiple fields. The synthesis approach enables comprehensive analysis that reveals emergent principles invisible in isolated datasets.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a structured analytical pipeline, leveraging expertise across our multidisciplinary team.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization (Months 1-6): We will systematically compile proteostasis-relevant data from established repositories. Protein-protein interactions will be extracted from BioGRID (focusing on human, mouse, and yeast chaperone systems) and IntAct, with quality filtering based on evidence codes and experimental methods. Structural data on chaperone-client complexes will be retrieved from the Protein Data Bank, supplemented by AlphaFold2 predictions for complexes lacking experimental structures. Client protein properties will be compiled from multiple sources: aggregation propensity scores from TANGO and Zyggregator algorithms, thermodynamic stability measurements from ProTherm, and turnover rates from systematic proteomics studies in PRIDE. Disease variant data will be extracted from ClinVar, with population frequency information from gnomAD. Phenotypic data on stress responses and aging will be compiled from GEO expression datasets and published proteomics studies. All data will be harmonized to common identifiers (UniProt accessions) and quality-controlled for consistency.

Network Construction and Analysis (Months 4-12): We will construct multi-layer proteostasis networks representing different interaction types: physical interactions (chaperone-client, chaperone-cochaperone), functional relationships (shared clients, regulatory connections), and structural similarities. Network analysis will employ graph-theoretic methods including community detection algorithms (Louvain, Infomap) to identify modules, centrality measures to identify hubs, and network motif analysis to characterize regulatory architectures. We will develop novel metrics for proteostasis-specific network properties including client coverage, redundancy indices, and adaptive capacity measures. Machine learning approaches (random forests, gradient boosting) will identify features predictive of network organization.

Client Triage Modeling (Months 8-18): We will develop computational models predicting client fate from integrated features. Training data will combine client properties, interaction patterns, and fate outcomes from published studies. We will implement multiple modeling approaches: logistic regression for interpretable feature importance, neural networks for capturing nonlinear relationships, and Bayesian networks for representing conditional dependencies. Models will be trained on well-characterized clients and validated on held-out datasets. Cross-species analysis will identify conserved versus species-specific triage principles. Uncertainty quantification will accompany all predictions.

Emergence Analysis (Months 12-24): We will correlate network properties with cellular phenotypes using regression modeling and causal inference methods. Stress response data from GEO will be analyzed to identify network features associated with resistance. Aging datasets will be examined for network fragmentation signatures. Disease variant effects will be modeled using network perturbation analysis, predicting phenotypic impact from network position and connectivity. We will develop a theoretical framework linking network organization to emergent properties using concepts from complex systems theory.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis will employ Python-based workflows (NetworkX, scikit-learn, PyTorch) with version control through GitHub. Computationally intensive analyses will utilize NCEMS computational resources. All code will be documented and containerized (Docker) for reproducibility.

Team Coordination: Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate activities across institutions. Quarterly in-person workshops at NCEMS will enable intensive collaborative analysis. A shared data infrastructure (using NCEMS resources) will enable real-time collaboration. Working groups organized around each aim will include members with complementary expertise.

Validation Strategy: Predictions will be validated against independent datasets not used in model training. Cross-validation and bootstrap resampling will assess model robustness. Predictions will be prioritized for experimental testing by collaborating laboratories outside this proposal.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple transformative outcomes advancing our understanding of proteostasis emergence.

Primary Deliverables: (1) The Proteostasis Network Atlas—a comprehensive, publicly accessible database integrating chaperone-client interactions, cochaperone networks, and degradation machinery connections across human, mouse, and yeast systems, with standardized annotations and quality metrics. (2) Client Triage Predictor—a validated computational tool predicting protein fate (refolding, degradation, sequestration) from sequence and structural features, enabling proteome-wide assessment of quality control outcomes. (3) Network-Phenotype Models—quantitative frameworks linking proteostasis network properties to cellular outcomes including stress resistance and aging trajectories. (4) Testable Hypotheses Catalog—prioritized predictions for experimental validation, including candidate regulatory hubs, predicted disease variant effects, and proposed intervention targets.

Scientific Impact: This project will establish foundational principles for understanding emergence in proteostasis networks. By revealing how molecular interactions produce mesoscale organization and cellular phenotypes, we address fundamental questions about biological complexity. Our findings will transform the field from component-focused studies toward systems-level understanding, enabling predictive models of proteostasis function and dysfunction.

Broader Impacts: Understanding proteostasis network organization has direct implications for aging research and therapeutic development. Our predictions of disease variant effects will inform clinical interpretation of genetic data. The network-based framework will identify novel therapeutic targets for protein misfolding diseases. Training activities will develop the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of synthesis research.

Community Resources: All deliverables will be publicly released following open science principles. The Proteostasis Network Atlas will serve as a community resource for hypothesis generation. Computational tools will be documented and accessible to researchers without specialized expertise. Training materials developed for workshops will be publicly available.

Success will establish a model for future synthesis projects addressing emergence in other biological systems.
