title: The Emergence of Signaling Specificity: Synthesizing Interaction, Localization, and Kinetic Data to Understand Pathway Insulation

original.abstract:
Cells use a limited repertoire of signaling molecules to control diverse responses, yet how signaling pathways maintain specificity despite shared components remains a fundamental puzzle. This proposal assembles signaling biologists, systems biologists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the principles underlying emergent signaling specificity.

Signaling specificity arises from spatial organization, temporal dynamics, and scaffolding proteins, but comprehensive understanding of how these mechanisms integrate is lacking. We will integrate protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, phosphoproteomics data from PRIDE, subcellular localization data from Human Protein Atlas, kinetic measurements, and structural data on signaling complexes.

Our first aim maps the signaling interaction landscape by synthesizing protein-protein interactions across signaling pathways, identifying shared components and pathway-specific factors. We will analyze scaffolding protein networks. Our second aim examines spatial organization's role in specificity by integrating localization data with interaction information to understand compartmentalized signaling. Our third aim develops predictive models of signaling specificity by integrating interaction, localization, and kinetic data to understand how pathways achieve insulation.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding signaling specificity requires expertise spanning signal transduction, cell biology, and systems biology. Data integration across interaction, localization, and kinetic data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning signaling biology, systems biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated signaling specificity database, (2) models predicting pathway insulation, (3) identification of key specificity mechanisms, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges, workshops on signaling data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about cellular signaling: how do cells achieve emergent pathway specificity despite using shared molecular components?
original.background_and_significance:
Cellular signaling networks represent one of the most remarkable examples of biological information processing, enabling cells to sense environmental cues and coordinate appropriate responses across diverse physiological contexts. A fundamental paradox lies at the heart of signal transduction: cells employ a surprisingly limited repertoire of core signaling molecules—including kinases such as ERK, PKA, and AKT, and second messengers like calcium and cAMP—yet achieve exquisite specificity in controlling hundreds of distinct cellular outcomes. This apparent contradiction between molecular economy and functional diversity constitutes one of the most compelling puzzles in molecular and cellular biology.

The emergence of signaling specificity represents a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon, arising from the integration of molecular interactions across spatial and temporal dimensions that cannot be predicted from individual components alone. While decades of reductionist approaches have catalogued individual signaling pathway components, the principles governing how specificity emerges from shared molecular machinery remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap has profound implications for understanding disease mechanisms and developing targeted therapeutics, as aberrant signaling specificity underlies numerous pathologies including cancer, metabolic disorders, and developmental abnormalities.

Three primary mechanisms have been proposed to explain signaling specificity: spatial compartmentalization, temporal dynamics, and scaffolding protein organization. Spatial compartmentalization restricts signaling components to specific subcellular locations, effectively creating parallel signaling channels within the same cell. Temporal dynamics, including signal duration, amplitude, and frequency encoding, enable cells to extract distinct information from shared pathways. Scaffolding proteins physically organize signaling components into functional modules, insulating pathways from crosstalk while facilitating efficient signal transmission.

Despite significant progress in understanding individual specificity mechanisms, a comprehensive framework integrating these principles remains elusive. This gap persists largely because the requisite data—spanning protein interactions, subcellular localization, phosphorylation dynamics, and structural organization—exist in disparate databases generated by different research communities using incompatible methodologies and nomenclatures. No single laboratory possesses the expertise or resources to synthesize these heterogeneous datasets into a coherent understanding of emergent signaling specificity.

The current moment presents an unprecedented opportunity for synthesis research in signaling specificity. Public repositories now contain millions of protein-protein interactions (BioGRID, IntAct), comprehensive subcellular localization data for thousands of proteins (Human Protein Atlas), extensive phosphoproteomics datasets capturing signaling dynamics (PRIDE), kinetic parameters for enzymatic reactions (BRENDA, SABIO-RK), and structural information on signaling complexes (PDB, AlphaFold). These resources collectively represent the accumulated knowledge of thousands of laboratories worldwide, yet their integration requires coordinated efforts spanning multiple disciplines.

This proposal directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Signaling specificity emerges precisely at this intermediate scale—between individual molecular interactions and cellular phenotypes—where spatial organization, temporal dynamics, and molecular assemblies create functional properties not predictable from components alone. Our synthesis approach will reveal fundamental principles governing how cells achieve robust information processing using shared molecular components, advancing both basic understanding and potential therapeutic applications.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses one overarching question: How do cells achieve emergent signaling pathway specificity despite extensive sharing of core signaling components? We decompose this fundamental question into three interconnected research aims, each with specific hypotheses amenable to testing through data synthesis.

Research Question 1: What is the architecture of component sharing and pathway insulation across human signaling networks?

Hypothesis 1a: Signaling pathways exhibit a hierarchical organization where highly shared "hub" components (kinases, phosphatases, second messengers) are insulated by pathway-specific "adapter" proteins that restrict their functional connectivity. We predict that adapter proteins will show stronger evolutionary conservation than hub components, reflecting their critical role in maintaining specificity.

Hypothesis 1b: Scaffolding proteins function as pathway insulators by creating mutually exclusive interaction interfaces that prevent simultaneous engagement of competing pathways. We hypothesize that scaffolding proteins associated with high-specificity pathways will exhibit structural features (binding domains, disordered regions) distinct from those in promiscuous pathways.

Research Question 2: How does spatial organization contribute to signaling specificity at the mesoscale?

Hypothesis 2a: Subcellular compartmentalization creates effective "pathway channels" where shared components achieve specificity through restricted spatial access. We predict that proteins functioning in multiple pathways will show dynamic localization patterns correlated with pathway activation, while pathway-specific components will exhibit constitutive localization.

Hypothesis 2b: Membrane microdomains and phase-separated condensates serve as mesoscale organizing centers that concentrate pathway-specific components while excluding competing factors. We hypothesize that proteins with intrinsically disordered regions enriched for specific sequence features will preferentially partition into signaling condensates, providing a structural basis for spatial specificity.

Hypothesis 2c: The spatial proximity of pathway components, as measured by co-localization scores, will correlate with functional pathway coherence more strongly than binary interaction data alone, suggesting that mesoscale spatial organization provides information beyond molecular contacts.

Research Question 3: Can integration of interaction, localization, and kinetic data predict emergent signaling specificity?

Hypothesis 3a: Signaling specificity can be quantitatively predicted by a multivariate model incorporating interaction network topology, subcellular localization overlap, and kinetic parameters. We hypothesize that kinetic insulation (differential reaction rates) and spatial insulation (compartmentalization) contribute additively to pathway specificity.

Hypothesis 3b: Pathways with high specificity requirements (developmental signaling, stress responses) will exhibit multiple redundant insulation mechanisms, while pathways tolerating crosstalk (metabolic regulation) will show fewer insulation features. This "belt and suspenders" principle predicts that specificity mechanisms will be non-uniformly distributed across the signaling landscape.

Hypothesis 3c: Machine learning models trained on integrated multi-modal data will identify novel specificity determinants not apparent from single data types, revealing emergent organizational principles operating at the mesoscale.

These hypotheses are specifically designed to be testable through synthesis of existing public data without requiring new experimental data generation. Each hypothesis generates specific predictions that can be validated computationally and subsequently prioritized for experimental follow-up by the broader research community. The hierarchical structure of our hypotheses—from network architecture through spatial organization to predictive modeling—ensures systematic progress toward understanding emergent signaling specificity.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates heterogeneous public datasets through standardized data processing pipelines, network analysis frameworks, and machine learning models. We organize our methods around three synergistic aims.

Aim 1: Mapping the Signaling Interaction Landscape

Data Sources and Integration: We will compile protein-protein interactions from BioGRID (>2.5 million interactions) and IntAct (>1.1 million interactions), applying standardized quality filters based on experimental evidence codes. Pathway annotations from KEGG, Reactome, and WikiPathways will classify interactions into canonical signaling pathways. We will develop a unified interaction confidence scoring system incorporating experimental method reliability, publication support, and cross-database validation.

Network Analysis: Graph-theoretic approaches will quantify pathway overlap through shared node analysis, identifying hub proteins participating in multiple pathways. We will compute network modularity metrics to assess pathway insulation and employ community detection algorithms (Louvain, Infomap) to identify functional modules. Scaffolding protein networks will be analyzed separately, characterizing their interaction profiles, domain architectures (from InterPro/Pfam), and pathway associations.

Comparative Analysis: We will compare interaction architectures across well-characterized pathway pairs (MAPK/PI3K, Wnt/Hedgehog) representing different specificity requirements, identifying structural features distinguishing high-specificity from promiscuous pathway organizations.

Aim 2: Integrating Spatial Organization with Interaction Networks

Localization Data Processing: Subcellular localization data from Human Protein Atlas (>12,000 proteins with validated localizations) will be mapped onto interaction networks. We will compute localization overlap scores for interacting protein pairs and pathway components, distinguishing constitutive from dynamic localizations using available cell-type and condition-specific data.

Spatial Interaction Networks: We will construct compartment-specific interaction subnetworks, analyzing how pathway architecture changes across subcellular locations. Co-localization analysis will identify spatial clusters of pathway components, testing whether interaction partners show greater co-localization than random protein pairs.

Condensate and Microdomain Analysis: Proteins associated with membraneless organelles and signaling condensates will be identified from published proteomics datasets and literature curation. Sequence features (intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains) will be analyzed using IUPred and other predictors to identify structural determinants of condensate partitioning.

Aim 3: Predictive Modeling of Signaling Specificity

Kinetic Data Integration: Enzyme kinetic parameters (Km, kcat, Ki) from BRENDA and SABIO-RK will be compiled for signaling enzymes. Phosphoproteomics time-course data from PRIDE will provide dynamic information on pathway activation kinetics. We will develop methods to estimate missing kinetic parameters using machine learning trained on available data.

Multi-Modal Feature Engineering: For each signaling pathway pair, we will compute feature vectors incorporating: network topology metrics (shared nodes, modularity), spatial overlap scores (co-localization indices), kinetic parameters (rate constant ratios), and structural features (binding interface properties from PDB/AlphaFold).

Machine Learning Framework: We will train ensemble models (random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks) to predict pathway specificity from integrated features. Cross-validation and held-out test sets will assess model performance. Feature importance analysis will identify key specificity determinants, generating prioritized hypotheses for experimental validation.

Computational Infrastructure: All analyses will utilize reproducible workflows implemented in Python and R, with version control through GitHub. Computationally intensive analyses will leverage NCEMS computing resources. We will develop standardized APIs for accessing integrated datasets.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple tangible outcomes advancing our understanding of emergent signaling specificity while providing lasting resources for the research community.

Primary Deliverables: (1) The Signaling Specificity Atlas (SSA), a comprehensive database integrating interaction, localization, and kinetic data for human signaling pathways with computed specificity metrics and insulation scores. This resource will be accessible through a web interface and programmatic API. (2) Validated predictive models quantifying pathway insulation from multi-modal features, enabling researchers to assess specificity mechanisms for pathways of interest. (3) A curated catalog of scaffolding proteins annotated with pathway associations, structural features, and predicted insulation functions. (4) Prioritized hypotheses identifying key specificity determinants suitable for experimental validation.

Scientific Impact: Our synthesis will transform understanding of signaling specificity from descriptive pathway-by-pathway accounts to quantitative principles governing emergent pathway insulation. By revealing how spatial organization, temporal dynamics, and scaffolding proteins integrate to achieve specificity, we will establish a conceptual framework applicable across signaling systems. Identification of specificity mechanisms will inform therapeutic strategies targeting pathway-selective interventions while minimizing off-target effects.

Broader Impact: This project exemplifies synthesis research addressing mesoscale emergence, demonstrating how integration of heterogeneous public data reveals principles invisible to single-laboratory approaches. Our methods and workflows will serve as templates for similar synthesis efforts in other biological domains. Training activities will develop the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of leveraging public data resources.

Community Resources: All databases, models, analysis code, and training materials will be publicly released under open licenses, maximizing accessibility and enabling community extension. We anticipate our resources will become standard references for signaling research, cited in hundreds of subsequent studies investigating pathway specificity mechanisms.

title: Emergent Properties of the Centrosome: Integrating Structural, Compositional, and Functional Data to Understand Microtubule Organizing Center Function

original.abstract:
The centrosome serves as the primary microtubule organizing center in animal cells, yet how its complex architecture enables emergent functions in cell division, signaling, and cilia formation remains incompletely understood. This proposal unites centrosome biologists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode centrosome organization and function.

The centrosome comprises centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material containing hundreds of proteins in a highly organized architecture. We will integrate structural data from cryo-ET and super-resolution microscopy, proteomics data on centrosome composition, protein interaction data, cell cycle-dependent localization data, and disease-associated variant information.

Our first aim constructs an integrated centrosome architecture model by synthesizing structural data with compositional information to map protein organization within the centrosome. We will identify organizational principles and structural modules. Our second aim examines cell cycle-dependent remodeling by integrating time-resolved proteomics and imaging data to understand how centrosome composition and architecture change during division. Our third aim connects centrosome organization to emergent functions by integrating structural and compositional data with functional measurements of microtubule nucleation, signaling, and ciliogenesis.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding centrosome function requires expertise spanning structural biology, cell cycle biology, and cilia biology. Data integration across structural, proteomic, and functional data types requires diverse approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning centrosome biology, structural biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) an integrated centrosome architecture database, (2) models of cell cycle-dependent remodeling, (3) predictions linking organization to function, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations, workshops on centrosome biology, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about cellular organization: how does centrosome architecture enable emergent microtubule organizing center functions?
original.background_and_significance:
The centrosome represents a paradigmatic example of biological emergence at the mesoscale—the critical interface between individual biomolecules and functional organelles that NCEMS seeks to understand. Comprising paired centrioles surrounded by a dynamic pericentriolar material (PCM) matrix, the centrosome orchestrates microtubule organization essential for cell division, intracellular transport, cell polarity, and cilia formation. Despite decades of research, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how the centrosome's complex architecture—involving over 500 proteins organized across multiple structural layers—gives rise to its emergent functional properties.

The significance of this knowledge gap extends beyond basic cell biology. Centrosome dysfunction underlies numerous human diseases, including cancer, microcephaly, ciliopathies, and developmental disorders. Mutations in centrosomal proteins cause primary microcephaly through aberrant neural progenitor division, while centrosome amplification drives chromosomal instability in tumors. Understanding the organizational principles governing centrosome function is therefore essential for comprehending both normal cellular physiology and disease pathogenesis.

Recent technological advances have generated unprecedented data on centrosome biology, yet these datasets remain siloed across disciplines. Cryo-electron tomography has revealed the nine-fold symmetry of centriolar architecture and the layered organization of PCM components at nanometer resolution. Super-resolution microscopy studies have mapped the concentric arrangement of PCM proteins, identifying distinct functional zones. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics has catalogued cell cycle-dependent changes in centrosome composition, while proximity labeling approaches have defined the local protein environment. Protein interaction databases contain thousands of interactions among centrosomal components. Additionally, clinical databases document hundreds of disease-associated variants in centrosomal proteins, providing natural experiments linking structure to function.

Despite this data abundance, no systematic effort has integrated these diverse datasets to construct a unified model of centrosome organization and function. This represents a classic synthesis challenge: individual laboratories possess expertise in specific data types or biological questions, but comprehensive integration requires transdisciplinary collaboration. The centrosome field exemplifies the fragmentation that NCEMS aims to address—structural biologists, cell cycle researchers, and cilia biologists study the same organelle but rarely integrate their findings systematically.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. The centrosome exhibits hallmark features of emergence: its microtubule organizing capacity, signaling functions, and ability to template cilia formation cannot be predicted from the properties of individual components. These emergent functions arise from the precise spatial organization of hundreds of proteins across length scales spanning 10 nanometers to 2 micrometers—precisely the mesoscale regime NCEMS prioritizes.

Our synthesis approach will transform centrosome biology by creating the first integrated computational model linking molecular composition, structural organization, and emergent function. By leveraging publicly available data across structural, proteomic, and functional domains, we will identify organizational principles that enable centrosome function, generate testable predictions about structure-function relationships, and establish a framework applicable to other mesoscale assemblies. This project exemplifies how data synthesis can answer questions impossible to address through traditional reductionist approaches, advancing our understanding of how complex cellular machines emerge from their molecular constituents.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions that collectively illuminate how centrosome architecture enables emergent microtubule organizing center functions.

Research Question 1: What organizational principles govern protein arrangement within the centrosome?

We hypothesize that centrosomal proteins are organized into discrete structural modules with defined spatial relationships, and that these modules correspond to functional units. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) PCM proteins organize into concentric layers with characteristic radial positions determined by their interaction partners and post-translational modifications; (H1b) Structural modules identified through interaction network analysis will correspond to spatially coherent protein clusters in super-resolution data; (H1c) Disease-associated variants will cluster at module interfaces, disrupting inter-module communication rather than intra-module structure. These hypotheses will be tested by integrating cryo-ET structural data, super-resolution localization measurements, protein interaction networks, and disease variant databases to construct a comprehensive spatial model of centrosome organization.

Research Question 2: How does centrosome composition and architecture change during cell cycle progression?

We hypothesize that cell cycle-dependent centrosome remodeling follows predictable trajectories governed by the sequential recruitment and removal of protein modules. Our specific predictions include: (H2a) Mitotic PCM expansion involves coordinated recruitment of pre-assembled protein modules rather than individual protein accumulation; (H2b) Temporal proteomics data will reveal distinct phases of centrosome remodeling corresponding to specific cell cycle transitions; (H2c) Proteins recruited simultaneously will occupy adjacent spatial positions within the centrosome architecture. We will test these hypotheses by integrating time-resolved proteomics datasets with cell cycle-staged imaging data, constructing dynamic models of centrosome remodeling that capture both compositional and structural changes.

Research Question 3: How do centrosome organization and composition determine emergent functional outputs?

We hypothesize that specific structural configurations enable distinct emergent functions, and that functional transitions require coordinated reorganization of multiple protein modules. Our testable predictions are: (H3a) Microtubule nucleation capacity correlates with the spatial arrangement of gamma-tubulin ring complexes and their anchoring factors, not simply their abundance; (H3b) The transition from mitotic spindle organization to cilia formation requires wholesale reorganization of centriolar satellite positioning and PCM composition; (H3c) Signaling pathway activity at centrosomes depends on scaffold protein positioning that creates specific protein interaction microenvironments. These hypotheses will be evaluated by correlating structural and compositional features with functional measurements extracted from published imaging, biochemical, and phenotypic datasets.

Methodological Research Questions:

Beyond biological questions, our project addresses methodological challenges in mesoscale data integration: (M1) How can we effectively integrate structural data at different resolutions (cryo-ET at nanometer scale, super-resolution at tens of nanometers) into unified models? (M2) What computational frameworks best capture the dynamic, probabilistic nature of centrosome organization? (M3) How can disease variant analysis inform structural models when variant effects are context-dependent?

These questions will drive development of novel analytical approaches applicable beyond centrosome biology. Our hypotheses are designed to be testable through data synthesis while generating specific predictions amenable to future experimental validation, ensuring our work advances both fundamental understanding and provides a roadmap for hypothesis-driven research.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our synthesis approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a structured workflow designed to address each research aim while maintaining data provenance and analytical reproducibility.

Data Acquisition and Curation (Aim 1-3 Foundation):
We will systematically compile centrosome-related data from public repositories. Structural data will be obtained from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) for cryo-ET tomograms and the Image Data Resource for super-resolution microscopy datasets. We will extract protein localization measurements from published expansion microscopy and STORM/PALM studies, creating a standardized database of radial positions for PCM components. Proteomics data will be compiled from ProteomeXchange, including centrosome-enriched proteomics, proximity labeling (BioID/APEX) datasets, and quantitative cell cycle proteomics. Protein interaction data will be integrated from BioGRID, IntAct, and STRING databases, supplemented with curated interactions from primary literature. Disease variant information will be extracted from ClinVar, OMIM, and gnomAD, focusing on centrosomal genes implicated in microcephaly, ciliopathies, and cancer.

Aim 1 - Integrated Architecture Model:
We will develop a multi-scale spatial model of centrosome organization using a hierarchical integration approach. First, we will construct a reference coordinate system based on the conserved centriolar structure, using averaged cryo-ET data to define the nine-fold symmetric scaffold. Protein localization data from super-resolution studies will be registered to this coordinate system, accounting for methodological differences between studies. We will apply network analysis algorithms (community detection, module identification) to protein interaction data, identifying functionally coherent protein clusters. Machine learning approaches will predict spatial positions for proteins lacking direct localization data based on their interaction partners and biochemical properties. Disease variants will be mapped onto the spatial model, and enrichment analysis will identify structural regions sensitive to perturbation.

Aim 2 - Cell Cycle Dynamics:
Temporal analysis will integrate time-resolved proteomics with cell cycle-staged imaging data. We will construct trajectories of centrosome composition changes using published quantitative proteomics from synchronized cells. These compositional trajectories will be correlated with structural measurements from imaging studies at defined cell cycle stages. Dynamic Bayesian network modeling will infer causal relationships between protein recruitment events. We will develop predictive models of centrosome maturation that capture both the sequence and kinetics of compositional changes.

Aim 3 - Structure-Function Relationships:
Functional integration will correlate organizational features with emergent outputs. We will compile quantitative measurements of microtubule nucleation rates, spindle assembly metrics, and ciliogenesis efficiency from published studies. Statistical modeling will identify structural and compositional features predictive of functional outcomes. We will develop a computational framework that predicts functional consequences of compositional or structural perturbations, validated against published RNAi/knockout phenotypes.

Computational Infrastructure:
All analyses will be implemented in reproducible workflows using Snakemake/Nextflow. We will develop a centrosome-specific data model accommodating multi-scale spatial information. Machine learning models will utilize established frameworks (scikit-learn, PyTorch) with documented hyperparameter optimization. Visualization tools will enable interactive exploration of the integrated centrosome model.

Team Coordination:
Biweekly virtual meetings will coordinate efforts across institutions. Annual in-person workshops will facilitate intensive collaboration and training. A shared computational environment will ensure all team members can access and contribute to analyses.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate transformative resources and insights for the centrosome and broader cell biology communities.

Primary Deliverables:
(1) The Integrated Centrosome Architecture Database (ICAD): A comprehensive, queryable resource mapping protein positions, interactions, and disease variants within a unified centrosome coordinate system. ICAD will serve as the definitive reference for centrosome organization, enabling researchers to contextualize new findings within the established structural framework.

(2) Dynamic Centrosome Remodeling Models: Quantitative models capturing cell cycle-dependent changes in centrosome composition and architecture, providing the first comprehensive view of how this organelle transforms during division.

(3) Structure-Function Prediction Framework: Computational tools predicting functional consequences of compositional or structural changes, enabling hypothesis generation for experimental studies.

(4) Testable Hypotheses: A curated set of predictions linking specific organizational features to functional outputs, prioritized for experimental tractability and biological significance.

Scientific Impact:
This project will establish organizational principles governing centrosome function, advancing our understanding of mesoscale emergence. By demonstrating how complex cellular machines arise from component interactions, our work provides a template for studying other membraneless organelles and macromolecular assemblies. The disease variant analysis will generate hypotheses about pathogenic mechanisms in centrosome-related disorders, potentially informing therapeutic strategies.

Methodological Impact:
Our data integration approaches will establish best practices for multi-scale biological data synthesis, directly applicable to other mesoscale assemblies (nuclear pore complex, kinetochore, cilia). The computational frameworks developed will be released as open-source tools for the broader community.

Training Impact:
Through workshops, student rotations, and collaborative research, we will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of addressing complex biological questions through synthesis approaches. Our inclusion of PUI researchers and early-career investigators will broaden participation in cutting-edge computational biology.

This project exemplifies NCEMS's vision of leveraging existing data to answer fundamental questions about biological emergence, generating insights impossible through traditional single-laboratory approaches.

title: The Emergence of Autophagosome Selectivity: Synthesizing Receptor, Cargo, and Membrane Data to Understand Selective Autophagy

original.abstract:
Selective autophagy targets specific cellular components for degradation through cargo receptor recognition, yet how selectivity emerges from molecular interactions remains poorly understood. This proposal assembles autophagy researchers, structural biologists, proteomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode selective autophagy principles.

Selective autophagy involves cargo receptors that bridge targets to autophagosome membranes, but comprehensive understanding of receptor-cargo relationships and their regulation is lacking. We will integrate protein interaction data, structural data on receptor-cargo complexes, proteomics data on autophagy substrates, ubiquitin modification data, and phenotypic data connecting autophagy to cellular outcomes.

Our first aim maps the selective autophagy interaction landscape by synthesizing receptor-cargo interactions across autophagy pathways. We will identify recognition motifs and predict new receptor-cargo pairs. Our second aim examines structural principles of selectivity by integrating structural data to understand how receptors achieve specific cargo recognition. Our third aim connects selective autophagy to emergent cellular outcomes by integrating interaction data with phenotypic measurements of organelle quality control and stress responses.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding selective autophagy requires expertise spanning autophagy biology, structural biology, and proteomics. Data integration across interaction, structural, and functional data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning autophagy biology, structural biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a comprehensive selective autophagy database, (2) models of cargo recognition, (3) predictions for new receptor-cargo relationships, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges, workshops on autophagy analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about cellular quality control: how do molecular interactions produce emergent selectivity in autophagy?
original.background_and_significance:
Autophagy is a fundamental cellular degradation pathway conserved across eukaryotes that maintains cellular homeostasis by sequestering cytoplasmic components within double-membrane autophagosomes for lysosomal degradation. While bulk autophagy non-selectively captures cytoplasmic material during nutrient deprivation, selective autophagy pathways specifically target damaged organelles, protein aggregates, and invading pathogens for degradation. This selectivity is mediated by cargo receptors—proteins that simultaneously recognize specific cargo through ubiquitin-binding domains or direct interactions and recruit the autophagosome membrane machinery through LC3-interacting regions (LIRs). The emergence of selectivity from these molecular interactions represents a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon where individual protein-protein interactions collectively produce specific cellular outcomes.

Despite three decades of autophagy research, fundamental questions about selective autophagy remain unanswered. How do approximately 30 known cargo receptors achieve specificity for hundreds of potential substrates? What determines whether a ubiquitinated protein is degraded by the proteasome versus selective autophagy? How do post-translational modifications regulate receptor-cargo interactions to respond to cellular stress? These questions persist because existing studies examine individual receptor-cargo pairs in isolation, lacking the systems-level perspective necessary to understand emergent selectivity.

The significance of understanding selective autophagy extends beyond basic cell biology. Defects in selective autophagy pathways contribute to neurodegeneration, cancer, infectious disease susceptibility, and aging. Mitophagy dysfunction causes Parkinson's disease through accumulation of damaged mitochondria. Xenophagy defects permit intracellular bacterial proliferation. Aggrephagy failure leads to toxic protein aggregate accumulation in Huntington's and Alzheimer's diseases. Understanding the principles governing cargo selectivity could reveal therapeutic targets for modulating specific autophagy pathways without disrupting bulk autophagy essential for cellular survival.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal because publicly available data on selective autophagy has reached critical mass. The Protein Data Bank contains over 200 structures of autophagy proteins and receptor-cargo complexes. BioGRID and IntAct databases document thousands of autophagy-related protein interactions. PhosphoSitePlus catalogs post-translational modifications on autophagy machinery. Large-scale proteomics studies have identified autophagy substrates across conditions and cell types. Phenotypic databases link autophagy gene perturbations to organelle quality and stress responses. However, these data remain siloed in discipline-specific repositories, preventing integrated analysis.

This project directly addresses NCEMS priorities by investigating emergence at the mesoscale—how molecular receptor-cargo interactions produce cellular-level selectivity in degradation. The transition from individual binding events to pathway-specific autophagy represents emergent behavior that cannot be predicted from studying components in isolation. Our synthesis approach will reveal principles governing this emergence by integrating structural, interaction, and phenotypic data across scales.

No single laboratory possesses the expertise to address this challenge. Understanding selective autophagy requires deep knowledge of autophagy biology, structural biology expertise to interpret receptor-cargo complexes, proteomics knowledge to analyze substrate identification studies, and computational skills for data integration and machine learning. This project assembles a transdisciplinary team uniquely positioned to synthesize disparate data types into mechanistic understanding of how selectivity emerges in autophagy.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions examining how selectivity emerges in autophagy from molecular to cellular scales.

Research Question 1: What is the complete landscape of receptor-cargo interactions in selective autophagy, and what sequence and structural features determine recognition specificity?

Hypothesis 1a: Cargo receptors exhibit overlapping but distinct substrate specificities that can be predicted from sequence features in cargo proteins beyond canonical ubiquitin modifications. We hypothesize that receptor specificity depends on combinatorial recognition of multiple cargo features including ubiquitin chain types, phosphorylation states, and intrinsic sequence motifs.

Hypothesis 1b: The selective autophagy network contains significant undiscovered receptor-cargo relationships that can be predicted by integrating interaction data with sequence analysis. We predict that machine learning models trained on known interactions will identify novel receptor-cargo pairs with high confidence.

Research Question 2: How do structural features of cargo receptors enable specific recognition while maintaining the flexibility to accommodate diverse substrates?

Hypothesis 2a: Cargo receptor binding domains utilize a limited repertoire of structural mechanisms to achieve specificity, including conformational selection, induced fit, and multivalent binding. We hypothesize that integrating structural data across receptors will reveal conserved recognition principles.

Hypothesis 2b: The structural basis of selectivity involves dynamic conformational states that are not captured in static crystal structures. By integrating structural data with molecular dynamics simulations and hydrogen-deuterium exchange data, we will identify flexibility signatures that correlate with substrate promiscuity versus specificity.

Hypothesis 2c: Post-translational modifications modulate receptor-cargo binding through predictable structural mechanisms. Phosphorylation sites on receptors and cargo localize to binding interfaces and allosteric sites in patterns that can be systematically classified.

Research Question 3: How do molecular-level receptor-cargo interactions translate to emergent cellular outcomes in organelle quality control and stress responses?

Hypothesis 3a: Selective autophagy pathway activity correlates with specific cellular phenotypes in a manner dependent on receptor-cargo network topology. We hypothesize that highly connected cargo receptors produce broader phenotypic effects than receptors with limited substrate ranges.

Hypothesis 3b: Cellular stress responses activate selective autophagy through coordinated changes in receptor-cargo interactions rather than simple upregulation of autophagy machinery. Integration of stress-responsive proteomics with interaction data will reveal rewiring of the selective autophagy network.

Hypothesis 3c: Emergent selectivity in autophagy arises from competition between receptors for shared substrates, creating a prioritization system for degradation. Mathematical modeling of receptor-cargo networks will predict how competition shapes cellular outcomes.

These hypotheses are testable through data synthesis and generate specific predictions for experimental validation. For example, predicted novel receptor-cargo pairs can be validated through co-immunoprecipitation. Structural predictions about binding mechanisms can be tested through mutagenesis. Phenotypic predictions can be evaluated against existing genetic screening data.

The hierarchical organization of our questions—from interaction landscape to structural mechanisms to cellular outcomes—reflects the emergence framework central to NCEMS. We examine how properties at each scale constrain and enable properties at higher scales, building toward understanding how molecular specificity produces cellular-level selectivity in autophagy. This multi-scale approach distinguishes our synthesis project from reductionist studies of individual components.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates publicly available data across four domains: protein interactions, structural biology, proteomics, and cellular phenotypes. We employ a phased strategy progressing from data assembly through integration to predictive modeling.

Phase 1: Data Assembly and Harmonization (Months 1-6)

We will systematically retrieve selective autophagy-related data from public repositories. Protein interaction data will be extracted from BioGRID, IntAct, and STRING databases, filtering for autophagy-annotated proteins and their interactors. Structural data will be obtained from the Protein Data Bank, including crystal structures, cryo-EM structures, and NMR ensembles of autophagy proteins and receptor-cargo complexes. AlphaFold predicted structures will supplement experimental data for proteins lacking solved structures. Post-translational modification data will be retrieved from PhosphoSitePlus, focusing on phosphorylation and ubiquitination of autophagy machinery. Proteomics data identifying autophagy substrates will be compiled from published mass spectrometry studies deposited in PRIDE and ProteomeXchange. Phenotypic data will be extracted from genome-wide screening databases including DepMap and published autophagy-focused screens.

Data harmonization will standardize identifiers using UniProt accessions, map interactions to consistent confidence scores, and annotate data provenance. We will develop a unified data schema accommodating heterogeneous data types while preserving source-specific metadata essential for quality assessment.

Phase 2: Interaction Network Analysis (Months 4-12)

We will construct a comprehensive selective autophagy interaction network integrating physical interactions with functional relationships. Network analysis will identify hub receptors, characterize network topology, and detect community structure corresponding to selective autophagy subtypes (mitophagy, xenophagy, aggrephagy, etc.). We will apply machine learning approaches to predict novel receptor-cargo interactions. Features will include sequence motifs, domain architecture, subcellular localization, and co-expression patterns. Random forest and gradient boosting classifiers will be trained on validated interactions and evaluated through cross-validation. High-confidence predictions will be prioritized for experimental validation by collaborators.

Phase 3: Structural Integration and Analysis (Months 6-18)

Structural analysis will examine receptor-cargo binding interfaces across available complex structures. We will calculate interface properties including buried surface area, hydrogen bonding patterns, and electrostatic complementarity. Comparative analysis will identify conserved versus receptor-specific recognition features. Integration with post-translational modification data will map phosphorylation and ubiquitination sites relative to binding interfaces. We will employ molecular dynamics simulations using publicly available trajectories from MoDEL database and generate new simulations for key complexes to characterize binding dynamics. Machine learning models will predict binding affinity changes upon mutation or modification.

Phase 4: Phenotypic Integration and Modeling (Months 12-24)

We will integrate interaction networks with phenotypic data to connect molecular interactions to cellular outcomes. Statistical approaches will identify correlations between network properties and phenotypic measurements. We will develop mathematical models of selective autophagy incorporating receptor-cargo competition, binding kinetics, and membrane recruitment dynamics. Agent-based modeling will simulate autophagosome formation and cargo capture to test hypotheses about emergent selectivity. Model predictions will be validated against published experimental data and generate testable hypotheses.

Computational Infrastructure

Analysis workflows will be implemented in Python and R using established bioinformatics libraries. We will utilize NCEMS computational resources for large-scale data processing and machine learning. All code will be version-controlled through GitHub with continuous integration testing. Jupyter notebooks will document analysis procedures for reproducibility.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple outcomes advancing understanding of selective autophagy and demonstrating the power of data integration approaches.

Primary Outcomes:

1. Selective Autophagy Database (SelectAuto): A comprehensive, publicly accessible database integrating receptor-cargo interactions, structural data, post-translational modifications, and phenotypic associations. SelectAuto will serve as a community resource enabling researchers to query relationships across data types and generate hypotheses for experimental investigation.

2. Predictive Models of Cargo Recognition: Machine learning models predicting receptor-cargo interactions from sequence and structural features. These models will identify recognition principles and predict novel interactions with quantified confidence scores. We anticipate predicting 50-100 high-confidence novel receptor-cargo pairs for experimental validation.

3. Structural Atlas of Selectivity: Systematic characterization of receptor-cargo binding interfaces revealing conserved and divergent recognition mechanisms. This atlas will establish design principles for engineering selective autophagy, potentially enabling therapeutic modulation of specific pathways.

4. Network Models of Emergent Selectivity: Mathematical and computational models explaining how molecular interactions produce cellular-level selectivity. These models will generate quantitative predictions about autophagy pathway behavior under perturbation.

Broader Impact:

Our findings will transform understanding of selective autophagy from cataloging individual interactions to comprehending system-level principles. The synthesis approach demonstrates how integrating publicly available data generates insights beyond individual datasets. Methodological advances in multi-scale data integration will be applicable to other biological systems exhibiting emergent properties.

The project will produce trained researchers skilled in synthesis science approaches. Graduate students and postdocs will gain experience in transdisciplinary collaboration, data integration, and open science practices. Undergraduate researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions will participate in authentic research experiences.

All outcomes will be publicly released following FAIR principles, maximizing impact and enabling community building upon our work. We anticipate our database and models will accelerate autophagy research and inspire similar synthesis approaches in related fields.

title: Decoding Emergent mRNA Fate Decisions: Synthesizing RNA-Protein Interaction, Localization, and Decay Data

original.abstract:
mRNA fate—including translation, localization, storage, and decay—is determined by combinatorial RNA-binding protein interactions, yet how these interactions produce emergent fate decisions remains poorly understood. This proposal unites RNA biologists, systems biologists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode mRNA fate determination principles.

mRNA fate involves hundreds of RNA-binding proteins recognizing sequence and structural elements, but comprehensive understanding of their combinatorial logic is lacking. We will integrate CLIP-seq data from ENCODE and published studies, RNA localization data, decay rate measurements, translation efficiency data from ribosome profiling, and structural data on RNA-protein complexes.

Our first aim maps the mRNA-protein interaction landscape by synthesizing CLIP-seq data across RNA-binding proteins and conditions. We will identify co-binding patterns and competitive interactions. Our second aim examines how interaction patterns determine fate by integrating RBP binding data with localization, decay, and translation measurements. Our third aim develops predictive models of mRNA fate by integrating sequence features, RBP binding, and outcome data.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding mRNA fate requires expertise spanning RNA biology, systems biology, and computational modeling. Data integration across CLIP-seq, functional measurements, and structural data requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning RNA biology, systems biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) an integrated mRNA-RBP interaction database, (2) models predicting mRNA fate from RBP binding, (3) identification of combinatorial binding rules, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations, workshops on RNA data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about gene expression: how do RNA-binding protein interactions produce emergent mRNA fate decisions?
original.background_and_significance:
Messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules serve as the essential intermediaries between genetic information and protein synthesis, yet their journey from transcription to degradation is far more complex than simple linear progression. Each mRNA molecule faces multiple potential fates: immediate translation into protein, localization to specific subcellular compartments, storage in cytoplasmic granules, or targeted degradation. These fate decisions are not predetermined but emerge dynamically from the combinatorial interactions of hundreds of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) with sequence and structural elements within each transcript. Understanding how these molecular interactions produce coherent fate outcomes represents a fundamental challenge in molecular and cellular biology and exemplifies emergence at the mesoscale—the scale between individual biomolecules and organized cellular structures.

The human genome encodes approximately 1,500 RBPs, each recognizing specific sequence motifs or structural features within mRNAs. Individual mRNA transcripts typically contain binding sites for dozens of different RBPs, creating an extraordinarily complex regulatory landscape. Studies have demonstrated that RBPs rarely act in isolation; instead, they engage in cooperative binding, competitive displacement, and hierarchical regulatory relationships. For example, the stress granule proteins G3BP1 and TIA1 cooperatively promote mRNA sequestration during cellular stress, while the decay factor UPF1 competes with translation factors for access to specific transcripts. These interactions create emergent regulatory behaviors that cannot be predicted from studying individual RBP-mRNA pairs.

Despite decades of research on individual RBPs and their targets, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how combinatorial RBP binding produces specific fate outcomes. This knowledge gap persists because traditional experimental approaches examine one or few RBPs at a time, missing the systems-level interactions that determine fate. However, the field has now generated unprecedented amounts of publicly available data that, when synthesized, can reveal these emergent principles. The ENCODE consortium alone has produced CLIP-seq data for over 150 human RBPs, while published studies contribute data for hundreds more. Complementary datasets measuring RNA localization, decay rates, and translation efficiency provide functional readouts of mRNA fate.

This synthesis project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. mRNA fate determination exemplifies mesoscale emergence: individual RBP-RNA interactions occur at the molecular scale, but fate decisions manifest at the scale of ribonucleoprotein complexes and subcellular organization. The combinatorial logic governing these decisions represents precisely the type of complex, multi-scale phenomenon that requires synthesis research to understand.

The significance of understanding mRNA fate extends beyond basic biology. Dysregulation of mRNA fate contributes to numerous diseases, including neurodegeneration, cancer, and developmental disorders. Mutations in RBPs cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, frontotemporal dementia, and muscular dystrophies. Cancer cells exploit altered mRNA fate to promote proliferation and survival. Therapeutic approaches targeting mRNA, including antisense oligonucleotides and mRNA vaccines, require understanding of fate determination for optimal design. By decoding the combinatorial logic of mRNA fate, this project will provide foundational knowledge for both basic science and translational applications, representing a transformative advance in our understanding of gene expression regulation.
original.research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build toward a comprehensive understanding of emergent mRNA fate determination.

Research Question 1: What is the complete landscape of mRNA-RBP interactions, and how do RBPs exhibit co-binding, competition, and context-dependent binding patterns?

Hypothesis 1a: RBPs form distinct functional modules characterized by consistent co-binding patterns across transcripts, reflecting cooperative assembly of regulatory complexes. We predict that clustering analysis of genome-wide binding data will reveal 10-20 major RBP modules corresponding to distinct regulatory functions.

Hypothesis 1b: Competition between RBPs for overlapping binding sites creates mutually exclusive binding patterns that define regulatory switches. We hypothesize that competitive relationships will be enriched between RBPs promoting opposing fates (e.g., translation factors versus decay factors).

Hypothesis 1c: RBP binding patterns exhibit cell-type and condition-specific variation that reflects differential RBP expression and activity. We predict that binding site occupancy can be partially predicted from RBP expression levels, but that additional factors including post-translational modifications and cofactor availability contribute to binding specificity.

Research Question 2: How do combinatorial RBP binding patterns determine specific mRNA fates, including translation efficiency, subcellular localization, and decay rate?

Hypothesis 2a: mRNA fate outcomes are determined by the quantitative balance of fate-promoting RBPs rather than presence or absence of individual factors. We hypothesize that the ratio of translation-promoting to decay-promoting RBP binding correlates with translation efficiency and mRNA stability.

Hypothesis 2b: Specific RBP combinations create emergent fate outcomes not predictable from individual RBP effects. We predict the existence of "fate codes"—specific RBP binding configurations that reliably produce particular outcomes. These codes may involve three or more RBPs acting in defined spatial arrangements.

Hypothesis 2c: mRNA localization is determined by hierarchical RBP binding, where localization-promoting RBPs must outcompete retention factors. We hypothesize that localized mRNAs exhibit characteristic binding signatures distinguishing them from non-localized transcripts.

Research Question 3: Can we develop predictive models that accurately forecast mRNA fate from sequence features, structural elements, and RBP binding patterns?

Hypothesis 3a: Integration of sequence features, predicted RNA structure, and RBP binding data will enable accurate prediction of mRNA half-life, translation efficiency, and localization. We predict that multi-feature models will substantially outperform single-feature approaches.

Hypothesis 3b: Deep learning models trained on integrated datasets will identify novel sequence and structural features associated with specific fates, revealing previously unrecognized regulatory elements.

Hypothesis 3c: Model interpretability analysis will reveal the relative contributions of different features to fate determination, identifying the most influential RBPs and sequence elements for each fate outcome.

These hypotheses are designed to be testable through synthesis of existing data and will generate specific predictions for future experimental validation. The hierarchical structure—from interaction mapping to fate correlation to predictive modeling—ensures that each aim builds upon previous findings while maintaining independent value. Importantly, these questions directly address emergence: we seek to understand how molecular-scale interactions produce coherent mesoscale outcomes that govern cellular function.
original.methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates computational biology, machine learning, and systems biology techniques to synthesize diverse publicly available datasets into a unified framework for understanding mRNA fate determination.

Aim 1: Mapping the mRNA-RBP Interaction Landscape

We will systematically compile CLIP-seq datasets from ENCODE, GEO, and published studies, encompassing data for over 300 human RBPs across multiple cell types and conditions. Data processing will employ standardized pipelines using CLIPper and Piranha for peak calling, with cross-method validation ensuring robust binding site identification. We will develop a unified coordinate system mapping all binding sites to transcript annotations from GENCODE.

To identify co-binding patterns, we will calculate pairwise binding correlations across all RBP combinations using Jaccard similarity and mutual information metrics. Hierarchical clustering and non-negative matrix factorization will identify RBP modules with coherent binding patterns. For competitive interactions, we will analyze binding site overlap and develop statistical tests for mutual exclusivity, controlling for sequence motif similarity. Network analysis using weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) will reveal higher-order organizational principles.

Aim 2: Integrating RBP Binding with Fate Outcomes

We will compile fate outcome datasets including: (1) mRNA half-life measurements from metabolic labeling studies (SLAM-seq, TT-seq), (2) translation efficiency data from ribosome profiling experiments, (3) subcellular localization data from fractionation-seq and APEX-seq studies, and (4) stress granule association data from proximity labeling experiments. All datasets will be mapped to common transcript identifiers and normalized for cross-study comparison.

Statistical modeling will relate RBP binding patterns to fate outcomes using multivariate regression and random forest approaches. We will test for non-additive interactions between RBPs using interaction terms and gradient boosting methods that capture complex feature relationships. Bayesian network inference will model causal relationships between RBP binding and fate outcomes, distinguishing direct effects from indirect correlations.

Aim 3: Developing Predictive Models of mRNA Fate

We will develop deep learning models integrating sequence features, predicted RNA secondary structure (from RNAfold and SHAPE-MaP data), and RBP binding profiles to predict fate outcomes. Model architectures will include convolutional neural networks for sequence features and graph neural networks for structural features, with attention mechanisms enabling interpretability.

Training will employ cross-validation with held-out test sets stratified by gene function to ensure generalizability. Transfer learning approaches will leverage models pre-trained on large sequence databases. Model interpretation using integrated gradients and attention visualization will identify influential features and generate hypotheses about regulatory mechanisms.

Data Integration Framework

We will develop a unified data infrastructure using standardized formats (BED, BigWig) and common APIs enabling cross-dataset queries. Quality control pipelines will assess data completeness, batch effects, and technical artifacts. Meta-analysis methods will combine results across studies while accounting for heterogeneity. All analysis workflows will be implemented in reproducible Snakemake pipelines with containerized environments ensuring computational reproducibility.
original.expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will produce four major outcomes with transformative impact on molecular and cellular biology.

First, we will deliver a comprehensive mRNA-RBP Interaction Atlas—an integrated database containing harmonized binding data for over 300 RBPs across human cell types and conditions. This resource will include binding site coordinates, confidence scores, and annotations linking sites to transcript features. The Atlas will serve as an essential community resource, enabling researchers to query RBP binding for any gene of interest and identify candidate regulators for functional studies.

Second, we will establish quantitative models linking RBP binding patterns to mRNA fate outcomes. These models will predict translation efficiency, half-life, and localization from binding profiles with accuracy exceeding current approaches. Importantly, models will identify combinatorial binding rules—specific RBP configurations that determine fate—revealing the emergent logic of post-transcriptional regulation.

Third, our analysis will generate testable hypotheses about mRNA fate determination mechanisms. We will identify candidate RBP interactions for experimental validation, predict consequences of RBP perturbation, and nominate therapeutic targets in diseases involving mRNA fate dysregulation. These hypotheses will be compiled in a publicly available repository with supporting evidence and suggested experimental approaches.

Fourth, we will develop analytical methods and software tools applicable beyond this project. Our data integration pipelines, statistical frameworks, and machine learning models will be released as documented, user-friendly packages enabling other researchers to apply our approaches to new datasets and questions.

The broader impact extends to understanding fundamental principles of gene expression regulation. By revealing how combinatorial RBP interactions produce coherent fate decisions, we address a central question in molecular biology with implications for development, disease, and evolution. Our findings will inform therapeutic development targeting mRNA, including antisense oligonucleotides, RNA interference, and mRNA-based medicines. Training outcomes will develop the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of synthesis research approaches.

This study decodes mRNA fate principles to provide foundational knowledge for understanding disease and developing new RNA based therapeutics.
